units.la: Operis mei est & studii, multos legere, ut ex plurimis diversos flores carpam, non tam probaturus omnia, quam quae bona sunt, electurus. Assumo multos in manus meas, ut a multis multa cognoscam, secundum illud quod scriptum est: omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete.
units.tr: It is my task and my study to read many authors, so that I may pluck diverse flowers from many, not so much intending to approve of everything as to choose what is good. I take up many books in my hands, so that I may learn many things from many, according to what is written: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.

units.la: Sunt qui scire volunt, eo fine tantum, ut sciant; & turpis curiositas est: Et sunt qui scire volunt, ut scientiam suam vendant; & turpis quaestus est: Et sunt qui scire volunt, ut sciantur ipsi; & turpis vanitas est: Sed sunt quoque qui scire volunt, ut aedificent; & charitas est: Et sunt qui scire volunt, ut aedificentur; & prudentia est.
units.tr: There are those who wish to know only so that they may know, and this is idle curiosity; there are those who wish to know so that they may sell their knowledge, and this is shameful gain; there are those who wish to know so that they themselves may be known, and this is shameful vanity; but there are also those who wish to know so that they may build up, and this is love; and there are those who wish to know so that they may be built up, and this is prudence.

units.tr: Thus the meaning must be placed before the words, as the soul is placed before the body.

units.la: ECulum est, Reuerendissimi Patres, Clementissimi Domini, PATRONI gratiosissimi, seculum, inquam, est & quod excurrit, ex quo volantibus vexillis, infestis armis, & dubio Marte concursum ac depugnatum hactenus est de Fide iustitia, & eius forma, causis, effectis, &c. Neque adhuc cantatur receptui; quod quam recte quamve secus factum sit, fiatve, arbitrum me modo constituere, aut amplius etiam disceptare instituti mei prorsus non est, hoc saltem liceat mihi bona scientia & conscientia affirmare ac deplorare, eo rem esse redactam, ut dum de fide digladiamur, & hostilibus admodum armis utrinque decernimus, Diuæ Charitatis & Theoriam & praxin fere in totum obsoleuisse, & hunc Ecclesiastici coeli phosfera amabilissimum iamplurimos annos miserandam Ecclypsin pati, idque in omnibus omnino Hierarchiis, ordinibusve sacris, nullo omnino excepto, neque arbitror, quen quam bonum atque cordatum esse, qui hoc non agnoscat, apudque animum suum mecum deploret, nedum ut inficias ire possit: adeo plane incidi-
units.tr: The age, most reverend Fathers, most gracious Lords, gracious PATRONS, the age, I say, and what is beyond it, has been the time in which, with banners flying, weapons drawn and the outcome of war uncertain, there has been conflict and battle over faith, righteousness, and its form, causes, effects, and so on. Nor is the retreat yet sounded. Whether this has been done rightly or otherwise, or is still being done, it is not my task now to judge, nor to dispute further, as my purpose requires. Let me only be allowed to affirm and lament, with good knowledge and a clear conscience, that matters have been brought to such a state that while we fight with one another over faith and decide the matter with weapons almost wholly hostile on both sides, the Theory and the Practice of divine Charity have nearly wholly fallen into disuse, and this most lovely light of the ecclesiastical heaven has for many years suffered a pitiable eclipse. This is so in all the hierarchies and sacred orders without exception. I do not think any good and sensible person exists who does not recognise this, and who does not lament it inwardly with me, much less one who could deny it. Indeed, we have plainly fallen

units.la: (*) 2 incidimus in ea tempora, de quibus Spiritus sanctus praesagit, Iniustitiam superabundaturam, & defecturam charitatem; fore homines seipsos amantes, cupidos, ela-tos, superbos, blasphemos, αθεοι, ἀσπονδοι, ἀκαρόσθυς, ἀλαζονες, ἀφιλαγαθοι, φιλήδονοι .
units.tr: (*) 2 into those times of which the Holy Spirit forewarns: that iniquity will abound and love will grow cold; that men will be lovers of themselves, covetous, boastful, proud, blasphemers, atheoi [ἀθεοι], aspondoi [ἀσπονδοι], akarosthus [ἀκαρόσθυς], alazones [ἀλαζονες], aphilagathoi [ἀφιλαγαθοι], philēdonoi [φιλήδονοι].

units.la: Et quae sequuntur: haecque adeo non tam Urbis quam Orbis Christiani, esse crimina, omnes boni gemunt ac dolent. Quocirca nemo pius dubitat, quin quoquo modo id agendum sit, ut ostracismi damnata dudum D. Alma, chara charitas ab exilio qua primum quasi postliminio revocetur, eiusque Praxis in integrum prisf numque florem ac nitorem cum Theoria restituatur, ut, quae omnibus adhibus nostris, iuxta Apostolum moderari debeat.
units.tr: And what follows. That these crimes are found not so much in the city as in the whole Christian world, all good people groan and grieve. Hence no pious person doubts that, by whatever means it must be done, dear Charity, long condemned to ostracism, should be recalled from exile as if by a right of return, and that her practice should be restored to its former integrity and brightness together with her theory, so that she may govern all our endeavours, as the Apostle says she ought to.

units.la: In Ecclesiastico statu, si linguis hominum loquar & Angelorum, charitatem autem non habeam, factus sum velut aes sonans, & cymbalum tinniens. Et si habuero prophetiam, & noverim omnia mysteria, & omnem scientiam, & si habuero omnem fidem, ita ut montes transferam, charitatem autem non habuero, nihil sum. In saecularibus, si distribuero in cibos pauperum omnes facultates meas, & si tradidero corpus meum ut ardeam, charitatem autem non habuero, nihil mihi prodest. Dicam cum Apostolo: charitas patiens est; benigna est; non aemulatur; non agit perperam; non inflatur; non est ambitiosa; non quaerit quae sua sunt; non irritatur; non cogitat malum; non gaudet super iniquitate, congaudet veritati; omnia suffert, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet; nunquam excidit; manet in aeternum, & est maior omnibus virtutibus.
units.tr: In the ecclesiastical state: if I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries, and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. In secular affairs: if I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing. I will say with the Apostle: charity is patient; charity is kind; it envies not; it does not act perversely; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own; it is not provoked; it thinks no evil; it does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; it never fails; it abides for ever, and is greater than all the virtues.

units.la: Erat autem (ut cum B. Augustino loquar) est regula dilectionis, ut quae sibi bona vult proventire, & proximo velit; & quae sibi accidere mala non vult, & illi nolit. Et: Omnia praecepta vastissimo charitatis complexu comprehenduntur. Charitas causa & mater est omnium virtutum, quae si defit, frustra habentur catera, si autem adsit, habentur omnia. Omnia fiunt facilia charitate. Mandatum Dei non habet grave: Aut enim quis non diligit, & iam grave est, aut diligit, & grave esse non potest. Totam magnitudinem divinorum eloquiorum & latitudinem securam possidet Charitas, qua Deum proximumque diligimus. Si ergo non vacat omnes paginas sanctas perscrutari, omnia involucra sermonum evolvere, omnia scripturarum secreta penetrare, tene charitatem: in ipsa pendent omnia, ita tenebis quod ibi non didicisti, tenebis & quod didicisti.
units.tr: There is, moreover (to speak with Blessed Augustine), a rule of love: that one should wish for one's neighbour the good that one wishes for oneself, and should not wish on him the evil one does not wish on oneself. And: All the commandments are contained in the vast embrace of charity. Charity is the cause and mother of all the virtues; without it the rest are held in vain, but with it all are possessed. All things become easy through charity. God's commandment is not burdensome: for either a man does not love, and then it is burdensome, or he loves, and then it cannot be burdensome. Charity, by which we love God and our neighbour, secures the whole greatness and breadth of the divine words. If therefore there is no time to search through all the holy pages, to unroll all the wrappings of the words, and to penetrate all the secrets of the Scriptures, hold fast to charity: all things hang upon it. Thus you will hold what you have not learned there, and you will also hold what you have learned.

units.la: Sicut enim radix omnium malorum est cupiditas, ita & radix omnium bonorum est charitas. Quapropter sectamini charitatem, dulce ac salubre vinculum mentium, fine qua dives pauper est, & cum qua pauper dives est. Haec in adversitatibus tolerat, in prosperitatibus temperat, in duris passionibus fortis, in bonis operibus hilaris, in tentatione tutissima, in hospitalitate latissima, inter veros fratres latissima, inter falsos patientissima. In Abel sacrificio grata, in Noe per diluvium secura: in Abraham peregrinationib. mansuetissima: in tribus pueris iugulandis ignes innocenter expectat, in Maccabaeis septem ignes fortiter tolerat; casta in Susanna erga virum, in Anna post virum, in Maria prater virum. Libera in Paulo ad arguendum: Humilis in Petro ad obediendum: humana in Christianis ad confitendum: divina in Christo ad ignoscendum, &c. Sola facilis est charitas: ieiunii corpus sentit iniuriam, Vigilia carnem macerant, eleemosyna labore quaeruntur, sanguis in martyrio, quamvis ardeat fides, non tamen sine dolore & timore funditur. Haec omnia sunt qui faciant, sola charitas sine labore est.
units.tr: For as the root of all evils is covetousness, so also the root of all goods is charity. Therefore pursue charity, the sweet and wholesome bond of minds, without which the rich man is poor, and with which the poor man is rich. It bears adversities, tempers prosperities, is strong in harsh sufferings, cheerful in good works, most safe in temptation, most generous in hospitality, most wide-embracing among true brethren, most patient among false ones. In Abel's sacrifice it is pleasing; in Noah it is safe through the flood; in Abraham's wanderings it is most gentle; among the three youths about to be thrown into the fire it awaits the flames innocently; among the Maccabees it bravely endures seven fires; chaste in Susanna towards her husband, in Anna after her husband, in Mary apart from a husband. Free in Paul to rebuke; humble in Peter to obey; human in Christians to confess; divine in Christ to forgive, and so on. Charity alone is easy: the body feels the injury of fasting, vigils weary the flesh, alms are sought with labour, blood is shed in martyrdom, and although faith burns, it is not poured out without pain and fear. All these things are for those who do them; charity alone is without labour.

units.la: Haec charitas subiectum nostrum est, Reuerendissimi Patres, Clementissimi Domini, gratiosissimi PATRONI, quod praesens hic noster libellus tractat, partim fieri commendans, partim omitti gemens dolensque. Verbo dicam: Ἀφιλαργυρίαν detestamur ac prohibemus, charam charitatem persuadere satagimus. Quare non litigamus de Authoritate vel Maioritate summi in plebe Christi sacerdotis: non disputamus: an & quibus, quomodo expendenda sint in Purgatorii foro supplicia: non rixamur de carnib. vel vescedis vel secus, alia res nobis, alia scena q. agitur. Moralia tractamus. Dogmatica aut plane no attingimus, aut, si qua extremis digitulis libamus, ea dicimus, quae ex omni parte ἀναμφισβήτητα sunt, & extra controversiae aleam posita, quocirca & eo confidentius ut in omnium, ita in vestrum singulariter Venerandum atque Magnificum conspectu producere gestim.
units.tr: This charity is our subject, most reverend Fathers, most gracious Lords, gracious PATRONS, which the present little book of ours treats, partly commending what should be done, and partly lamenting with grief what is left undone. To put it in a word: we detest and forbid φιλαργυρία (love of money), and we strive to persuade men to the dear love of charity. For this reason we do not quarrel over the authority or greater dignity of the chief priest in the people of Christ; we do not dispute whether, or to whom, or in what manner, the punishments are to be assessed in the court of Purgatory; we do not brawl over meats, whether eaten or not. Those are other matters, and another stage on which they are played out. We treat morals. Dogmatic matters we either do not touch at all or, if we taste some of them with the tips of our fingers, we say only what is beyond dispute in every respect and placed outside the hazard of controversy. Therefore we are the more confident in wishing to bring this before the sight of all, and of you, most venerable and magnificent men, in particular.

units.la: Modum tractandi talem fore confidimus, qui homine SS. Theologiae & Studioso & praeconi indignus censeri non possit, Hieroglyphicus, nimirum & Moralis: nam per hieroglyphicas literas arcanos sensus adumbramus, & sapientibus pia, prudenti, dextra, varia (quemadmodum titulus nullo jota frustra redundante loquitur) evolutione intimamus. Is autem modus neque novus est Theosophiae Professoribus, neque singulari sua suavitate, oblectatione, utilitate, fructuque caret. Quis non similitudinibus, ἱερογλυφοις, parabolis, eiconibus, picturis, fabulis, & similibus vim maximam inesse neget; at vere Horat. Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci, Lectorem delectando pariterque monendo, Hic meret aera liber, &c.
units.tr: We trust that our method of treatment will be such that it cannot be judged unworthy of a man learned in sacred theology, a student, and a herald: it is hieroglyphic, and moral. For through hieroglyphic letters we shadow forth hidden meanings, and we make them known to the wise, to be unfolded devoutly, prudently, skilfully, and variously (as the title says, with no letter added in vain). Nor is this method new to the professors of theosophy, nor does it lack its own singular charm, delight, usefulness and fruit. Who would deny that great power resides in similitudes, hieroglyphs, parables, images, pictures, fables and the like? Horace truly says: He has won every point who has mingled the useful with the pleasant, delighting and at the same time instructing the reader; this book earns its price, etc.

units.la: Non is, inquam, ut redeamus, Aegyptiorum mos tantum est, nec soli Niliaci hoc studio ducuntur imo ne nostri quidem, qui multi sunt, soli, in prophanis, ipse Spiritus S. ab Hieroglyphis non abhorrere videtur, siquidem rem aequabiliter & absque adfectibus aestimare velimus. Quid enim? an non Iob Interroga inquit, iumenta, & docebunt te: & volatilia caeli, & indicabunt tibi. Loquere terra & respondebit tibi, & narrabunt tibi pisces maris.
units.tr: I do not say this, I repeat, merely as the custom of the Egyptians, nor is it only the Nile peoples who are led by this zeal; nor, among the profane writers, are only the many of ours; the Holy Spirit himself does not seem to shrink from hieroglyphs, if we wish to judge the matter evenly and without prejudice. For what? Does not Job say: Ask the beasts and they will teach you; the birds of the air and they will tell you. Speak to the earth and it will answer you, and the fishes of the sea will declare to you.

units.la: Quis in sacris tam imperitus est & hospes, qui nesciat, Aquilam divina providentia esse hieroglyphicam. Quis ignorat serpentes obthurantes aures ad verba incantatoris typum praestare refractariorum verbi divini auditorum? quem latet linguam calumniatricem, novacula, & labia dolosa illita oleo romphaea adsimilari? Serpentinam prudentiam & columbinam simplicitatem ipse Dominus Salvator in Euangelio commendat. Formica ἱερογλυφον est apud Salomonem. Vitis & oliva apud S. Psalmographum. Amorem ac beneuolentiam suam erga Hierosolymitanos & quoscunq; commendat Dn. Salvator per Gallina alas, quibus pullos suos tegit. Et quis omnia percesse potest? Inde autem perspicue apparet, quanta nobis etiam in Sacrof. Bibliis huius seges sit. Quisquis ergo putavit hactenus, in profanis tantum scriptoribus extare Emblemata, Flosculos, pictas sententias, Hieroglyphica &c. is corrigat mentem. Non est sterilis huius nostr agellus, imo feracissimus. Quare qui institutum nostrum improbaverit, is infscitiam potius & ofcitantiam suam agnoscat & improbet, & corrigat; consulat idem canam ac SS. vetustatem, legatq; B.Patres, Ecclesiae Prisca Lumina, obvia ubivis Hieroglyphices vestigia deprehendet: sat scio. B. Augustinus Curiosulos huius aevi piscibus maru adsimilat, qui in profundo huius seculi tantum quaerunt temporalia, & discurrut tanquam magna tracaturi nequicquam. Impium fumo comparat. Anchoram Spei cum Apostolo hieroglyphicum facit. Invidam navigio interfluctus jactato pingit. Avarum inferno aequiparat. Concentum scripturarum Harmonia vel organo Musico similem esse dicit, &c. B. Hieronym. Architectantem mala comparat sagitta, quae si contra duram materiam mittatur, revertitur in mittentem. Lyncem cuius hieroglyphi rei faciat, ex Epl.ad Chrysogonum Monachum perspicere est. Aquila iridem typum vide in c.1. Mich. Et in Epl.ad Rustic. Monach. inquit: sicut mordet serpens in silentio, sic qui fratri suo in occulto detrahit, &c. Ut jam desinam de B. Clemente Alexandrino in Paedagog. & in Stromatib. & de B. Irenaeo. B. Tertulliano, B. Cypriano, B. Origene, B. Athanasio, B. Lactantio Firmiano, B. Ambrosio Mediolanensi, B. Basilio Magno, B. Gregorio Nazianzeno Theologo dicto, BB. Cyrillo utroq., B. Ioan. Chrysost. Constantinopolitano, B. Fulgentio Episcopo Ruspensi, Venerabili Beda, B. Bernhardo Clarevallensi, & aliis compluribus, ex quibus non nemo tales literas hieroglyphicas studiose atque aptissime conquisivit, in fasciculum compegit, & justa tractatione profequutus absolvit. Ut omnino saniores inter profanos atque Gentiles mittam.
units.tr: Who is so unskilled and a stranger in sacred things as not to know that the eagle is a hieroglyph of divine providence? Who does not know that serpents stopping their ears prefigure, in the words of the charmer, the type of the refractory hearers of the divine Word? Who does not know that the calumniating tongue, the razor, and deceitful lips smeared with oil, the sword are likened to it? The Lord Saviour himself commends in the Gospel serpentine prudence and dovelike simplicity. The ant is a hieroglyph in Solomon. The vine and the olive in the Psalmist. The Lord Saviour commends his love and goodwill towards Jerusalem, and towards all, by the wings of the hen with which she covers her chicks. And who can survey everything? From this it clearly appears how rich a harvest of this kind there is also in the Holy Bible. Whoever therefore has thought hitherto that emblems, little flowers, painted sayings, hieroglyphics, etc. are found only in profane writers, let him correct his mind. This little field of ours is not barren, but most fertile. Therefore, whoever has disapproved of our undertaking, let him acknowledge and disapprove his ignorance and carelessness, and correct it; let him consult the old and holy antiquity, and read the blessed Fathers, the bright lights of the early Church; he will find traces of hieroglyphics everywhere. I know this well. Blessed Augustine compares the curious of this age to fish of the sea, who in the depths of this world seek only temporal things, and run about as if about to catch great things, to no purpose. He compares the impious to smoke. He makes the anchor of hope, with the Apostle, a hieroglyph. He paints the envious man as a ship tossed among the waves. He equates the avaricious with hell. He says that the agreement of the Scriptures is like a harmony or a musical organ, etc. Blessed Jerome compares one who plans evil to an arrow, which, if shot against hard material, returns upon the shooter. What hieroglyph the lynx makes can be seen from his letter to Chrysogonus the monk. For the rainbow as a type, see chapter 1 of Micah. And in his letter to Rusticus the monk he says: as a serpent bites in silence, so he who slanders his brother in secret, etc. To pass over Blessed Clement of Alexandria in the Paedagogus and the Stromata, and Blessed Irenaeus, Blessed Tertullian, Blessed Cyprian, Blessed Origen, Blessed Athanasius, Blessed Lactantius Firmianus, Blessed Ambrose of Milan, Blessed Basil the Great, Blessed Gregory Nazianzen called the Theologian, both Cyrils, Blessed John Chrysostom of Constantinople, Blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, the Venerable Bede, Blessed Bernard of Clairvaux, and many others, of whom not a few have diligently and most aptly gathered such hieroglyphic letters, compiled them into a little bundle, and finished them with a fitting treatment. Not to mention the more sensible among the profane and Gentile writers.

units.la: Illorum igitur vestigia legimus, premimus, illos imitamur, cum illis loquimur in Iconibus hisce nostris hieroglyphicis, & arcanos sensus oratione explicata indicamus atq; evolvimus, ut plane inhumanum fore arbitremur, quem hic modus tractandi non moveat. Sicut enim vinum semper bibere, aut semper aquam, contrarium est, alternis autem uti delectabile: ita legentibus ut semper exactius fit sermo, non erit gratus: nec semper graviora legenda sunt, sed fastidium suaviorum & utilium tamen lectione abstergendum est, quam ad rem haec nostra appositissime quadrabunt. Quibus explicatis & intellectis eadem opera rationem reddimus atq; reddidimus, quare Viridarium Hieroglyphico-Morale inscribere placuerit; De Hieroglyphico jam nunc plus satis. Bene Viridarium, nam odoratiss. mes flosculos lentiarum ac rerum cum ex sacris tum ex profanis transplantantes huc infevimus, plures etiam insituri, nisi chartae angustia prohibu. ffet, nihil autem vetat, quo minus quisque pius, cordatus, ac doctus pro cuiusque ingenii ductu ac lubitu plures huc transferat, inferat. Et hoc Viridarium nostrum sibi efficiat instar instructissimi ac locupletissimi, Topicorum Virtutum vice fungetis, perq; virtutes atque contraria vitia discurrentis Promptuarii, in quod quodlibet eximium con-
units.tr: We therefore read their footsteps, we press on them, we imitate them, and in these hieroglyphic pictures of ours we speak with them. Having explained the hidden meanings in prose, we unfold them, so that I judge anyone to be inhuman whom this way of treating the subject does not move. For just as to drink wine always, or water always, is disagreeable, but to use them by turns is pleasant, so a discourse that always grows more exact will not please the reader. Nor must we always read weightier matters; the weariness must be wiped away by reading more pleasant and useful things, and these pages of ours will fit that purpose very well. Having explained and understood these things, we also give, and have given, the reason why we chose to entitle it The Hieroglyphic-Moral Garden. As for Hieroglyphic, enough has already been said. The title Garden is apt, for we have transplanted here the most fragrant little flowers of sayings and things, taken from both sacred and profane sources, and we would have planted more had the narrowness of the paper not prevented us. Nothing, however, forbids any pious, judicious and learned reader to bring in and add more, as his own talent and inclination lead him. Let him make this Garden of ours serve him as a most well-stocked and rich Storehouse, taking the place of the Topics of the Virtues, a Handbook running through the virtues and the contrary vices, from which anyone may gather together whatever choice thing he needs, and draw it out again as the necessity requires.

units.la: gr:gare gregare, & vicissim ex eodem depromere possit, necessitate ita exigete. Accedit, quod de quavis fere materia ita dissertavimus, ut de hac vel illa virtute, vel etiam vitio disceurrete, ut vocant, volenti, eximia & utilissima futura sit manuductio. Certe inventis facile addere est: Et (ut cum B. Hier. loquar) in terra aurum quaritur, & de fluviorum alveis splendens profertur glarea. Pactolusq; ditior est coeno quam fluento. Meum propositum est, antiquos legere, probare singula, retinere quae bona sunt, & a fide Catholica Ecclesiae non recedere: cur igitur me lacerant amici mei?
units.tr: Besides, we have discussed almost every subject in such a way that anyone wishing to range over this or that virtue, or even vice, as they say, will find here an excellent and most useful guide. Certainly it is easy to add to what has been found; and (to speak with St. Jerome) gold is sought in the earth, and shining gravel is brought from the beds of rivers. The Pactolus is richer in mud than in its stream. My purpose is to read the ancients, to test each thing, to keep what is good, and not to depart from the Catholic faith of the Church. Why, then, do my friends tear me to pieces?

units.la: Deniq; tempus etiam monet, & jubet Papyri ratio, ut etiam explicemus finem, scopumq; ac mentem nostram in inventione hac nostra τολμήσει, & evolutione, quo de etiam supra breviter admodum attigimus: caput & summa est: Virtutem commendamus, taxamus vitia, illam persuasuri, his nigrum Theta scribimus, & munimus contra ea mentes animosq; cordatorum, Deiq; timentium. Varios ac multiplices huius mundi mores, machinationesque graphice depingimus, & bonis atque honestis contra fucos praesentissima pharmaca exhibemus. Nemini injuriam inferimus, labem nulli adspergimus, virtutem, ubi reperimus, laudamus in quibusvis vitia, ubi inoleuerint, perstringimus, detestamur, missa fieri monemus, in nullis αδικως, φυχως in omnibus: adeoq; neminem, quasi speciatim suggilletur ipse, jure conqueri posse scimus, nisi si quis animum gerat exacerbatum, exasperatum, effascinatum, malevolentia, rancore, invidia, aemulatione, deniq; illis ipsis vitiis, quae in hoc opusculo maxime reprehenduntur: idem plane propositum nobis quod Martialis:
units.tr: Finally, the time also warns, and the nature of this paper requires, that we explain also the end, aim and intention we had in this our invention and its unfolding, which we touched on briefly above. The head and sum of it is this: we commend virtue and censure vices, urging the one and marking the other with a black theta, and we fortify the minds and courage of the judicious and God-fearing against them. We vividly portray the various and manifold customs and devices of this world, and we offer the good and honest the most effective remedies against its deceits. We do injury to no one, we cast blame on no one; wherever we find virtue we praise it, and wherever vices have taken root we rebuke and denounce them, and we warn that they be given up. We are in no case unjust [ἀδίκως], and in all things we are [ψυχῶς]. Hence we know that no one can rightly complain that he is singled out for abuse by name, unless he bears a soul embittered, exasperated and bewitched by malice, rancour, envy, rivalry, and, finally, by those very vices which are chiefly rebuked in this little work. Our purpose is the same as that of Martial:

units.la: Hu c ser vare modum nostri novere libelli, Parcere personis dicere de vitiis. Erunt forte.
units.tr: My little books have learned to keep this measure: to spare persons, to speak of vices. Perhaps they will.

units.la: Si forte futurus sit non-nemo, qui Satyrici crimen mihi obiiciat, cum Persius: Omne vafer vitium ridenti Flaccus amico Tangit, & admissus circum praecordia ludit;
units.tr: If perhaps there should be someone who will charge me with the fault of satire, I answer with Persius: Flaccus, the crafty one, touches every vice with a friend who laughs, and plays about his heart once admitted.

units.la: Eidem iterum ego cum B. Hier. Nemo, inquam, reprehendat, quod in opusculis aliquos aut laudamus aut carpimus. Cum in arguendis malis correctio fit caeterorum, & in optimis praedicandis bonorum ad virtutem studia concitentur. Condemnatio autem malorum, laus bonorum est. Nec detrahere est, verum dicere. Quare (eiusdem sunt verba) Hoc obsecro, ut si mordacius quippiam scripsero, non tam mea quam putet auferitatis esse, quae morbi. Putridae carnes ferro curantur & cauterio, venena serpentina pelluntur antidoto. Quod satis dolet, maiori dolore expellitur, &c. Hisce non contentis respondeo cum Poeta: Latratus relinqui canum manipli Omnes unius est: mamus asis.
units.tr: Again, I answer with St. Jerome: Let no one, I say, find fault that in these small works we either praise or criticise certain persons; since in denouncing evils there is correction for others, and in proclaiming the best things the zeal of good men towards virtue is stirred up. The condemnation of evils, however, is the praise of the good. Nor is it detraction to speak the truth. Therefore (these are his words) I beg this, that if I have written somewhat more biting, it may be seen to belong not so much to my temper as to the disease. Rotting flesh is cured with iron and cautery, serpent poisons are driven out by an antidote. What causes sufficient pain is expelled with greater pain, etc. To those who are not satisfied with these things I answer with the poet: Let the barking of dogs be left to them; the whole troop is of one kind, and they are asses.

units.la: Amara (inquit B. Hier.) est veritas, nihil igitur mirum, si illi, qui praedicant eam, amaritudine replentur. Fruimur equidem testimonio bonae conscientiae, quod scopus atq; finis hujus nostrae scriptiunculae fuerit atq; fit: Prodesse multis, obesse nemini; gloria Dei, bonum bonorum: quare confidenter cum eodem B. Hieron. exclamamus: Spernentes hominum iudicia, nec laudibus eorum extollimur; nec obtrectationibus contristamur, sed ingredimur rectam viam, & tritas a S. Prophetis ac patribus semitas. Sed quo delabor?
units.tr: Truth (says St. Jerome) is bitter; so it is no wonder if those who proclaim it are filled with bitterness. Indeed we enjoy the witness of a good conscience, that the aim and end of this our little writing has been, and is: to benefit many, to harm no one; the glory of God, the good of goods. Wherefore we confidently exclaim with the same St. Jerome: Scorning the judgements of men, we are not lifted up by their praises, nor saddened by their detractions, but we walk the straight way and the paths trodden by the holy prophets and fathers. But where am I drifting?

units.la: B.Hier. in Ep. ad Minerium & Alexandrum tom 2 Oper. Exomnib. aliquid: ut est 1. Tbiff v 21 Finu & Scopi huius scripturis.
units.tr: St. Jerome, in his letter to Minerius and Alexander, vol. 2 of his works, on certain matters: as it is, 1 Thess. 5:21. The end and aim of this writing.

units.la: Ad vos autem, Reverendissimi Patres, Clementissimi Domini, gratiosissimi PATRONI conuertor, apud Vestrarum Reverend. Illustr. & Magnific. Dominationum pulvinaria hoc quicquid est opellæ, depono, memoris certe atq; gratissimi animi χάριν, quod me nuper PATRONI, ad ovilis Dn. ac Servatoris nostri Iesu Christi, quod ipsi Nauhaimij colligitur, pascitur q;, curam, tam benigne atq; gratiose admisistis, atq; adeo hoc gratissimæ recordationis μνήμην, cum aliud non liceat mihi, infimorum subselliorum homini, apud Rev. Illustr. & Magnif. Vestr. Dominat. deponere summo gaudio fuit, fructum laborum meorum quantorumcunq; abunde præclarum mihi inde retulisse visurus, vbi quam sincero, humili ac Vestris Rev. Illustr. & Magnif. Domination. devoto plane animo offero, tam sereno vultu ac gratioso affectu à Rever. Illustr. & Magnif. Domination. Vestris suscipietur. Dn. noster Iesus Christus salus ac salvator noster Vestras Rever. Illustr. & Magnif. Domination. omni benedictione corporis atque animæ cumulate benedicat, & florentes-vigentes conservet ex hoc nunc & perpetim, quod animitus voveo lucubrans, properans in nostro (imo vestro) musæolo Nauhaimiano. Calend. Mart. 1619.
units.tr: But to you, Most Reverend Fathers, Most Clement Lords, most gracious PATRONS, I turn, and lay down at the cushions of your Most Reverend, Illustrious and Magnificent Lordships this little work, whatever it is, in thanks [χάριν] of a grateful and mindful heart, because you so kindly and graciously admitted me, a man of the lowest rank, recently, to the care of the flock of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, which is gathered and fed at Naumburg. Since I am allowed nothing else, I have found it a great joy to lay before your Most Reverend, Illustrious and Magnificent Lordships this memory [μνήμην] of most grateful remembrance, and I expect to have reaped from it abundantly a most excellent fruit of my labours, of whatever kind. I offer it with a sincere, humble and wholly devoted mind to your Most Reverend, Illustrious and Magnificent Lordships, and I trust it will be received with a serene countenance and a gracious feeling. May our Lord Jesus Christ, our health and Saviour, bless your Most Reverend, Illustrious and Magnificent Lordships abundantly with every blessing of body and soul, and keep you flourishing and vigorous from now on and for ever. This is what I wholeheartedly vow, writing by lamplight, hurrying in our (nay, your) little muse-house at Naumburg. Kalends of March, 1619.
Address [Πρόσφωνησις], humble dedication.

units.la: REV. ILLUSTR. ET MAGNIF. VESTRAS DOMINAT. humili observantia & obsequiis colens
units.tr: To your Reverend, Illustrious and Magnificent Lordships, whom I honour with humble respect and service
Henricus Oraeus.
EPIGRAM

units.la: Præsens qui placide pieq; seclum Vult transmittere, vir bonusq; haberi, Curis abstq; meris, molestiisq; Is ante omnia maximum Iehouam Sincere vereatur, atque amet, nec Non & ante oculos sibi reponat Verbi iussa salutis, exsequatur Gnauus officia & vocationis: Suum diligat intimoq; amore Proximum, pariter suas agat res: Non sese ἀλλοτρίοις det implicatum, Vt sortem placide ferat, vel unum Curet; diuitiis hiet ne opimis: Aulai atq; fori pericla mille Et discrimina sed [?]dolus vitabit: Immittet rigidos subinde frenos Linguæ, det labiis suis capistrum: Γλωσσαγώγος non agat perinde, Quod est esse velit, nihilq; malit, Esse quenq; sinat, quod est, simulq; Sic est ille futurus idem & usq; Tum cubilia vitet inquinare, Et thorum fugiat coinquinatum Purum a crimine corpus, & sagacem Conseruans animum, piumq; pectus, Infami abstineat manusq; furto, Sensus dirigat atq; cautus actus: Non sit alterius, suis licet dum Esse, nemine obesse, adesse cunctis: Hoc emblemata nostræ docebunt, Quod ipsum fauet aduouens Oraeus.
units.tr: He who wishes to pass this life peacefully and piously, and to be counted a good man, free from cares and mere troubles, above all must sincerely fear and love the greatest Jehovah, keep before his eyes the commands of the saving Word, and diligently carry out the duties of his calling. Let him love his neighbour with heartfelt affection and manage his own affairs in the same way. Let him not give himself over entangled in other men's affairs [ἀλλοτρίοις]. Let him calmly bear his lot and not trouble himself over a single thing, nor gape after rich wealth. He will avoid the thousand dangers and perils of court and forum, and deceit. From time to time he will put firm bridles on his tongue and a muzzle on his lips. Let him not act the babbler [γλωσσαγώγος], but wish to be what he is, want nothing more, and let each man be what he is. So he will remain the same man in the future and always. Then let him avoid defiling beds and flee the polluted marriage bed. Keeping his body pure from crime, his mind shrewd and his breast pious, let him abstain from infamous theft with his hands, and let him direct his senses and his actions with caution. Let him belong to no one else, provided he can be of use to all and harm no one. Our emblems will teach this, which Oraeus himself favours and avows.
ALL THINGS FROM ONE.

units.la: Omnia diuina subsistunt condita dextra, Illa eadem Verbo, Flatuq; reguntur louæ.
units.tr: All things subsist, founded by the divine right hand, and the same things are governed by the Word and the breath of Jehovah.

units.la: Omnibus hæc ergo prima & siet vnica cura Debita diuinæ vt dicat præconia MENTI.
units.tr: So this should be the first and only care of all: to proclaim the praises owed to the divine MIND.
From the Beginning, the Beginning.

units.la: PANTOPLASTES Deus, qui est PATER, FILIVS, SPIRITVS SANCTVS, vnessentia, trinus personis, homousiis, homodoxis, homotimiis, †vere ENSENTIVM & Deus super omnia benedictus atque laudatus in omne aeuum, Condidit totum hoc vniuersum, calum empyreum cum suis Archangelis atque Angelis, Orbes caelestes cum toto ipsorum exercitu, ornatu, virtutibus atque influentiis, Luce primigenia, Sole, Luna, Stellis tum erraticis tum fixis, Aerem cum volucribus & toto Alituum genere, terramque cum eius incolis homine & animantibus vt quadrupedibus ita bipedibus, reptilibus atque infectis, substantiisq; minutissimis: Oceanum & maria quoq;, vna cum Balaenis & omnis generis piscibus: OMNIA.
units.tr: PANTOPLASTES, God, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one in essence, three in persons, of one essence [homoousios], of one glory [homodoxos], of one honour [homotimos], truly being, and God, blessed and praised above all things for ever, created this whole universe: the heavens, the empyrean heaven with its archangels and angels, the celestial spheres with their whole host, their adornment, powers and influences, the primal light, the sun, the moon, the stars both wandering and fixed; the air with its birds and the whole race of winged creatures; the earth with its inhabitants, man and animals, both four-footed and two-footed, reptiles and insects, and the smallest substances; the ocean and the seas also, together with the whales and fish of every kind: ALL THINGS.

units.la: Condidit totum hoc vniuersum Pater per Filium λόγον & Spiritum utrique ὁμοούσιον, ἐνυπόστατον, ταυτόσημον: sicut dicitur in sacris: In principio creauit Elohim, calum & terram, & Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas: Verbo Domini caeli firmati, & Spiritu oris eius, &c.
units.tr: The Father created this whole universe through the Son, the Word [logos], and through the Spirit, who is of one essence [homoousios] with both, subsisting in himself [enhypostatos], and of the same substance [tautosemos]. As it is said in the sacred writings: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, and the Spirit of the Lord moved upon the waters." "By the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth," etc.

units.la: Condidit omnia EX NIHILO. Nulla vel praeexistente vel praeiacente materia: ipse creauit OMNIA in principio ἐκ τῶν μὴ ὄντων.
units.tr: He created all things OUT OF NOTHING. No matter, either pre-existing or lying beneath, was present: he himself created ALL THINGS in the beginning, out of things that were not [ek tōn mē ontōn].

units.la: Condidit in principio, temporis, scilicet, ante quod non erat tempus: tum erat illud principium, antea pura puta aeternitas incomprehensibilis.
units.tr: He created in the beginning of time, that is, before which there was no time. Then that beginning was; before it there was pure eternity, incomprehensible.

units.la: Condidit omnia LIBERE, sed postquam tamen condidit, necessario: Nam libertas non necessitatem sed coactionem excludit.
units.tr: He created all things FREELY, yet, having created them, he acts necessarily; for liberty excludes not necessity but compulsion.

units.la: Condidit omnia GRATIOSE, nullo praeexistente cuiusquam merito: Quis enim prior illi dedit aliquid, quod retribueretur?
units.tr: He created all things GRACIOUSLY, with no prior merit of anyone to precede it. For who first gave him anything that might be repaid?

units.la: Condidit omnia POTENTER, potentia infinita, & incomprehensibili, qua omnia sibi subiecit, omniaq; potest & facit, quae vult, in calo & in terra, vltra quam nos vel petere vel cogitare possumus.
units.tr: He created all things POWERFULLY, with an infinite and incomprehensible power, by which he has subjected all things to himself; he can and does do whatever he wills, in heaven and on earth, beyond what we are able either to ask or to think.

units.la: Condidit omnia SAPIENTER, & disposuit in numero, pondere & mensura, is cuius sapientia non est numerus.
units.tr: He created all things WISELY, and arranged them in number, weight and measure; he whose wisdom has no number.

units.la: Condidit omnia SEX DIEBVS non vno momento, non tantum vt sint, sed etiam vt cursum obtineant ἐμφυτον, quoad ei videretur.
units.tr: He created all things in SIX DAYS, not in a single moment, and not merely so that they might exist, but also so that they might hold their inherent course, as far as seemed good to him.

units.la: Condidit omnia PROPTER semetipsum, h. e. ad gloriam suam, bonumque suorum electorum & dilectorum, vt inde reluceret ipsius.
units.tr: He created all things FOR HIMSELF, that is, for his own glory and for the good of his chosen and beloved, so that his own glory might shine forth from them.

units.la: Gratia: qua fertur erga omnia opera sua, in primis electos.
units.tr: Grace: by which he extends himself toward all his works, and especially toward the elect.

units.la: Libertas: quod in manu eius sumus, tanquam lutum in manu figuli.
units.tr: Liberty: that we are in his hand, as clay is in the hand of the potter.

units.la: Potestas: quod ex omnibus miseriis, quae, quales, quantae, cumque illae sint, adeoque ex morte ipsa resuscitare nos possit.
units.tr: Power: that from all miseries, whatever their kind and however great they may be, and even from death itself, he is able to raise us up.

units.la: Condidit, conseruat, & regit omnia, sustentatque verbo potentia.
units.tr: He creates, preserves and rules all things, and sustains them by the power of his word.
Who has set you above others?

units.la: Quod sumus & gerimus diuino munere constat: Ex nobis aliud non nisi bulla sumus. Ergo cuiq; fiet magnæ sua lectio curæ, Vt domus officiis fiet bene iuncta suis.
units.tr: What we are and what we do is established by divine gift; of ourselves we are nothing but a bubble. Therefore each person will make his own reading a matter of serious care, so that the household is well joined together by its own duties.
Piously
II. HIERARCHIES.

units.la: Pie vereq;,Nemo,inquit Baptistes,sibi sumere quicquam potest, nisi datum sit ei cœlitus. Figurat id nostrum Emblema: Nam in medio Ecclesiasticus seu persona quædam Ecclesiastica, Episcopusve, cum Pileo seu Infula & pedo Episcopalibus sursum arrecta dextra cœlitus sibi datum librum captans, probare nititur. Diuinitus dari sacros ordines, & cognitionem ad ministeria Ecclesiastica functionesque scholasticas necessariam. Quis enim ad hæc munia idoneus? Nemo certe. Quis te pratulit? Deus. Omnes necesse habemus cum Apostolo fatendo gloriari, & gloriando fateri: Gratia Dei sum, id quod sum. Et: Neque qui plantat, est aliquid, neque qui rigat, sed qui incrementum dat Deus. Diversitates donorum sunt, sed idem spiritus. Diversitates ministeriorum sunt, sed idem Dominus. Diversitates facultatem sunt, sed idem est Deus, efficiens eas omnes in quibusvis. Unicuique vero data declaratio Spiritus ad utilitatem. Spiritus Patris loquitur. Loquebantur, iniquiunt Actus Apostolici, prout cuique Spiritus dabat eloqui. Verbo dicam: Nemo sibi sumit honorem. Adeo quidem ut ipse Dominus & Saluator de vocatione & donis, augematibusque excellentissimis secundum humanam naturam glorietur, nec ab similiter Prophetæ atque Apostoli.
units.tr: Rightly the Baptist says: A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven. Our emblem illustrates this. In the middle stands an ecclesiastic, a bishop, with mitre and episcopal crozier, his right hand raised aloft, grasping a book given him from heaven, and seeks to prove that holy orders and the knowledge needed for ecclesiastical ministries and scholastic duties are given by God. For who is fit for these offices? No one, surely. Who has set you above others? God. We must all, with the Apostle, boast in confessing, and confess in boasting: By the grace of God I am what I am. And: Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord. There are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who works them all in everyone. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. The Spirit of the Father speaks. They spoke, say the Acts of the Apostles, as the Spirit gave them utterance. In a word, no one takes honour to himself. So much so that the Lord and Saviour himself glories in his calling and gifts, and in the most excellent endowments according to human nature; nor do the prophets and apostles do otherwise.

units.la: Claudit huic dextrum latus Vir paludatus, vel chlamydatus, idemque sursum extensa dextra, è cœlo sibi porrectum ensem arripiens significare satagit, etiam magistratus recognoscere Deum authorem ac superiorem, nec sibi ipsis acceptum referre honorem istum, sed soli & uni Archontotetha Deo, cui omnes etiam Maximi supplicare & homagium præstare obligantur. Omnipotestas à Deo est: Unde & nomen Deorum cum Deo uno & solo participant. Deus instituit reges, & transfert Regna; Ideoque sub DEO sunt, exemplum præeunte Vice-Rege Ægypti Iosepho: quod ipsum ipsi efferunt diplomatum proceris: Nos, inquiunt, Dei gratia. Denique.
units.tr: On the right side of this figure stands a man in a military cloak or mantle, who, with his right hand raised aloft and seizing a sword held out to him from heaven, strives to show that magistrates too acknowledge God as author and superior, and do not ascribe that honour to themselves, but to the one God alone, the Ruler of rulers, to whom even the greatest are bound to supplicate and render homage. All power is from God. Whence they also share the name of gods with the one God alone. God sets up kings and transfers kingdoms; and so they are under God, following the example of Joseph, viceroy of Egypt. Their own decrees of the nobles say the same: We, they say, by the grace of God. Enough on this.

units.la: Siniistram stipat vir rusticus superne delatum ligonem eleuata dextra sumpturus, indicat: Esse se diuino munere, qui sit; nec suum se sibi fictorem factorumve esse, sed diuina sibi gratia locum adsignari.
units.tr: On the left side a rustic man, his right hand raised to take up a mattock let down from above, shows that he is what he is by divine gift, and that he is not the maker of himself or of his deeds, but that divine grace assigns him his place.

units.la: Quæ cum ita se habeant, quis non videt in id sibi incumbendum totis viribus; quod diuino sibi munere, mandatum esse sentit: ut ille loquatur λογιά ἁ ἐξ. Iste feliciter imperet. Hic in sudore vultus sui manducet panem. Omnes autem & singuli splendorem sui ordinis & operis in timore Domini agnoscat, faciant officia singuli vocationum, & ut quisque accepit, ita alius in alium illud (donum suum) administret, ut boni dispensatores variagratia Dei: istud tenentes, singulos quicquid fecerint boni, hoc reportaturos à Deo, in nouissima de gesta dispensatione reddenda ratione, & cui multum concreditum fuerit, ab eodem multum flagitatum iri: qui autem in minimis fidelis fuerit, eum super multa constituendum fore.
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, who does not see that each must strive with all his strength at what he perceives to be enjoined on him by divine gift: that the one should speak logia ha ex [λογιά ἁ ἐξ]; that the other should rule happily; that this one should eat bread in the sweat of his face. Let each and every one recognise the splendour of his own order and work in the fear of the Lord; let each perform the duties of his calling, and as each has received, so let him administer it to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God, holding this: that each will receive from God whatever good he has done, in the final reckoning to be rendered of his stewardship, and that from him to whom much has been entrusted, much will be demanded; but he who has been faithful in little will be set over much.
QUEEN MONEY.

units.la: Et genus & formam Regina pecunia donat, Omnia facit pecunia, Excæcat magnos, Medioxymosq;,& Paruos: Quid non potest pecunia?
units.tr: Money gives both birth and form, queen money. Money makes all things; it blinds the great, the middling and the small. What can money not do?

units.la: Sapientes sapienter credunt ita sapienti: Pecunia obediunt omnia. Aureum est hoc & argenteum seculum, auro ducuntur omnes status & ordines, auro capiuntur & argento magni, parui, medioxymi; auro denique & argento reguntur summa & ima. nec abs re est, quod Regina titulo pecuniam ornat Vates Venusinus Horatius. Quid enim? An non auro temeratur illibatus verbi diuini honos? Certe: vel ipso Domino teste: Sacerdotes pretio docent, & Prophetae pecunia diuinant; interea Iehova nituntur, dicendo: An non Iehova in medio nostri est, non superuenient nobis malum. Vireret adhuc intemeratus flos diuinae veritatis, absque pecunia & opimis praebendis si esset: Auro inflectitur rectus iuris bacillus, & Nomothetae muneribus excaecantur, vt absoluant impium & condemnent iustum, hi furum socii sunt, de quibus Propheta Euangelicus: Quomodo effecta est meretrix vrbs fidelis? & plenissima iure, in qua iustitia pernoctabat, ea nunc homicidarum plena est? Argentum tuum abijt in scoriam, merum tuum infurcatum est aqua; Principes tui contumaces & socij furum; vnusquisque amat munus & sectatur retributiones, &c. In vita ciuili seu communi, quid non fit auri fame studioq;: vt non immerito exclamare libeat, liceat: auri sacra fames quid non mortalia cogis pectora? Mortalibus nil charius pecunia, atq; inter homines vna plurimum valet. Vnde iterum alius intonat:
units.tr: The wise, wisely, believe this saying: All things obey money. This is a golden and silver age; by gold all ranks and orders are led; by gold and silver the great, the small and the middling are caught; in short, by gold and silver the highest and the lowest are ruled. Not without reason does the Venusian poet Horace adorn money with the title queen. For indeed, is not the untainted honour of God's word also defiled by gold? Surely, and the Lord himself bears witness: The priests teach for hire, and the prophets divine for money; yet they lean upon the LORD, saying, Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No evil shall come upon us. The flower of divine truth would still flourish unspoiled if there were no money and rich stipends. By gold the straight rod of justice is bent, and lawgivers are blinded by bribes so that they acquit the wicked and condemn the just; these are companions of thieves, concerning whom the evangelical prophet says: How has the faithful city become a harlot? She who was full of justice, in whom righteousness lodged, is now full of murderers. Your silver has turned to dross, your wine is mixed with water; your princes are rebellious and companions of thieves; every one loves gifts and pursues rewards, etc. In civil or common life, what is not done from hunger and eagerness for gold? So one may rightly exclaim: Accursed hunger for gold, to what do you not drive mortal hearts? Nothing is dearer to mortals than money, and among men it alone is worth the most. Whence another again thunders:

units.la: Prob vt nihil sanum reperias vspiam! Sed pariter omnes seruiunt vili lucro!
units.tr: Alas, you will find nothing sound anywhere! But all alike serve base gain!

units.la: Auro blasphematur nomen Dei. Auro fiunt parricidia ministrorum. Auro excitantur seditiones. Auro patrantur homicidia. Auro committuntur stupra, adulteria, incestus. Auri studio exercentur latrocinia. Auro ferūtur falsa testimonia. Aurum & argentum, anima sunt & sanguis mortalibus, hoc qui caret, nec sibi parauit sedulo viuos hic inter, mortuus circum ambulat. Pudor per aurum soluitur, Violatur auro integritas, Pax occidit, fides perit. Legesq; & ipsa intercidunt.
units.tr: For gold the name of God is blasphemed. For gold the ministers are murdered. For gold seditions are stirred up. For gold homicides are committed. For gold fornications, adulteries and incests are committed. From the pursuit of gold robberies are carried out. For gold false testimonies are given. Gold and silver are the life and blood of mortals; whoever lacks them, and has not diligently provided for himself among the living here, walks about as one dead. Shame is dissolved by gold, integrity is violated by gold, peace dies, faith perishes; even the laws themselves fall.

units.la: Si ius violandum est, auri (regnandi) gratia violandam est, in caeteris pietatem solas: Sine me vocari pessimum, vt diues vocer, Nemo an bonus; an diues omnes quaerimus. Aut diues opto viuere aut pauper mori.
units.tr: If right must be violated, let it be violated for the sake of gold (of ruling); in other things let piety alone be spared. Let me be called the worst, so that I may be called rich; no one asks whether a man is good; we all ask whether he is rich. I would rather live rich, or die poor.

units.la: Verum, heus tu, bone, quid vanius auro; quid fluxius argento; quid denique fragilius pecunia? adeo vt, si vel totum mundum lucreris, iacturam animae patiaris: nam aurum & argentum non vindicant in die irae, imo testabuntur aduersus cultores, adeo pretiosa est redemptio animae. Quare si diuitiae affluant, noli apponere cor, auri massae caue sacra facias, nec spem ponas in pereuntibus diuitiis, sed in solo Deo viuo. Ibi thesauriza, vbi thesaurus manet aeternum.
units.tr: But listen, good sir: what is emptier than gold, what more fleeting than silver, what finally more fragile than money? So that if you should gain the whole world, you would suffer the loss of your soul; for gold and silver do not avenge in the day of wrath, indeed they will testify against their worshippers, so precious is the redemption of the soul. Therefore, if riches flow in, do not set your heart on them; beware of making sacred the heaps of gold; nor place your hope in perishing riches, but in the living God alone. Lay up your treasure there, where the treasure remains for ever.
Aristoph. in Tlut.
RAMPANT SINS.

units.la: Infima cum summis miscentur, turpia dictu Facilia facTu nemo est qui pudori habet Inde grauem Ecclypsin Ecclesia, Curia, Priua Patitur.Beatus, ille est qui minimis studet.
units.tr: The lowest mingle with the highest; things shameful to speak of are easy to do, and no one is ashamed of them. Hence the Church, the Court and private life suffer a grievous eclipse. Blessed is he who devotes himself to the smallest things.

units.la: Summa totius huius emblematis consistit in illo Hoseæ dicto, capite quarto, cum quo vocem tollere lubet: Audite Verbum Iehoua (o populares!) nam contentio est Iehoua cum habitatoribus terra huius, quod nulla sit fides, nullaq; benignitas, & nulla agnitio Dei in hac terra. Peierando & mentiendo, & occidendo, furando, & adulterando effringunt legem, & cædes aliæ aliis sunt contiguæ. Propterea lugebit hæc terra, & languebit quicquid habitat in ea. Talia plane, o diuine Hoschea, sunt tempora nostra, ad quæstus collata tuos, quum vt quo similius esse non possit, tempora quam sunt nostra tuis.
units.tr: The whole sum of this emblem rests on that saying of Hosea in chapter four, with which I am glad to raise my voice: Hear the word of the LORD, O you people, for the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of this land, because there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in this land. By swearing and lying, by killing, stealing and committing adultery, they break the law, and murder follows upon murder. Therefore this land shall mourn, and everything that dwells in it shall languish. Truly, O divine Hosea, our times are such, and so like yours, that nothing could be more alike than our times are to yours.

units.la: Vis & violentia primum locum occuparunt. Pellitur e medio iustitia & Sapientia, vigeritur res: Perstrepit illud Caligulæ: Oderint dum metuant, quod acinaces tibi tu cruento impositio capite significare debet, cædes aliæ aliis sunt contiguæ, cædes, inquam, cordis, odium, invidia æmulatio. cædes oris, mendacia, calumnia obtrectatio: cædes deniq; operis, persecutio, oppressio, cruentatio.
units.tr: Force and violence have taken first place. Justice and wisdom are thrust out of the way, and might rules. That saying of Caligula echoes loudly: Let them hate, so long as they fear, which the sword hanging over your head, ready to fall on your bloody neck, ought to signify. Murder follows upon murder: murder, I say, of the heart, by hatred, envy and rivalry; murder of the mouth, by lies, slander and detraction; and finally murder of deeds, by persecution, oppression and bloodshed.

units.la: Scortari, stupra adulteria, incestus committere turpe non esse putant, adeo frequenter, licentiose, & impune etiam, quod mali caput est, perpetrantur, adulterantur, & domum meretricis turmatim conveniunt, vt quipasti sunt, cum mane surgunt, quisq; ad vxorem proximi sui adhinniunt.
units.tr: Whoring, debauchery and adultery: men do not think it shameful to commit fornication and incest. These are committed so often, so wantonly and even with impunity, which is the head of all evils, that they commit adultery and crowd into the house of the harlot in troops; like well-fed stallions, each one neighs after his neighbour's wife in the morning when he rises.

units.la: De superbia & ambitione si dicere connitar, verbis facta æquare scio, non sufficiam, ita plerique primas in congressibus & consessibus captant, & plus de se, quam oportet, sapiunt, quod patula pauonum cum impositis arijs penna, manifestum faciunt.
units.tr: If I try to speak of pride and ambition, I know that words fall short of deeds, and I shall not be equal to the task. So many people strive for the first places in meetings and assemblies, and think more of themselves than they ought, for they make it plain by spreading the peacock's feathers, with their showy eyes set out.

units.la: Ad hunc modum tota mundi sphæra æruginem induit, obscuratur & patitur Ecclypsin perpetuam per continua crimina, vitia ac turpitudinem.
units.tr: In this way the whole sphere of the world has taken on rust, is darkened, and suffers a perpetual eclipse through its constant crimes, vices and filth.

units.la: Luce quidem sua radiat verbum, & flammas longe lateque eiaculatur suas, sed nemo curat, nemo suscipit, nemo cognoscit, Lucet lux in tenebris, sed tenebra non comprehendunt, adeo nulla est Dei cognitio in mundo hoc.
units.tr: Indeed the Word shines with its own light, and sends out its flames far and wide, but no one heeds it, no one receives it, no one knows it. The light shines in the darkness, but the darkness does not comprehend it; so there is no knowledge of God in this world.

units.la: Crescit avaritia studium indies, & ingravescit habendi insana libido, unde fas nefas pari trutina librantur, & æqua lance.
units.tr: Greed grows day by day, and the mad lust of having grows more severe, so that right and wrong are weighed on the same scales, with equal balance.

units.la: Iniustitia sumit incrementa per momenta, fides autem per charitatem efficax labascit & refrigescit: Multis annis iam peractis nulla fides est in pactis, mel in ore, verba lactis, fel in corde, fraus in factis.
units.tr: Injustice gains strength by the moment, while faith, which works through love, grows faint and cold. Many years now have passed, and there is no faith in covenants: honey in the mouth, words like milk, gall in the heart, and fraud in deeds.

units.la: Quare cum crescant delicta, pœnas etiam crescere, & vltionem diuinam non morari credere fas est: Impleta enim mergitur vrna.
units.tr: Since, then, offences are increasing, it is right to believe that the punishments are increasing too, and that divine vengeance will not delay, for when the urn is full, it sinks.

units.la: Vigilantibus ergo esse nobis conuenit, nec [Greek] iuxta Apostolum: [Greek], cuius Aduentum tam accelerare consentaneum, quam vera est Domini saluatoris assertio: Quæ cum fieri videatis, [Greek], quoniam redemptio vestra prope est. Beata autem prudentes virgines, seruique fideles, omnes ardentes gestantes lampades semper parati, ibunt in occursum sponsi & introibunt ad æternas nuptias.
units.tr: It is therefore fitting for us to be watchful and not sleep, as the rest do, according to the Apostle: [γρηγορῶμεν] let us watch. It is as fitting to hasten his coming as it is true, in the words of the Lord and Saviour: When you see these things come to pass, [γινώσκετε] know that your redemption is near. But blessed are the wise virgins and the faithful servants, who, always ready and carrying their burning lamps, will go out to meet the bridegroom and will enter into the eternal marriage feast.
THE CAPTIVE VIRTUE.

units.la: Laudatur virtus, sed non transfertur ad vsum,
units.tr: Virtue is praised, but it is not put into practice:

units.la: Dic mihi, quid, quaeso? vanius esse potest?
units.tr: Tell me, I beg you, what could be emptier?
Who does not feel the dreadful fires
Of divine wrath? Yet who now takes heed? Alas!

units.la: De extremis temporibus osDei,Sapientia Patris,veritas ipsa,Dn.Saluator noster,ita ait: Scandalizabuntur multi,& inuicem tradent,& odio habebunt inuicem: abundabit iniquitia, refrigescet charitas. Subscribit Dn.Saluatori Organon electum: Hoc, inquit ad Timotheum Ephesiorum Episcopum, Discipulum & Filium in fide γνήσιον: Hoc scito, quod in nouissimis diebus instabunt tempora periculosa; &erunt homines seipsos amantes, cupidi, elati, superbi, blasphemi, parentib. non obedientes, ingrati, scelesti, sine affectione, sine pace, criminatores, incontinentes, immites, sine benignitate, Proditores, proterui, tumidi, voluptatum amatores, magis quam Dei: Habentes speciem quidem pietatis, virtutem autem eius abnegantes. Concludit (in ore enim trium consistit omne verum) os Apostolorum: Scitote primum, quod venient in nouissimis diebus in deceptionem illusores iuxta proprias concupiscentias ambulantes. Hos tales depingere,& viuis coloribus depictos ob oculos nobis statuere praesens conatur ἐμφάνισις.
units.tr: Concerning the last times, the mouth of God, the Wisdom of the Father, truth itself, our Lord and Saviour, speaks thus: Many shall be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another. And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold. The chosen vessel agrees with our Lord. He writes to Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians, his disciple and true son in the faith [γνήσιον]: Know this, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, without natural affection, implacable, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof. The mouth of the Apostles, which cannot err, sums it up (for "in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word is established"): Know this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts. The present work sets out to paint such men and, with vivid colours, to place them before our eyes: a portrayal [ἐμφάνισις].

units.la: Manicas simul ac pedicas patitur chara charitas, captiua tenentur virtutes. charitas omnibus in ore versatur, sed pedicis irretita in cor descendere non permittitur; Excidit enim huic peruerso seculo illud Ioannis: Τεκνία, μὴ ἀγαπᾶτε λόγῳ μηδὲ γλώσσῃ, ἀλλὰ ἔργῳ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ: Vt de chara charitate vsurpare liceat illud Iuuenalis: Rara auis in terris nigroque simillima Cygno.
units.tr: Dear Charity suffers manacles and fetters, and the virtues are held captive. Charity is on everyone's lips, but once it is entangled in fetters it is not allowed to come down into the heart. For this perverse age has forgotten the words of John: Little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth [Τεκνία, μὴ ἀγαπᾶτε λόγῳ μηδὲ γλώσσῃ, ἀλλὰ ἔργῳ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ]. So, of dear charity, we may apply the line of Juvenal: a rare bird on earth, very like a black swan.

units.la: Ostracismi rea semel perac̈ta est, ab exsulio immerentem nemo reuocat, ab ἀσπόνδοις hostibus constricta praeseruatur: inuidia, dico & auaritia.
units.tr: A woman once condemned to ostracism has been driven out, and no one recalls the innocent from exile. She is held fast by implacable enemies, with whom there is no truce [ἀσπόνδοις]: envy, I mean, and avarice.

units.la: Inflatis multi buccis optume-meritae praeconia dicunt virtuti, captiuitate tamen non exonerant, sed quo magis commendatur, hoc magis premitur: Speciem virtutis habentes, virtutem eius abnegant. Pulpita obsederunt, tententq; clauos ἀδίκοι, dolosi, hypocritae, auari, μισοδιδάσκαλοι, αὐθάδεις, ... omnium horarum homines, indocti, quorum Deus venter est, huius seculi homines, qui palia, quod aiunt, ventorum intemperiae accommodate obuertere sciunt: Virtus non tam spernitur, cum suis clientibus (quod ferri quidem posset) sed premitur, proculcatur, demergitur. Optume senties, si mecum senties: Quod si: esse velis, nihil q; malis.
units.tr: Many men with puffed-out cheeks offer praises to virtue, yet they do not release her from captivity; the more she is commended, the more she is oppressed. They have the appearance of virtue, but deny its power. They have besieged the pulpits and seized the nails: the unjust [ἀδίκοι], the deceitful, the hypocrites, the greedy, the haters of teachers [μισοδιδάσκαλοι], the self-willed [αὐθάδεις], men of every hour, the unlearned, whose god is their belly, the men of this age, who know how to turn their cloaks to the winds, as they say. Virtue is not so much despised along with her followers (which might perhaps be borne) as pressed down, trampled and sunk. You will feel this best if you feel it with me: If you wish to be, then prefer nothing else.

units.la: Et praxi dona illud Spiritus S. per calamum Dauidis sonori: Noli amulari in malignantibus, neq; zelaueris facientes iniquitatem: Quoniam tanquam foenum velociter arescent, & quemadmodum herba cito decidunt: Tu vero delectare in Domino, & dabit tibi petitiones cordis tui.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit's words, sounded through the pen of David, agree with this: Do not envy the evildoers, nor be jealous of those who work iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb. Trust in the Lord, and delight thyself in the Lord; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
CHRIST, THE TREE OF LIFE.

units.la: [Woodcut engraving: Christ crucified on a tree, the titulus INRI above, with kneeling figures at the foot. Not text.] Planiciem quærit, vitat præruptaviator, Indagat gratam fessus arator opem. Planicies Christus cæli est, atq; vmbra salutis. Nec venit ex alio lux, via, vita, salus.
units.tr: [Woodcut engraving: Christ crucified on a tree, the titulus INRI above, with kneeling figures at the foot. Not text.] The traveller seeks a level plain and avoids the steep path; the weary ploughman looks for welcome help. Christ is the level plain of heaven and the shade of salvation. Light, way, life and salvation come from nowhere else.

units.la: Quód Dominus Saluator apud Matthæum, Venite, ait; ad me, omnes qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego reficiam vos. Tollite iugum meum super vos, & discite à me quoniam mitis sum & humilis corde, & invenietis requiem animabus vestris, quoniam suave est iugum meum, & leve meum onus: hoc ipsum ad oculum demonstrare nititur emblema praesens, sub typo arboris a qua Christus [ endet, cum inscriptione: Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum. Non est absonum a sacris hoc ἀνθος dicitur enim Christus: Surculus ex radice Iesse. Vocatur non tantum Iehouah iustitia nostra, sed & Germen Dauidis. Nam
units.tr: That the Lord Saviour says in Matthew, "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls, for my yoke is easy and my burden light": this very thing the present emblem seeks to show to the eye, under the type of a tree from which Christ hangs, with the inscription "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews." The flower [ἄνθος] is not out of keeping with the sacred writings, for Christ is called "a shoot from the root of Jesse." He is called not only "Jehovah our righteousness" but also "the Branch of David." For

units.la: Arbor summa & ima coniungit: Reconciliat Christus caelum & terram, Deum & homines, vnitque.
units.tr: The tree joins the highest and the lowest. Christ reconciles heaven and earth, God and men, and unites them.

units.la: Arbor semitam q. praebet ad superiora. Ita Christus est via, veritas & vita, nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per ipsum. Estque adeo vere scala illa Iacobaea, per quam ascendimus ad patrem.
units.tr: The tree offers a path to the heights. So Christ is "the way, the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through him." He is indeed that ladder of Jacob by which we ascend to the Father.

units.la: Arbor extendit ramos ad quatuor partes orbis: ita Iesus Christus crucifixus praedicatus per quatuor partes orbis terrarum, Gentibus, stultitia: Iudaeis, scandalum: sed vt Iaiuifica, omnibus fidelibus.
units.tr: The tree extends its branches to the four quarters of the world: so Jesus Christ crucified is preached through the four quarters of the earth, to the Gentiles foolishness, to the Jews a stumbling block, but to all the faithful a saving power.

units.la: Arbor etiam sub terram spargit radices: Nam a morte etiam redimit nos Christus & resuscitabit de puluere terra in nouissimo die: in Christo omnes viuificantur.
units.tr: The tree also spreads its roots under the earth: for Christ also redeems us from death and will raise us from the dust of the earth on the last day; in Christ all are made alive.

units.la: Arbor praebet gratam vmbram fessis, anhelisque. Ita Christus in omnibus aduersis gratum solatium: In aestu peccati est nobis vmbra iustitiae: In feruore ira est nobis refrigerium gratiae: In calore precum, est nobis solamen certae exaud-itionis: In contentione laboris, est nobis dulcis quies: In errore profectionis, est nobis regia via: In tenebris ὑποδοχεῖον, est nobis saluifica veritas: In tentatione opacat solatio spiritus: in morte refrigerat vmbra Passionis: in cruciatibus Gehennae praebet gratam vmbram aeternae felicitatis; humiliores sunt omnes humanae myricae, quam vt nobis vmbram vitae, pietatis, iustitiaeque coram Deo, aeternaeve salutis praestare possint. Quare verbo dicam cum Phostere Mediolanensi: Omnia nobis Iesus est, si volumus. Curari desideras; medicus est: si Febribus aestuas, fons est: si gravaris iniquitate; iustitia est: si auxilio indiges; virtus est: si mortem times; vita est: si ire desideras; via est: si tenebras fugis; lux est: si cibum appetis; alimentum est: gustate igitur & videte, quoniam suavis est Dominus!
units.tr: The tree offers a welcome shade to the weary and panting. So Christ is a welcome comfort in all adversities: in the heat of sin he is the shade of righteousness for us; in the fervour of wrath he is the refreshment of grace for us; in the heat of prayers he is the solace of certain being heard; in the strain of labour he is our sweet rest; in the error of setting out he is the royal road; in darkness he is the refuge [ὑποδοχεῖον], our saving truth; in temptation he shelters us with the comfort of the Spirit; in death the shade of his Passion cools us; in the torments of Gehenna he offers the welcome shade of eternal happiness; all human tamarisks are too lowly to afford us the shade of life, piety and righteousness before God, or of eternal salvation. Therefore, to put it in a word, with Phostere of Milan: Jesus is all things to us, if we will have him. Do you desire to be cured? He is the physician. If you burn with fevers, he is the spring. If you are weighed down by iniquity, he is righteousness. If you need help, he is strength. If you fear death, he is life. If you wish to go, he is the way. If you flee darkness, he is the light. If you crave food, he is nourishment. Taste, therefore, and see that the Lord is sweet!
Ambr. lib. 1 de Virgin.
SIMPLICITY IS CROWNED

units.la: Mirae, nec vnquam satis decantatae cum corporis tum animi tarditatis animal est asinus, vt multis inde dicteriis ortum locumq; dederit, vt ii homi-nem tardum, rudem, ἀπαίδευτος dicere velis; Asinū, Asinum Thessalicum, Asino indoctiorem, &c. voces: Vtut autem contemptum sit hoc animal, est tamen multorum in animali rationali exemplar & typus. Est enim simplex. Ἁπλοῦς. Naturae ductui à Deo ingenito obsequeus. Tanto affectus impete ad foetum ὁμοιοτρόπως rapitur, vt medius per ignem eius gratia feratur. Iusti aequique tenax. Non nocet morsu; non laedit calce; sed potius ictus & verbera patitur, subinde ad plura excipienda paratum. Vnde nec Christo equite ac sefore indignum.
units.tr: The ass is a creature of wonderful slowness, both of body and of mind, never sufficiently praised, and it has given rise to many taunts, so that you would call a man slow, dull or untaught [ἀπαίδευτος]. "An ass, a Thessalian ass, more ignorant than an ass," and so on. However despised this animal is, it is nonetheless the model and type of many in the rational animal. For it is simple [ἁπλοῦς], obedient to the leading of nature implanted by God. It is driven with such impulse toward its young, in like manner [ὁμοιοτρόπως], that it will pass through fire for its sake. It is tenacious of what is just and fair. It does not harm with a bite, nor hurt with a kick, but rather suffers blows and beatings, and is ready to bear more. Hence it is not unworthy even of Christ as its rider.

units.la: Asino certe quouis (liceat barbarizare) asiniores sunt, qui vel ab asino has virtutum vmbras ad rem & corpus transferre non conantur.
units.tr: Surely there are more asinine than the ass itself (let me coin a barbarism), those who do not even try to carry these shadows of the virtues from the ass over into their conduct and their body.

units.la: Simplicitas, à Christo ipso commendatur, & iniungitur, vt optume credere & optume ambulare putetur is, qui simpliciter credit & ambulet, absque carnali sapientia, quae stultitia coram Deo est, & ab eodem confunditur. Vide sis autem, ne dum simplex haberi vis, duplex euadas vel omnino ἁπλοῦς.
units.tr: Simplicity is commended and enjoined by Christ himself, so that he is thought to believe and walk very well who believes and walks simply, without carnal wisdom, which is foolishness before God and is confounded by him. But see to it that, while you wish to be thought simple, you do not turn out double, or not simple at all [ἁπλοῦς].

units.la: Ita enim simplex est, vt ductum ingenitum à Deo sequatur: tu lucem & Ducem λόγον sequere, & nunquam errabis.
units.tr: For you are simple insofar as you follow the leading implanted by God. Follow the light and the Guide, the Word [λόγον], and you will never go astray.

units.la: Ad ὁμοιοτρόπως, ad fratres, singulari te amoris adfectu trahi, diuinum est. Dei genus es, hunc diligere ante omnia, super omnia, post omnia, eumq; propter ἀδελφῷ amare ὁμοιοτρόπως debes, sicut teipsum, id nisi feceris, sub homicidarum censum cades.
units.tr: Likewise [ὁμοιοτρόπως], that you are drawn by a singular affection of love toward your brothers is a divine thing. "You are of God's offspring; love him before all, above all, after all," and you ought to love him, for the sake of his brother [ἀδελφῷ], likewise [ὁμοιοτρόπως], as you love yourself. If you do not do this, you will fall into the number of murderers.

units.la: Iustus vt sis & habeare, iusti, aequique tenax esse debes, & suum cuiq; tribuere. Qui facit iustitiam, iustus est.
units.tr: That you may be and be considered just, you must be tenacious of what is just and fair, and render to each his due. He who does righteousness is righteous.

units.la: Morsu oris ladere debes neminem, falsum testimonium non dicere, mendaciis non ferire, calumniis non lacerare.
units.tr: You must harm no one with the bite of your mouth, not bear false witness, not strike with lies, not tear with calumnies.

units.la: Imperitus non recalcitrare. Lacessitus non reuerberare: maledicta, maledictis, iniurias, iniuriis; damna, damnis; non copensare fi d bono malum vince. Et id teneas, te ad plura atq; maiora sustinenda Lex Christi obligari queest: si quis te percusserit dextram maxillam, praebe illi & alteram. Non excidat Asini Apologus.
units.tr: Do not kick back at the unskilled. Do not strike back at one who provokes you: curses with curses, injuries with injuries, damage with damage. Do not repay evil with evil, but overcome evil with good. And keep this in mind: the law of Christ obliges you to endure more and greater things, for "if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also." Let not the fable of the ass escape you.

units.la: Sedet pro confessionibus audiendis Νεῖο-Ἀρχῶν Leo, audit & absoluit Lupum ἰεροφάγον, rapinas ouium: Confitentem Laniatus anserum &c. Vulpem, & alios id genus, consueta absolutione: Tace frater mihi & tibi haec sunt communia. Asinum, quod manipulum foeni casu delapsum voraffe fateretur, solum sublimem rapi & in crucem à lorariis agi iubet. Intelligs quo tendam?
units.tr: The Lion, the new ruler [Νεῖο-Ἀρχῶν], sits to hear confessions. He listens to and absolves the Wolf, the temple-robber [ἰεροφάγον], the plunderer of sheep; the Fox, confessing the slaughter of geese, and others of that kind, he absolves in the usual way: "Be silent, brother; these things are common to you and me." The Ass, which confessed that it had gulped down a bundle of hay that had fallen by chance, he alone orders to be seized, lifted up, and dragged to the cross by the whip-men. Do you understand where I am heading?

units.la: Quare ad verbera te para, qui Christi discipulus clues: Mitto vos, inquit, vt oues in medium luporum. Fieri non potest quin lupus in infimo fontis loco iuxta se stantem agnum turbatae aquae teum peragere satagat.
units.tr: Therefore prepare yourself for blows, you who call yourself a disciple of Christ. "I send you," he says, "as sheep in the midst of wolves." It cannot be that the wolf, standing at the lowest point of the spring, does not strive to drive off the lamb standing beside him by stirring up the water.
THE NATURE OF TRUE AND SAVING FAITH.

units.la: Perpetuas tibi fundit aquas fons viuus, & vsum Multiplicem præstat vena perennis aquæ: Sic fidei veræ soboles dilectio præsto est, Corpus vt vmbra, fidem sic comitatur amor.
units.tr: A living spring pours out for you perpetual waters, and the vein of an ever-flowing fountain offers many uses. So true faith is accompanied at once by its offspring, love: as the shadow goes with the body, so love goes with faith.

units.la: Pie ac vere August.fides, inquit, est honorum omnium fundamentum:Fides est humana salutis initium, sine hac nemo ad filiorum Dei numerum potest peruenire, quia sine ipsa nec in hoc seculo quisquam iustificationis gratiam consequitur, nec in futuro vitam poss debit aeternam. Est autem fides (vt idem inquit Augustinus) credere in eum qui iustificat impium: credere in Mediatorem sine quo nemo reconciliatur Deo: credere in Saluatorem,qui venit quaerere & saluare quod perierat,&c.
