units.tr: OF THE FAITHFUL. The eagle is dear to God: the faithful are dear to God, both actively and passively, since without faith it is impossible to please God.

units.la: Aquila omnium summe volat altitudum: fideles non sunt graculi in terrenis nidos figentes, sed alas fidei librant in caelum usq; caelorum ad Thronum Maiestatis in excelsis.
units.tr: The eagle flies highest of all: the faithful are not jackdaws building their nests on earthly things, but they poise the wings of faith up to heaven, even to the throne of majesty on high.

units.la: § Aquila oderantur cadauera: Oderantur fideles Christum crucifixum, ita vt alta licet sit terra. altumq; caelum, fides tamen omnem omnino altitudinem, omnem omnino penetrat profunditatem, vt de fideli oratione loquitur Augustus. Fides omnem altitudinem transcendit.
units.tr: The eagle scorns carcasses: the faithful scorn Christ crucified. Although the earth is deep and the heaven high, faith nevertheless penetrates every height and every depth entirely, as Augustine says concerning the prayer of the faithful. Faith transcends all height.

units.la: Aquila in lucidissimos solis radios irretortis oculis perspicere potest. Ita fideles per ipsas nubes, per caelum sydereum vident in sclium diuinae maiestatis. His solis aperiuntur oculi vt dicere cum Stephano possint: Video caelos apertos & filium hominis stantem ad dextram Dei.
units.tr: The eagle can gaze at the brightest rays of the sun with unwavering eyes. So the faithful see through the very clouds and through the starry heaven into the sanctuary of the divine majesty. For these eyes are opened so that they can say with Stephen: "I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."

units.la: Aquila non agnoscit profuis, qui radios solis apertis, & irretortis oculis ferre non possunt. Ita nec Deus pro suis agnoscit, nisi fideles, & recto vultu Christum solem iustitiae contuentes. Oculi enim Domini requirunt fidem & fideles respectant.
units.tr: The eagle does not acknowledge those chicks which cannot bear the rays of the sun with open and unwavering eyes. So God too acknowledges as his own only the faithful, who behold Christ the sun of righteousness with a steady countenance. For the eyes of the Lord seek faith, and look upon the faithful.

units.la: Aquila tametsi super maria immobil. penna altissime feratur, de tanta tamen sublimitate despectat inferne, quae humanis non patent obtutibus: Ita fidelium oculis omnia sunt praesentia, licet humanis oculis non pateant, & ea quae in inferis & ea quae in superis sunt. Quare de his omnibus Hieronymus in hunc modum: Aquilam cunctis auib. altius volitare, (inquit) ettam h qui de natura auium disputant, memoriaprodiderunt, tantique con-uentus esse dicitur &c. quae sequuntur: Quae exponens Chrysostomus: Aquilas (inquit) appellat, vt ostendat ad alta eum (fidelem quemuis) oportere contendere, & nihil cum terra et esse debere commune, neque ad inferiora trahi ac repere, sed ad superiora semper volare, & in solem iustitiae intueri, multumque oculum acutissimum habere.
units.tr: Although the eagle flies very high on unmoving wings over the seas, from such a height it nevertheless looks down upon things below which are not open to human sight. So to the eyes of the faithful all things are present, although they are not open to human eyes, both those things which are below and those which are above. Concerning all these things Jerome writes in this manner: "The eagle flies higher than all birds," he says; and those who discuss the nature of birds have recorded this as well, and it is said to be of such great concord... ," and what follows. Expounding this, Chrysostom says: "He calls them eagles to show that the faithful man ought to strive upward, and that he should have nothing in common with the earth, nor be dragged and crawl down to lower things, but always fly up to higher things, and look upon the sun of righteousness, and have a most keen eye."

units.la: Aquila cum serpentibus bella ἀσπίδας: ita fidelibus cum serpentibus infernalib. Leonibus. Principibus. Dominis. Duisq; huius seculi.
units.tr: The eagle wages war with serpents [aspidas]: so the faithful with the infernal serpents. Lions, princes, lords and rulers of this world.

units.la: Aquila a fulmine immunis. Ita fideles ab ira Dei & maledictione aeterna: Nihil enim damnationis his qui in Christo Iesu sunt.
units.tr: The eagle is immune to the thunderbolt. So the faithful are immune to the wrath of God and to eternal condemnation: "For there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus."

units.la: Aquila annosa ad solem pennas exurens salubriq; inde mersata lympha reinuenescit: Quod indicium est fidelium regenerationis in hac & altera vita h.e. tum renouationis in tempore: & resurrectionis in nouissima die.
units.tr: The aged eagle, scorching its wings in the sun and then renewed by the healing water, grows young again. This is a sign of the regeneration of the faithful in this life and the next, that is, of their renewal in time, and of their resurrection on the last day.

units.la: IVSTITIAE quoq; non contemnendum σημεῖον est: librat iustitia alas in liquidum aera supremum, & inania tranant ad vsq; ἐπιτροπον. Pati iusf pre miq; iustitia ad tempus potest, opprimi nunquam. Vsq; ad iustitiam reuerturum est ludicium, & post illud omnes recti corde.
units.tr: The justice of the eagle is also a sign not to be despised: justice lifts its wings into the highest liquid air, and passes over emptiness as far as the guardian [epitropon]. The just man can suffer and be rewarded by justice for a time, but can never be crushed. There will be a judgment that returns to justice, and after it all who are upright in heart.

units.la: AMORIS deniq; diuini erga nos: Vt aquila excitat nidum suum: pandit alas suas, assumit pullum & portat super alas suas: sic Iehouah solus duxit eum, nec fuit cum Deus fortis alienigena.
units.tr: Finally, the love of God towards us: As an eagle stirs up its nest, spreads its wings, takes its young and carries it on its wings, so the LORD alone led him, and there was no foreign god with him.
THE JUST MAN SUFFERS FOR THE TIME BEING.

units.la: [Engraving: emblem picture, described under notes; no printed text in it.] Quisquis in hoc Diui tractas præconia iuris Æuo, hos in scopulos ingrediare, caue. Æmulus ille Dei est qui ius dispensat & æquum Iusteziniustitiæ dum arbiter ipse perit.
units.tr: [Engraving: emblem picture, described under notes; no printed text in it.] Whoever in this age of yours undertakes to proclaim the praises of divine law, let him beware of entering these rocks. That man is a rival of God who dispenses law and equity, while he himself perishes as judge, as Justice is wounded by injustice.

units.la: Multa sunt quae cursum iustitiae in hoc seculo peßumo remorari solent, vt similis sit catenato mo osso, & gladio feraq; obferatu, vtpote:
units.tr: There are many things which are wont to hold back the course of justice in this most wicked age, so that it is like the chained mouth and the sword locked up in its sheath, namely:

units.la: 'Αφοβία, seu vacuitas Timoris Domini: Vt enim ex tali securitate non nisi omnia mala in genere, ita in primis maxima oritur iniustitia, docente Dn. Salvatore parabola illa sua, Luc.18.Iudex quidam erat in quadam civitate, qui Deum non timebat, & hominem non reuerebatur, &c. Eiusmodi autem homo αφοβος Deo placere non potest: Et monenti tales essent, quod, SINT SVB DEO: Occinendumque illud piissimi Regis Iosaphat: Quare nunc infit pauor Iehoua vobis, observate & facite cum Timore Iehoua, cum fide & animo integro: Non enim pro homine iudicaturi estis, sed pro Iehoua, qui vobiscum futurus est in rebus iudiciariis.
units.tr: Aphobia, or the absence of the fear of the Lord. For just as all evils in general arise from such security, so above all the greatest injustice arises from it, as our Lord the Saviour teaches in his parable, Luke 18: "There was a certain judge in a certain city, who did not fear God and did not regard man," etc. Moreover a man of this kind, being without fear (aphobos), cannot please God. And to those who are such, he gives the admonition: "Be under God." And that most pious king Jehoshaphat's words should be sung: "Now therefore let the fear of the LORD be upon you; take heed and do it with the fear of the LORD, with faithfulness and with a perfect heart. For you judge not for man but for the LORD, who will be with you in judgment."

units.la: Πρόσωπο λῆψις Capitalis iniustitiae pestis hostisque est respectus personarum, fit fauore iniustus iusti ficatur: & condemnatur odio qui iustus. Communissimum simul atq; turpissimum hoc vitium seu crimen est, & diuinae capitaliter infestum iustitiae, quare tam seuere a iust.issimo Deo prohibetur: Personam ne respicito in iudicio, abominatio enim est Dn. Deo tuo. Non est profopolepsis Deus, ‘iuste iudicat, vnumquemq; secundum opera sua, cuius vestigiis insistere Iudices aquos ac bonos decet. Qui autem iustificat impium ac damnat iustum, vterq; abominatio est coram Deo.
units.tr: Respect of persons (prosopolepsia) is the plague and enemy of capital injustice: by favour the unjust is justified, and by hatred the just is condemned. This is the most common and at the same time the most shameful vice or crime, and it is mortally hostile to divine justice; therefore it is so severely forbidden by the most just God: "You shall not respect persons in judgment, for it is an abomination to the LORD your God." "God is not a respecter of persons" (Acts 10); he judges justly, each according to his works, and in whose footsteps fair and good judges ought to walk. But he who justifies the wicked and condemns the just, both are an abomination before God.

units.la: Δωροφαγία seu acceptio munerum iniustitiae genetrix dici potest, & iustitiae gradum sistit. Iudicium, inquit Dominus, non peruertito, a verbo mendacij proculabesto: & innocentem ac iustum ne occido: quia non absoluam improbum. Munus ne accipito, nam munus ipsum excaecat oculatos, & peruertit verba iustorum. Et iure naturae hoc crimen abominandum patet. Socii furum hi tales sunt. Nota est historia Cambysis Persarum Regis Cyri illius Magni filii, qui Sisamni iniusto & Δωροφάγῳ iudici pellem detrahi & tribunali assui iussit, filiumque Sisamnis Otanem tribunali imposuit, vt intuitu corii paterni recte ac iuste sine acceptione personarum ac munerum iudicaret. Regnet in iure dicendo istud: Fiat iustitia, & pereat mundus.
units.tr: Bribery, or the acceptance of gifts, may be called the mother of injustice, and it stands on the step of injustice. "Judgment," says the Lord, "do not pervert; keep far from a lying word, and do not kill the innocent and just, for I will not acquit the wicked. Do not accept a gift, for a gift blinds the seeing and perverts the words of the just" (Exod. 23; Deut. 16). And by the law of nature this crime is clearly to be abhorred. "Such are the companions of thieves." The story is well known of Cambyses, king of the Persians, son of that great Cyrus, who ordered the skin of Sisamnes, an unjust judge who took bribes, to be flayed off and sewn onto the judgment seat, and placed Sisamnes' son Otanes on the seat, so that by looking at his father's hide he might judge rightly and justly without respect of persons or gifts. Let this rule in the administration of law: "Let justice be done, though the world perish."

units.la: 'Αυθάδεια ac peruicacia: eo enim peruicaciae seu pertinaciae multi prouehuntur, vt non tantum scientes ac volentes iniustas sententias rogent, sed etiam admoniti iniustitiae corrigere tamen detrectent, imo iustum magis magisq, odio, calumniis, & oppressione persequantur: nimirum Ecclesiasticus sic docuit hos tales: ne fusc̈pias personam damno animae tuae. Ne contendas veritati vllo modo, sed verecundia cohibitor ne mentiaris. Ne confiteri verecunderis peccata tua, neq; rursus affer. &c. ô temporalo mores!
units.tr: Arrogance and obstinacy: for by obstinacy or stubbornness many are carried so far that they not only knowingly and willingly pronounce unjust sentences, but even when admonished refuse to correct the injustice; indeed they pursue the just man ever more with hatred, slander and oppression. Ecclesiasticus taught such people thus: "Do not accept a person to your soul's hurt. Do not contend for the truth in any way, but be restrained by modesty; do not lie. Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, nor resist the flow of the river," etc. O the manners of this age!

units.la: Prudentia carnalis: qua saepe premitur iustus spe imaginariae cuiusdam emendationis, & in gratiam aliorum. Quemadmodum Pilatus in gratiam Iudaeorum flagellauit Dominum, vt furor Iudaeorum mitigaretur: Magna haec est iustitiae Remora: verum non faciendi mala sunt, vt eueniant bona. &c: interim patitur iustus.
units.tr: Carnal prudence: by which the just man is often oppressed, in the hope of some imagined reform, and for the favour of others. Just as Pilate, to please the Jews, scourged the Lord so that the fury of the Jews might be calmed. This is a great hindrance to justice; but "evils must not be done that good may come," etc.; meanwhile the just man suffers.

units.la: Cuius iustitia postliminio retegitur & instar orientis ex alto stellae prodit cum iniustitiae & iniustorum confusione atque opprobrio. Quare commenda Domino viam tuam, ipse faciet, proferet tanquam lucem iustitiam tuam, & ius tuum tanquam meridiem.
units.tr: Whose justice is brought back by the right of return and appears like a star rising from on high, when injustice and the unjust are confounded and put to shame. "Therefore commit your way to the LORD; he will bring it to pass, and he will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your judgment as the noonday."
A Kind of Equity [ΕΠΙΕΙΚΕΙΑΣ ΕΙΔΟΣ]

units.la: Hispida latrantem laedit dum forte catellum Bellua, sit stricti iuris imago tibi: Nam rigoris nimius, strictum qui persequitur ius: Laedit, & infesto Dica mucrone secut.
units.tr: As a bristly beast, by chance biting a barking puppy, may be an image of strict law for you: for he who pursues strict right with too much rigour does harm, and Justice cuts with a hostile sword.

units.la: Summum, aiunt, ius summa saepe iniuria est. Eleganter hoc quidem & vere! Non enim semper sequendum est ἀκριβοδίκαιον, sed pro re nata poena sentetiaq; mitiganda est. Leuius lenitate ac mansuetudine, grauius, crudelitate peccatur. Pia (dixerunt veteres) seueritas crudelitas non est, non autem transgrediendi sunt limites seueritatis, alioquin facile in turpem degenerabit & cruetam crudelitatem: crudelitas in saeuitiam: saeuitia in tyrannidem; Tyranno autem nihil dici detestabilius potest, nec magis exsecrandum. Notum illud est Imperatoris: Imperare nescit, qui dissimulare nescit. Nec abludit ab illo sapientis: De vlla iniuria ne irascaris proximo, & ne agas quicquam contumeliosis factis. Quod Germanice in nostrum sensum sonat significantius: Recht nicht zu genaw alle Mißethat/vnd fühle dein Müthlein nit/ wann du straffen solt. Luculenta iniuria est, si poena delictu excedat. Poena peccato debet commensurari seu: inter delictu & poena debet esse proportio. Nec in iniuria vacare arbitramur, si in commensuratione nulla omnino personarum, temporis, loci, aetatis, similiumue circumstantiarum ducatur ratio. Vbi legis rigor mitigari potest, & delictum siue delinquens sine graviori poena & sine scandalo emendari, ibi clementiori poena vtitur pius ac sapiens Iudex: De ipso Deo Opt. Max. constat, iustum eum quidem esse, sed prauaiere tamen apud ipsum misericordiam: Non enim secundum peccata nostra facit nobis, neque secundum iniquitates nostras reddit nobis. Quare nulla re propius ad Deum accedimus, quam beneficentia atque mansuetudine. Et quemadmodum diuina sapientia gladium iustitia oleo misericordiae semper inungit: ita moderationem adhibere Iudex prudenter debet, vt inter iustitiam & clementiam currat ac medietur clemens iustitia & iusta clementia.
units.tr: "The highest law," they say, "is often the highest injustice." This is certainly elegantly and truly said! For one must not always follow strict justice [ἀκριβοδίκαιον], but as the case requires the punishment and sentence must be softened. Wrong is done more lightly by gentleness and mildness, and more gravely by cruelty. The ancients said that duty-bound severity is not cruelty, but the limits of severity must not be overstepped, or else it will easily degenerate into shameful and bloody cruelty: cruelty into savagery, savagery into tyranny. Nothing can be said to be more detestable than a tyrant, nor more accursed. That saying of the Emperor is well known: "He does not know how to rule who does not know how to overlook." Nor does the saying of the wise man differ from it: "Do not be angry with your neighbour over any wrong, and do not do anything by insulting deeds." In German this sounds more pointedly in our sense: "Do not be too exact in examining every misdeed, and do not feel your little spirit when you ought to punish." It is a manifest injustice if the punishment exceeds the offence. "Punishment ought to be measured to the sin; that is, there ought to be proportion between the offence and the punishment." Nor do we think there is no injustice if, in the measuring, no account is taken of the persons, time, place, age, or similar circumstances. Where the rigour of the law can be softened, and the offence or the offender can be corrected without a heavier punishment and without scandal, there the pious and wise judge uses a milder punishment. It is agreed about God Himself, the Best and Greatest, that He is indeed just, but mercy prevails with Him: "He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities." Therefore we draw near to God by nothing more closely than by beneficence and gentleness. And just as divine wisdom always anoints the sword of justice with the oil of mercy, so the judge ought prudently to apply moderation, so that justice and clemency run together, and merciful justice and just clemency temper each other.

units.la: Est piger ad poenas Princeps, ad praemia velox;
units.tr: The prince is slow to punishments, swift to rewards;
and he grieves whenever he is forced to be fierce.

units.la: Notaest historia de Theodosio Imper. qui Thessalonicae absque fere clementiae ac moderationis respectu aliquot millia ciuium furenter occidi iussit, vbi certe poena delictum excessit longissime, quare à S. Ambr. à communione abstentus, & ab omnib. sacris, in loco peccatorum poenitentiam egit in cilicio atq; cinere. Nimius rigor nocet ipsi exercenti rigorem sicut acies nimis exacuata conuertitur in acuentem ac vibrantem: prorsus vt canis aculeos erinacei ore excipit ac sauciatur: ita strictus iustitiae vindex extremo rophaeae laeditur. Moniss wendet sich, vnd leget den Der es so gesch\u00e4rpft hat. Monet Apostolus: Τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ὑμῶν innotescat omnibus, quod vt omnibus omnino piis, ita inprimis iudicibus atq; magistratib. dictum esto. Similem esse collationem philosophus inquit, Regis cum subditis, qualis est Pastoris ad boues, patrisq; ad filios seu liberos. Nullum violetum est diuturnum: Neq; vllius magistratus crudelis exitus fuit bonus, vt exempla Pharaonis, Saulis, Balthazaris seu Labynithi; Antiochi, Herodis, Neronis & similium abunde testatum faciunt. Commendatur autem iustitia mixta ἐπιεικεία, vt in Dauide, Iosaphato, Salomone, Hiskia, Iosia, Augusto, &c. Zaleuco, &c.
units.tr: The story of the Emperor Theodosius is well known, who at Thessalonica, with almost no regard for clemency and moderation, ordered several thousand citizens to be slaughtered in a rage, where the punishment far exceeded the crime. Therefore Ambrose kept him from communion and from all the sacred rites, and he did penance in the place of sinners, in sackcloth and ashes. Excessive rigour harms the one who exercises it, just as a blade sharpened too finely turns back upon the one who sharpens it and wounds him when it is brandished; just as a dog takes the spines of a hedgehog into its mouth and is wounded, so the stern avenger of justice is hurt at the end. "Gentleness turns itself around and lays it back upon the one who sharpened it so." The Apostle admonishes: "Let your gentleness [Τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ὑμῶν] be known to all," which ought to be said to all pious people, and above all to judges and magistrates. The philosopher says that the comparison of a king with his subjects is like that of a shepherd with his oxen, or of a father with his sons or children. No violence is lasting, and no cruel magistrate has had a good end, as the examples of Pharaoh, Saul, Belshazzar or Labynitus, Antiochus, Herod, Nero and the like bear abundant witness. Justice tempered with gentleness [ἐπιεικεία], however, is commended, as in David, Jehoshaphat, Solomon, Hezekiah, Josiah, Augustus, etc., and Zaleucus, etc.
THE SLIPPERY LAW.
O mortal, you tread slippery paths of law,
whoever you are, when you follow ambiguous ways:

units.la: Aerea vt incautum laedunt[?] tormenta virum, sic
units.tr: as bronze cannon harm an unwary man, so

units.la: Aurea & incauto iura nocere solent. Sclopetum(siue, quam à sono, quem edit, dicunt bombardam) ius seu iuris tractationem:gladius & libra utrinq; extensa iustitiam hëic figurat.Qui sic?ais;Totus sclopeti vel vsus,vel vtilitas, vel pernicies est penes vtentem. Si rectè vtaris ac moderate, defendet te:sin imprudenter ac temerarie, laedet te. Certe quicunq; iura tractant & dispensant summa prudentia atque cautione opus habent, ne dum ius dicunt, iniustas sententias dicant, & eo per ius iniusti iuste accusentur,damnenturq;.Non sane immerito Gracorum Oratorum Aquila atq; Coryphaus,si dua, inquit,sibi monstrarentur via, altera ad iuris dispensationem seu iudicis officium, altera ad mortem ducens, se hanc pra illa electurum. Quid ita miDemosthenes?Quoniam tam ambigua lubricaq; dicendi iuris prouincia est. Quam difficile enim est non moueri vel personis vel muneribus vel alia quauis fere re externa! Ne dum ius dicere velis,iniustum dicas; dum æquum iniquam;dum phas,nephas;.quis omni æquabiliter videt tempore,vt fieri potè non sit, qui hodie non impingit, cras non impingat itidem. Nota est similis illius historia, qui cum proue&tæ nimis ætatis essent, moribundus dicebat,scribiq; pro Epicedio manibus imperabat: Simlis hi. iacet, cuius atas quidem multorum annorum fuit, septem tamen dumtaxat annis vixit: Adriani Imp.h.c Aulicus fuerat & ius dixerat, solu supremu septennium exegerat priuatus. Totam igitur priorem vitam pro dispendio ac damno reputabat, vltimum septennium ponebat in lucro. Haud aliter sentiebat de administrandis LL. fasciLus Æschines, quo de Plutarcho testatur, quod à foro discundoq; iure liber factus ita gestierit,atq; qui liberatus fuerit à morsu rabiosi canis.Officium ipsum non sugillamus, de modo administrandi nobis sermo est.Spinas tractant quicunq; ius tractant, cura opus habent, & summa niti ope debent vt insistant. Quod de LL.ministris ac viudicibus diximus, idem de iis dicimus qui iure volunt vti, nam & Themistoclis ea fuit electio, vt si duae sibi monstrarentur semitę,ad ius vna,altera ad mortem,se hac potius iturum:Ita eodem plane modo fieri poterit,vt dum ius captas, iniuria tibi obtingant. Tanta cautione nemo tractat sclopetum, quin maiori opus fit: ita nemo ea Prudentia quaerit,vtiturq; iure, quin maiori nec esse habeat. Nam sive vincat sive minus, nunquam id fiet sine damno. Exempla ac dicteria odiosa sunt. Cui bombardae simile non sapit,mellis degustet:moderate hoc quis vtatur oportet,vt non noceat. Melinueniens comedis quod satis est tibi,ne saturatus illo,euomas illud.
units.tr: golden laws too are wont to harm the unwary. The arquebus (or, from the sound it makes, the bombard) is the image of the handling of law. The sword and the balance, both held out, here represent justice. How so? Whether the arquebus is useful or harmful depends entirely on the one who uses it. If you use it rightly and moderately, it will defend you; if rashly and carelessly, it will harm you. Certainly, all who handle and administer law need the greatest prudence and caution, lest in pronouncing law they pronounce unjust sentences, and so are justly accused and condemned under the law for injustice. Not without reason did the eagle and chief of the Greek orators say that, if two ways were shown to him, one leading to the administration of law or the office of judge, the other to death, he would choose the latter rather than the former. Why so, Demosthenes? Because the province of speaking and administering law is so slippery and uncertain. For how hard it is not to be moved by persons, by bribes, or almost by any external thing! Not only, when you wish to declare what is law, do you declare what is unjust; when you declare what is fair, you declare what is unfair; what is right, what is wrong. Who sees everything evenly at all times, so that it is not possible that one who does not stumble today will not stumble likewise tomorrow? The story of that man is well known, who, since he had lived far too long, on his deathbed commanded that this be written for his funeral epitaph: Here lies this man, who lived many years of age, yet lived only seven years. He had been a courtier of the Emperor Hadrian and had administered law, but he had spent only the last seven years in private life. He therefore reckoned his whole earlier life as loss and damage, and counted the last seven years as gain. Æschines thought much the same about administering the laws, as Plutarch reports of him, that once he was freed from the forum and the administration of law he rejoiced as one who had been freed from the bite of a mad dog. We do not disparage the office itself; our discussion concerns the manner of administering it. All who handle law handle thorns; they need care and must strive with all their might to keep their footing. What we have said of the ministers and judges of law, we say likewise of those who wish to use law, for Themistocles too made this choice: if two paths were shown him, one to law, the other to death, he would rather go by the latter. So in exactly the same way it may happen that, while you seek law, injury befalls you. No one handles an arquebus without great care, and so no one who seeks and uses law with such prudence can avoid a greater one. For whether he wins or not, it never happens without loss. Examples and sayings are wearisome. Let him who does not like the bombard taste honey: one must use this in moderation, so that it does no harm. If you find honey, eat what is enough for you, lest, being sated with it, you vomit it up.
The diversity of the jurists.
Demosthenes, in Erasmus' Apophthegms.

units.la: Similis historia apud Dion. Cass. Nican. Adr. Imp.
units.tr: A similar story in Dio Cassius, on the Emperor Hadrian of Nicaea.
Plutarch, in Aeschines.
Themistocles.
Prov. 25. vs. 16.

units.la: SCINDITVR HVMANVM STV-dia in contraria vulgus.
units.tr: MANKIND IS DIVIDED INTO CONTRARY PURSUITS, THE COMMON HERD.

units.la: Laudis opes, dotesq; tagi, venerisq; latebras, Sectatur stolidum nunc ubicunq; genus: Quæ bona de cœlo CHRISTI quoq; sanguine partæ, Dat Deus, hæc amens spernere munde soles!
units.tr: The foolish race now pursues wherever it can the riches of praise, the gifts of wealth, and the hiding-places of lust; the good things that God gives from heaven, won by the blood of Christ, you, mad world, are willing to spurn!

units.la: Sumus quidem principaliter conditi ad gloriam & cognitionem Dei, indeq; ad vitam adsequendam possidendamq; æternam, hæc autem vita & domicilium terrenum, tanquam vestibulum illius alterius inhabitandum seu incolendum potius interim datur, dum præstituto à Deo tempore ad illam diuina gratia transferamur, hac lege, vt hic Deum agnoscere, timere, diligere, quærere, atq; colere discamus, inchoemus, isthic perficiamus: sed tanta nostra cæcitas, vt & malitia est, vt spretis posthabitisq; cœlestib tantū terrenis inhiemus, & tales nos præbeamus, vt ad cælicā apprehendendam possessionem plane reddamur inhabiles. Id q; præsens noltiū emblema liquido ostendere cónitur, p diuersissima mūdi studia, à regno Dei aliena.
units.tr: We are indeed created chiefly for the glory and knowledge of God, and thence to attain and possess eternal life. This life, and this earthly dwelling, is given us for the time being to be inhabited or rather lived in, as a vestibule of that other life, until at the time appointed by God we are transferred to it by divine grace, on this condition: that here we should learn to know, fear, love, seek and worship God, begin it here and perfect it there. But our blindness is so great, and our malice so great, that, scorning and setting aside the heavenly things, we gape only after earthly ones, and show ourselves such that we are wholly unfit to take hold of the heavenly possession. This present emblem attempts to show plainly this by the most diverse pursuits of the world, which are alien to the kingdom of God.

units.la: Sunt qui captent honores & laudes in hoc seculo: inidonei sunt illi ad regnum cœlorum, quod v.g. Dn. Saluator Pharisæis & Scribis in Euangelio obiicit, tanquam insigne à regno cœlesti auocamentum, dicens: Quomodo vos potestis credere, qui gloriam ab inuicem accipitis, & gloriam quæ à solo Deo est non quæritis? q.d. fieri id non posse. Et iterum: Dilexerunt n. gloriam mundi magis quam gloriam Dei. Quare studium mundanæ gloriæ & studium gloriæ cœlestis ita sese mutuo tollunt, vt vna consistere non possint: quanto ergo hæc illa præstat, tanto magis huic quam illi sudare debemus. Illa vitrea est, cum splendet, frangitur, hæc manet in æternum: illa croci dili instar est, persequentem fugit, fugientem persequitur: hæc vero à persequentibus apprehenditur: violenti rapiunt eam.
units.tr: There are those who seek honours and praise in this age. Such people are unfit for the kingdom of heaven. The Lord Saviour, for example, puts this to the Pharisees and Scribes in the Gospel as a notable hindrance from the heavenly kingdom, saying: How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone? As if to say, that this cannot happen. And again: For they loved the glory of the world more than the glory of God. Therefore the pursuit of worldly glory and the pursuit of heavenly glory so cancel each other out that they cannot stand together. Since the latter surpasses the former by so much, we ought to labour all the more for it than for the former. The one is like glass: when it shines, it is broken; the other remains for ever. The one is like a crocus-lily: it flees the one who pursues it, and pursues the one who flees; but the other is seized by those who pursue it: the violent take it by force.

units.la: Sunt qui opes ac bona huius mundi sectantur, & id studio habent, vt magnos thesauros auri, argentiq; corradant, & laute ac opipare victitent in hoc seculo: sed & hi vanis ducūtur & seducuntur adsectibus, nā spinæ sunt terrenæ opes, quas caute ac prudenter tractare oportet, ne pungat, nec animam lædant, quod certe non cuiusuis esse ex dominica assertione patet, qui ait, fieri perinde facile posse, vt camelus (seu maximus funis nauticus) per foramen acus transeat, quā diues vt intret cœlorum in regnum: rationem subdit Apostolus: Qui diuites fieri volunt, incidunt in tentationem & laqueos & desideria multa, quæ demergūt hominem in interitum & damnationē. Monendi igitur diuites sunt, ne cor appendat nec confidant in terrenis opibus, sed thesaurisent in cœlis. ¶ Sunt qui potentiam quærunt in hoc æuo, & eminere gestiunt, vt vbiuis conspiciant in alto, & sedeant ad clauū. Nimis fatui ac curiosi sunt hi: dum n. alas pauonias ita librant, quid faciunt aliud, q; vt vigilias, curas, molestias, & nihil non incomodi mercetur, & suo sibi iumento mala attrahā: iuxta q; et à calle cœlestis regni deuiant, de quo dicitur: Qui inter vos eminere vult, fiat sicut iunior, & qui præcedere, fiat sicut omnium minister. His occinendū illud: dulcis inexpta cultura potetis amici, expertus metuit. ¶ Sunt denique, quos stimulatur luxuria, & furor beluinus pronos ad cocitat in venerē, adeo vt exserto ore dicere nō horrent, se tales illecebras vel ipso cœlo (horresco referens) commutaturos. Plane aguntur hi infernalib. furiis, qui scortari adolescentem nec turpe putant, nec pro peccato reputāt: Vxorem aiunt duxi, venire non possum. Ita indiem heluantur, scortantur, pergræcantur, adulterantur, incestus & sodomias, multaq; peccata alia muta Hagitiose perpetrant, de quibus aperte oraculo diuino conclamatum est. Non gustabunt coenam meam. Non intrabunt in requiem meam. Nolite errare, non possidebunt regnum cœlorum.
units.tr: There are those who chase the riches and goods of this world, and make it their aim to heap up great treasures of gold and silver, and to live sumptuously and lavishly in this age. But these too are led and seduced by vain affections, for earthly riches are thorns, which must be handled cautiously and prudently, lest they prick and wound the soul. That this is certainly not for everyone is clear from the Lord's saying, who said that it is just as easy for a camel (or the largest ship's cable) to pass through the eye of a needle as for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. The Apostle adds the reason: Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and snares and many desires, which drown a man in destruction and damnation. The rich must therefore be warned not to set their heart on, nor trust in, earthly riches, but to store up treasure in heaven. ¶ There are those who seek power in this age, and long to stand out, so that they may be seen on high everywhere, and sit at the helm. These are too foolish and too curious: for while they poise their peacock's wings in this way, what else do they do but earn for themselves watches, cares, troubles, and nothing but discomforts, and draw evils upon their own beast of burden; and so they stray from the path of the heavenly kingdom, of which it is said: Whoever wishes to stand out among you, let him become as the youngest, and whoever would go before, let him become as the minister of all. To these is fitting that saying: sweet is a friend's cultivation, untested; he who has tested it fears. ¶ Lastly, there are those whom lust goads, and beastly fury drives headlong into the pursuit of love, so that they do not shrink from saying openly that they would exchange such allurements even for heaven itself (I shudder to relate it). Plainly these are driven by infernal furies, who think it neither shameful nor reckon it a sin to whore after a young man: They say, I have taken a wife, I cannot come. Thus they waste their days in gluttony, whoring, drunkenness, adultery, and commit incest and sodomy and many other sins, unmentionable, shameful, and concerning these the divine oracle has openly cried out: They shall not taste my supper. They shall not enter into my rest. Do not err: they shall not possess the kingdom of heaven.
Emblem of the Jurists: Prudence

units.la: Prudens te pietas, pia te prudentia stipet, Quisquis es, vt populis iura verenda roges. Tale olim te iudicium, mihi crede, manebit, Quale heic in plebem forte tuere tuam.
units.tr: Prudent piety and pious prudence attend you, whoever you are, that you may plead the laws that are to be revered for the peoples. Such a judgment, believe me, will await you as you have dealt with your own people here.

units.la: . Duæ sunt virtutes cardinales, quæ iuris & æqui prudentem maxime iuuant, ornantq;: Pietas vna, altera Prudentia. Res illa, rei hæc modus haud incongrue vocabitur: Magistra illa, hæc serua: Hera & Domina illa, hæc ancilla: illa Deo, hæc LL. seu δικαίῳ ἡ νομίμῳ vt vocant, nititur.
units.tr: There are two cardinal virtues that greatly help and adorn the prudent person in matters of law and equity: piety, the one, and prudence, the other. The one may fitly be called the matter, the other its measure. The one is the mistress, the other the servant; the one is the lady and mistress, the other the handmaid. The one rests on God, the other on the law [by the just or the lawful δικαίῳ ἢ νομίμῳ], as they say.

units.la: Quicunque n. Deum toto corde reueretur, ille haud difficulter iuris & æqui se vt consultissimum ita studiosissimum præbebit, nec rebus iniustis consentiet vnquam: Timor Dn. reuocat à peccando. Impius neq; Dei nec iuris æquiue ratione ducet, quare necesse est, vt Pietas cordi & oib. actibus moderetur. Timor Dn. Sapientiæ initium, quare generum Moschen Sacerdos Midianiticus Iethro viros Dei timentes ante omnia conquirere & constituere iubet: & à iudicibus Pius Rex Iosaphatus, primitus requirit Pietatem, & Timorem Iouæ, quoniam in huius honorem iudicia maxime exercentur. Ipseq; Adsessore se in omnib. iudiciis ingerat, & primos captet accubitus. Quare nō abs q; ratione fuit illorū mos, qui vacuam timoriIouæ sellam iuxta sestatuerūt. hæc res & forma est fori aciudiciorū, qua sine nihil Deo placere pōt.
units.tr: Whoever reveres God with his whole heart will without difficulty show himself most learned and most diligent in law and equity, and he will never consent to unjust acts: The fear of the Lord restrains from sin. The impious man is guided neither by the reason of God nor by that of law and equity; hence it is necessary that piety govern the heart and all actions. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. For this reason Jethro, the Midianite priest and father-in-law of Moses, bids him above all to seek out and appoint men who fear God; and the pious king Jehoshaphat requires of the judges, first of all, piety and the fear of Jehovah, since judgments are exercised chiefly for the honour of Jehovah. Piety should also press itself upon the judge as adviser in all judgments, and seize the first place at the table. Hence it was not without reason that they had the custom of setting an empty seat beside the judge, to represent the fear of Jehovah. This is the form and the manner of the court of judgments, without which nothing can please God.

units.la: Quo aūt Iudex ius pie ac iuste administret, opus est ipsi Prudentia, cuius triplex facies hieroglyphicum est, ac Sapientia, q pietati ancilletur, qua sine Pietas, simulacrū potius pietatis vel stoliditas erit: Prudentiā aut dico, qua in pietate fundatur, & ex ea mediantib. LL. cū diuinis tum positiuis oritur, piam ac iustam prudentiā, q omnia accurate perpendit, & neruū prudenter intēdit in.
units.tr: But so that the judge may administer law in a pious and just way, he needs prudence itself, whose threefold face is the hieroglyph, and wisdom, which serves piety; without wisdom, piety will be a mere image of piety, or foolishness. I mean prudence, which is founded on piety, and which arises from it, through laws both divine and positive: a pious and just prudence, which weighs all things carefully and prudently directs its effort to the matter at hand.

units.la: I. Oculos. Vultus animi Index est, & ex faciei, quæ vocant, lineamentis à prudentibus de cordis vel simplicitate vel duplicitate haud difficulter iudicari pōt. Fieri vix potest, vt quis monstrum, qui in corde alit, in vultu prorsus tegere possit, quin p licet. Qui conuiuet oculu suu, inquit Regum sapientiss. & sapientum R. x, cogitat res peruersas, contendens sermones suos, perficit malum. Rotatus, nictationes & similes oculorū gestus duplicis cordis & peruersi nebulonis indicia haut obscura præbent, hæc ἐφ' ἀλμοσωτεία raro fallit, vt in specie Sapiēs de dubiæ pudicitiæ muliere adserit: Sicortario mulieris in elatu oculu ac pa pebris eius cognoscitur.
units.tr: I. The eyes. The face is the index of the mind, and from the lines of the face, as they call them, the prudent can judge without difficulty whether a heart is simple or double. It can hardly happen that a man who nourishes a monster in his heart can hide it entirely in his countenance without it showing. He who winks with his eye, says the wisest of kings, plans perverse things, and with his words he works evil (R. x). Rolling of the eyes, winking and similar movements of the eyes give clear signs of a double heart and a perverse scoundrel; this (ἐφ' ἀλμοσωτεία) rarely deceives, as the Wise Man says of a woman of doubtful chastity: The harlot is known by the haughtiness of her eyes and the lifting of her eyelids.

units.la: II. Os. Sermo, aiunt, animi Index: Loquere, dicebat Philosophus, vt te videam verba præcipitata, distorta, semesa, tertiata, ambigua, & c. sufficientia sunt, quid de re ipsa statuere habeas. Vide mihi Sapientiam seu Prudentiam Salomonis, ex cruentis profligatę prostibuli pudicitiæ verbis arguebat, veram illam matrem esse non posse. Omnia igitur ac singula verba pio iudici aurea lance sunt trutinanda, vt ius inde extricet.
units.tr: II. The mouth. Speech, they say, is the index of the mind: Speak, the philosopher used to say, that I may see you. Hasty, distorted, half-swallowed, garbled, ambiguous words and the like are enough to show what you ought to judge about the matter itself. Consider Solomon's wisdom or prudence, which argued from the bloodthirsty words of the shameless harlot that she could not be the true mother. Therefore every word, one and all, must be weighed by the pious judge on a golden scale, so that he may disentangle the right from them.

units.la: III. Deniq; & manum obseruare debet: nam si illa spōte acemere in duos priores & extensos digitos se porrigat, haud dubie stultum malumq; ibi latere aīm arguet. Pii & bonæ restimonio conscientię freti iuramenta horrent tanq; sacra & φῦκ. Deinde si cuius manus videant complicatas & auri argentiue honorario (sic iniquitatis mercedem vocar) onustas, malæ causæ propugnatorem inde intelliget. Pii, boni, iusti causæ bonitate freti à munerib. dādis vltro abstinent, nec iustitiæ mercantur patrocinium, cum diuini interdicti, tum æternæ honestatis, tum et propriæ conscientiæ respectu absterriti, qui v. quāuis tueri causam non abhorrent, quomodo non eidem eam quouis modo licito, illicito; honesto, inhonesto; bono, malo; obtinere satagant.
units.tr: III. Finally, he must also observe the hand. For if it stretches out of its own accord with the first two fingers extended, it will undoubtedly show that a foolish and wicked mind lies hidden there. Those who trust in the testimony of a good and pious conscience shrink from oaths as from holy things [φῦκ.]. Again, if people see someone's hands folded and laden with gold or silver fees (thus he calls the wage of iniquity), the judge will understand from this that he is a defender of a bad cause. The pious, good and just, trusting in the goodness of their cause, abstain of their own accord from giving bribes, and do not buy the patronage of justice; they are deterred both by the respect owed to the divine prohibition, by eternal honesty and by their own conscience. But those who do not shrink from defending a cause, how do they not strive to win it by any means whatever, lawful or unlawful, honest or dishonest, good or bad?
DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE.

units.la: Sancta Themis, iustiq; tenax ter virgo beata, Quæq; cuiq; soles distribuisse suum! Dispereat precor ille, tuæ, O Astræa, sacratum Corpore qui florem virginitatis auet!
units.tr: Holy Themis, steadfast in justice, blessed thrice-virgin, who alone givest to each his own! Perish, I pray, that man who covets the flower of virginity consecrated to your body, O Astraea!
Equality [Ισότης]

units.la: ’Ιστίτις, inquit Græcus, ... Iustitiæ igitur distributiuæ hic vides ... : Est autem iustitia distributiua, quæ suum cuiq; abíq; prauis adfectibus, malis consultoribus, muneribus, respectu personarum, & aliis iniustitiæ hærentibus criminibus distribuit, in gloriam Dei & bonorum commodum, salutemq;. Habet hæc distributiua iustitia sua encomia cum in sacris, tum in prophanis plurima. Iudicate, inquit Dn. Saluator, rectum iudicium. Non assumes personam in iudicio, nec munera captabis, abominatio sunt huiusmodi Iehoua. Lauate, purifi ate vos, auferte malignitatem actionum vestrarum ex aduerso oculorum meorum, desinite male facere: discite benefacere, quærite ius: beate oppressum, ius dicite pupillo, suscipite causam viduæ, &c. Hac δικαιοσύνη ... maxime opus est in omnibus omnino statibus, vt cuiq; detur secundum quod meruit vel laus, vel vituperium: vel præmium vel pœna, dicente Apostolo: Vnicuiq; quod debetis, vectigal, cui vectigal: tributum, cui tributum: timorem, cui timorem: honorem, cui honorem: Vergit id in honorem Dei, conducit ad communem tranquillitatem ... coseruandam & animos pacat: vt perpendiculum recte in medio pendeat, & æqua omnia librentur lance, serpentina prorsus hanc ad rem opus est prudentia: vt figura declarat. Hoc est Periandri illius Corinthii: quod iusum est imitare. Et Pittacus Mitilenaeus: iuste, inquit, iudicato. Vir iustus simulacrum Dei, inquit Diogenes. Cicero, inquit, primum fundamentum iustitiæ est, ne cui noceatur, deinde communi utilitati seruiatur. Imo Dn. Saluator. Quacunq; vultis vt faciant vobis homines, eadem & vos facietis illis. Seminate iustitiam, &c. Capitales iustitiæ hostes sunt plurimi maximiq;.
units.tr: "Equality," says the Greek, ... Here you see distributive justice ...: distributive justice is that which gives each person his own, free from perverse feelings, bad counsellors, bribes, partiality towards persons, and other crimes that cling to injustice, for the glory of God and the advantage and salvation of good people. This distributive justice has very many commendations, both in sacred and in secular writers. Judge, says the Lord Saviour, true judgement. You shall not respect persons in judgement, nor take bribes; for such things are an abomination to Jehovah. Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes; cease to do evil, learn to do well; seek judgement, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow, etc. This justice [δικαιοσύνη] is most needed in absolutely all estates, so that each person receives according as he has deserved, whether praise or blame, reward or punishment, as the Apostle says: Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour. This tends to the honour of God and conduces to common tranquillity ... to preserve it and to calm minds, so that the plumb-line hangs straight in the middle and all things are weighed on an even scale; for this purpose prudence is altogether required, as the figure shows. This is the saying of Periander of Corinth: what is just, that you should imitate. And Pittacus of Mytilene: judge justly, he says. A just man is an image of God, says Diogenes. Cicero, he says, the first foundation of justice is that no one be harmed; then that common advantage be served. Indeed the Lord Saviour: Whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you even so to them. Sow for yourselves justice, etc. The chief and greatest enemies of justice are very many.

units.la: Acceptio personæ seu Prosopolepsia, quemadmodum Agesilaus Rex ait: Nicia, si non habet iniustam causam, dimitte & absolue. Si vero habet iniustam causam, mea causa dimittere: omnino autem dimitte.
units.tr: Respect of persons, or prosopolepsia, as King Agesilaus said: Nicias, if he has no unjust cause, dismiss him and acquit him. But if he has an unjust cause, dismiss him for my sake; but in any case, dismiss him.

units.la: Acceptio munerum, quæ summa iniustitia est: iustitiæ neruus, à sumendis muneribus super pio ac iusto, abstinere, talis habitabit in mente S. Domini, vt Psaltes ait.
units.tr: Acceptance of bribes, which is the greatest injustice: the sinew of justice is to abstain from taking bribes against the innocent and just; such a man shall dwell in the holy hill of the Lord, as the Psalmist says.

units.la: Temeritas, vis, violentia, quando dicitur: Sic volo, sic iubeo. An nescis, habere mepotestatem tui vel absoluendi, vel condemnandi: adeoq; vel vitæ, vel necis in te? An nescis Imperatorem esse te, leges ferre non pati. Et quæ sunt similia.
units.tr: Rashness, force, violence, when one says: Thus I will, thus I command. Do you not know that I have power over you either to acquit or to condemn, and so over your life or death? Do you not know that you are an emperor, and do not suffer laws to be made? And other things like these.

units.la: Præcipitantia: deliberandum autem diu meminera esse, quod semel iudices, statuasue. In præcipiti furore si quid statueris iuste, iniustum te statuisse vel ad minimum iniustum esse te crede.
units.tr: Precipitancy: remember that what you judge or decide once must be considered at length. If in headlong fury you decide anything rightly, believe that you have decided unjustly, or at least that you are unjust.

units.la: Odium, si condemnes, quem odio habes: non quod iniustam tueatur causam, sed tm q oderis, violentus es & iniustus: affectus mali sunt conciliarij.
units.tr: Hatred: if you condemn the man whom you hate, not because he defends an unjust cause but merely because you hate him, you are violent and unjust: evil passions are counsellors.

units.la: Somnolentia itidem. Quemadmodum Demosthenes (vel, vt volunt alii, Empedocles) somnolentiam suorum scabinorum asinina umbra apologo corrigit: & Machetes prouocat à somnolento Philippo ad expergefactum, & attentum.
units.tr: Drowsiness likewise. As Demosthenes (or, as others will have it, Empedocles) corrected the drowsiness of his jurymen with the fable of the donkey's shadow; and Machetes calls from the drowsy Philip to the wide-awake and attentive one.

units.la: Eadem autem mensura, qua mensus fueris, metientur tibi
units.tr: With the same measure that you mete, it shall be measured to you.
CANDOUR AND TRUTH.

units.la: [woodcut emblem: an engraving with two figures, a staff bearing a banner inscribed FIDES, a sword, a tablet of the Ten Commandments, an arrow, and scales; no printed text beyond the banner word.] Ne pia diuini violes sacraria iuris, Sed clauie vtaris legis ad arbitrium: Candor, & Alma fides, studium SEVERI ac VERI Ornent iudicium, singulaq; acta, tuum. Clauis, iustitiæ; Sagitta, ignoratio veritatis; crux, fidei hieroglyphica intellige, duæ facies denotant candorem ac veritatem. Scopus huius ἐμφλήμματος est, inhibere corrupta iudicia, promouere recta. Clauibus inter alia vtimur ad magnos recludendos thesauros. Maxim9 Thesaurus est iustitia: hanc vt recte administres, quicunq; dicis ius, summopere necessarium est: ne connumereris illis, de quibus Poeta:
units.tr: Do not violate the sacred shrines of divine law, but use the key as the law directs. May candour and kindly faith, zeal for what is stern and true, adorn your judgment and every one of your acts. Key, of justice; Arrow, ignorance of truth; cross, of faith: understand these as hieroglyphs. The two faces denote candour and truth. The aim of this emblem [ἐμφλήμματος] is to restrain corrupt judgments and promote right ones. Among other things, we use keys to unlock great treasures. The greatest treasure is justice, and it is supremely necessary that you administer it rightly, you who pronounce the law, so that you are not counted among those of whom the poet speaks:

units.la: Οἱ βίη ὁ ἀγορὴ σχολιὰς κείνων ὑμιστὰς Ἐκ δὲ δίκην ἰλάλωσι, ἡ δὲ ὁ ἀπὸ αὐτοῦ ἱ ἄλλο ὄντες.
units.tr: Those who by force pervert judgments, [Οἱ βίη ὁ ἀγορὴ σχολιὰς κείνων ὑμιστὰς Ἐκ δὲ δίκην ἰλάλωσι, ἡ δὲ ὁ ἀπὸ αὐτοῦ ἱ ἄλλο ὄντες.]

units.la: Fidelitate cum primis opus est iudici tanquam diuino administro: nā in ministrū non requiritur nisi vt sint fideles. Fideles respiciunt oculi pij magistratus: vt Dauid in Psalmis loquitur. Nec non & seueritate: Verum enim imo verissimum est illud Mimi: Bonis nocet, qui malis parcit. Nota est historia Saulis parcentis Agago regi Amalecitarū, qui perpetuæ propterea internecioni à Deo Opt. Max. deuotus est. Nec ignota illa de Ahabo, parcenti Benhadø Syrorum Regi, id propter à Deo abiecto. Maledictus qui facit opus Dn. fraudulenter, & retinet gladiū, ne effundat sanguinem. Pia seueritas non est crudelitas. Non frustra gladium gerit magistratus, &c. Totus Spartanorum exercitus deletus est propter duorum adolescentum scelus in Seedasi filias patratum: non enim moratur nemesis Adrastia diuina.
units.tr: Above all, a judge needs fidelity, as one who serves God: for in a minister it is required only that they be faithful. The eyes of a godly magistrate look upon the faithful, as David says in the Psalms. Severity is needed too. That saying of Mimus is true, indeed most true: he harms the good who spares the wicked. The story is well known of Saul, who spared Agag, king of the Amalekites, and for this was doomed by God the Best and Greatest to perpetual destruction. Nor is that unknown story of Ahab, who spared Ben-hadad, king of the Syrians, for which he was rejected by God. Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord fraudulently, and withholds his sword from shedding blood. A godly severity is not cruelty. The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain, and so on. The whole army of the Spartans was destroyed because of the crime committed by two young men against the daughters of Seedasus; for divine Nemesis Adrastia does not delay.

units.la: Quare iudices corrumpi se non sinant, sed legitima cognitione praevia veritatem inquirant, quodque iustum est decernant: insontes tueantur: nec maleficis parcāt, sed vt lex quenq; vel absolui vel damnari iubet, ita vel absoluant vel condemnent.
units.tr: Therefore judges must not allow themselves to be corrupted, but after a lawful and prior examination let them seek out the truth and decide what is just. Let them protect the innocent, and let them not spare wrongdoers; but as the law commands each person to be either acquitted or condemned, so let them either acquit or condemn.

units.la: Nemo praeficiatur iurisdictioni, nisi qui scientiam legum habeat & conscientiam, quiq; ius dicere, suumq; cuiq; tribuere velit ac possit ἀνδ ἀκρ-ωπαλήψιας quas pestes Deus exsecratur, & iura Caesarea prohibent ac plectunt.
units.tr: No one should be placed in a judicial office unless he has knowledge of the laws and a conscience, and is willing and able to declare the law and render to each his due; and not one who respects persons [ἀνδ ἀκρ-ωπαλήψιας]. These are the plagues that God abhors, and that the imperial laws forbid and punish.

units.la: Εἰλικρινεια siue candor si vspiam laudabilis est, in iudice certe laudibus ad caelum vsq; est euehendus: estq; muri instar ahenei, non egit Mauri iaculis nec arcu. Recte faciendo neminem timeo, ait ille.
units.tr: Sincerity [εἰλικρινεια] or candour, if it is praiseworthy anywhere, certainly in a judge it must be lifted up to heaven with praise. It is like a bronze wall; he did not drive off the Moor with arrows or bow. "By doing right I fear no one," as that man says.

units.la: Nec minus diuina veritas vtilis simul ac laudabilis est. Veritate stabilitur thronus regis. Quare iudices, vt veraces ipsi sint oportet, ita veritatem, amare & inquirere debent. sunt quiliure dicundo ita ludunt, quemadmodum pueri ludunt astragulis: quemadmodum Dux Albanus vitam Harlemensibus ciuibus stipulatus, fame eos necat, vitam ipsis non victum se promisisse ditans. Et Paisės Ducis Colophonio promittit saluum con: & reductum: sed reducto in vrbem ceruicem demi demetrique iubet. Cruenta haec veritatis laesio est, & candoris, cruentaque calumnia.
units.tr: Divine truth is no less useful than it is praiseworthy. The throne of the king is established by truth. Therefore judges ought to be truthful themselves, and so they ought to love and seek the truth. There are those who in pronouncing law play with it as boys play with knucklebones: as the Duke of Alba, when he had promised the citizens of Haarlem their lives, starved them to death, claiming he had promised them life, not food. And Paeso, the Duke, promised the Colophonians safety and return, but once they were brought back into the city he ordered their necks cut off. This is a bloody violation of truth and of candour, and a bloody calumny.
It is a fine thing to die for one's country.
It is also lawful to resolve upon savage war,
Not otherwise to live safely, when it is permitted:
But let the prudent man first weigh the cause,

units.la: Quæ nisi iusta subest subtrahat arma pudor:
units.tr: Which, unless it is just, let shame withdraw the arms:

units.la: Omnia prius verbis ac sapienti consilio experiri, quam decernere armis, sapientem decet. Verum si aliter non liceat aris focisq; uti integris, non est contra diuina neq; humana iura etiam armis experiri. Pro aris autem & focis, aiunt, quibus duae iuste gerendi belli adsignantur causae: defensio religionis seu fidei: & defensio patriae, bonorum & fortunarum, coniugum, liberorum, & omnium. &c. Alphonsus Rex Neapolitan, in clypeo gestat Pellicanum, sanguinem rostro è pectore elicientem, & mortuos pullos viuificantem, cum inscripto Noemate: PRO LEGE ET PRO GREGE: idem prorsus subindicans.
units.tr: Everything should first be tried with words and wise counsel before deciding by arms; this befits a wise man. But if there is no other way to keep our altars and hearths unharmed, it is not against divine or human law to try arms as well. They say that for altars and hearths two just causes of waging war are assigned: the defence of religion or faith, and the defence of the fatherland, of goods and fortunes, of spouses, of children, and of all else. Alphonsus, King of Naples, bore on his shield a pelican drawing blood from its breast with its beak and bringing its dead chicks back to life, with the motto PRO LEGE ET PRO GREGE, hinting at exactly the same thing.

units.la: Et quidem pro patria ac focis ferro decertandum esse cum sacratum profana abunde comprobant. Pro patria, aiunt, mori gloriosum est. Quanquam & hic summa prudentia opus est: Ne quem tibi hostem vltro accersas, vt fecit Abias Rex Iudae. & Iosias post eum. Neq; nimio furore ad arma praeceps rapiare. Non deponuntur ea facilitate arma qua sumuntur. Quae momento arripueris, per multos fere annos vix deponere, & non nisi cum summo damno liceb[it], vbi defecerit & pecunia & sapientia, quemadmodum sapientiss. Imp. Carol. V olim dicebat. Turrim qui aedificare vult, sumptos praemesos ac praesuppuratos h beat oportet: ideoq; ad arma rapiare caue, si hic te belli neruus destituerit: vel ad arma si raptus es, pacem, quam potes, quaere. Vbi vero & iusto bello peteris occuparisve, velim te nulli parcere sumptu, notu est de Mauritio Imp. qui intempestiua auaritia militem irritauit, & in se, domumq; Imp. totam concitauit, quam non nisi interitu liberorum, coniugis suiq; ipsius piauit. De Constantino Palaeologo extremo Orientis Imp. ferut, quod propter nimiam tenacitatem Vibem nec stario praesidio nudarit, ac tandem amiserit, cum perpetuo & Imperatorii numinis in Oriente & Christiani nominis dedecore ac damno.
units.tr: Indeed, that one must fight with the sword for fatherland and hearths is amply proved by sacred and profane examples alike. For one's country, they say, it is glorious to die. Yet even here great prudence is needed: do not invite an enemy upon yourself unprompted, as Abijah, king of Judah, did, and Josiah after him. Nor should you be rushed headlong to arms by excessive fury. Arms are not laid down with the same ease with which they are taken up. What you seize in a moment you can scarcely lay down again for many years, and it will not be done except at great cost, when both money and wisdom have run out, as the most wise Emperor Charles V used to say. Whoever wants to build a tower must first have the costs measured out and laid by; so beware of taking up arms in haste, lest the sinews of war fail you there; and if you have been swept into arms, seek peace as far as you can. But when you are going to seek or seize something in a just war, I would have you spare no expense. It is well known of Maurice, Emperor, that by untimely avarice he provoked his soldiers and roused the whole imperial household against himself, and he atoned for this only with the death of his children, his wife and himself. It is said of Constantine Palaeologus, the last emperor of the East, that because of excessive thrift he stripped the city of a standing garrison, and at last lost it, to the lasting dishonour and loss both of the imperial majesty in the East and of the Christian name.

units.la: Pacta etiam ac foedera de induciis aliisque rebus vtilibus, necessariis bonis & honestis etiam hosti seruabis: Magna nominis decessione labor at Card. Iulian. qui Ladislao suaserit, foedus frangendum cum Amurathe Turcorum ictum.
units.tr: You will also keep pacts and treaties concerning truces and other useful matters, which are good and honourable, even with an enemy. Cardinal Julian laboured under a great loss of reputation, for he advised Ladislaus to break the treaty struck with Amurath, the Turkish ruler.

units.la: Pro religione ac fide an arma sumenda sint, quaesitum est, & in vtrāq; partem disputatum; Videtur autem quod sic: Ex loco Israelitarum qui ob probabilem laesi religionis suspicionem copias coegerunt contra fratres. Quod & Maccabai factitarunt. Et Imper. Constantinus Magnus Christianis propter religionem patientibus contra sex tyrannos Diocletianum, Maximianum, Galerium, Maxentium, Maximin. & Licinium suppetias tulit, & Christianos in libertatem vindicauit. Quae in contrariam partem oggeruntur non est loci huius refutare.
units.tr: Whether arms should be taken up for religion and faith has been asked and disputed on both sides. It seems that they should, from the example of the Israelites, who, on a probable suspicion that religion was harmed, gathered forces against their brothers. The Maccabees also did this. And the Emperor Constantine the Great, when Christians were suffering for their religion, brought aid against six tyrants, Diocletian, Maximian, Galerius, Maxentius, Maximin and Licinius, and vindicated the Christians into liberty. It is not the place here to refute the arguments brought against this.
To fight with a silver spear.

units.la: [woodcut emblem: a halberd with sword, two hands, scales, money bags and an inkstand with quills] Ærea piscaris munuscula, & aurea præstas, Quantæ id (crede mihi) est fatuitatis opus. Munera captantes, eadem quoq; munera dantes, Hos turpes simili crimine vtrosq; puta!
units.tr: [woodcut emblem: a halberd with sword, two hands, scales, money bags and an inkstand with quills] You offer bronze and gold gifts to fishermen, and believe me, that is a work of great folly. You who seek gifts and you who give gifts alike, consider both of them base, guilty of the same crime!

units.la: Vtilissimum instrumentum est bipennis, ad configendum simul ac percutiendum, ad trahendum æque atq; amoliendum coducibile, sed pe-nes vtentem est eius vsus & arbitrium; vt bene vel male adhibeatur, cadatque. Huic nostrum ἐμέλησε comparatius sive forum, sive instrumenta iustitiæ, bona ea per se & vtilia, sed male à multis vsurpantur, qui LL. figūt, refigunt; torquent ac retorquēt, put ipsis volupe, atq; crumenę proficuū fore colligere possunt, nulla Dei, propriæq; & conscientiæ ac famæ ratione ducti. Magna huius seculi labes ac profanitas, vt non immerito vulgus luristarum (quos vocant) male audiat, iam inde à multis annorum centenariis. Fit autem istud quacunque acceptione vel personarum vel munerum: qua de re pernitiosissima multa hactenus: & constat illicitum id esse ex iure
units.tr: The bipennis (double-headed axe) is a most useful tool: it serves to pierce and strike, and to pull or push away equally well. But its use and judgment rest with the one who wields it, so that it may be applied well or badly and fall accordingly. Our care [ἐμέλησε] applies in the same way to the forum and to the instruments of justice, which are good and useful in themselves, but are misused by many who fix and unfix the laws, twist and turn them, so that they can gather profit for themselves and money for their purse, guided by no regard for God, for their own honour, conscience or reputation. This is a great blemish and profanity of this age, so that the crowd of lawyers (as they are called) rightly has a bad name, and this has been so for many centuries. This happens under any kind of pretext, whether of persons or of gifts, a matter on which much very harmful material has been written hitherto; and it is clear that this is unlawful by the law

units.la: Diuino. Ne suscipias personam in Iudicio, neq; captes munera, sunt enim hæc abominatio coram Deo.
units.tr: of God. Thou shalt not respect persons in judgment, neither shalt thou take gifts, for these are an abomination before God.

units.la: Canonico. Non debet (inquit) Iudex vendere iustum iudicium, aut testis verum testimonium. Cum autem iudicia & testimonia quæ nec iusta nec vera vendenda sunt, iniqua & falsa venduntur, multo sceleratius vtiq; pecunia sumitur, quia sceleratè sumitur, licet à volentibus detur, &c.
units.tr: Of canon law. A judge (he says) ought not to sell a just judgment, nor a witness a true testimony. Since judgments and testimonies, which ought not to be sold whether just or true, are sold unjust and false, the money is taken all the more wickedly, because it is taken wickedly, even if it is given by those who are willing, etc.

units.la: Ciuili. Vt in l. plebiscito. ff. de offic. præsid. &c: in authentic. §. Quapropter in sin. col. 2. iuxta textum in c. summopere. 11. qu. 3. quæ posteriora ad ius canonicum pertinent. vid. nouell.
units.tr: Of civil law. As in the law Plebiscito, Digest, on the office of the governor, etc.; in the authentic Quapropter, at the end, column 2, following the text in the chapter Summopere, 11 q. 3; those later ones pertain to canon law. See the Novels.

units.la: Naturali. Ex lumine iuris naturæ scit Cambyses ὑποφαγίαν esse prohibitam. Ex eodem detestatur Poeta, aliud q. agendo
units.tr: Of natural law. By the light of natural law Cambyses knew that bribery [ὑποφαγίαν] was forbidden. By the same law the poet also condemns doing the opposite:
Believe me, gifts placate both men and gods,
and Jupiter himself is placated by gifts given.

units.la: Quare significanter admodum Thebani seu Athenienses suos iudices pinxerunt simulacra quædam ante altaria Deorum sedentia, omnia manibus truncatis, præter supremum, manibus quidem integrum, sed oculis captum. Vnde præclare Alciatus:
units.tr: Accordingly, the Thebans or the Athenians very significantly pictured their judges as certain statues sitting before the altars of the gods, all with their hands cut off except the foremost, which had its hands whole but its eyes blinded. Whence Alciato aptly says:

units.la: Effigies manibus trunca ante altaria Diuum Hic residént, quarum lumine capta prior: Sic næ potestatis summa, sanctiq; senatus, Thebanis fuerant ista reperta viris: Cur resident? quia mente graues decet esse quieta Iuridicos, animo nec variare leui: Cur sine sunt manibus? apiant ne Xenia, necsé Pollicitis flecti munera bis sine sinant: Cæcus adest Princeps, quod solis auribus absq; Affectu, constans iussa senatus agit.
units.tr: Figures with maimed hands sit here before the altars of the gods, and the first of them is blind in its sight. Thus the highest power and the holy senate were devised by the Theban men. Why do they sit? Because judges ought to be grave and quiet in mind, not changing with light spirit. Why are they without hands? So that they may not seize gifts, and may not let gifts bend them twice by promises. The Prince is blind, so that he acts upon the decrees of the senate, steadfast, with ears alone and without feeling.
With time and manner.

units.la: Quisquis es in speculo tanquam tua discute facta: Et quid te deceat, dispice, quidue minus; Censorem alterius nunquam tu te oggere labis, Quin prius explores singula quæq; tua.
units.tr: Whoever you are, examine your deeds as if in a mirror, and see what befits you and what less so. Never set yourself up as a censor of another's fault before you have first searched out each of your own.

units.la: Tria Prudentiæ Hieroglyphica in vno & breui hoc vides Emblemate,Gallum,speculum, & Serpentem. Temporis rationem si ducendam cum in verbis tum in factis,monent. Serpentinam prudentiam ipse Dominus comendat in Euangelio. Prudentissimus autem, h. e. astutissimus bestiarum omnium ita dictus est serpens (inquit Augustinus) propter astuciam diaboli, qui illo & de illo ages- bat dolum. Serpens prudentissime cauet, ne vulnus capiat in capite, quare gyros torquet, fibula edit, & quoque modo potest se defendit. Gallus temporis horologus est, quod intelligentia (inquit Gregor.) accepit, vt prius nocturni temporis horas discutiat, & tunc demum voces ex itatione emittat. Pretiosissima certe temporis iactura est,fugit irreuocabile tempus, ars longa vita breuis, quare, quam accuratissima potest, eius habenda est ratio, vt nefine linea, quod aiunt, prætereat. Nam etiam minutissimi temporis acti, vel momenti, reddeda olim ratio erit. Serutte tempori, ait Apostolus, quoniam mali dies. Multus & grauis est Bernhardus in temporis subducenda ratione.
units.tr: In this one short emblem you see three hieroglyphs of prudence: the cock, the mirror and the serpent. They advise that the reckoning of time be taken into account both in words and in deeds. The Lord himself commends serpent-like prudence in the Gospel. The serpent is called most prudent, that is, the most crafty of all beasts (says Augustine), on account of the craft of the devil, who carried out and worked his deceit through it. The serpent, most prudently, takes care lest it receive a wound on its head, so it twists in coils, hides its face, and defends itself in whatever way it can. The cock is the clock of time, which (says Gregory) it understood, so that it first shakes off the hours of the night and only then sends out its voice in the morning. Certainly the loss of time is most costly: time flies never to return, art is long and life is short; so the reckoning of time must be kept as carefully as possible, so that, as they say, no day passes without a line. For even the smallest moment or instant of past time will one day have to be accounted for. Redeem the time, says the Apostle, because the days are evil. Bernard is long and weighty on the reckoning of time.

units.la: Serpentis aliam adfert Augustin.: Quemadmodum (inquit) serpentu quoddam genus, cum it ad bibendum, priusquam ad fontem venit, omne venenum euomit: ita Christianus cum adorandum accedit omnem iracundiam & odium proximi deponat.
units.tr: Augustine brings forward another image from the serpent: Just as a certain kind of serpent, when it goes to drink, before it reaches the spring, spits out all its venom, so the Christian, when he approaches to worship, ought to lay aside all anger and hatred toward his neighbour.

units.la: Seruit etiam Gallus considerationi proprię nostræ, infirmitatis, & ad labendum pronitatis, monetq; eo mitius de proximi nequis sentire, statuere, ac loqui, nam cum edere cantus parat, (verba sunt D.Greg. Magni Epist. Romani) prius alas soluerter excutit, & semetipsum feriens, vigilantiorem reddit: ita pii sese in sanctis actionibus exercent, ne in semetipsis torpentes opere, alios excitent voce, sed ante se per sublimia facta excutiunt. Et tunc ad bene agendum alios sollicitos reddunt.
units.tr: The cock also serves our consideration of our own weakness and proneness to falling, and warns us to think, decide and speak more gently about our neighbour's faults. For when it prepares to sing (these are the words of St Gregory the Great's letter to the Romans), first it shakes its wings and, striking itself, makes itself more watchful. So the godly exercise themselves in holy actions, so that, sluggish in their own works, they do not rouse others by voice, but first shake themselves by lofty deeds. And then they make others anxious to act well.

units.la: Singularis ac rarae prudentiae ac pietatis opus est à se ipso censuram eiusque initium facere, nam iustus est accusator sui ipsius. Tanto laudabilius, quanto grauius exerceturillud γνῶθι σεαυτόν. Sculpi non scribi istud vbiq; conueniebat, quemadmodum Ausonius: Commendo nostrum γνῶθι σεαυτόν nosce te Quod in columna iam tenetur Delphica.
units.tr: It is a singular and rare work of prudence and piety to begin censure with oneself, for the just man is his own accuser. It is all the more praiseworthy the more earnestly one practises that know yourself [γνῶθι σεαυτόν]. It was fitting that this saying be carved everywhere, not written, as Ausonius has it: I commend our "know yourself" [γνῶθι σεαυτόν], which is already held on the Delphic column.

units.la: Plerumq; fieri solet vt non videamus id mantica quod in tergo est,eoq; confidentius iudicamus proximum: sed facile ab altero abstinet iudicando, qui sua facta dictaque recolit. Pessimæ indolis est, & hominis inuidi indicium atque vani, qui alios iudicat se non iudicat nec excutit.
units.tr: It often happens that we do not see the bag that is on our back, and so we judge our neighbour the more confidently. But one who recalls his own deeds and words will easily refrain from judging another. It is a sign of a wicked disposition and of an envious and vain man to judge others and not to judge and examine himself.

units.la: ὑψοῦ αὐ κρατησρίας γοῦς φθονερὸς. Sed de hoc infra.
units.tr: A man envious of those raised on high [ὑψοῦ αὐ κρατησρίας γοῦς φθονερὸς]. But of this more below.
LAW IN THE HANDS

units.la: [engraving: a lit candle on a tripod stand, a hand holding a balance with scales, a hand holding a sword, dice and playing cards on a table; no text] Flos vt odorus api mel præbet, lurida fella Ex quo sed contra toxica arachna bibit: Haud secus ex diuo probus haurit iure salutem, Per quod & iniustus iusta barathra subit.
units.tr: As the flower offers the bee both fragrant honey and bitter gall, yet the spider drinks poison from the same blossom, so the upright man draws health from the divine law, while the unjust man enters through the same law into deserved ruin.

units.la: Compedes aculeum semper erectum gerentes, iuris gerunt figuram, quod semper idem manet atq; æquabile, tametsi petulanter admodum à multis figatur, refigatur, & instar astragalorum, chartarumq; tractetur, quod scurrarum, mimorum, histrionum, & similium huius manipuli futurum est. Non secus ac cereus nasus ab aureis & auaris iuristis (quos vocant) torquetur. fitque adeo illis ipsis ius, & administratio iustitiae iniusta instar aurearum compedum, quibus ipsi laeduntur. Vt optimo in tales iure ludere liceat, quemadmodum mordax in coaeraneum Aristippum Diogenes; aureis eos compedibus infoliotenderi, ne avolare possint. Nemo autem sine laesione in compedes impingit, ita nec sine damno tales ius peruertent, sed sequetur illos hoc infamia, mala conscientia, & iustum odium, isthic autem iusta condemnatio. Ius hic iniuste dispensant, quare à iustissimo Deo haud iniuste aliquando iudicabuntur: Durum autem erit illis vt ad Saulum Dominus Seruator ait Iniusti non possidebunt regnum coelorum. Ne fallamini, Deus non irridetur. Risus vobis, ô boni, fiunt hic pauperes, presbyteri, sacerdotes, ministri, viduæ, orphani: ridebit & vos aliquando Deus, Angeli ridebunt, & subsannabit totus Electorum exercitus, Deus videt, Deus odit, Deus punit. Gladius iustitiae, quem pro lubitu versastis, vibrastis, torsistis, in vos ac viscera vestra conuertetur. Salua ac immota stabit iustitia maceries, sed vestra volus, quibus impingitis, capita diminuet, vt media crepent. Lapis offendiculi super vos cadet, qui comminuet fustatim. Compedes, quas pauperi ac derelicto iacitis, vestros vobis ipsis pedes confodient. Si non hic est qui vos excoriet Cambyses, at erit isthic qui vos iudicet atq; condemnet Deus. Via est vobis ius, quæ vestra vos iniustitia atq; culpa ad inferos ducit. Canis rabiosus est, cuius veneno certo occumbetis, nisi resipueritis. Quare in auribus vestris semper sonet illud Dauidicum: Quoniam iudicabitis iniquè, & personam impiorum suscipietis: summe. Iudicate tenuem & pupillum, afflictum & pauperem iustum pronunciate. Liberate tenuem, & egentem e manu improborum eripite. Ego dico, Dii quidem estis & filij excelsi omnes: At certe, vt plebeius homo moriuri estis, etiam sicut unus aliorum principum casuri estis. Potentes potenter patientur tormenta.
units.tr: Fetters, always holding their sharp point upright, represent the figure of law, which remains always the same and even-handed, although many handle it wantonly, fix it and unfix it, and toss it about like knucklebones and playing cards, as jesters, mimes, actors and others of this crew will do. Just so the wax nose is twisted by the so-called golden and greedy lawyers. Thus the law itself, and the administration of justice, becomes for them an unjust thing, like golden fetters, by which they themselves are harmed. Let the best of men be allowed to make sport of such law, as Diogenes, biting at his contemporary Aristippus, did: they are shackled in golden fetters so that they cannot fly away. No one steps into fetters without injury, and so such men who pervert the law do not do so without loss. Infamy, a guilty conscience and just hatred will follow them, and there, in the world to come, a just condemnation. They deal unjustly with the law here, and so the most just God will sometimes judge them not unjustly. It will be hard for them, as the Lord and Saviour said to Saul: The unjust shall not possess the kingdom of heaven. Do not be deceived, God is not mocked. Here the poor, the elders, the priests, the ministers, the widows and the orphans are a laughing-stock to you, good sirs; but God will one day laugh at you too, the angels will laugh, and the whole army of the elect will mock you: God sees, God hates, God punishes. The sword of justice, which you have wielded, brandished and twisted at your pleasure, will turn against you and your vitals. The wall of justice stands safe and unmoved, but the stone of stumbling, against which you dash, will break your heads so that your brains burst out. The stone of offence will fall upon you and grind you to dust. The fetters you cast upon the poor and forsaken will pierce your own feet. If no Cambyses flays you here, there will be God there to judge and condemn you. The law is a road for you which, by your own injustice and fault, leads down to hell. It is a mad dog, and you will perish by its certain poison unless you repent. Therefore let that Davidic word always sound in your ears: Since you judge unjustly and accept the persons of the wicked, mark this: judge the lowly and the fatherless, do justice to the afflicted and the poor. Deliver the lowly and the needy, rescue them from the hand of the wicked. I say, you are indeed gods and all sons of the Most High: yet surely, like a common man, you shall die, and fall like any one of the other princes. The powerful will suffer mighty torments.
PATIENCE CONQUERS ALL THINGS.

units.la: Disce sed ex verbo mentem firmare Iehouæ, Rebus in aduersis rupis vt instar ouet: Grata Deo nulla est patientia, quam nisi firmet Ex verbo diuus Spiritus ille suo.
units.tr: Learn from the Word to fix your mind on Jehovah, to stand like a sheep upon the rock in adversity. No patience pleases God unless the divine Spirit confirms it by his own Word.

units.la: Varie & infirmis admodum rationum fundamentis prudentiores Philosophorum Gentilium labores ac ærumnas huius æui solati sunt, vt quod necesse sit feras, quæ non possis mutare. Patientiam talem esse virtutem, quæ dolori longe anteponenda sit. Exemplis fulti collationeq; euentuum: & si quæ sunt similia. Sed nimis arida hæc fuerunt, vt in exitu videre fuit.
units.tr: The wiser philosophers of the Gentiles consoled the labours and hardships of this age in various ways, and on very weak foundations of argument, by teaching that one must bear what one cannot change.
