They held that patience is a virtue to be placed far above pain. They supported this with examples, comparisons of outcomes, and similar arguments. But these were too dry, as the outcome showed.

units.la: Sola religio Christiana, & purum putum Dei verbum solida fundamenta consolationum submi-nistrat, quibus cor fidele rebus in incertis atque adhuc ætis niti ac saluari potest. Voluntatem diuinam, cui necesse est obedire, respicere patiens ante omnia debet ac potest. Habet autem Deus causas, cur suos premi in hoc æuo atq; discruciari permittit. Liberrimum agens est, & potestatem habet facere de suo quod vult, neq; est quod dicat lutum factori suo: cur me talem fecisti; Habet vitæ simul atq; necis in nos ius, & voluntati ipsius refragari nephas. Ita autem decretum est apud ipsum vt vel probet vel castiget: & fauillas fidei, spei, patientiæ, humilitatis, inuocationis exsuscitet, moueat, augeat, vt in magna incendia Amoris exardescant. Vultnos conformes fieri imagini filij sui tum patientia & exaltatione. Hæc autem omnia non nisi ex solo ac solido diuino verbo addiscuntur, vides igitur agnum libro verbi insistere: Verbum autem immotaæ rupi imponitur. Rupes Christus est: qui verbi est scopus, hoc est vtriusq; testamenti caput: nam ei omnes Prophetæ testimonium perhibent: propter Christum patiens abnegat semetipsum, suscollit crucem suam & sequitur ipsum. Inde certam spem gerit corona immarcescibilis vitæ atq; gloriæ. Patientia enim corona sanctorum est. Premitur patiens à mundo iuxta quod dictum à Seruatore: In(a)mundo pressuram habetis: Lupus ail gat agnum turbatæ aquæ: Sed iustus nititur fide & bonæ conscientiæ testimonio. Estq; aliquid magnum crimen abesse malum. Et sustentat se breuitate horæ, qua sunt finienda huius æui mala: vt Sapores Persa seni Ananiæ. Claudemo mentum oculos. Et patiêter expectat mortem, quæ gloriosa simul ac pretiosa est in conspectu Dei, finis malorum, atq; vitæ ianua. Sed & considerat fragilitatem honorum, opum, & omnium eorum, quæ in aliqua existimatione sunt in seculo isthoc, non obliti istius Apostolici: Πεχομανα τολμωσ... Inprimis autem copiosam mercedem in cœlis repositam: Cum momentanea leuitas afflictionis æternum pondus gloriæ pariat: disperuntibus improbis, oforibus, liuidis, instar fumi diplofis, & dicunt cum Propheta, imo cum Ecclesia: Iram Domini portabo, quoniam peccaui ei, vsque dum contendat contentionem meam, & exerceat ius meum: producens me in lucem, vt fruar iustitia eius.
units.tr: The Christian religion alone, and the pure Word of God alone, provides solid foundations of consolation, on which a faithful heart can rest and be saved amid uncertain and still unsettled circumstances. The patient person ought above all, and is able, to regard the divine will, to which one must submit. God has reasons for allowing his people to be oppressed and tormented in this age. He is the most free agent, and has power to do with his own what he wills, nor is there anything that the clay may say to its maker: why did you make me thus? He has the right of life and death over us, and it is impious to resist his will. It is decreed by him so that he may either prove or chasten us, and he may stir up, move and increase the sparks of faith, hope, patience, humility and invocation, so that they may blaze into a great fire of love. That we should be made conformable to the image of his Son, both in patience and in exaltation. All these things are learned only from the solid and sure divine Word. You see, therefore, that the lamb stands upon the book of the Word, and the Word is laid upon the immovable rock. The rock is Christ, who is the goal of the Word, that is, the head of both Testaments, for all the prophets bear witness to him. For Christ's sake the patient person denies himself, takes up his cross and follows him. From this he has the sure hope of the unfading crown of life and glory, for patience is the crown of the saints. The patient person is oppressed by the world, according to the saying of the Saviour: In the world you have tribulation. The wolf seizes the lamb in troubled waters. But the righteous man rests on faith and the testimony of a good conscience, and it is a great thing not to have a bad crime. He sustains himself by the brevity of the hour in which the evils of this age must end, as Sapor the Persian did with the old man Ananias. I close my eyes. And he patiently awaits death, which is glorious and at the same time precious in the sight of God, the end of evils and the gate of life. He also considers the frailty of honours, wealth, and all those things that are held in esteem in this world, not forgetting that Apostolic saying [Πεχομανα τολμωσ...]. Above all, he considers the abundant reward laid up in heaven, since the momentary lightness of affliction produces an eternal weight of glory. The wicked perish, the proud, the envious and the malicious perish like smoke that dissolves, and he says with the Prophet, indeed with the Church: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes my judgment, bringing me forth into the light, that I may enjoy his righteousness.
Do Not Stir Up the Common People

units.la: [Woodcut: owl perched on a column with scales, city and fields behind; not transcribed as text.] Quæritur immani nece cur perit hicce vel ille?: In promptu causa est: seditiosus erat. Crede, magistratus frustra non promicat ense: Disperiit, qui vnquam seditiosus erat.
units.tr: [Woodcut: owl perched on a column with scales, city and fields behind; not transcribed as text.] One asks why this man or that perished by a savage death. The cause is at hand: he was a seditious man. Believe me, the magistrate does not draw the sword in vain. He has perished who was ever a seditious man.
The Owl

units.la: Nocturnam seditionis ac seditiosorum faciunt hieroglyphicum. Est autem se-
units.tr: They make the night owl the hieroglyph of sedition and of seditious men. Now sedi-

units.la: ditio non tantum resistere ac repugnare ordinario atq; legitimo magistratui in rebus divinis atq; licitis, sed etiam alios in societatem perditissimi huius criminis adlegere, & ipso opere crimen committere laesa maiestatis. Turpissimum & exsecrandum hoc est crimen, & tam in sacris quam in prophanis meritissime damnatum. Sicut dicitur: Nefis seditiosus, neq; cum tumultuante plebe commiscetor. Et nota sunt exempla seditiosorum pessimo semper letho extinctorum. Horrendum sane quod de Coraho, Dathane, atq; Abirone legitur, est, qui cum tabernaculis, uxoribus, liberis, pecoribus, iumentis, & omnibus viui in infernum descenderunt. Simri seditiosus & alii male perierunt. Seba interiit. Iudai aduersum ordinarium Magistratum Romanum seditiosi decantatissimum punitae seditionis atq; rebellionis exemplum nobis reliquerunt: quid dicam de Catilina? quid de Cassio, Bruto, & scelecтis aliis coniuratoribus? Quemadmodum noctua no-
units.tr: Sedition is not merely to resist and oppose the ordinary and lawful magistrate in matters that are divine and lawful, but also to draw others into partnership in this most desperate crime, and to commit the crime of treason by the very deed. This is a most shameful and accursed crime, and it is rightly condemned both in sacred and in secular affairs. As it is said: A seditious man, do not mix with a people in uproar. The examples of seditious men destroyed by the worst kind of death are well known. Truly dreadful is what is read of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who went down alive into hell with their tents, their wives, children, flocks, beasts of burden, and all their goods. Zimri, a seditious man, and others perished miserably. Sheba perished. The Jews against the ordinary Roman magistrate left us the most famous example of punished sedition and rebellion. What shall I say of Catiline? What of Cassius, Brutus, and the other wicked conspirators? Just as the owl misuses the darkness of night for its flight and for uttering its seditious cry, so they too scattered their libels in the dark, by which they urged one another to dare the most seditious and detestable parricide. This is still today the habit of seditious men: to plot in secret and to devise mischief. For whoever…

units.la: ctis tenebris ad suum volatum, seditiosamq; aedendam vocem abutitur: ita & illi in tenebris suas eiaculabantur schedulas, quibus sese mutuo ad audendum seditiosissimum & detestabilissimum parricidium exhortati sunt, qui adhuc hodie seditiosorum mos est, clam machinari, malumque architectari, nam qui mala agit, odit lucem, eamq; fugit, sicutes opera sua a luce arguipropalat. Capitalis etiam poena, eaq; gravissima LL. statuta est seditiosis. Docentque exempla, nunquam cuiuspiam vspiam seditiosi felices fuisse exitus. Videatur Valer.Maxim.lib.non.capit.septim. Nec hodienum moratur Adrasteia iustissima Iehouae contra mouentes plebem, & concitantes seditionem, ut exempla recentia in Galliis. Anglia. nec non & Germania nostra luculenter testantur. Hoc non semel ex bonis audierunt boni: Nunquam vidi bona exitum morte, qui cum ordinario ac legitimo magistratu seditiose contenderit. Nondum B. Augustus seditionis originem ad ipsum Sathanam referre: Vitium, inquit, malum, (seditio) vitium primum! Primus enim homo dominari voluit, dominum habere noluit. Et alibi bestias immanitate superare scribit idem: Contemptor gloriae, Dominationis est auidus, bestias superat, sine crudelitate vita, sine fluxu luxuriae. vid. Alexandr. ab Alexand. in Genialibus diebus.
units.tr: Like the owl that abuses the dark nights for its flight and for raising its seditious cry, so these men scattered their pamphlets in the dark, by which they urged one another to dare the most seditious and detestable parricide. This is still the habit of seditious men today: they plot in secret and devise mischief. For everyone who does evil hates the light and shuns it, lest his works be exposed by the light. The law also lays down the gravest capital punishment for sedition. Examples teach that seditious men have never had a happy outcome anywhere. See Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 7. Nor does the most just Adrasteia of Jehovah, which punishes those who stir up the people and incite sedition, delay even now, as recent examples in France, England and our own Germany clearly attest. Good men have often heard from good men: I have never seen good men come to a good end who have contended seditiously against a lawful and legitimate magistrate. Blessed Augustine traced the origin of sedition to Satan himself: Sedition, he says, is an evil, a first vice! For the first man wished to rule and did not want to have a master. And elsewhere the same writer says that the seditious man surpasses beasts in savagery: the despiser of glory is greedy for domination, he surpasses the beasts, his life is without cruelty but also without the flow of luxury. See Alexander ab Alexandro, in the Genial Days.
You shall swear and you shall keep (it).

units.la: Μηδ' ἐπιορκήσεις, μητ' ἀγνῶς, μηδὲ ἐκῶν πῃ Phocylidis vatis pagina scripta docet. Nam miser est quisquis temere periuria fundit, Cum veniat tacitis poena frequens pedibus. Iuramenta semper religiosa habita sunt, etiam à vanis ac profanis ethnicis. Nulla enim gens vnquam tam rudis tamq; barbara fuit, quin crediderit esse Deum, eumq; cum timore Θεοῦ venerandum. Quare etiam iuramenta quæ contestationes sunt diuini numinis, non potuerunt non in summa veneratione haberi. Quare etiam omnibus atq; singulis fidelibus iuramenta licere, imo pro re nata incumbere, æquum & liquidum est. Possunt & debent persona Ecclesiastica iurare, se pro ea facultate, quam diuinus suggerit Spiritus fidelíter administraturos officium, acuendo legem, docendo Euangelium, præstare obedientiam & fidelitatem in rebus diuinis, licitis atq; honestis. Itidem & magistratus, huiusq; locum tenentes, & officiarii, se ius dispensaturos recte & absq; respectu vel personarum vel munerum. Omnes deniq; quibus iuramentum præstandum legitime offertur vel imponitur: Iurandum a est & Deo & per Deum. Iurandum quoq; hominibus per Deum, sed non per homines neq; per vllam rem aliam creatā extra ac præter Deum: Nam Per nomen, inquit Propheta: Iurabis in veritate, in iustitia, in iudicio, &c. Quod enim Dn. Saluator ait: Omnino non iuretis, istud de temerariis peierationibus accipiendum esse, nemo pius negauerit. Ideoq; & ea, quæ pie, legitimeq; iurata sunt, omnino seruanda esse iura omnia manifeste clamant. Ea autem pia & legitima iuramenta sunt, quæ fiunt secundum verbum Dei, de rebus piis, honestis, licitis, possibilibus, &c. inq; iurantium potestate existentibus: secus non sunt legitima, neque etiam seruanda: Præstaret autem omnino non fieri talia iuramenta, quam facta rescindi. Verum si facta, sine impietate vel scelere compleri non possint, præstat rescindi quam seruari. Vota enim atque iuramenta non debent esse vincula iniquitatis: neq; obligant tenentur ad impossibilia, inhonestaq;, vel contra Deum contraq; communem honestatem militantia. Rescindere poterat paterfamilias filiæ suæ incautum votum. Stulte simul atque impie sustulit filiā Iephthes, siquidem Holocautomatis vice sustulit. Impie ac stulte Saul filiū Ionathanem ad mortem poscit. Impie Baptista necat Antipas: Rectius Hippolytus: lingua iuraui, mentem iniuratam tento. In malu paētis rescinde fidem inquit Isidorus, &c. Si quid autem iurasti, id vt seruet, summa ope nitere. Extremæ impietatis est, legitime iurata infringere, & Deum falsi testem facere, quod omnium ordinum homines hodie frequenter faciunt, & non minori impietate quam leuitate. Inprimis autem in iudicio attendendum, ne quid tale committatur, vel iuramentis ludatur, maxime per magistratum.
units.tr: Do not swear falsely, nor deceitfully, nor knowingly in any way [Μηδ' ἐπιορκήσεις, μητ' ἀγνῶς, μηδὲ ἐκῶν πῃ], as the page of the poet Phocylides teaches. For wretched is whoever rashly pours out perjuries, since punishment often comes on silent feet. Oaths have always been regarded as sacred, even among the vain and profane heathen. For no nation was ever so rude and barbarous that it did not believe there is a God, and that he is to be revered with the fear of God [Θεοῦ]. Therefore oaths, which are appeals to the divine power, could not but be held in the highest reverence. Hence it is fair and clear that oaths may be taken by all and each of the faithful, and indeed should be undertaken when the occasion arises. Ecclesiastical persons may and must swear that they will faithfully discharge their office, as far as that ability which the divine Spirit supplies allows: sharpening the law, teaching the Gospel, and rendering obedience and fidelity in divine matters that are lawful and honourable. Likewise the magistrates, and those who hold their place, and officials, swear that they will administer justice rightly and without regard to persons or offices. Finally, all to whom an oath is legitimately offered or imposed must swear by God and through God. One must also swear to men through God, but not through men, nor through any other created thing outside or beside God. For the prophet says: "In the name" of the Lord "you shall swear in truth, in justice, in judgment, etc." As for the Lord Saviour's words, "Swear not at all," no pious person will deny that they must be understood of rash perjuries. Hence all lawful oaths that have been sworn piously and legitimately clearly cry out that they must be kept in full. Those oaths are pious and lawful which are made according to the word of God, concerning things that are pious, honourable, lawful, possible, and so on, and which lie within the power of those swearing; otherwise they are neither lawful nor to be kept. Yet it would be far better that such oaths were never made than that they were broken once made. But if what has been sworn cannot be fulfilled without impiety or wickedness, it is better to annul it than to keep it. For vows and oaths ought not to be chains of iniquity; nor are people bound to what is impossible, dishonourable, or opposed to God and common decency. A father of a household could have annulled his daughter's rash vow. Jephthah foolishly and impiously sacrificed his daughter, since he offered her in place of a burnt offering. Saul impiously and foolishly demanded the death of Jonathan his son. Herod Antipas impiously put the Baptist to death. More rightly Hippolytus said: "I have sworn with my tongue, but I try to keep my mind unsworn." Isidore says, "Break faith in an evil pact," and so on. But if you have sworn anything, strive with all your might that you keep it. It is the utmost impiety to break lawfully sworn oaths and to make God a false witness, which men of every rank do frequently today, with no less impiety than levity. Above all, in judicial matters one must take care that nothing of this sort is committed, or that oaths are not trifled with, especially by the magistrate.

units.la: Ecclesiastici. 2. Tim. 4. v. 1. Paulus sapiss. Secularet. Idiota. Exod 20. v. 7. Levit. 19. v. 12. Ierem. 4. v. 2. Matt. 5. v. 34. Qualia iuramenta. Vid. Aug. de verb. B. Ap. Iacob. serm. 30. Num. 30. v. 4. Iudic. 11. v. 39. 1. Sam. 14. Matt 14. Exir. XXII. 9. 2. late. Nostrum fo-tum.
units.tr: Ecclesiasticus. 2 Tim. 4 v. 1. Paul very often. Secular. Layman. Exod. 20 v. 7. Lev. 19 v. 12. Jer. 4 v. 2. Matt. 5 v. 34. Kinds of oaths. See Augustine, on the words of the blessed Apostle James, sermon 30. Num. 30 v. 4. Judg. 11 v. 39. 1 Sam. 14. Matt. 14. Exod. 22 v. 9. 2 late. Our own forum.
EMBLEM: NOT TO RESIST THE WINDS [Μὴ τ' ἀντιγνώειν ἀνέμοισιν].

units.la: [woodcut emblem: a globe-shaped ship's hull with a column topped by a cockerel, two banners reading FIDES and IVSTITIA, a sun, a town on a hill, and a winged figure at a steering oar in rough sea] Temporibus, siquidem sapias, seruire memento, Atq; malos noris seculi adesse dies. Ut refles ventis, caueas, polypiq; teneto Mentem, qui quœuis saxa colore refert.
units.tr: If you are wise, remember to serve the times, and know that evil days of this age are at hand. So that you may bend with the winds and avoid them, hold to a mind like the polyp, which takes on the colour of any rock.

units.la: Nauigium, quod vides, statum, conditionem qi huius aeui tibi figurat, in quo Diabolus, horologij obseruans remigem agit, crux fidei; & gladius, iustitiae sunt hieroglyphica: saccus cum gallo versatili studia mundi significant, & cupiditates, quibus deflagrat mundus: Sol vero occumbens, finem mundi ob oculos ponit.
units.tr: The ship you see represents for you the condition and state of this age. In it the Devil, watching the hourglass, acts as the rower. The cross stands for faith, and the sword for justice. The sack with the weathercock that turns about signifies the pursuits of the world and the desires by which the world burns. The setting sun sets before your eyes the end of the world.

units.la: Non abluduntur haec nec a sacris nec ab experientia, magistra stultorum. Vehitur hic mundus instar nauigii in altissimo atq; profundissimo mari, in quod vna Eurus Nothusq; ruunt, creberq; procellis Africus incumbit, & a fluctibus hinc inde iactatur, concutiturq;: Ita innumeris atq; perpetuis rerum aduersarum procellis impetuntur, quicunq; huic nauigio imponuntur: & mors a vita (quemadmodum ille non minus eleganter quam vere dixit) vnum tantum distat affeum: Pauci cum Deo, cum superis, cum felicibus nauigamus. Paucis iuxta terram nauigare, h. e. sauum sine iactatione atq; concussione transfigere, datur. Πλῶς ἡ ποτὲ γῆν, ὡς ἡ ποτὲ θάλασσαν ἡδῶς, vt Plutarch.
units.tr: These emblems are not idle, either by Scripture or by experience, the teacher of fools. This world is carried like a ship on the deepest and highest sea, upon which the east and south winds rush, and the south-west wind presses with frequent storms, and it is tossed and battered by waves on every side. So too those who are placed in this ship are assailed by countless and unceasing storms of adverse things. And death is separated from life (as that man said, no less elegantly than truly) by only a single thread. Few of us sail with God, with the heavenly ones, with the fortunate. Only a few are allowed to sail near the land, that is, to cross the sea safely without tossing and shaking. [Πλῶς ἡ ποτὲ γῆν, ὡς ἡ ποτὲ θάλασσαν ἡδῶς], as Plutarch says.

units.la: Remex Diabolus nauigium, quo vult, impellit, est enim Princeps, imo Deus τὰ ἀῖδια τὰ τῆς: & est efficax in filiis ἀπειθείας: Horologii sane obseruantissimus, ne quid temporis elabatur sine linea: quae diuini illius oraculi etiam mens est ac sententia: Vae (dicentis) terra ac mari, quia descendit Diabolus ad vos, habens iram magnam, sciens quod modicum tempus habet.
units.tr: The rowing Devil drives the ship wherever he wishes, for he is the Prince [of this world], indeed the God of [this] age [ta aidia ta tēs]. He works in the sons of disobedience. He is most attentive to the hourglass, lest any time slip away without a line. This is also the mind and meaning of that divine oracle: Woe (it says) to the earth and the sea, because the Devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has but a short time.

units.la: Pecunia obediunt omnia fides per aurum soluitur. Iustitia per aurum intercidit: Quarendam pecuniam primum esse omnes fere uno ore clamitant, & virtutem post nummos ponunt. ὦ φίλοι! (exclamamus) ὦδ' ὡς φίλῳ: ἡ ὦ πιστὴν δὲ ἡ ... &c. Nulla fides pietas, locu reperitur in vllis.
units.tr: All things obey money; faith is bought off with gold. Justice perishes through gold. First of all, money must be sought, almost all cry with one voice, and they put virtue after coins. O friends! [ὦ φίλοι] we cry, as to a friend [ὦδ' ὡς φίλῳ]: and faithful [ἡ ὦ πιστὴν δὲ ἡ] ... etc. No faith, no piety, is to be found in anyone.

units.la: Gallo plæriq; versatiliores sunt templario, quo se ventus potrigit, eo pallium ibuertunt: quo se Fortuna, eo etiam fauor hominum inclinat. Polypi mentem obtinent, quouis Proteo vel vertumno mutabiliores, πολύτροπον, falsarii, hypocritae, inconstantes; & Morpheo genitos dicas, adeo vti foro, & seruire scenae norunt, Alcibiadem agunt, & Vlyssem.
units.tr: Most men are more changeable than the weathercock: as the wind turns it, so they turn their cloak; as Fortune turns, so too the favour of men inclines. They have the mind of the polyp, more changeable than any Proteus or Vertumnus, πολύτροπον: they are forgers, hypocrites, inconstant. You would say they were born of Morpheus, so well do they know how to suit the marketplace and serve the stage. They play Alcibiades and Ulysses.

units.la: Sed moribus hisce suis imminens indicium, horamq; nouissimam prænuntiant, & ad occasum vergere solent, condocefaciunt. Quare quicunq; sunt boni, vt corruptissimos prauissimi huius saeculi mores detestantur, eaque propter mœrent, ita non possunt non gestire ob instantem finem, inclamareque: veni Domine.
units.tr: But those who are good, foretelling the judgement and the last hour that hangs over such ways, are accustomed to teach that the end is near. So whoever is good, detesting the most corrupt morals of this most wicked age, and therefore grieving over them, cannot but rejoice at the approaching end, and cry out: Come, Lord.
Let not the cobbler go beyond his sandal.
Ihovah, the wise one, has ordered his offices in due sequence,
and it has been given to no one to rule over all things at will.

units.la: Ergo cuiq; sient primum sua munia curæ,
units.tr: Therefore let each man first attend to his own duties,
lest the avenging wrath of God strike him.

units.la: Pie ac vere, Initium, inquit Sapiens, Omnis peccati superbia, qui tenuerit illam, adimplebitur maledictis, & subvertit eum in finem: Quae si superiores ordines invadat, occupet, ducat, multa mala committuntur in Deum, Ecclesiam, Pios.
units.tr: Piously and truly the wise man says: Pride is the beginning of all sin; whoever holds it shall be filled with curses, and it will overthrow him in the end. If pride invades, seizes and leads the higher orders, many evils are committed against God, the Church and the godly.

units.la: Sacerdos μεγαλοπρεπῶν, μεγαλοφρύων, καὶ φιλόπμῳ in sacri Codicis adyta temere se ingerit, sua sensa importat, fingit, refingit: figit, refigit, & hoc cogit significare, quod ille mente prius concepit. Ut exempla: Pauli Samosateni: Arrii: Nestorii & similium Haeresiarcharum prisci & nostri temporis ostendunt. Vtinam vero talibus hominum φιλαυτῶν monstris saeculum nostrum vel careret vel caruisset! Is talis etiam verbum salutis ac veritatis ὀρθοπραξίας haud curat, sed mutum canem praestat, puluinaria confuit, vulpem agit, & quoquo modo honorem captat, & applausum tam a vulgo quam a proceribus. Si qui sunt ex fratribus boni, & pio zelo praediti, hos in odium apud superiores inducunt, calumniantur, & nullum non lapidem movent, ut supprimantur, quo tales Morphistae, Ecceboliste, & devota Satanae mancipia soli regnent atque dominentur: nec desunt hoc nostro saeculo tales perfidi ferui conservos ferientes, & primas in omnibus congressibus atque consessibus captantes.
units.tr: A priest of lofty, haughty and ambitious spirit [μεγαλοπρεπῶν, μεγαλοφρύων, καὶ φιλόπμῳ] rashly thrusts himself into the sanctuaries of the sacred Scripture. He brings in his own notions, invents, reinvents, fixes and refixes, and forces the text to signify what he has first conceived in his mind. Examples: the earlier and our own times show Paul of Samosata, Arius, Nestorius and similar heresiarchs. Would that our age had no such monsters of self-lovers [φιλαυτῶν], or had never had them! Such a man also cares nothing for the word of salvation and truth, of right conduct [ὀρθοπραξίας], but acts as a dumb dog, sews cushions for the elbows, plays the fox, and by every means seeks honour and applause, from the common people as well as from the nobles. If there are good brethren among us, endowed with godly zeal, such men stir up hatred against them among the superiors, slander them, and move every stone to have them suppressed, so that Morphists, Eccebolists and devoted slaves of Satan alone may reign and rule. Nor in this our age are lacking such faithless fellow-servants who beat their fellows and seek the first places at every gathering and every seat.

units.la: Politicus elato ingenio, & libidine dominandi perdite flagrans, hos fouet, quos sibi genua flectere ac se adorare sentit, reliquos Mardochaeos, vtcunq; pios, vtcunq; doctos, vtrumque Ecclesiae vel reipublicae valde vtiles tales oderunt, aspernantur, naso suspendunt adunco, premunt, pro derisu habent; & id solum agunt, ut ne pro virtutum suarum dignitate emergant, nihil veriti oppressorum clamores, neque vindicem oculum Dei αἰσθητήριος aliquando iuste iudicaturum.
units.tr: The politician, with his lofty mind and his ruinous passion for domination, cherishes those whom he feels bowing their knees to him and worshipping him, while such men as the rest of the Mordecais, however godly and however learned, and however very useful to Church and commonwealth, he hates, despises, turns up his hooked nose at, oppresses and holds in derision. He does only this, that they may not rise according to the worth of their virtues, having no fear of the cries of the oppressed, nor of the eye of God, which [αἰσθητήριος] perceives and will one day judge justly.

units.la: Hoc vero Caput labis ac mali est, si soli Politici in diuina atq; Ecclesiastica iura inuolent, ministros verbi vocent, examinent, ordinent, id docere cogant, quod ipsis arridet, & Theologiam in Ecclesia, Theologosq; moderentur, vt quid vel quomodo hi proponant pro suggestu, ex solo ipsorum arbitrio sumant. Ministri in Consistoriis tolerantur tantum, siquidem tolerantur: decreta autem a solis, puris, putis Politicis pendentia, in Persicorum ordinem abeunt. Horrenda haec est αὐθαδεια-ἐπισκοπία & si non hic (quae optimi ac sanctissimi Dei est longanimitas!) certe isthic infernalibus prunis aeternum mulctanda. Dudum invasit Ecclesiam haec lues, estq; a multis hactenus deplorata, sed Caesareus ille Papatus non refipit, & plura damna dat quam Papaeus Caesareatus.
units.tr: This is indeed the head of the disease and the evil, if politicians alone break into divine and ecclesiastical rights, call and examine and ordain ministers of the Word, compel them to teach what pleases themselves, and govern theology and the theologians in the Church, so that they take what or how they are to set forth from the pulpit solely at their own discretion. Ministers are tolerated in the consistories only, if indeed they are tolerated; but decrees depending solely on pure, mere politicians pass into the Persian order. This is a dreadful self-will and episcopal presumption [αὐθαδεια-ἐπισκοπία], and if it is not punished here (O the long-suffering of the best and most holy God!), it is certainly to be punished there with infernal coals for ever. This plague has long invaded the Church, and it has hitherto been lamented by many; but that Caesarean Papacy does not come to its senses, and it inflicts more harm than the Papal Caesarism.

units.la: Haeretico-rum morere. Hilar. libr. de Trinit. 1 Confull. histor. Eccl. & quid. cent. 4. horum
units.tr: Die the death of heretics. Hilary, On the Trinity, book 1; Consult.; Histor. Eccl.; and Quid., century 4. These things
EMBLEM: DO NOT THINK TOO HIGHLY OF YOURSELF
Whoever is lifted up on high with headlong step,
those men will then fall with a far heavier fall.
But those who, with daring that aims high, seek the lowest place,

units.la: Hos in fine tamen gloria digna manet. Vetustissimum, communissimum, turpissimum crimen est SVPERBIA: quae est, plus de semetipso sapere ac sentire, quam decet: definiente Apostolo vetustissimum recte dixerimus, quoniam peccati initium est, ex quo omnia peccata, tanquam ex pestifera scaturigine promanant. Ipse Satanas, quae communis Dd. sententia est, primo per superbiam lapsus est, Filio Dei incarnando subiici detrectans, unde haud abs re D. Bernardus. τῷ φαεσφόρῳ dicenti, non sum sicut ceteri homines, subiicit: Ergo sicut ceteri daemones: Et Chrysostom. Tolle, inquit, hoc vitium, ut non velint homines hominibus praevalere, et sine labore caeterae resecabuntur: nec quenquam latet lapsus Evae protoplastae, quomodo superbia et diuinitatis adfectatione primum lapsa fit: quare vetustissimum merito dici quis diffitebitur? Communissimum itidem: de primatu altercantur omnes: digladiantur, et de primis plerique, superbiae currum voluunt, rotae, impellunt: Ecclesiastici, seculares, plebeii, omnes, idque stultissime, unde non illepide exclamatur: Stultorum plena sunt omnia. Πλεῖν γὰρ κακῶν ἢ μεγάλων. Stulta sapit vulgus, nemo vult esse quod hic est, praeferri autem et mansuetudine gestari omnes, pennas pavonias omnes iactant, horridos contemplari pedes, et miseriam, turpitudinemque suam agnoscere nemo vult.
units.tr: yet at the end a worthy glory awaits them. Pride is the most ancient, most universal and most shameful sin. It is to think and feel more of oneself than is fitting. Following the Apostle's definition, we may rightly call it most ancient, since it is the beginning of sin, from which all sins flow as from a poisonous spring. Satan himself, as the common opinion of the doctors holds, first fell through pride, refusing to be subject to the Son of God made flesh. Hence St Bernard not without reason adds, to the one who is bright-bearing [τῷ φαεσφόρῳ] saying, I am not like other men: Therefore like the other demons. And Chrysostom says: Take away this vice, so that men do not wish to prevail over men, and the rest will be cut away without labour. Nor is it hidden from anyone how the fall of Eve, our first parent, came about through pride and the desire to be like God; so who will deny that it may rightly be called most ancient? It is equally most universal: everyone quarrels over precedence. Churchmen, laymen, common folk, all of them struggle, and most of them, even the first among them, push and strain to drive the chariot of pride, and that most foolishly. Hence it is aptly exclaimed: All things are full of fools. Better to have many evils than great ones [Πλεῖν γὰρ κακῶν ἢ μεγάλων]. The common crowd is foolish in its wisdom; no one wishes to be what he is. All want to be preferred and carried aloft in gentleness, all display peacock's feathers, and no one wishes to look at his own ugly feet or to recognise his wretchedness and baseness.

units.la: Turpissimum denique ex iis, quae diximus, esse vltro apparet. Est enim, ut Gregorius inquit, certissima nota reproborum, filiorum, ac mancipiorum Satanae, impossibile enim est (ut exstat in vitis Patrum) ut simul habeamus seculi gloriam et coelestem. Non itur certius ad gehennam quam superbia, fastu, supercilio. Superbia virtutes turpantur et charismata minuuntur: quemadmodum dicitur: Si tibi gratia, fisapientia, formaque detur, destruit omnia, sola superbia, si comitetur. Ut iam non dicam, quam molestum iuxta atque grave sit pati inuidiam superbiae indiuiduam comitem, iuxta illud τῆς ὕβρεως ... vt exempla Hamonii. Antipatri. Alexandri. Pausaniae. Et aliorum innumerorum liquido ostendunt
units.tr: Finally, that pride is most shameful from what we have said appears of its own accord. For, as Gregory says, it is the most certain mark of the reprobate, of the sons and bondslaves of Satan; for it is impossible (as stands written in the lives of the Fathers) that we should have both the glory of the world and the heavenly one at once. No one goes more surely to hell than the proud man, with his haughtiness and arrogant brow. Pride spoils the virtues and diminishes the gifts of grace, as the saying goes: If grace, if wisdom, if beauty is given to you, pride alone destroys all, if it accompanies them. I need not now say how troublesome and how grievous it is to suffer envy, the inseparable companion of pride, according to that saying of insolence [τῆς ὕβρεως] ... as the examples of Hamonius, Antipater, Alexander, Pausanias and countless others clearly show.

units.la: Vt denique non dicam de diuina ἀδεσπότεια, quae omnia excellentia solet mutilare. Vnde vere ex Esopo Chilon: ... Certe Sapius ventus agitatur ingens Pinus, et celsa graviore casu Decidunt turres, feriuntque summos Fulmina montes.
units.tr: Not to mention the divine ἀδεσπότεια [sovereignty, lit. having no master], which is wont to mutilate all excellence. Whence Chilon rightly said, in the words of Aesop: ... Surely the great pine is more often shaken by the wind, and high towers fall with a heavier crash, and lightning strikes the highest mountains.
MODERATE THINGS ENDURE.

units.la: [Engraving: a king seated on a throne under a canopy, with a counsellor, a scribe and a figure of an angel in a framed picture; a cloak-shaped sheet on the floor is inscribed with the words Philosophia, Philargyria, Vis, Ius civile, Pietas and Ius aequum, with a globe, a set square, a sceptre and sheaves of grain.]
units.tr: [Engraving: a king seated on a throne under a canopy, with a counsellor, a scribe and a figure of an angel in a framed picture; a cloak-shaped sheet on the floor is inscribed with the words Philosophia, Philargyria, Vis, Ius civile, Pietas and Ius aequum, with a globe, a set square, a sceptre and sheaves of grain.]

units.la: Prima ministrorum in nostro sit Principe cura, vt
units.tr: Let the first care of the ministers be in our prince, that
When he himself fears God, let him rejoice and likewise
That with equal zeal all protect the needy,
And press the necks of the unjust beneath their feet.

units.la: Quinq; pestes sunt pestilentissimæ regnorum atq; impe- rior ... Philotomia. Philargyria. Vis. Ius ciuile. Prudentia politica seu carnalis. Hisce talibus sucris finitatur vel Imperium, vel Respublica, vel ciuitas, necessario tandem corruet, atq; interim infelicibus syderibus regetur. Philotimia certe pestundat regna ac Respublicas, ac promouet luxum, qui luxus requirit sumptus, vt lapsu sumptus autem non nisi ex sudoribus subditorum exsugunturatq; comparantur. Quare qui feliciter atq; pacate præesse Imperiis volunt, Philotimia se nimia abdicent oportet, seque sub Deo esse meminerint.
units.tr: There are five plagues most pestilential to kingdoms and empires: Philotimia, Philargyria, Vis, Ius civile, and Prudentia politica seu carnalis. By such evils an empire, or a commonwealth, or a city is brought to an end and must at last fall, and meanwhile it is governed under unhappy stars. Philotimia certainly destroys kingdoms and commonwealths, and promotes luxury; luxury requires expenses, and as it were these expenses are drawn and gathered only from the sweat of the subjects. Therefore those who wish to rule empires happily and peacefully must renounce excessive Philotimia, and remember that they are under God.

units.la: Philargyria absit quam longissime a meo magistratu: census non duplicentur, nec intendantur exactiones, melius in duab. (quam in vna) thesaurus conseruatur arculis. Boni Pastoris est tondere pecus non deglubere. Ludovicus IX. Rex Galliarum per totam suam vitam nil fere pœnituit magis quam quod tributum aliquando intenderit, & duplicarit exactionem, filiumque moriturus, vt ne tale quid committat, monuit: quod idem de Turcorum quodam Imperatore literis proditum est. Tales enim Auari principes consiliarii subditorum in se concitant animos precesq; quæ non possunt a Deo non exaudiri. Nota sit historia de Constantino Magno, cui cum Licinius collega paupertatem, lenitatem atq; moderationem exprobraret, subditos suos conuocati iussit, & ad necessitates Imp. tributum exigi, id omnes & singuli pro virili cum exsequerentur & penderent, immensum thesaurum pi⁹ ac moderatus Imp. collegit, & quidem a voluntariis, & ad dandum promptissimis, vltroneisq;, cum quod multi a subditis extorquentur plagosi, id necipsi habent nec subditi, nam diuina et iusta maledictione disperit, vt & Principes & subditi pauperentur.
units.tr: Let Philargyria be as far as possible from my magistracy: the taxes are not to be doubled, nor the exactions increased; treasure is better kept in two chests than in one. It is the mark of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not to flay it. Louis IX, King of the French, repented almost nothing during his whole life more than that he had once increased the tax and doubled the exaction; and when dying he warned his son not to commit any such thing. The same is recorded in writing of a certain Emperor of the Turks. For such avaricious princes stir up against themselves the minds of their subjects, and prayers which cannot fail to be heard by God. Let the history of Constantine the Great be noted: when his colleague Licinius reproached him with poverty, gentleness and moderation, he called together his subjects and ordered that a tax be levied for the needs of the Emperor. All and each paid it according to their means, and the pious and moderate Emperor gathered an immense treasure, and indeed from willing givers, most ready and spontaneous in giving. For what many extort from subjects with blows, they have neither themselves nor do their subjects keep it; for it perishes under a divine and just curse, so that both princes and subjects are impoverished.

units.la: Vis & violentia tyrannorum est, & bono Principe e diametro contrarium: vt concupiscentia Eunuchi de vitianda puella, ita est quisquis vi exercet iudicia. Lateres nemo pius duplicauerit: & ipsorum met Impp. est obseruare δίκαιον ...
units.tr: Force and violence belong to tyrants, and are diametrically opposed to a good prince, just as the lust of the eunuch to violate the girl; whoever administers judgments by force is of that kind. No pious man will have doubled the bricks; and it is the duty of the emperors themselves to observe what is just [δίκαιον].

units.la: Obtentus iuris ciuilis multos fallit: non est regula quæ exceptionem nō patiatur. Iustissimum iniuriam esse sæpe compertum est. Prudentis ac moderati Imperatoris est etiam de lege secundum legem aliquid remittere, si pacate atq; feliciter regnare volet.
units.tr: The pretext of civil law deceives many: there is no rule that admits no exception. It has often been found that the highest justice is the highest injury. It is also the mark of a prudent and moderate emperor to remit something from the law according to the law, if he wishes to reign peacefully and happily.

units.la: Prudentia carnalis coram Deo fatuitas est, soletq; Deus talia talium cōfilia plerumq; infatuare, ipsosq; in sua ipsorum astutia capere, vt in exemplo Achitophelis luce meridiana clari relucet. Qui igitur sapit, in Domino sapiat.
units.tr: Worldly wisdom is folly before God, and God is wont mostly to confound the counsels of such men, and to catch them in their own cunning, as shines forth clear as midday in the example of Ahithophel. Let him therefore who is wise be wise in the Lord.

units.la: Inprimis exitialis pestis Dominis est minister, qui auribus Domini seruit, & verbum Iehuae ad Principis nutum fingit, tales nebulones diuini fures honoris vel primi digni sunt, quibus laqueus gulam frangat.
units.tr: Above all, the deadly plague for lords is the minister who serves in the ear of the lord and fashions the word of Jehovah at the prince's nod. Such scoundrels, thieves of divine honour, deserve the first place, for whom a noose should break the throat.

units.la: IMPIA FEX HOMINVM REgum mercatur honores.
units.tr: IMPIOUS BREED OF MEN, THEY BUY THE HONOURS OF KINGS.

units.la: [Engraving: a crowned king pointing, with two fur-cloaked courtiers in conversation, one holding a bag; no text in the picture.] Regis in aspectu didici seruire, fauorem Vt mihi blanditiis conciliare queam: Omne malum Domino clam mens aliena precatur, Dum facit officium lingua manusq; suum.
units.tr: [Engraving: a crowned king pointing, with two fur-cloaked courtiers in conversation, one holding a bag; no text in the picture.] I have learned in the king's presence to serve, so that I may win his favour by flattery. While the disloyal mind prays for every evil to befall its lord, the tongue and hand carry out their duty.

units.la: Vides peridiffimum & profligati honoris, honeftatifq; genus hominum versutorum aulicorum, quod mores Dominorum nolle, atq; imitari, omnia laudare propter offam, taxare nihil didicit. Quæ hominum sentina iam inde ab initio & semper male audiit apud bonos ac prudentes: nam in Deum & homines iniurii sunt. Misso Deo in Principibus confidunt. Reges ac Dominos idola faciunt: In dominorum gratiam preces missas faciut, exsecrantur, blasphemant, hariolantur, &c. Diuinas per ministerium monitiones sufq; deq; faciunt. Sub prætextu obedientiæ reges ac regna sæpe in extrema pericula coniiciunt, lingua occidunt innocentes, crudelissimi sunt lenoniam exercent, si Dominis ita lubet: depeculantur thesauros, per calumnias: furantur insontibus famam, quod furtum omnium turpissimum est: Nam fama & vita æquiparantur: Verbo dicam nihil non mali faciunt, ut satius sit Principi incidisse in κολακας quam in κολακας: nec truculentius animal (tyranno excepto) inuenias assentatore aulico. Vnde recte Menander.
units.tr: You see the most pernicious kind of men, the crooked courtiers, lost to all honour and decency. They have learned not to dislike their masters' ways and imitate them, to praise everything for the sake of a morsel, and to criticise nothing. This sink of men has from the beginning and always been ill spoken of by good and prudent people, for they wrong both God and men. Having dismissed God, they trust in princes. They make idols of kings and lords. For the favour of their lords they offer prayers, curse, blaspheme, practise soothsaying and so on. They treat the divine admonitions delivered through the ministry as worth nothing. Under the pretext of obedience they often thrust kings and kingdoms into extreme dangers. They kill the innocent with their tongues, and they are most cruel, practising pimping whenever their lords please. They plunder treasuries by slander and rob the blameless of their reputation, which is the most shameful of all thefts, for reputation and life are equal in value. In a word, they do every kind of evil, so that it is better for a prince to fall among flatterers [kolakes] than among sycophants [sykophantai]. And you will find no more savage creature (apart from the tyrant) than the courtier-flatterer. Hence Menander rightly says:

units.la: Ὀσὶ ⊗ κολακες τὰς τυραννους ἢ δεσποτας
units.tr: Those who flatter tyrants or masters [kolakes]...

units.la: Πρὸς τὰς δὲ ὁ κόλαξ ἀρέσκει τυράννων, δὲ πρὸς ⊗
units.tr: The flatterer pleases tyrants, and ...

units.la: Ὁ Συκοφάντης, ὁ δὲ κόλακος τέλος τ ⊗.
units.tr: The sycophant, and the end of the flatterer ...

units.la: Magna igitur cautione opus est Domino, ut sibi à talibus caueat, & pios iniquirat ministros, exemplo Dauid, Psal. 101. & Constantini Magni, ut in hiftor. Ecclesiast. Nec difficile foret Principibus talia carcinomata dignoscere, siquidem Prudentiæ Sprm Deum orarent, & non scientes volentes decipi mallent: Quid enim? an non omnia Principis laudare, assentatoris est? an non mores imitari Principis, assentatoris est? an non συκοφαντειν & frequenter calumniari, assentatoris est? Ipse Satyricus tale genus hominem irridet: Rides maiore cachinno; Concutitur: flet, cum lacrymas conspexit amici: Nec dolet igniculum brumæ si tempore poscas Accipit Endromeden: si dixeris, æstuo: sudat.
units.tr: Great caution is therefore needed on the part of the lord, so that he guards himself against such men and seeks out pious ministers, following the example of David in Psalm 101, and that of Constantine the Great, as in the Ecclesiastical History. Nor would it be difficult for princes to recognise such crabs, provided they prayed to God for prudence and did not, through ignorance, prefer to be deceived. For what? Is it not the mark of a flatterer to praise everything the prince does? Is it not the mark of a flatterer to imitate the prince's morals? Is it not the mark of a flatterer to play the sycophant [sykophantein] and to slander often? The satirist himself mocks this kind of man: You laugh with a louder guffaw; he shakes, he weeps when he has seen his friend's tears. Nor does he feel the little fire of winter; if you ask for Andromeda's cloak, he gets it; if you say, "I am sweating," he sweats too.

units.la: Theodoricus Veronensis Diaconum adulantem decapitari iubet. Imp. Severus adulatorem Thurinum Verconium fumo necat.
units.tr: Theodoric of Verona ordered a flattering deacon to be beheaded. Emperor Severus killed the flatterer Thurinus of Verconium by smoke.

units.la: Noti sunt adulatores Dionysii Siracusani, is cum cæcutiret, tum adulatores etiam cæcutientiam simulabant, ita, ut alius in alium impingeret.
units.tr: The flatterers of Dionysius of Syracuse are well known. When he was going blind, they even feigned blindness, so that one of them bumped into another.

units.la: Noti Alexandri, qui inflexam ceruicem & vocis asperitatem, quæ omnia erant in Alexandro, imitabantur: nimirum in regum domibus sunt qui mollibus vestiuntur. Exeat oportet qui pius, candidus, &c. esse volet, talem nec herus nec serui ferre possunt. Sed de his multi alias. Eheu! nunquid adhuc regnat scelus istud in aulis, Trudat ut hic illum de statione sua! Hei mihi quot numerant hæc ferrea secula vulpes, Qui graue mellito virus ab ore vomunt!
units.tr: The flatterers of Alexander are well known, who imitated his bent neck and harsh voice, all of which were in Alexander. Certainly in kings' houses there are those who are dressed in soft clothing. Whoever wishes to be pious, honest, and so on, must leave, for neither master nor servants can bear such a man. But of these things many have written elsewhere. Alas! Does this wickedness still reign in the courts, so that it thrusts this man from his post! Woe is me, how many foxes this iron age counts, who vomit grievous poison from honeyed mouths!
THE GOOD SHEPHERD SHEARS THE FLOCK.

units.la: Regis ad ingenium seruorum turba paratur, Aurum cor radunt si sit auarus homo: Detestanda fames auri, quæ non nisi tandem Expletur sæui sub Phlegetontis aquis.
units.tr: The crowd of slaves is prepared to suit the king's temper; they scrape the heart of gold if the man is greedy. Detestable is the hunger for gold, which is never sated until it is finally satisfied in the waters of savage Phlegethon.

units.la: Qui fisco, thesaurisq; augendis regiis nimis intenti sunt Reges, Principes, Proceres, næ illi quiduis facile committunt potius quam vt abstineat ab iniustitia tali: vt quod Apostolus ingenere de omnib. ditescere cupientibus pronunciat, id αἰσχρὸν & quidem φιλαργυρία in tales competat maxime: Incidere eos in tentationes & laqueos, & desideria multa, qua demergant eos in perditionem ac interitum. Nam
units.tr: Those kings, princes and nobles who are too intent on swelling the treasury and the royal coffers readily entrust themselves to anything rather than refrain from such injustice. What the Apostle says generally of all who want to grow rich, that it is shameful and indeed love of money [philargyria], applies most of all to such men: they fall into temptations and snares, and many desires which drown them in ruin and destruction. For

units.la: Tales Harpyiæ ne à sacris quidem manus abstinent, quin in bona Ecclesiastica inuolent, vt fami inde sitiq; suæ satisfaciant. Horredum hoc icelus est, iniurium in Ecclesiam, contumeliosum in Deum Ec lesiæ Protectorem atq; vindicem: quare & E. Laurentius Diaconus Romanus & Martyr Christi tali Harpyiæ ad necem vsque & rogum se opposuit pro thesauro Ecclesiæ: ignotum nostris esse non potest illud iuris canonici:Semel Deo dicatum, non estad humanos vsus transferendum vlterius, nec manus tamen abstinent mastigiæ, priusquam prunis adustas infernalibus gerant. Libet exclamare cum Germanis:ô S. Martine, offerunt tibi obolum & equum furantur:Omnes thesauros Ecclesiæ abstulerunt, ministrantibus autem altari vix suppetit vnde viram sustentent & cutem trahant. Exp rg scere vindex Deus Iimo etiam cutem de-trahunt ministris, & si quid reliquerunt, rapiunt tamen & illud & insues ac porcos distribuunt.
units.tr: Such Harpies do not keep their hands even from sacred things, but pounce on ecclesiastical property to satisfy their hunger and thirst. This is a horrible crime, wrongful against the Church and insulting to God, the Church's protector and avenger. Therefore E. Laurentius, Roman deacon and martyr of Christ, opposed such a Harpy even to death and the pyre, in defence of the Church's treasure. The rule of canon law cannot be unknown to our people: What has once been dedicated to God is not to be transferred to human uses any further. Yet they do not keep their hands from the plunder until they have brought the scorched coals of hell upon themselves. One is moved to cry out with the Germans: O Saint Martin, they offer you a penny and steal your horse! They have carried off all the treasures of the Church, and for those ministering at the altar there is scarcely enough to sustain life and keep the skin on their bones. Awake, avenging God! They even strip the skin from the ministers, and if they have left anything, they seize that too and distribute it to their asses and pigs.

units.la: Sanguinem & sudores sub diterum fugere, bibere, indeq; saginari non horrent: Pastores vocantur, sed lupi sunt, non tondent sed deglubunt & excoriant pecus: etiam proprionum redemptiones corporum (longe vltra Turcicam tyrannidem prouecti) imperant: Rustico ne caseus quidem à vectigali immunis relinquitur. Occlamare illis Esaias & Michæas: aliiq; deberent, sed horum clamores non ferunt, audiant igitur Hybream: Messem duplicate & vindemiam, si tributa duplicare vultis, vel ab his etiam abstinete.
units.tr: They do not shrink from draining blood and sweat from their subjects, from swallowing them and growing fat on them. They are called shepherds, but they are wolves; they do not shear the flock but flay it and strip off its skin. They even impose ransoms of the bodies of their subjects, having advanced far beyond Turkish tyranny. Not even cheese is left to the peasant free from tax. Isaiah and Micah and others ought to cry out to them, but these men cannot bear their outcries. Let them then hear Hybreas: Double the harvest and the vintage, if you wish to double the taxes, or at least refrain from these things.

units.la: Tales sibi iæpe quærunt ministros, per quos ditescant, qui impleant de-mos dominorum suorum violentia ac dolo, fisci consiliarios, qui in id tantum incubunt, vt modos inueniant, quibus rusticos argento emungant: quas spongias suas vocitare Imp. Vespasianus solebat, quib. impletis aurum redextorqueat: Nota est Tiberii Imp. historia, cui obuiam factus domum enunti hulcerosus & mendicus, cum ab eo saturas mustas depellere vellet, dicebat: hæc turba quiescat Quasi forte abeat, nostro quæ sanguine dudum Iam tumet: accedet subito noua copia, rursus It ie una cohors, nostri quæ sanguinis omne Quod reliquat capiet, magis atq; infesta nocebit.
units.tr: Such men often seek for themselves ministers through whom they may grow rich, who fill up the measures of their lords by violence and deceit: the fiscal advisers, who devote themselves only to finding ways by which they may squeeze money from the peasants. The Emperor Vespasian used to call them his sponges, which he squeezed to wring out the gold once they were filled. The story of Emperor Tiberius is well known: when a sore-ridden beggar met him on the road and said he was bringing home what he had been given, Tiberius wished to drive off the swarming flies. The beggar said, Let this crowd rest, lest perhaps they go away, which already swell with our blood; a new supply will come suddenly, again a crowd of such flies which will take whatever blood is left to us and harm us more and more fiercely.

units.la: Denique hi tales fisco parcunt, sæpe cum irreparabili damno, πανώλεθρία, totiusq; totali Imp. Regni. Reipublic. interitu, vt supra aliquibus exemplis probatum fecimus.
units.tr: Finally, such men spare the treasury only rarely, often to the irreparable loss of the whole kingdom and commonwealth, through total [panolethria] destruction, as we have shown above by several examples.

units.la: QVI SIBI NIMIVM SAPERE videtur, nequicquam sapit.
units.tr: He who thinks himself too wise is wise to no purpose.

units.la: [Woodcut illustration: a man in a fur-trimmed robe and hat holding a globe aloft, with a skeleton at right holding an hourglass, a fox at his feet, a cart and a walled town in the background.] Est leuis ac vanus qui plus sibi vendicat ipse, Demonstrare sua quam potiatur ope. Ne nimium sapias, pudor est mage velle videri: Qui sapit hoc vere quod sapit, ille sapit.
units.tr: He is light and vain who claims more for himself than he can show by his own resources. Do not seem too wise: it is shameful to wish to appear so. He who is wise in truth is wise in what he really is.

units.la: Financiarum heic vides magistrum, qui altissimum, profundissimum, longissimum, latissimum, adeoq; totum prudentiae exantlasse sibi videtur, adeo sapientiae opinione turget. Eximius est Theologus, qui de rebus diuinis profunda habet & appositè differere de iisdem potest: cerebro vtitur pro scrinio iuris canonici: in iurisprudentia regnat & excellit: Principis hoc nemo melius medicum agit. Linguas callet plurimas; mores multorum regnorum atq; nationum peregrinus dudum didicit atq; tenet, deque omnibus discurrere (vt vocant) congrue potest, nec est Sapientiae pars, quam ille non (non dicam a limine quod aiunt, salutarit, sed) integram & totam vorarit. Hinc sinistra mundum, dextra cælum tangit, nam mundi sibi lux esse, & ipsis Diis imponere se posse sibi persuadet, vel, vt loquitur Psaltes, in cælum exponit. Et quibus Luciani in morem ipsi super risus fiunt. Stellas dinumerare potest, calices tussire, herbas crescere, & pisces screare audir, estq; adeo talis, quale inter tot chiliadum myriadas vix inueneas vnū. O hominum genus odiosissimi nū!quod semper studere, discere semper, sed ad ἐπίγνωσιν peruenire potest nunquam, de quibus merito vsurpare possis illud Senecæ: Multi ad veram ac solidam sapientiam peruenirent, nisi se dudum peruenisse putarent: quibus, quod nesciunt, discere pudor est: alienissimi ab illo Socratis: hoc scio me nihil scire. Verum illi, quod sciunt, scire se sciunt, imo scire, quæ nesciunt etiam, sibi ipsis splendide mentiuntur: hos si commentitiæ laude amplius inflas, turgebunt, vt vel medii crepent, rumpantur. Singula horum talium verba, singula continent oracula Delphica, similes Buzitę: Plenus sum sermonibus, coartat me spiritus ventris mei: Ecce venter meus vt vinum cui non aperitur? sicut vtres noui finderetur: eloquar, vt respiratio fit mihi, aperiens labia mea respondebo, &c. Verum hominibus tam arrogantibus & iactabundis cum Deus tum homines infesti sunt, & tandem manifestu fit, nihil minus quam sapientiam cum ipsis habitasse. Sapientia certe cum Ahitophele moritura videbatur, cuius consilia pura oracula habebantur. Consilium enim Ahitophelis (inquit scriptura) quod consulebat illis diebus erat ac siquis consuluisset ipsum verbum Dei, sed summa eius stultitia tum patefiebat, quum posthabitum suum consilium cernens, instrato asino suo surgens domum abiit suam, & suspendio vitam sibi ipsi finiuit. Hunc finem sortiuntur tales ardeliones & philautoi, quare & Heraclitus Athenien-sibus risum mouit, cum se præter modum iactaret. Pythagoras autem qui moderate de se sentiebat, non Sophum sed Philosophum voci cari discupiens, æternum sapientiæ præconium nactus est: Itidemq; Thales recusata mensa aurea: & alii. Consilium igitur Apostoli est:
units.tr: Here you see a master of finance, who thinks he has mastered everything that is highest, deepest, longest, broadest, and so the whole of prudence, and he swells with the reputation of wisdom. He is an outstanding theologian, who has profound knowledge of divine things and can discourse on them aptly. He uses his brain as a chest for canon law. He reigns and excels in jurisprudence; no one acts as the prince's physician better than he. He knows many languages. As a stranger he has long learned and holds the customs of many kingdoms and nations, and he can discourse on all of them, as they say, appropriately. There is no part of wisdom which he has not (I will not say greeted from the threshold, as they say, but) devoured whole and entire. Hence he touches the world with his left hand and heaven with his right, for he persuades himself that he is the light of the world and can impose himself even on the gods, or, as the Psalmist says, he sets his mouth against heaven. And, in the manner of Lucian, he himself becomes a laughingstock. He can count the stars, cough up the cups, see the herbs grow and hear the fish sing, and he is such that among so many myriads of thousands you would scarcely find one like him. O most hateful kind of men! They are always studying, always learning, yet they can never attain to knowledge. Of them you may rightly use that saying of Seneca: Many would attain to true and solid wisdom, were it not that they long ago thought they had attained it. For such men it is a shame to learn what they do not know, and they are most alien to that saying of Socrates: I know that I know nothing. But they, as to what they know, think they know it, and indeed they splendidly deceive themselves even about what they do not know. If you puff them up further with fictitious praise, they swell until they burst, and even burst in the middle. Every word of such men contains the oracles of Delphi, like those of Buzi: I am full of words; the spirit of my belly constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins it will burst. I will speak, that I may find relief; I will open my lips and answer, etc. But God and men are both hostile to men so arrogant and boastful, and in the end it becomes plain that wisdom has dwelt with them not at all. Wisdom seemed certainly about to die with Ahithophel, whose counsels were regarded as pure oracles. For the counsel of Ahithophel (says Scripture) which he gave in those days was as if a man had consulted the word of God; but his great folly was then revealed, when, seeing his counsel set aside, he rose, saddled his ass, went home and ended his life by hanging. Such vain and self-loving men meet this end. For this reason Heraclitus also made the Athenians laugh when he boasted beyond measure. Pythagoras, however, who thought modestly of himself and desired to be called not Sophos but Philosopher, gained the everlasting praise of wisdom. So too Thales, who refused the golden table, and others. Therefore the counsel of the Apostle is:

units.la: Μὴ ὑψηλοφρονεῖν παρ ὁ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν, &c.
units.tr: Not to think highly beyond what one ought to think, but to think so as to be sober-minded, etc. [Μὴ ὑψηλοφρονεῖν παρ' ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν]
Let the other side also be heard.
Press your little lip with your finger.

units.la: Multarum nos rerum vtilium admonet hic vir Purpuratus hieroglyphice, sed ante omnia iustitia: quod significare videntur cum gladio, enseue, libra iustitiae hieroglyphica: deinde & comprimens aurem sinistra manus. Ensis seueritatis monet: Non enim frustra gladium gerit, &c. Oculus, inquit Iehoua, tuus non parcat. Libra iuste iudicare docet, vt causas aequa lance ponderes, & sententiam roges ex iure, aequo, bonoq;, & iusto. Manus extensa, inq; duos porrecta digitos, iuris te admonet iurandi, quod ab initio praestitisti, ne contra datam venias fidem. Magna huius aeui labes est, inprimis in iudicibus, quod datae fidei tam leuiter obliuiscuntur, & conscientiam propriam vel personis vel muneribus vel aliis rebus externis posthabent. Quo pertinet Iudaei illius cum Christiano disputatio, cur inter Christianos plures inueniantur male affecti quam inter alios, & periuria Christianorum causatus Iudaus, ruborem Christiano incussit. Fortassis non ablusit. Fama conscientia, oculus, lusum non patiuntur. Arista honoris hieroglyphicum, honores in iudicio captare prohibet, iuxta illud sapientis. Ne quaras fieri iudex, nec requiras a Domino principatum, neque a rege cathedram gloriae: ne iustitiam tibi afferas coram Domino, neq; coram Rege sapientiam, ne non valeas iniuste facta tollere. Et quae sequuntur. Descriptio Decalogi per numeros, pie indicat, secundum ius & LL. scriptas rogandam sententiam, non secundum proprii cerebri dictamen fallibile. Bonus enim Index nihil ex arbitrio suo facit, sed iuxta legis & iura pronunciat. Estque exemplum in Paedagog. Cyri: qui Cyrus adolescens cum absoluisset puerum grandiusculum apud se accusatum, quod alteri minori prolixiorem vestem eripuisset, & suam tanquam breviorem & ad modum corporis magis congruentem, tradidisset, reprehendit magister iudicium Cyri, eiq; dat plagas, monens: non iusta esse quae ipsi videantur, sed quae nitantur legibus. Quod vero Purpuratus hic noster sinistra sinistram manu comprimit aure, commode monere vult iudicem aequitatis & iustitiae Alexandri Magni, de quo Plutarchus commemorat, quod quoties accusatorem audiuerit, altera aurem manu obturauerit, integram eam reo delatoque referuans. Qpidem sapientis monitum est: Priusquam perquisieris, ne criminetis, cognosce primum atque tum increpa: Quare etiam digito labella comprimit, innuens non praecipitandum esse iudicium, sed deliberandum diu quod semel statuendum sit: quocirca idem sapiens monet. Priusquam audiueris ne respondeas, & in medium sermonum ne immittas verbum. De regimine linguae alius dicendi dabitur locus & occasio, sufficit modo dixisse, quam non praecipitanda sit iudici sententia: Nam qui statuit aliquid inaudita altera parte, aequum licet statuerit, haud aequus est: ac proinde Leg. Attic. cautum:
units.tr: Here this man in purple reminds us, in hieroglyphic form, of many useful things, but above all of justice, which the sword, the blade and the scales seem to signify as hieroglyphs of justice. Then the left hand pressing the ear. The blade warns of severity: for he does not bear the sword in vain, etc. Your eye, says Jehovah, shall not spare. The scales teach you to judge justly, so that you weigh causes in an even balance and ask for judgment according to law, equity, goodness and righteousness. The outstretched hand, it says, holding up two fingers, reminds you of the oath of law which you took at the beginning, so that you do not come against the pledge given. This age has a great blot, especially among judges, that they forget the faith given so lightly, and set their own conscience aside for persons, bribes or other external things. To this belongs that disputation of the Jew with the Christian, why more ill-disposed people are found among Christians than among others; and the Jew, charging the Christians with perjury, struck the Christian with shame. Perhaps he was not wide of the mark. Conscience, the eye, do not allow mockery. The ear of grain, the hieroglyph of honour, forbids seeking honours in judgment, according to that saying of the wise man: Do not seek to become a judge, nor ask the Lord for rule, nor the king for a seat of glory; do not claim justice for yourself before the Lord, nor wisdom before the King, lest you be unable to remove unjust deeds. And what follows. The description of the Decalogue by numbers rightly indicates that judgment must be sought according to law and written statutes, not according to the fallible dictate of one's own brain. For a good judge does nothing by his own will, but pronounces according to the law and the rights. There is an example in the Pedagogy of Cyrus: when the young Cyrus had acquitted a rather large boy who had been accused before him of snatching a longer garment from a smaller boy and giving his own shorter one, which was more fitting to the body, the master rebuked Cyrus's judgment and struck him, warning that those things are not just which seem so to him, but those which rest on the laws. As to the fact that this purple-clad figure of ours presses his left ear with his left hand, he wishes to remind us fittingly of the judge of equity and justice, Alexander the Great, of whom Plutarch relates that whenever he heard the accuser he stopped the other ear with his hand, reserving it whole for the accused. And there is the saying of the wise man: Before you inquire, do not accuse; first learn, and then rebuke. Hence he also presses his lips with his finger, signifying that judgment is not to be rushed, but that what is to be decided once must be long deliberated. Therefore the same wise man advises: Before you have heard, do not answer, and do not put in a word in the midst of speeches. An opportunity and occasion for another discourse on the government of the tongue will be given; it is enough to have said that a judge's sentence must not be hastened. For whoever decides something without hearing the other party, even if he decides fairly, is not fair. Accordingly the Attic law provided:
To hear both sides equally [Ὁμοίως ἀμφοῖν ἀκροᾶσθαι].
THE ASS AND THE LYRE.

units.la: Si quæras, quæres ancipiti Fortunæ lusui maximè expositá sit, dicam: Fauor Principum:nam his proclive admodum amare, odisse: amare immerentes: & odisse bonos. Necabsonum est comune Prouerbium: fidelis seruus semper asinus. Improbi zizaniorum instar se habent, quæ succulentiora semper occupare loca solent: talem nugiuendam & Cumanum asinum hic vides, ad clauum quidē & honorum falsigium euectum, qui gladium semper, & rophaeam crepat, sed mensus est, & leuis inuentus nimis, aurefq; asininas longe supra caput extulit. Indignissimum (per Deum immortalem!) fuerit, tales asinos euehi, sed non minus tamen frequens quam indignum esse cotidiana clamat experientia. Vere istud quidem quo quis doctior & sapientior, eo erit & humilior, verissimum autem contra & illud: Quo quis rudior & magis barbarus, eo felicior atq; insolentior, nesciunt enim tales asini fortuna uti, sed exemplo comprobant: Asperius nihil esse stulto cum surgit in altum: vbi non mores sed honores tantum mutantur. Quare occinendum erat talibus Itali Poetæ Ausonii illud:
units.tr: If you ask who is most exposed to the doubtful play of Fortune, I will say: the favour of princes. For it is very easy for them to love and to hate: to love the undeserving and to hate the good. There is the common proverb: a faithful servant is always an ass. Wicked men are like tares, which usually occupy the richest places. Here you see such a worthless, Cumaean ass, raised to the helm and to false honours, who is always rattling his sword and his trophy, but he was weighed and found too light, and he has lifted his asses' ears far above his head. It would be most unworthy (by the immortal God!) that such asses be raised, yet daily experience cries out that it is no less frequent than it is unworthy. The more learned and wise someone is, the humbler he will be: that is certainly true, but the opposite is most true too: the ruder and more barbarous someone is, the happier and more insolent he will be. Such asses do not know how to use fortune, but they prove it by example: nothing is more harsh than a fool when he rises on high, where only honours change and not manners. Therefore the Italian poet Ausonius' verse had to be sung to such fellows:
Treat Fortune with reverence, you who, suddenly
Rich, step forward from a humble place.

units.la: Laudabiliter Epaminondas: qui cum antea consueuisset quidem aucto corpore, hilariq; vultu prodire in publicum, postridie tamen eius diei, quo ipsius auspiciis feliciter pugnatum erat in Leuctris, squallidus ac submissus processit: cumq; amici scisciarentur, num molesti aliquid accidisset; nihil, inquit, sed heri sensi me plus aquo mihi placuisse, hodie illius gaudii insolentiam castigo. Talis fuit moderatio Epaminondæ hominis ad gloriam ac sublimitatem facti, natiq;: quæ non fuerit nostra;
units.tr: Praiseworthy was Epaminondas, who, although he had been accustomed to come out in public with a healthy body and a cheerful face, went out on the day after the battle at Leuctra, fought successfully under his command, squalid and subdued. When his friends asked whether something troublesome had happened, "Nothing," he said, "but yesterday I felt I had pleased myself more than was right; today I am chastising the insolence of that joy." Such was the moderation of Epaminondas, a man of glory and high rank by his deed and birth; our age has not matched it.

units.la: Sed gigantum nostrorum insolentia tanta est, vt ab ebrietate Fortunę non euigilare, nec arrogantię crapulam edormire vnquā possint, velint: quare & vindicis ira Dei in omnibus statibus non cessat. Audacia quidem ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς virum bonum non dedecet, sed ostentatio & vanæ præsumptio gloriæ vt stultorum ita improborum quoq; est. Longius prouehi quam conueniat raro felicem sortitur euentum. Vere enim Lotichius:
units.tr: But the insolence of our giants is so great that they neither can nor will wake from the drunkenness of Fortune or sleep off the hangover of arrogance. Therefore the wrath of God the avenger does not cease in every estate. Boldness indeed does not disgrace a [ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς] good man, but ostentation and vain presumption of glory belong to fools and wicked men alike. Going further than is fitting rarely meets a happy outcome. For truly Lotichius says:
Rash courage does not have calm outcomes.

units.la: Exemplis id demonstrare est cum sacris tum prophanis: quis enim insolentior Hamane, sed suspendio finit vitam: tales fuerunt: Epicurus, Palamon, Gorgias Leontinus, Menecrates, Hippias, Pompeius & sexcenti alii: μεγάλα διάχειν ... vt verum sit maneatq; diuinum oraculum sapientissimi Regis: Aduersus superbia erit ignominia. Ὅταν ὕβρις ...
units.tr: This can be shown by examples, both sacred and profane. For who was more insolent than Haman? Yet he ended his life on the gallows. Such were Epicurus, Palamon, Gorgias of Leontini, Menecrates, Hippias, Pompey, and six hundred others. [μεγάλα διάχειν] ... so that the divine oracle of the wisest King is true and stands: Where there is pride, there will be dishonour. [Ὅταν ὕβρις ...]

units.la: [Greek verse lines printed in the text block at the foot, partly illegible.]
units.tr: [Greek verse lines printed in the text block at the foot, partly illegible.]
THE ASS AND THE FLUTE.

units.la: Qui sua prudenti committit munia seruo, De euentu vnquam non ambiget ille bono. Sed quisquis stolido magno discrimine: certus De euentu optato non erit iste diu.
units.tr: He who entrusts his duties to a prudent servant will never doubt a good outcome. But whoever entrusts them to a fool, in great danger, will not for long be certain of the outcome he hopes for.

units.la: Similis simili gaudet. Qualis herus, talis servus, tales & mores: ut lepus lepori, ita stultus stulto mento conuiuit. Vere illud: Noscitur ex comite, qui non cognoscitur ex se.
units.tr: Like delights in like. As the master, so the servant. And so too the manners: as the hare keeps company with the hare, so the fool keeps company with the fool in mind. True is that saying: one is known by the company he keeps, who is not known from himself.

units.la: Vides hominem Apollinis sibi scientiam atq; sapientiam arrogantem Delphici, asinus autem reapse est ad cibiam. Tot sibi artes atq; disciplinas fingit mentitur; ipse, ut fumario opus sibi fore arbitratus sit, per quod humores vaporesq; nonnulli exhalarent, ne cerebrum rumpatur. O lepidum caput! o festiuum ingenium! sed o ineptum hominem! tales sunt quibus honores decernuntur amplissimi, minime omnium dignis, quod tamen hoc exulceratissimo seculo frequentissimum est in omnibus statibus. In Ecclesiastico statu extolluntur rudes & omnium rerum ignari, in quos competit illud Prophetæ: Dicunt: Dominus dixit: & non est verbum Domini: dum tatum implere aures grauieloquentia & magnidicentia possunt, & magnos exhalare strepitus, magno conatu magnas recitare nugas, officio se suo probe defunctos esse arbitrantur: maxime si vel populus applaudat, vel illa crymetur, ut olim ad boatus monachorum & frigidos passionales actus histrionicos factum. Ita asininæ asini ruditati populi inequitant, & laudantur ieiuni & aridissimi ipsorum sermones, de quibus si interroges quid fuerint vel continuerint, tantum scibunt, quantum de colore cæcus, vel minus. Mundus vult decipi In statu Politico tales nugiuendas inueniãs quamplurimos, qui tantum fumos vendunt Dominis atq; servis, quos caro sæpe mercantur utrique, digni qui vel ipsi fumo pereant, Pygopolynices simulatque Parasiti, de quibus non illepide Poeta noster sub ipsorum persona: Quodcunq; Princeps expetit | Mensq; mandat, consulo: Quamuis id vrbes perderet | Aut etiam concordiam Tantum meam si consequor | Partem vel omnes rideo.
units.tr: You see a man who arrogates to himself the knowledge and wisdom of Apollo of Delphi, yet in truth he is an ass fit only for fodder. He feigns and lies that he has so many arts and disciplines; he thinks he needs a smoking-room, through which some humours and vapours might be exhaled, lest his brain burst. O charming head! O witty mind! But O silly man! Such are those to whom the highest honours are decreed, least of all those worthy of them, which nevertheless in this most ulcerated age is most frequent in every estate. In the ecclesiastical estate the rude and ignorant in all things are exalted, to whom that saying of the prophet applies: They say: The Lord has said, and yet it is not the word of the Lord. While they can fill the ears with heavy eloquence and grand talk, and utter great noises, and with great effort recite great trifles, they think they have discharged their office properly, especially if the people applaud, or if that crowd roars, as once was done at the howling of monks and cold passion-plays and theatrical acts. Thus asses ride upon the asinine rudeness of the people, and their empty and dry sermons are praised; if you ask them what these contained, they will know as much as a blind man about colour, or less. The world wishes to be deceived. In the political estate there are very many such trifling fellows who sell only smoke to lords and servants, which both often buy at a dear price; they deserve to perish by that very smoke, Pygopolynices as much as Parasites, about whom our poet, speaking in their own persona, says not unpleasantly: Whatever the Prince desires | and his mind commands, I advise. Even if that should ruin cities | or even if I should win his concord, | only my share, I laugh at them all.

units.la: Ideoq; sedulo in id incumbet noster Princeps, ut in delectu seruorum sit cautus ac prudens: Et sexaginta si ipsi consiliarii fuerint, anima tamen sua consilium, ne dispexerit. A caueat rudibus ne quid committat asellis, Qui bene curatas res volet esse suas:
units.tr: Therefore our Prince should apply himself diligently to this, that he be cautious and prudent in choosing his servants. Even if there were sixty counsellors, let him not despise his own soul's counsel. Let him beware of entrusting anything to the rude donkeys, if he wishes his affairs to be well managed.

units.la: Sed heu! ingenio celebres non amat aula viros. Fatui, dementes, stolidi, qui magnos emittere elenchos possunt, quibus tectum diabolis fumat, & moribus ducuntur suis tales euehuntur. Exeat ex aula, dixit ille, qui volet esse pius. Non intret aulas Principum | Ex corde qui Deum colit Hic regnat inconstantia | Et sæpe peruersissimus Est administer principi | Acceptior sit iisdem. Proinde, quisquis gloria | Abhorret & mendacium Quem nuda stipat veritas | Non intret aulas principum.
units.tr: But alas! The court does not love men famed for their talent. Fools, madmen and dullards, who can utter great boasts, by whom the house is smoked for the devils, and such people are promoted by their own manners. He said: let him who wishes to be godly leave the court. Let him not enter the courts of princes. | Where one worships God from the heart, there inconstancy reigns, | and the most perverse man is often the prince's minister, | more acceptable to them. Therefore, whoever shrinks from glory | and from lies, and whom naked truth surrounds, | let him not enter the courts of princes.
Hartman. Scopper.

units.la: AN H ΛEONTH MH ΕΞΙΚΗΤΑΙ, ΤΗΝ ΑΛΩ-ΠΕΚΗΝ ΠΡΟΣΑΨΟΝ.
units.tr: If the lion cannot reach it, attach the fox's skin [ΑΝ ΛΕΩΝ ΜΗ ΕΞΙΚΗΤΑΙ, ΤΗΝ ΑΛΩΠΕΚΗΝ ΠΡΟΣΑΨΟΝ]

units.la: Sit Princeps mitis, constans, mansuetus, & absq; Ira præcipiti, fraudibus, atq; dolo: Tardus & ad pœnas, velox ad præmia danda, Et doleat quotiens cogitur esse ferox.
units.tr: Let the prince be gentle, steadfast and mild, free from headlong anger, from deceit and from guile. Slow to punish, swift to give rewards, let him grieve whenever he is forced to be harsh.

units.la: Nicolaus Machiauellus Florentinus, vir doctissimus & peritissimus, sed impius ac malus, in quo virtutes vitiis certant, si non a vitiis longo interuallo relinquuntur: Is edito libro (quem de Principe vel Princeps inscripsit) persuadere magistratibus conatus est, ne religionem in cordibus suis curent vllâ, interim tamen vt eam externa specie simulent. Fidem nec subditis nec aliis magistratibus seruent etiam sanctissime promissam: denique hortatur magistratus, vt omnes actiones suas ad priuatum commodum referant, vt facultatibus & dignitatibus augeantur, etiamsi iniquissimis hoc consequantur rationibus. Has impietates & in Christianis auribus paradoxa horrenda recensere, vel recitare refutare est. Eas taxare nostrum emblema conatur.
units.tr: Nicolaus Machiavellus of Florence, a man most learned and skilled, but impious and wicked, in whom virtues contend with vices, if they are not left far behind by vices. In his published book, which he titled De Principe or The Prince, he tried to persuade magistrates not to care for religion in their hearts at all, but to feign it by outward show.
