They should keep faith neither with their subjects nor with other magistrates, even where they have promised most solemnly. Finally, he urges magistrates to refer all their actions to private advantage, so that they may be enriched in wealth and honours, even if they achieve this by the most unjust means. To list these impieties and horrible paradoxes to Christian ears is to refute them merely by reciting them. Our emblem seeks to censure them.

units.la: Corradians, intus periuriis plenum & caedibus, vna cum vulpe nequitiæ, doli & fraudis hieroglyphico, Pellacis magistratus indicium est: serpentes versutiæ typum præstant. Lupus crudelitatem: Pileus amplia-tus, dilatationem regnorum, significant: sed aristæ cum clepsydra breuitatem simul ac fragilitatem Imperiorum, dolo, fraudibus, truculentia & crudelitate partorum innuunt. Digna certe figura, quæ non æreis sed aureis laminis, & cordib. magistratuum digito diuini Spiritus insculpatur. Quam grata Deo vulpina sit maxime in magistratibus, ostendit Christus, quando de Herode pronunciat, quod vulpes sit & in eodem vulpinam taxat. Veritas & iustitia stipent meum principem, non vulpina pellis, quæ durabilis non est, & vel à Gentili homine derisa: ὁ ἀλώπηξ ἱλαρὸς ὡμένης ἀλλὰ πίχοῦσι. Laudabunt Deum omnes recti corde: vt in-tem sanguinum & dolosi non dimidiabunt dies suos. Prudentiam serpentum Christus imitari iubet, non vulpinam nequitiam ac fraudes. Quod autem si vulpina non succedat, lupinam induere iubet Machiauellus, & vicissim, id in tyrannos non in Christianos ac pios. Deinque timentes magistratus comperet, à quibus Sophistica & Tyrannii abesse & exulare debent quam longissime: nec contra datam fidem & fœdera veniet Princeps meus, sed contra pacta & compactata quanta potest induistria seruabit, cum iure gentium etiam, & merito quidem, infames censeantur, qui contra datam fidem veniant, & iura fœderum leuiter violent: Iosua atque populus Israeliticus, dolis licet atq; mendaciis circumscripti à Gabaonitis, fidem tamen non fregerunt, sed propter timorem Iehouæ seruarunt: alia exempla vetera ac recentia sciens volens omitto. Pistaret aut tam multa sudare ac facere propter regna cæli, quam propter terrena, nam culmo quouis hæc fragiliora sunt, & subinde mutantur, transeunt, intereunt, in quibus incola tantum ac peregrini sumus, in illis veri ciues futuri. Quærendum ergo regnum Dei & eius iustitia, vt elapsa huius ævi clepsydra in possessionem illorum totalem intromittamur.
units.tr: The corn-ears with the water-clock, along with the fox, the hieroglyph of cunning, deceit and fraud, are a sign of a deceitful magistrate, full within of perjuries and slaughters. The serpents stand for craftiness, the wolf for cruelty, and the enlarged cap signifies the widening of kingdoms. But the ears of grain with the water-clock indicate the brevity and fragility of empires won by guile, fraud, savagery and cruelty. It is certainly a fitting figure, to be engraved not on bronze but on gold plates, and on the hearts of magistrates by the finger of the divine Spirit. That the fox-like cunning is most displeasing to God in magistrates, Christ shows when he calls Herod a fox and in the same place rebukes his foxiness. Truth and justice should surround my prince, not a fox's skin, which does not last and has been mocked even by a heathen man [ὁ ἀλώπηξ ἱλαρὸς ... ἀλλὰ πίχουσι]. All the upright in heart shall praise God; but bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days (Ps. 64.; Ps. 55.). Christ bids us imitate the wisdom of serpents, not the foxy wickedness and frauds. But if the fox's skin does not serve, Machiavelli bids us put on the wolf's, and in turn; but that is for tyrants, not for Christians and the pious. Finally, magistrates who fear God will see that sophistry and tyranny must be kept far away and banished as much as possible. My prince will not break faith or covenants given, but will keep pacts and agreements with all his industry, since by the law of nations, and rightly so, those who break a given promise and lightly violate the laws of covenants are counted infamous. Joshua and the people of Israel, though deceived by the Gibeonites through guile and lies, did not break their word but kept it for the fear of Jehovah. I knowingly and willingly pass over other examples, old and recent. Let no one grudge to toil and labour as much for the kingdom of heaven as for earthly kingdoms; for these are more fragile than any straw, and are constantly changing, passing away and perishing, while we are only sojourners and strangers in them, and are to be true citizens in the other. Therefore we must seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness (Matt. 6.), so that, once the water-clock of this age has run out, we may be admitted to full possession of that kingdom.
Hunting Is Lawful.

units.la: Venandi studium licitum mortalibus esse, Hæc præsens docte sculpta tabella monet: Est tamen in rebus modus, & sunt limina fixa, Ultra quos ratio recta salire vetat.
units.tr: This tablet, skilfully carved here, warns that the pursuit of hunting is lawful for mortals. Yet there is a measure in all things, and fixed thresholds beyond which right reason forbids us to leap.

units.la: Venandi studium non omnino improbamus, nedum damnamus. Cum Deus ipse communem ferarum vel animalium vsum concesserit post diluuium, atq; posteros Nohæ Nohamq; ipsum dixit: Timor vester super bestias agri, vt viridem herbam, sic illa omnia dedi vobis. Est ad multa vtilis venatio. Nam ferae conducunt ad alimenta hominum, quo fine Romulus vrbis conditor, quandoq; venabatur, vt se sociosq; aleret: eo fine Æneas ex cineribus Troianus exul ceruum venatum fuisse Virgilius testis est: & adhuc hodie hoc fine tolerari venationes possent, vt victui & amictui hominum seruirent: Omnia n. propter hominem, homo autem conditus est propter Deum. Deinde exercet iuuentutem & homines prauis alioquin studiis intentos, ne otio simul & luxu, luxuriaque diffluant. Homines enim nihil agendo, male agere discunt, & otium fulminar Satanæ dicitur. Quocirca de Diana fabulatur Poetæ, quod a iaculis cupidinis prorsus fuerit immunis, eo quod venationum exercitio dedita amoribus non vacarit. Et sane venatum quam mœchatu fuisse Dauidem Ægyptium, aliosq; præstitisset. Res age, tutus eris, inquit Ouid. Inprimis autem venationes q progymnasmata sunt bellandi, vt sapientibus visum: magna enim inter venationes & instructiones bellorum confinitas est, & Persarum reges venationes tanquam verissimam rerum bellicarum meditationem frequentes coluerunt. Vt iam non dicam de damno, quod fera sylvestres frugibus inferunt, quod deinceps in ipsum Humanum Genus deriuatur: non dicam de herbis & graminibus, quae a feris detonsa maiorem animalibus domesticis nutriendis vtilitatem exhibere possent: satius igitur est venationibus tolli quam tolerari feras. Quid quod hanc voluptatem & non inutile exercitium magnatibus nemo bonus inuidebit nec reprehendet. Quare & a Platone diuino, Academiarum principe legimus commendatam venationem, & Timotheus quidam Atheniensis Princeps, celebratur, cuius plagis Fortuna semper adstitit, & feras in eas coegit, quod felicitatis exemplum vbiq; decantatum reperitur. Denique scriptura quando de exercitiis pietatis atque iustitiae loquitur, venandi verbo non illepide nec infrequenter vtitur. Quamuis neque negare neq; dissimulare possimus, multa inesse venationibus immodicis mala, propter quae apud bonos pessime audiant frequentissime. Nullum prima ævi primi ætate venandi fuit exercitium, quando herbulis atq; radicib. victitabant sancti. Venationibus nusquam legeris in sacris deditos fuisse sanctos, sed homines truculentos, crudeles, profanos, ἀφέσεις, & eos deniq; a quibus tyrannis initium sumsit: Nimrodem, dico, Ismaelem, Esauum, Dardanios, Thebanos, Cretenses, alios, imo Sathanæ fraudes venationibus comparantur, suntque venationes, si pensiculatius excutere velimus, gymnasiae potius ad sæuitiam atque crudelitatem quam ad virtutes. Vluq; compertum est, Sarhanæ sæpe organon fieri, per quod mala quam plurima, parricidia, cædes, latrocinia, &c. operetur: vt in exempl. Fulconis Regis Hierosolymorum Imp. Maximiliani. & aliorum videre est.
units.tr: We do not wholly disapprove of the pursuit of hunting, much less condemn it. For God himself, after the Flood, granted to Noah and his sons the common use of wild beasts and animals, saying: The fear of you shall be upon every beast of the field, as the green herb have I given you all these things. Hunting is useful for many purposes. For wild beasts serve as food for humans, and to this end Romulus, the founder of the city, used to hunt, so that he might feed himself and his companions. To this end, Virgil bears witness, Aeneas, the Trojan exile from the ashes, hunted a stag. And even today hunting could be tolerated for this purpose, to serve the food and clothing of men: for all things are for man, and man is made for God. Further, hunting trains young people and keeps men, who would otherwise be given over to wicked pursuits, from dissolving in idleness and luxury at once. For men who do nothing learn to do evil, and idleness is called the devil's anvil. For this reason the poets tell the story of Diana, that she was wholly free from Cupid's darts because, being devoted to the exercise of hunting, she had no leisure for love. And indeed hunting served David the Egyptian better than adultery, and others as well. Be active, and you will be safe, says Ovid. Above all, hunts are the training exercises of war, as the wise have judged: for there is a great affinity between hunts and the drilling of armies, and the kings of Persia frequently cultivated hunting as the truest rehearsal of martial affairs. Not to mention the damage that wild beasts of the woods do to crops, which in turn rebounds upon the human race itself; not to mention the herbs and grasses, cropped by the wild beasts, which could provide greater benefit for nourishing domestic animals: it is therefore better to remove the wild beasts by hunting than to tolerate them. What is more, no good man will begrudge or condemn this pleasure and useful exercise to the great. Hence we read that hunting was commended by the divine Plato, prince of the Academies, and a certain Timotheus of Athens, a prince, is celebrated, to whose blows Fortune always stood by, and who drove the wild beasts into his nets, an example of happiness found proclaimed everywhere. Finally, when Scripture speaks of the exercises of piety and righteousness, it uses the word hunting not inelegantly and not infrequently. Yet we can neither deny nor conceal that immoderate hunting contains many evils, on account of which it very frequently meets with the worst reputation among good people. In the first age of the world there was no practice of hunting, when the holy men lived on herbs and roots. You will nowhere read that holy men were given to hunting in the sacred writings, but rather fierce, cruel, profane men, dismissals [ἀφέσεις], and those from whom tyranny at last took its beginning: I mean Nimrod, Ishmael, Esau, the Dardanians, the Thebans, the Cretans, and others. Indeed, if we wish to examine more carefully, the snares of Satan are compared to hunts, and hunts are rather training grounds for savagery and cruelty than for virtues. And it has been found by experience that Satan is often made into an instrument, through which he works very many evils: murders, slaughters, robberies, and so on, as may be seen in the examples of Fulco, king of Jerusalem, and the emperor Maximilian and others.
HUNTING AND ITS EVILS

units.la: [Woodcut: a huntsman with antlers and spear, a skeleton with bow and hourglass, a horned satyr with horn, dogs and a stag.] Multa intemperiei venandi incommoda subsunt Adfectus ratio quod nisi recta domet. Concurrunt fraudes, & vafri dæmonis astus, Dulcia patrantur cædibus aucta mala.
units.tr: [Woodcut: a huntsman with antlers and spear, a skeleton with bow and hourglass, a horned satyr with horn, dogs and a stag.] Hunting brings many discomforts unless reason tames the passion. Deceit and the cunning of the crafty demon come together, and sweet pleasures bring about evils made worse by bloodshed.

units.la: Inter alia autem mala quamplurima, quae venationibus, vt plurimum adhaerent, est & hoc, quod Optimates huic dediti studio a grauioribus studiis & politicis exercitiis, officia vocationis quam maxime concernentib, abstrahuntur, & tandem in tyrannidem concedant: quod illustris comentator in Genesin, nostro tepore super exemplo Nimrodi in 10.c. Geneseos deplorat ac reprehendit his verbis: Vsitata est Principum venatio, cui Principes quidam insano studio sic indulgent, vt etiam feriis negotiis eam anteponant, & malint strenui venatores, quam sapientes gubernatores aestimari. Neq; dubitamus quin Gentilitia grauitas hoc studium eodem fine taxare atq; irridere voluerit sub Actaeonis cuiusdam persona, de quo fabulabantur a Diana in ceruum conuersum esse, quam de fabula neq; incongrue neq; illepide quidam sic commentatur: Actaeon in ceruum conuersus docet: Principes quodammodo exuere animum humanum, ac degenerare in naturam ferinam, dum ad fyluas agunt, ibiq; cum feris lustantur. Et quae sequuntur. Quid quod multi thorum coniugalem ferarum studio excubantes in discrimen adducunt non vno modo, quarum generosae vxores, zelotypiae forte oestro percitae, excurrerunt, actuum dominorum experimenta capturae, a quibus feraï loco misere traiectae globis, vel confixae iaculis fuerunt. Nil attineret dicere de eo, quod natura liberae ferae, earumq; vsus, iam potentioribus tantum cedant, nisi ab aliquibus modus ita excederetur, vt feras capientes agricolas non fortunis tantum, & exsulio multent, corpora mutilent, sed capitibus etiam plectant, & suspendio tollant. Vt certe ea est & a tyrannide vel nihil aberrat, vel parum admodum, latumve vix vnguem. Sane cum ferae nullius sint proprie iure naturali sed communes omnibus, at magistratus sibi solis earum ius ac potestatem vendicarint, frui hoc suo quodam iure possent, ad aliquantam recompens. grauis laborum, nec haberent subditi quod valde ringerentur. Esset tamen magistratus pii ac moderati subditos eorumq; bona a feris defendere: propter causas plurimas, & in transgressores non nimis esse feroces ac rigidos: de ultimo supplicio nihil statuunt LL. mitiore longe poena statuunt: pecuniaria carceraria: exsulii, & similem. Deniq; magna carnificina per venationes exercetur in rusticos, subditos, & agricolas, exiguntur illi e sedibus suis per aliquot milliaria, adhibetur etiam honesti ciues ad talia seruilia officia, quae veteres mancipiis vix imposuissent: non relinquitur ocium hominibus miseris & pauperibus, vt suis famelicis domesticis bolum panis lucrari pof. sint: ita perpetuantur, perennanturq; hae exactiones. Nemo igitur pius author aut suasor suo magistratui esse vel potest vel debet, vt tam iniurio studio tam insanum in modum indulgeat, nedum vt propter feram interfectam hominem ad imaginem Dei creatum prorsus e medio tollat.
units.tr: Among the many other evils that usually cling to hunting is this: nobles given over to this pursuit are drawn away from more serious studies and from political exercises, and from the duties of their calling as far as possible, and in the end they slide into tyranny. The distinguished commentator on Genesis laments and rebukes this in our own time, in his comment on the example of Nimrod in Genesis 10, with these words: The hunting of princes is a common practice, to which some princes give themselves with such a mad passion that they put it ahead even of their public business, and prefer to be esteemed vigorous hunters rather than wise governors. Nor do we doubt that the seriousness of the Gentiles wished to censure and mock this same pursuit under the figure of a certain Actaeon, of whom they told the fable that he was turned into a stag by Diana. Someone comments on this fable not inappropriately or without wit: Actaeon, turned into a stag, teaches that princes in some way strip off the human mind and degenerate into the nature of beasts, when they go about in the woods and there revel with the wild beasts. And what follows. Moreover, many who keep watch over their marriage bed for the sake of wild beasts bring it into danger in more ways than one, when their noble wives, perhaps stung by the gadfly of jealousy, run out to the trial of their lords' hunting, and are wretchedly pierced through by balls or struck by spears in place of the beast. There would be no point in saying that the natural liberty of wild beasts, and their use, now yields only to the more powerful, unless some have carried this so far that they punish farmers who catch the beasts not only with loss of property and exile, fining them and mutilating their bodies, but also with the loss of their heads, and hang them. Indeed this practice differs from tyranny either not at all, or very little, not even the thickness of a nail. Surely, since wild beasts belong to no one by natural right but are common to all, while magistrates have claimed for themselves alone the right and power over them, they might enjoy this right of theirs as a kind of compensation for the heavy burden of their labours, and their subjects would have nothing to complain of bitterly. Yet it would be the mark of a pious and moderate magistrate to defend his subjects and their goods from the wild beasts, and for many reasons not to be too fierce and harsh against transgressors: the laws do not lay down the ultimate punishment, but prescribe a far milder penalty: fines, imprisonment, exile, and the like. In short, a great slaughter is carried out through hunting among peasants, subjects and farmers; they are driven from their homes for several miles; respectable citizens are also made to perform such servile duties as the ancients would scarcely have imposed on slaves; no leisure is left to miserable and poor men to earn a morsel of bread for their hungry households; and so these exactions are perpetuated and kept going forever. No pious author or adviser, therefore, can or should advise his magistrate to indulge so immoderately in so unjust a passion, much less to remove completely from the midst a man created in the image of God for the sake of a slain beast.

units.la: Venationes impediunt officia vocationis. Vid. comment. Sabin. in lib. Ouid. metamorph. Meminit huius incommodi Ludou. Viues de instit. faemin. Christia. §. de Zelotyp. D. Nic. Selnec. pædagog. in f. præcept. Vid. Danaus in Ethic. Chriftian. in 6. L. Secund. tab. Allegat Selnec. in pad. C. non est. Saxon lib. 2. art. 2 & Iur. Francic. Remus in Spicileg. Lusus Domin. norum luftus subditorum.
units.tr: Hunting hinders the duties of one's calling. See the commentary of Sabinus on Ovid's Metamorphoses. Ludovicus Vives mentions this inconvenience in his De institutione feminae christianae, in the section on jealousy. Dr Nicolaus Selnecker, in his Paedagogia, at the end of the precepts. See Danaeus, Ethica christiana, on the sixth commandment, in the second table. Selnecker cites in Paedagogia, and the Saxon law book, book 2, art. 2, and the Frankish law. Remus, in Spicilegium: the sport of lords, the ruin of subjects.

units.la: DOLVS AN VIRTVS QVIS IN hoste requirat.
units.tr: Whether Guile or Courage Is to Be Sought Against an Enemy

units.la: Talia sunt belli incommoda, vt iure quis dubitare possit, an belli vnquam decertandum & experiundum sit. Verum cum & diuino mandato bella quodam gesta sint, & Deus exercituum Dominus in sacris literis appelletur: promiferitq; se iusta & Domini bellantibus bella potenter atq; gratiose adfuturum, etiamq; stratagemata docuerit, quibus circumscribendus sit hostis, bella legitima recte suscipi possunt, maxime v. si aliter non possis, & in solis sola spes armis proxime Deum posita esse videantur. Tum vero solicite admodum faciendum est Imperatori exercitus, vt vulpina vtantur astutia & prudentia serpentina: Verbis & consilio prius omnia experiatur quam armis: etiam ipsum hostem (si quidem fieri id vtiliter vllo modo potest) conueniat, si res transigi atq; coponi possit, quod quam fractuosum sit, multis exemplis probatum & compertum est. Si hac non succedat, & arma omnino capescenda sint, ante omnia Deum ... & felicem oret euentum: nam sola fere oratione hostem victum ac profligatum esse cum sacra tum profana et exempla docent. Moses oratione pro exercitu Israelitico pugnabat, & vincebat. Samuel itidem. Theodosius nocturnis precibus confudit ac dissipauit exercitum. Legio itidem tempore M. Antonini Imper. contra Marcomannos & Quados. Absq; fiducia auxilii diuini nihil faciat, nam cruentos hęc temeritas euentus sortitur, vt in exemplis videre est, quę annotamus. Positum castrorum prudenter consilerabit nostro Imperator. Neruum belli, sumptus duco, probe expendat mente & opere. In exploratores si quid expendat, pro lucro reputabit id vel sacra docent. In conferendis signis sit prudens ac animosus, nam fortitudo sine prudentia temeritas est. Stratagematu vtatur, quibuscunq; commode potest modis, saltem vt sanguini humano parcat effundendo: hic, si non alibi summam laudem obtinent fraudes ac doli: & quanto pretiosior est humanus sanguis, tanto gloriosius vincet, qui sine multo fusofanguine vincit. excubias solicite aget gruis instar nec dulci piius declinet lumina somno quam omnia in numero, pondere, atq; mensura q. disposuerit, & caverit. Deniq; in sola Cruce Christi ipsam victoria ponat: a Domino enim victoria est: qui aeque per paucos quam per multos vincit, quod illustrissimo Constantini Magni Imp exemplo (ad quod hoc notrum alludit) probatum, ei cum Licinio Collega & adfine signa collaturo pro re Christiana, & iam precibus pie ac prudenter excubanti apparet signum Christi crucifixi, in eoq; verba:
units.tr: Such are the inconveniences of war that one might well doubt whether war should ever be fought and undertaken at all. But since wars have been waged by divine command, and the Lord is called "the Lord of hosts" in the sacred writings, and he has promised to be powerfully and graciously present with the Lord's warriors in just wars, and has even taught stratagems by which an enemy may be outwitted, lawful wars may rightly be undertaken, especially if you cannot otherwise act, and when all hope seems to lie in arms alone, placed next to God. Then indeed the commander of an army must take great care to use the cunning of the fox and the prudence of the serpent. Let him try everything first by words and counsel before arms. Let him also meet the enemy himself, if this can be done profitably in any way, in case the matter can be settled and composed; how fruitful this is has been proved and established by many examples. If this does not succeed, and arms must in every case be taken up, then above all he must pray to God ... and for a happy outcome; for both sacred and profane examples teach that an enemy has been conquered and routed by almost prayer alone. Moses fought and conquered by prayer on behalf of the army of Israel. Samuel likewise. Theodosius by nocturnal prayers confounded and scattered his army. A legion likewise, in the time of M. Antoninus the Emperor, against the Marcomanni and Quadi. Let him do nothing without confidence in divine help, for such rashness brings about bloody outcomes, as may be seen in the examples which we note. Let the emperor prudently consider the placing of his camp. The sinews of war: let him weigh the expenses carefully, in mind and in deed. Whatever he spends on scouts, he shall count as gain; sacred writings also teach this. In joining battle let him be prudent and spirited, for courage without prudence is rashness. Let him use stratagem in whatever manner he conveniently can, at least so that he spares human blood from being shed. Here, if nowhere else, fraud and trickery win the highest praise: and the more precious human blood is, the more glorious the victory of him who conquers without much blood being shed. He shall keep watch diligently, like a crane, and not let his eyes droop in sweet sleep until he has arranged and guarded everything by number, weight and measure. Finally, let him place the victory itself in the Cross of Christ alone: for the victory is from the Lord, who conquers equally by few as by many. This was proved by the most illustrious example of Constantine the Great (to which this our emblem alludes), when, about to join battle for the Christian cause with his colleague Licinius, and already keeping devout and prudent watch in prayer, the sign of Christ crucified appeared to him, and with it these words:

units.la: ἐν τούτῳ νίκα: IN HOC VINCE.
units.tr: By this, conquer [ἐν τούτῳ νίκα]: IN HOC VINCE.
Until now I thought you had horns.

units.la: [Engraving: emblem picture, horseman on a horse with feathered hat, troops in background, a bird on a stone base at lower left; not transcribed as text.] Vt timidi lepores ad tympana rauca feruntur, Sic animos gestant ad fera bella pigri. Bella decent animos, & fortia pectora. quare Bella gerant alii: tu Pari semper ama.
units.tr: As timid hares are carried off to the harsh drums, so lazy men carry their spirits off to fierce wars. Wars suit spirited men and brave hearts. Let others wage wars; you, Paris, always love.

units.la: Bellum Coneni cura fuerit, aiunt: hoc est, fortibus, prudentibus, animosis bella gerenda committantur, qui vt maxime semel succumbat, & leui certamine superentur, animum tamen resumunt, vires reparant, & maioribus quam antea, prudentioribusque machinis hostem adoriuntur, iuxta illud: Ἀνὴρ φιλόνικος πολλὰ μαχόμενος.
units.tr: Let Conon's war be his concern, they say. That is, wars should be entrusted to brave, prudent and spirited men, who, even if they are overcome once, and defeated in a minor encounter, nonetheless take heart again, restore their strength, and attack the enemy with greater strength and wiser devices, according to the saying: "A man who loves victory, fighting often" [Ἀνὴρ φιλόνικος πολλὰ μαχόμενος].

units.la: Arma viri, bellumque gerant, quae bella gerenda.
units.tr: Let men bear arms and wage war, which wars are to be waged.

units.la: Turnus apud Virgilium: vir timidus, ignavus, meticulosus, ad colum magis quam ad Romphæam aptus, ad arma adhibendus non est: nunquam feliciter Martis cadet alea, quando γυνὴ τεχνηγής, ἡ γυνὴ τεχνηγή: vt ille ait: Ideoque alterutrum requisitorum adsit, aut animosus Imperator, & timidus exercitus, aut si Imperator meticulosus sit, fortem esse exercitum decet. Illud tamen malim, vt dicitur: Malo exercitum ceruorum, cuius dux sit Leo, quam exercitum Leonum cuius dux sit ceruus. Tota rei summa ab Imperatore pendet, quemadmodum Israelitae suo Regi Dauidi dicunt: Non es processurus, nam si plane fugeremus, non apponerent ad nos animum, sive morerentur dimidium nostrum, apponerent ad nos animum, si decies mille nostrum caderet: quare nunc melius fuerit, &c. ideoque Prudentia ac Fortitudine ante omnes opus est Imperatori. Is autem exercitus eminet, quando Leones Leonem Ducem gerunt.
units.tr: Turnus in Virgil: a man who is timid, lazy and fearful, fit for the distaff rather than the sword, is not to be employed in arms; the dice of Mars never fall happily when "a woman skilled in craft, a woman skilled in craft" [γυνὴ τεχνηγής, ἡ γυνὴ τεχνηγή]. As he says: therefore, let one of the two requisites be present: either a spirited commander and a timid army, or, if the commander is fearful, the army ought to be brave. Yet I would rather have the saying: "I would rather have an army of stags whose leader is a lion than an army of lions whose leader is a stag." The whole sum of the matter depends on the commander, just as the Israelites say to their king David: "You shall not go out, for if we indeed flee, they will not set their minds on us; or if half of us die, they will set their minds on us; but if ten thousand of us fall, now it will be better for you, etc." Therefore prudence and fortitude are needed above all in a commander. An army stands out when lions have a lion for their leader.

units.la: Ψιλάνθρωποι, & tales, quales Achilles Agamemnoni in decennali illa Graecorum ad Troiam expeditione obiicit:
units.tr: Weaklings [Ψιλάνθρωποι], and such men as Achilles reproached Agamemnon with in that ten-year Greek expedition to Troy:

units.la: Ὀνοβάρβαροι, κυνὸς ὑμμὴ ἴχων, χερσὶν ἐλαφοι qui non fœnum in cornu sed animum in pedibus habent, pectora ceruina, leporina, muliebria gestantes, armis tam apti, quam asinus lyrae, sunt, Tropæa nunquam statuunt: in conflictu fugiunt: Exemplo si opes sine nocent: quare etiam diuino oraculo ex authoriti, adq; domesticum larem remitti iubentur. In concionibus, (vt Demosthenis animoso Oratori, sed ignauo Bellatori, obiiciebant) fortes sunt, in hostili congressu vix ventris onus caninum in morem continent. Apage tales, plus oberunt quam proderunt, qui ne amicis quidem fideles sunt, vt docet exemplum Imp. Mauritii & successoris Parricida, Phocae de quo historiae referunt: Quod Mauritius somniauerit, se militi suo Phocae iugulandum tradi: quare Philippicum ex carcere eductum interrogat, qualis sit Phocas, qui respondet: Centurionem esse, eumque ambitiosum & timidum, subiicit gloriosus & Optimus Imp. Mauritius, si timidus est, homicida est: πὰρ ἢ δεινῶν φοβὸς. Certe si cululli euacuandi: Venus colenda: furandum deniq; sit, (vt haec tabula docet) Heroes tales sunt, iuxta Prophetam.
units.tr: "Ass-brained, with a dog's eyes, with a deer's heart" [Ὀνοβάρβαροι, κυνὸς ὄμμα ἔχων, καρδίην ἐλάφοιο]. They have not hay in their horns but spirit in their feet; they carry deer's breasts, hare's breasts, womanish breasts; they are as fit for arms as an ass for the lyre. They never set up trophies; in the fight they flee. Example: if resources do no harm without... For which reason they are also ordered, by divine oracle and by authority, to be sent back to their domestic hearth. In the assemblies they are brave (as they objected to Demosthenes, an animated orator but a cowardly warrior); in the encounter with the enemy they can scarcely contain the burden of their belly, like dogs. Away with such men! They do more harm than good, and they are not even faithful to their friends, as the example of the Emperor Maurice and his parricide successor Phocas teaches, of whom the histories tell: that Maurice dreamed he was to be handed over to his soldier Phocas to be slaughtered; so he asks Philippicus, brought out of prison, what sort of man Phocas is. He answers that he is a centurion, ambitious and timid. The glorious and excellent Emperor Maurice adds: "If he is timid, he is a murderer" [πὰρ ἢ δεινῶν φοβὸς]. Certainly, if chamber pots must be emptied, Venus must be worshipped, and finally stealing must be done, as this picture teaches, then such are the heroes, according to the Prophet.
ATROCIOUS CRIMES, ATROCIOUS PUNISHMENTS.
[engraving: emblem picture, not transcribed]

units.la: Auri sacra fames, madidi malus vsus Iacchi,Et venus, Imperiis vltima fata ferunt.Quo finis propior, magis hoc quoq; crimina crescunt,Præcipitat pœnas & mala turba graues. Multæ
units.tr: The accursed hunger for gold, the evil practice of drunken Bacchus, and lust bring about the final ruin of empires. The nearer the end, the more these crimes grow, and a crowd of evils hastens grievous punishments. Many

units.la: Multa sunt, quae animos frangunt, & gloriosam in expeditionib. victoriam mortalibus inuident, quae hoc nostro emblemate notantur ac perstringuntur, Germanis nobis vel inprimis euitanda ac fugienda.
units.tr: There are many things that break men's spirits and envy them a glorious victory in campaigns. These are marked and pierced by this emblem of ours, and they must be avoided and shunned above all by us Germans.

units.la: Primum est anaritia atq; φιλονεικία, cui si plerique deditì sint, haud dubie hostes externi sine labore fines inuadunt, depopulantur, vastant, vel nemine obsistente.Per hanc ciues pecuniam bello requisitam Imperatori negant, neruumq; belli subtrahunt.Per hanc Imperator, vrbes, oppida, ac regiones necessariis praesidiis nudar, & hosti Imperii q. claues tradit. Per hanc Duces exercitui & militibus stipendia suffurantur, ac minuunt salaria. Per hanc milites gregarius non quae belli pacisue, sed quae crumenae sunt suae curat. Quod crimen Prophetae pro causa excidii regni Israelitici allegant. Huic deditus caetera bonus Mauritius Imp. exosus militibus factus, & tandem obtruncatus est. Per hanc florentissimum Orientis Imperium Christianis ereptum est, & Imperatoria sedes Constantinopolis turpissime cessit Turcis. Er quis dubitabit adhuc, id criminis in causa fuisse hactenus, quod Turcico tyranno superiori seculo tot munimenta, propugnacula, castella, vrbes & regiones cum perpetua Christiani nominis infamia traditae sint? Taurinum certe (alia omitto) Christianis per hoc ereptum esse constat.
units.tr: The first is avarice and philonikia [φιλονεικία]. If most men are given over to it, foreign enemies undoubtedly invade our borders without effort, plunder and lay waste, with no one to resist. Through this, citizens refuse the money demanded for the war from the Emperor and withdraw the sinews of war. Through this, the Emperor strips cities, towns and regions of necessary garrisons and hands over the keys of the empire to the enemy. Through this, commanders embezzle the soldiers' pay and reduce their wages. Through this, common soldiers care not for the affairs of war or peace but only for their own purses. The prophets cite this sin as the cause of the ruin of the kingdom of Israel. Given over to this, among other things, the good Emperor Mauritius became hateful to his soldiers and was finally cut down. Through this the most flourishing empire of the East was snatched from the Christians, and the imperial seat of Constantinople shamefully surrendered to the Turks. Who will still doubt that this crime was the cause of the fact that, in the last century, so many fortresses, bulwarks, castles, cities and regions were handed over to the Turkish tyrant, with lasting disgrace to the Christian name? Taurinum, at least (I omit other examples), is known to have been taken from the Christians in this way.

units.la: Secundum Temulentia est & ebriositas, & inde dimanans armorum neglectus, vides hic acinacem acuentem suum Turcam, & res suas solicite agentem, nihilq; omittentem, quod ad gloriosam victoriam obtinendum, & regni dilatanda Turcici pomeria faciat, cum interim Dux Christianus suum Bacchum, i.e. vinum refrigerat, dolum frigida temperat, & culullos parat: dic quaeso? nunquid haec Sodoma & Gomorrha erat luxuries? an non idem exprobrat Deus suis per Prophetam: Vae valentibus potare vinum, & strenuis ad miscendum potum inebriantem! Ridiculum simul ac detestandum est quod de Sybaritis referunt, qui in comportationibus suis non taratantarae sonum classica cientis ferre, sed admotum tibiarum nymphę in more saltare assuefecerunt equos, eoq; merito a Crotoniatis superati. Quis Scytharum exercitum a Cyro per ingluuie casum non ignorat? in hoc vitio regnas, Germania! Exl.sunt odiosa.
units.tr: The second is drunkenness and intemperance, and from these flows neglect of arms. Here you see the Turk sharpening his scimitar and attending diligently to his affairs, omitting nothing that might help him win a glorious victory and extend the borders of the Turkish kingdom. Meanwhile the Christian commander cools his Bacchus, that is, his wine, tempers his drink with cold water and prepares his cups. Tell me, please: was this not the luxury of Sodom and Gomorrah? Does God not rebuke the same thing in his people through the prophet: Woe to those who are mighty to drink wine, and valiant at mixing strong drink! It is both ridiculous and detestable what they report about the Sybarites, who taught their horses not to bear the sound of the trumpet calling to battle during their marches, but to dance at the sound of approaching flute-girls, and for this reason they were defeated by the Crotoniates. Who does not know that the army of the Scythians was ruined by gluttony under Cyrus? You reign in this vice, Germany! Examples are tiresome.

units.la: Deniq; venus, luxuria, stupra, adulteria, sodomia, bestialitates mutaq; peccata alia omnium ordinum extremam virgae diuinae manum adferut, & per haec desuescentia armorum, vt equi ad vxores proximorum suorum adhinniunt, haec πανολιτεία Imperiis ac Rebuspublicis accersit, vt penes sacra etiam vnico profano testatum faciemus exemplo ex Iustino: Arma & equi ademptii illi (de Lydis loquitur) iussiq; cauponas & ludicras artes & lenocinia exercere. Et sic gens induistria quondam potens & manu strenua effeminata mollitie, luxuriaq; virtutem pristinam perdidit: & quos ante Cyrum inuictos bella praestiterant, in luxuriam lapsos otium ac desidia superauit.
units.tr: Finally, lust, luxury, debauchery, adultery, sodomy, bestiality and other unspeakable sins bring the last hand of the divine rod upon every rank of people. Through these, a neglect of arms, so that horses neigh after the wives of their neighbours, brings upon empires and commonwealths universal corruption of the state [πανολιτεία]. We shall make this clear even from sacred history, and also from one profane example, taken from Justin: They were deprived of arms and horses (he speaks of the Lydians) and ordered to practise the trades of innkeepers and actors and the arts of pimping. And so a people once powerful in industry and vigorous of hand, made effeminate by softness and luxury, lost its former valour, and those whom before Cyrus no wars had overcome, having fallen into luxury, were overcome by idleness and sloth.
Justin, book 1, p. 8, Wechel edition.
THE EMBLEM: MEN ARE IRRECONCILABLE [ἄσπονδοι].

units.la: [Engraving: a street scene with houses, a church spire and a fountain-like building at the back. In the foreground a man in a cloak draws a sword against a second swordsman. A skeleton with a spear stands behind them, and a dog runs at the lower left. Figures fight in the background, and a group of townspeople stands at the right.] Candida Mortales Concordia viseret oras, Imbueretq; animos Pax opulenta hominum: Tum Fortuna suas roraret diuite cornu Dotes, omnigenum deforet hautq; bonum.
units.tr: [Engraving: a street scene with houses, a church spire and a fountain-like building at the back. In the foreground a man in a cloak draws a sword against a second swordsman. A skeleton with a spear stands behind them, and a dog runs at the lower left. Figures fight in the background, and a group of townspeople stands at the right.] May bright Concord visit mortal shores, and rich Peace fill men's minds. Then Fortune would shower her gifts from her full horn and pour out every kind of good.

units.la: Nulla vnquam gens fuit tam barbara ac ferox, quæ non pacem bello, & discordiæ concordiam multis parasangis præstulerit, & merito quidem, nam tantum pacis atq; concordiæ bonum est, malumq; belli atq; discordiæ; vt verbis æquare rem nullius eloquentiæ flumen possit: quod vel ipsius Sallustii hominis alioquin Gentilis ac profani testimonio patefit: Concordia, dicentis, parua res crescunt, discordia vero magna dilabuntur. Si vero gentem vllã, certe Christianos decerete pax & concordia, dedeceret bellum ac discordia, qui singulari Spiritus vnitate conglutinamur. Sed eheu hostiliter inuicem dissidemus, infestis armis concurrimus, & de re saepissime leuissima tanquam de aris ac focis digladiamur: quod ipsum præsens nostrum ἐμφυλίωμα arguit ac sugillat. Per Hierarchias deducere placet.
units.tr: No nation has ever been so barbarous and fierce that it has not preferred peace to war and concord to discord by many leagues, and rightly so. For the good of peace and concord is so great, and the evil of war and discord so great, that no flood of eloquence could match the matter in words. This is shown even by the testimony of Sallust, a man who was otherwise a Gentile and a profane writer: "Through concord, small things grow; through discord, great things fall apart." But if any people should be bound by peace and concord, certainly we Christians should, who are joined together by the singular unity of the Spirit. Yet, alas, we are at odds with one another in hostile fashion; we rush together with weapons drawn, and we fight to the death over matters that are very often most trivial, as if over altars and hearths. Our present civil strife [ἐμφυλίωμα] itself proves and exposes this. I intend to lead this through the hierarchies.

units.la: In statu Ecclesiastico quam infesto atq; ancipiti pugnamus Marte: quam hostiliter digladiamur: quam temere decernimus: nulla fere honoris gloriæq; diuinæ, & ampliandorū Ecclesiæ pomeriorum, exædificandarum concscientiarum, sed saltem φιλονικίας, φιλοτιμίας, simultatum fouedarum ducitur ratio; Commendatur fraterna ἰσονοια, quæ in idem velle ac nolle consistit, & τοῖς φρονεῦσι ἐν κυρίῳ consistit, sed nemo sese huic obsequentem vel studiosum præbet: Mordemus inuicem, quam periculum etiam est ne inuicem consumamur, & veritas altercando amittatur, quemadmodum multis retro seculis cuenisse in propatulo est. De sacerdotibus inter se ipsis dicam: quam tenaciter hæreant odia, simultates, inimicitiæ: peius quam in Iuda & Leuissimis quibusque: vaticinium Pauli ... liquidissime completum cernitur.
units.tr: In the ecclesiastical state, how hostilely and doubtfully we fight; how savagely we fight to the death; how rashly we decide! Almost no account is taken of the honour and glory of God, of enlarging the borders of the Church, or of building up consciences. Instead, account is taken only of rivalry [φιλονικία], ambition [φιλοτιμία] and the nursing of grudges. Brotherly equality [ἰσονοια], which consists in wanting and not wanting the same things, and in being "of the same mind in the Lord" [τοῖς φρονοῦσι ἐν κυρίῳ], is commended, but no one shows himself willing or eager to obey it. We bite one another, and there is even danger that we will devour one another, and the truth will be lost in the quarrelling, as is plain to see has happened many times in past ages. I will speak of the priests among themselves: how tenaciously hatreds, grudges and enmities cling to them, worse than in Judas and in the most worthless men. The prophecy of Paul ... is seen to be most clearly fulfilled.

units.la: In Politico statu, quam rarus candor! quam frequentes pugnæ! quam horrida certamina! De vmbra asini quantæ sæpe lanienæ! de vno lepore quanti sæpe tumultus! de agri sulco quantæ altercationes! videlicet: Omne regnum inter se diuisum desolabitur, & domus cadit super domum. Exsurge Deus, & concede propitius, vt inhabitet gloria in terra nostra, vt misericordia & veritas obuient sibi, iustitia & pax osculentur se, vt veritas de terra oriatur, & iustitia de coelo prospiciat, &c.
units.tr: In the political state, how rare is candour! how frequent are the battles! how dreadful the contests! Over the shadow of an ass, how many butcheries there have often been! Over a single hare, how many uproars! Over a furrow of a field, how many quarrels! Clearly: "Every kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation, and house falls upon house." Arise, O God, and graciously grant "that glory may dwell in our land, that mercy and truth may meet together, righteousness and peace may kiss each other, that truth may spring out of the earth and righteousness look down from heaven," etc.

units.la: In Oeconomico ordine, & conuersatione ciuili præter, iurgia, altercationes, dissidia audias nihil, alter alterius iugulum petit, etiam & quidem haud infrequenter inter eos, quos Deus & natura peculiariter deuinxerunt diuina ἐκ ἐπιθυμίας Sapientia de nostro certe seculo gloriari non potest: Tribus rebus speciosa effecta sum, & surrexi speciosa coram Domino, coram Domino & hominibus: concordia, fratrum & amicitia propinqui, & viro ac muliere, quibus inter ipsos conuenit, &c.
units.tr: In the household order and in civil life, you hear nothing but wrangling, quarrels and dissensions; each seeks the other's throat, and this happens not infrequently even between those whom God and nature have bound together in a special way. Divine wisdom cannot boast of our age in this regard: "I am made beautiful by three things, and I stand up beautiful before the Lord and before men: the concord of brothers, the friendship of neighbours, and a husband and wife who agree together," etc.

units.la: Quare, omnibus seuere edictum esto: Alter alterius onera portate, & legem Christi implebitis.
units.tr: Therefore let this edict be strictly issued to all: "Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ."
NO SAFETY IN WAR.
When Bellona shakes her savage whip,
all the wealth of the lands is shaken.

units.la: Tot mala sunt bello, rutilo quot sydera cælo:
units.tr: As many evils attend war as stars in the ruddy sky.
The conquered weep, and the victor groans when Mars falls.

units.la: Inter discordiam & bellū hoc interest, vt illa priuatim, hoc publice exerceatur: illa paucorum, hoc multorum fit: illa fine singulari aliorum damno, hoc vero non nili etiam aliorū damno atq; iniuria geratur. Quare quo plures hoc occupantur & implicantur, eo et immanius est & inhumanius, vt omnem plane hominem exuisse videantur, qui tam infestis inter se armis breuiter concurrunt & decertant, & totas regiones nationesq; in extrema discrimina adducunt. Id quod à multis cum prisci tum recentioris aeui piis bonisq; agnitum ac deploratum est. Quo magis mirandum est inter nos Christianos esse qui tam leuiter ac praecipiti ad arma furore feratur, & quidem tam leuib. de caulis: Lepus captus est: manipulus leguminis ablatus: pedem pede pressit: & quæ sunt similia leuia & ludicra. Quod Gentilitius ille homo tanquam vanum ac temerarium non immerito deridet:
units.tr: Between discord and war there is this difference: discord is carried on privately, war publicly; discord involves few, war many; discord brings harm only to individuals, whereas war is waged not without harm and injury even to others. Therefore, the more people who are occupied and entangled in it, the more monstrous and inhuman it is, so that those who briefly engage and contend with such hostile arms, and bring whole regions and nations to the brink of ruin, seem to have wholly put off the character of man. This has been recognised and deplored by many pious and good men, both of ancient and of more recent times. All the more remarkable is it that among us Christians there are those who are carried away to arms so lightly and rashly, and indeed for such trivial causes: the hare was caught; a bundle of pulse was carried off; he pressed foot upon foot; and other such petty and foolish things. That heathen man rightly mocks this as vain and reckless:

units.la: Belli causa fuit violatus vulnere teruum.
units.tr: The cause of the war was the wound of a violated ... (a tender wound).

units.la: Quis vnquam sanus Græcorum decennalem expeditionem propter vnam fornicariam fæmellam imo propter putidum prostibulum aduersus Troianos gestam probauit? Tullius certe Hostilius Rex Romanus Legatis cum Numinis diuini summa obtestatione dicebat: Nuntiate regi vestro, Regem Roman. Deos facere testes, vt prius populus res repetetes legatos aspernatus dimiserit, vt in eum omnes expectant huiusce cladis belli. Hæc homo Gentilis. Vbi nunc est fidos tua, Iuliane Cardinalis, quæ et bene consopitum bellum è fauiliis & cineribus resuscitare, pactas inducias dissoluere, &numinis obtestatione fœdusq; tam leuiter frangere non exhorruisti? Arma sine damno nunquam arripiū tur, siue victor triumphes, siue victus lugeas. Omnia victoria cruenta est, nulla incruenta. Hoc vsu semper compertum, quod exactis inimicitiis, & depositis armis victor doleat, victus fleat, siue felici Marte, siue cum Erasina de, quod aiunt, sit decertatum. Quanta enim belli sint incommoda atq; damna, neq; cogitando mens, nec lingua fando vlla ... qui potest. Committuntur bello blasphemiae: silent leges diuinae & humanae patrantur periuria: Consulunt Pythones: ædunt hierarchiae: ædes ac latrocinia in infinitum exercentur: virgines nobiles constuprantur: designantur adulteria: fiunt incestus: rapinarum non est numerus: deuastantur omnia: mutantur ferro ac flamma in solitudines, exculti vici: artificiosa oppida: numerosæ vrbes: solo æquantur regiones: ius vicinorum & confœderatorum potenter est vt non violetur: deniq; multo facilius dixeris quæ bona non sunt, quam quæ committantur mala: hæc adeo vera sunt, vt etiam Poeta exclamet:
units.tr: Who in his right mind ever approved of the Greeks' ten-year expedition against the Trojans, waged for the sake of one harlot, indeed for a stinking brothel-girl? Tullus Hostilius, the Roman king, certainly said to the envoys, with the greatest invocation of the divine power: Tell your king that the King of the Romans calls the gods to witness that, since the people rejected the envoys who demanded the goods back, all expect this war to bring such a disaster upon him. So spoke a heathen man. Where now is your good faith, Julian the Cardinal, who did not shrink from reviving a war that had been well laid to rest out of its embers and ashes, from breaking agreed truces, and from so lightly violating a covenant made under invocation of the divine power? Arms are never taken up without loss, whether the victor triumphs or the vanquished mourns. Every victory is bloody; none is bloodless. Experience has always shown that, once enmities are ended and arms laid down, the victor grieves and the vanquished weeps, whether the battle was fought with fortune favouring one side or, as they say, with Erasinus. For the troubles and losses of war cannot be grasped by thought, nor described by any tongue... Blasphemies are committed in war; divine and human laws fall silent; perjuries are perpetrated; oracles are consulted; hierarchies are raised up; murders and robberies are carried on without end; noble virgins are violated; adulteries are plotted; incests are committed; plunder is beyond counting; everything is laid waste; by fire and sword, cultivated villages become wildernesses and well-built towns become desolate; populous cities are levelled with the ground; regions are reduced to bare soil; the rights of neighbours and allies are violated with impunity. In short, you could more easily name the things that are not good than the evils that are committed. These things are so true that even the poet cries out:

units.la: Nulla salus belli pacem te posci mus omnes.
units.tr: There is no safety in war; we all ask you for peace.

units.la: Angeli nato Pacis Principe, Orbis seruatore. Pacem non bella annunciant Vrbi & Orbi: ad cuius tempora dudum gestiit Prophe ta: Tu ... inquit, gladios suos in ligones, & hastas suas in falces: non attollet gens vlla in aitera jam gladium, neq; discent amplius bellum.
units.tr: The angels, announcing the birth of the Prince of Peace, the Saviour of the world, proclaim peace, not war, to the city and to the world. For his times the prophet long ago rejoiced, saying: He will beat their swords into mattocks and their spears into pruning hooks; no nation shall any more lift up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any more.
EVIL DOUBLED WITH EVIL
Not without reason are you armed with the two-pronged iron, Neptune,
For you are hostile and do harm by a double disaster and a double manner:
What madness, mortals, alas, has taken hold of you!

units.la: Non vnum satis est; nunc geminate malum!
units.tr: One evil is not enough; now double the evil!

units.la: Multa ac varia per se sunt mariis discrimina, ut non immerito gratesillii imperet diuinus Psalmographus, qui è maris procellu saluus emerserit: sed tanta humanarum mentium caecitas est, ut Neptunum cum Marte committere, seu nauali bus praeliis experiri, hoc est, malum malo conduplicare non horreant, in quos tamen & Mars & Neptunus (iniquissimi sancti!) insolubili foedere coniurarunt. Talé exemplum, in sacris, quod sciam, nusquam legi. Magna haec dementia! quoq; maius periculum, eo maior temeritas. Nota est Xerxis historia, qui mari compedes iniicere, virgis caedere, & ad libitum ut iret suum, cogere contendit, sed quae eius rei, imo quae eius stupendae temeritatis ac insaniae fuit epitasis? deplorabat ille humanam fragilitatem, qui de tanto suo undecies centum mille hominum numerante exercitu post elapsum unum seculum non superfuturus esset unus, suam ipsius calamitatem imminentem sapientius deplorasset, nam cum optimi & fidissimi Demarati consilio obsequi nollet, in eas redactus est angustias, ut toto suo exercitu caeso vsq; ad internuncionem, pauculis profligatis, ipse scapha auectus aegre euaserit, & turpi fuga salutem quaesierit. Pisator, aiunt, itaque sapit, id Cononi Atheniensium Duci praestantissimo contigit. Is cum à Lysandro Lacedaemoniorum Imperatore nauali praelio victus atq; superatus esset, Martis aleam Neptuno committere noluit amplius, quare recollectis copiis, & resumptis, auxiliis Regg. Cypri ac Persiæ, viribus terrestrib. ac pedestribus signis cum Pisandro Laconico congreditur, & superior euadit, non tantum Lacedaemoniorum classe ad Cnidum prostrata, sed ipso etiam Pisandro interfecto, itaque Patriae, Athenis, una cum ingenti praeda, & quinquaginta, hoc est, triginta millium coronatorum dono ad reparandos muros, libertatem restituit.
units.tr: The perils of the sea are many and various in themselves, so that the divine psalmist rightly bids men give thanks to God for those who have come safely out of the storm of the sea (gratias illi). Yet human minds are so blind that they do not shrink from pitting Neptune against Mars, or from trying out naval battles, that is, from doubling evil with evil, against those whom both Mars and Neptune (most unjust of saints!) have bound together in an indissoluble league. I know of no such example anywhere in Sacred Scripture. This is great madness! And the greater the danger, the greater the recklessness. The story of Xerxes is well known: he tried to put fetters on the sea, to beat it with rods, and to force it to go as he pleased. But what was the outcome of this, indeed of this stupendous recklessness and folly? He lamented human frailty, though he had an army of eleven hundred thousand men; yet, after a single century had passed, not one of them would survive. He would have lamented his own impending calamity more wisely, for when he refused to follow the counsel of the best and most faithful Demaratus, he was brought into such straits that, with his whole army cut down to a man and only a few put to flight, he himself escaped with difficulty in a small boat and sought safety in shameful flight. The fisherman, they say, therefore is wise; this happened to Conon, the excellent general of the Athenians. When he had been defeated and overcome by Lysander, the commander of the Lacedaemonians, in a naval battle, he refused to entrust the dice of Mars to Neptune any longer. Therefore, having gathered his forces again and received the help of the kings of Cyprus and Persia, he engaged Pisander the Laconian with land troops and infantry standards, and came off the victor, not only because the fleet of the Lacedaemonians was destroyed at Cnidus, but also because Pisander himself was killed. And so he restored liberty to his fatherland, Athens, together with great spoil and a gift of fifty, that is, thirty thousand crowns, for rebuilding the walls.

units.la: Hoc sapere erat. Semel feliciter pugnatum est mari superiori seculo inter Hispanum & Anglam, nostra memoria, vbi terribilis illa classis Hispana, toto fere triennio apparata, quae totam Angliam occupare, & multo longius progredi iussa erat, cum confusione rebus omnibus infectis, priusquam Angliam attingeret, turpiter & infeliciter aufugit: Epinicio Anglicano non incongrue nec illepide succinuit quidam cum Claudiano:
units.tr: This was wisdom. Once, in our own memory, in the last century, a battle at sea was happily fought between the Spaniard and the Englishman, when that terrible Spanish fleet, prepared over almost three years, which had been ordered to occupy all England and advance much farther, was thrown into confusion in every part and, before it reached England, fled shamefully and unhappily. Someone, with Claudian, sang an apt and witty song of triumph for the English:

units.la: O nimium dilecta Deo cui militat aether
units.tr: O too much beloved by God, for whom the sky fights,

units.la: Et conivrati veniunt ad praelia venti.
units.tr: And the winds come to battle in conspiracy.
Ibid., and read Philip in the Chronicle.
Erasmus, Adagia, Philippus, in Chrysostom.
Claud. Tetta.
THE AIM OF FAITH: CHRIST.

units.la: Vt si quid fragili nitatur fundamento Corruit, & fixum nescit habere locum:
units.tr: As, if anything rests on a fragile foundation, it collapses, and knows not how to keep a fixed place:

units.la: Sic qui non fidei solide fundamina iecit, Labitur, & firmum non facit ille gradum.
units.tr: So he who has not laid the firm foundations of solid faith slips, and that man does not take a firm step.

units.la: Alludit haec tabula ad illud Apostoli ad Corinthios: Fundamentum aliud ponere nemo potest, praeter id quod positum est, qui est Iesus Christus. Si quis autem superaedificat super fundamentum hoc aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, lignum, fœnum, stipulam: uniuscuiusque opus manifestum erit, dies enim declarabit, quia in igne revelabitur, & uniuscuiusque opus, quale sit, igni probabit. Facit se Architectum: Christum fundamentum: Fidem, aurum: argentum. Charitatem: lapides pretiosos, virtutes reliquas: Lignum, fœnum, stipulam facit affectus, cupiditates infirmitatesque fidelium: illa igne non consumi ait, sed purificari: haec consumi, non purificari. Pia sane atque ingeniosa tabula! Vere enim Christus salutis fundamentum est, estque solus, aperte alleuerate Apostolo, & praeeunte Dn. nostro Saluatore ipsomet, qui ait: Nemo venit ad patrem nisi per me. Is ipse lapis angularis est: λίθος ἀκρογωνιαῖος. Hoc fundamentum nisi bene iecteris, omne quod superstruxeris, corruet, quemadmodum de omni fundamento ille ait: Iecit Deus Pater praedestinatione aeterna, & praesentatione generali ad ripam Iordanis: superstruimus nos fidem: ὁ πρῶτος ... quare fides aurum est, quoniam etiam auro pretiosior, per ignem tribulationum excocta. Fides autem nititur aperto & expresso verbo, extra quod non fides sed opinio est: huius verbi hieroglyphicon hic est Candela, & tabulas Legis & Euangelii tenentia; nam quemadmodum in tenebris sine lege impingitur: ita sine praevio verbo non nisi tenebras errorum sequimur, & impingimus adeo ut vel praecipites tales dentur in barathrum aeternarum & exteriorum tenebrarum: Cauetis ergo ut in adyta praerupta diuinorum consiliorum te temere abdas, sufficit verbum quod prope & in ore est tuo: huic simpliciter crede, ut infantes, & columbinam (quas vides) simplicitatem imitare, optime is credit qui simpliciter sed praelucente verbo Dei, credit. Vides extra Christum non esse nisi tenebras, nec videre lucem Legisperitos, Philosophos, & quicunque extra & praeter verbum, Legem & Prophetas, Christi indices ductum atque dictamē corruptae rationis sequuntur: Talia inventa & ratiunculae fundamento superstructae non purificabuntur sed deflagrabunt, conflagrabuntque; & superstruentes, & instar fumi euanescent. Qui vero fidem veram ac synceram superstruunt, tametsi ... luctas, & scorias concurrere contingat, deflagrabunt tamen illa tantum, his perpetim saluis: sed de his etiam supra.
units.tr: This picture alludes to the Apostle's words to the Corinthians: "No one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each one's work will be made manifest; for the day will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one's is." He makes himself the architect: Christ is the foundation; faith is the gold, and silver; charity the precious stones, and the other virtues likewise; wood, hay and stubble he makes the affections, desires and weaknesses of the faithful. He says that the former are not consumed by fire but purified, and the latter are consumed, not purified. A truly pious and ingenious picture! For indeed Christ is the foundation of salvation, and the only one, as the Apostle plainly asserts, and our Lord and Saviour himself goes before, saying: "No one comes to the Father except through me." He himself is the cornerstone [λίθος ἀκρογωνιαῖος]. Unless you lay this foundation well, everything you build upon it will fall, just as that writer says of every foundation: "God the Father laid it by eternal predestination and by the general presentation at the bank of the Jordan; we build faith upon it: the first ... [ὁ πρῶτος ...]." Therefore faith is gold, since it is also "more precious than gold, refined by the fire of tribulations." Faith, moreover, rests on the open and express Word, outside of which there is not faith but opinion. The hieroglyph of this Word here is the lamp holding the tables of the Law and the Gospel; for as one stumbles in darkness without a law, so without a preceding Word we follow only the darkness of error and stumble, to such an extent that such men are even hurled headlong into the abyss of eternal and outer darkness. Beware, therefore, lest you rashly hide yourself in the steep sanctuaries of the divine counsels; "the word which is near you, in your mouth," is enough. Believe this simply, like infants, and imitate the dove-like simplicity you see; he believes best who believes simply, with the Word of God shining before him. You see that outside Christ there is only darkness, and that the experts in the Law, the philosophers, and all who follow, outside and apart from the Word, the Law and the Prophets, the witnesses of Christ, the guidance and dictate of corrupted reason, do not see the light. Such inventions and little reasonings built upon the foundation will not be purified but will burn and be consumed, and those who build them will vanish like smoke. But those who build true and sincere faith, although ... struggles and dross happen to meet them, will nonetheless see only those things burn away, while these remain safe forever; but of these things also above.
THE FULFILMENT OF THE LAW IS LOVE

units.la: Medallion: Lex frenum / Lex est speculum / Lex regula vitae
units.tr: The law is a bridle. / The law is a mirror. / The law is the rule of life.

units.la: Left pillar: Diligē Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo.
units.tr: Love the Lord your God with all your heart.

units.la: Right pillar: Et proximum tuum sicut teipsum.
units.tr: And your neighbour as yourself.

units.la: Est virtus geminis sublimibus alta columnis, Illa Deum prendens, [illegible, ~6 letters] hæcce suum: Inter namq; Deum currit dilectio, & inter Proximum, vt hunc propter seruiat illi etiam.
units.tr: Virtue is lofty, raised on two towering columns: the one grasps God, the other [illegible] its own. For love runs between God and the neighbour, so that for the neighbour's sake one also serves him.

units.la: Homo fidelis & solido fundamento Christo vera salvificaq, fide innixus, cuius equidem hieroglyphicon est iuuenis alatus, hoc: duas, stans super fundamine, tenet columnas ad idem vergentes, quarum altera dilectio Dei est, altera dilectio proximi: Nimirum hisce duabus piae charitatis & charae pietaris partibus Christiani hominis officium absoluitur. Τὸ τέλος τῆς ἐντολῆς ἐστιν ἀγάπη ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας καὶ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς καὶ πίστεως ἀνυποκρίτου. ΑΓΑΠΗΣΕΙΣ: ἡ γὰρ ἀγάπη τοῦ νόμου πλήρωμα. Præclare ergo August. Omnium quæ prædicta sunt, ex quo de rebus tractamus, hæc summa est, ut intelligatur legis & omnium diuinarum scripturarum plenitudo & finis esse: DILECTIO rei quæ fruendum est: & rei, quæ nobiscum ea frui potest, quia ut se quisque diligat præcepto non est opus. Sed multi hic in accusationem præceptí conuertuntur quod seruare non possunt, quasi offendiculum eo Deus posuerit; His respondendum: Bona lex est: & mandatum sanctum, bonum, iustum. In nobis autem hæret culpa, quod perfecte istud præstare non possumus. Verum si Euangelio credideris, & vera fide intueberis Christum, ille defectus restituet tuos, quoniam agnus ille Dei est, peccata mundi tollens. Interim obedientiam tuam ad legis νομοθεσίας exerce, eademq; vtere pro Speculo: ex quo, quid tibi ad perfectionem deest, addisce. FRENO: quo traharis ad obedientiam: Pædagogus enim est: & quidem ad Christum, vt, quod tibi deest, in vno & solo Christo quæras, nimirum: in ira, gratiam: in maledictione, benedictionem: in peccato, iustitiam: in tentatione, consolationem: in tenebris, lucem: in morte, vitam: Omnia enim Christus est, si credere volumus. Regula: eaq; bene viuendi, quam cynosuram & amussim semper ob oculos nos habere decet, neq; ab ea deflectere, vel ad dextram vel ad sinistram, vt ne nos ὑπερηφάνως inquinemus potius quam obedientes nos Deo probemus, qui vno omnes tales halitu difflat: Edixi enim filiis illorum: in statutis patrum vestrorum ne ambuletis, & iura illorum ne obseruetis: ego Iehouah Deus vester in statutis meis ambulate & iura mea obseruate ac facite ea. Id quod complebimus in illa vita, quum videbimus facie ad faciem, vt iterum Augustinus libr. de Spir, & litera c. 26.
units.tr: A faithful man, resting on the solid foundation of Christ and a true, saving faith, is represented by a hieroglyph of a winged youth, who stands on a base and holds two columns converging on the same point. One of them is the love of God, the other the love of neighbour. Indeed, the duty of the Christian is completed by these two parts of pious charity and dear piety. The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith [τὸ τέλος τῆς ἐντολῆς ἐστιν ἀγάπη ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας καὶ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς καὶ πίστεως ἀνυποκρίτου]. "You shall love": for love is the fulfilling of the law [ἡ γὰρ ἀγάπη τοῦ νόμου πλήρωμα]. Therefore Augustine rightly says: of all the things that have been said, since we are treating of things, this is the sum: that it is to be understood as the fulness and end of the law and of all divine Scriptures, namely the LOVE of the thing which is to be enjoyed, and of the thing which can enjoy it with us; for there is no need for a precept that each should love himself. But many here turn the precept into an accusation, because they cannot keep it, as if God had placed a stumbling block there. To these it must be answered: the law is good, and the commandment is holy, just and good. The fault lies in us, that we cannot perform this perfectly. But if you believe the Gospel and look upon Christ with true faith, that defect will be made good for you, since he is that Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. Meanwhile, exercise your obedience to the law-giving of the law, and use it as a mirror: from it learn what is still lacking to you for perfection. It is a bridle, by which you are drawn to obedience, for it is a pedagogue indeed leading to Christ, so that what you lack you may seek in him alone: namely, in wrath, grace; in curse, blessing; in sin, righteousness; in temptation, consolation; in darkness, light; in death, life. For Christ is all things, if we are willing to believe. It is a rule of living well, which we ought always to keep before our eyes as a guiding star and plumb-line, not to deviate from it, to right or to left, lest we defile ourselves through pride rather than prove ourselves obedient to God, who breathes out all such with one breath. For I have given the commandment to their children: "Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, nor keep their judgments; I am Jehovah your God: walk in my statutes, and keep my judgments and do them." This we shall fulfil in that life, when we see face to face; so again Augustine, in the book On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 26.
DO NOT HARM YOUR FRIENDS.

units.la: Dulce ut amicitiæ nomen, sic dulcior usus, Nil equidem patulus carius orbis habet. Unus sit Pylades fido tibi fidus Oresti Hic quoq; amicitiæ non levis usus erit.
units.tr: As sweet as the name of friendship is, its practice is sweeter still; indeed the wide world holds nothing dearer. Let there be one Pylades, faithful to you as he was to Orestes; this too will be no small use of friendship.
LVI.

units.la: Omnium rerum quas ad bene beateq; viuendum Sapientia comparauit, nihil est maius aut praestantius amicitia, quae consistit in IDEM VELLE & IDEM NOLLE. Est autem Deus, qui suis amicos conciliat, qui solus corda hominum in manu sua habet, & quocunq; vult, flectit illa: quae sapientissimi sententia est: Quum beneuolentia prosequitur Iehoua vias alicuius, etiam inimicos eius pacatos reddit et: quod exemplis Iacobi & Esau: Dauidis & Saulis apertum fit. Ad amicitiam non facile prosiliendum confirmandam, nam tales amicitiae non diu durant: sunt qui facilius parant amicos, quam conseruant, modium prius sal (iuxta Sapientum doctrinam) cum eo consumas, vel patrimonia diuidas, secus perfecte haud cognoueris: hoc IESV quoq; Syracidis monitum est: Si comparaturus es amicum, in adflictione compara eum, neq; cito credas teipsum ei: Nam est amicus, qui non permanet in die adflictionis. Est amicus qui ad inimicitiam traducitur. Est amicus mensarum particeps, cum quo ita comparatum, ut feruente olla feruEat amicitia, nam vulgus amicitias vtilitate probat: quare in deligendo amico summa prudentia opus est. Ad minimum autem vnum habeas amicum, iuxta versiculum: Vnus sit Pylades fido tibi fidus Orestes, Hic quoq; amicitia non leuis vsus erit.
units.tr: Of all the things that Wisdom has provided for living well and happily, nothing is greater or more excellent than friendship, which consists in WILLING THE SAME AND REJECTING THE SAME. God, moreover, joins friends together, he alone holds the hearts of men in his hand and turns them wherever he wills. This is the saying of the wisest man: When Jehovah looks kindly on a man's ways, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him, which is made plain by the examples of Jacob and Esau, and of David and Saul. One should not leap quickly into friendship, for such friendships do not last long. There are those who acquire friends more easily than they keep them. Unless you have eaten a bushel of salt with someone (according to the teaching of the wise), or divided your inheritance with him, you will not know him perfectly. Jesus, son of Sirach, also warned of this: If you are going to acquire a friend, acquire him in adversity, and do not trust yourself to him too quickly. For there is a friend who remains only so long as it is a day of comfort, and who will not stay in the day of affliction. There is a friend who turns into an enemy. There is a friend who is a companion at table, and who will not remain your friend when the pot boils. For the common people judge friendships by their usefulness. Therefore great prudence is needed in choosing a friend. At the very least, have one friend, according to the verse: Let there be one Pylades, faithful to you as Orestes was faithful; this too will be a friendship of no small use.

units.la: Amicitiam autem si cum quo contraxeris eam ne facile ruperis: est enim fidus amicus valida protectio, quem qui adeptus est, magnum adeptus est thesaurum: Ἀνὴρ δίκαιος ὁ μόνον πολίτης: Amicus, Salomone teste, fratre coniunctior est. Stabat Romae effigies AMICITIAE: iuuenis virente habitu: quoniam semper virere debet amicitia, in cuius fronte extabat: Hymns, aeternas: semper durat amicitia vera: circa locum pectoris: Prope, procul. Non enim militat hic procul ab oculis, procul a corde, &c. In extremo fimbriae: Mors, vita: per ea enim durat amicitia. Quare cum rebus in incertis cernatur amicus certus, memento contractu amicitiae vtriusque, vt illa ait, fortuna cum socio societatem initiate: Amicus enim in die adflictionis agnoscitur: vt exemplis Dauidis, & Ionathae: Pyladis & Orestis: Damonis & Pythiae illustrissime relucet. Nec tamen amicitia contractus ad iniquo ista aut impia obligare debet, sed amici esse debemus vsq; ad aras: non amicitia sed conspiratio est, qui consentiunt in malo, vt Catilinarii factio. Et illi qui ad occidendum Paulum conspirarunt. Propter calumnias inuidorum, ne temere rumpas amicitiam: quin potius legem amicitiae considera, quae est: Monere & moneri. A calumniis autem ipse abstineto, nihil enim frequentius quam calumnia. Suspicio quoq; abest ab amico. Difsutam quam primum redintegrato. Reconciliatum amicum ne facile offende. A reconciliato autem aliquantisper caue.
units.tr: Once you have entered into friendship with someone, do not break it lightly: for a faithful friend is a strong protection, and whoever has found one has found a great treasure. A just man is the only citizen [Ἀνὴρ δίκαιος ὁ μόνον πολίτης]. A friend, according to Solomon, is closer than a brother. At Rome there stood a statue of FRIENDSHIP: a young man in green clothing, since friendship ought always to flourish, and on its forehead was written: Hymn, eternal: true friendship always endures. On the area of the breast: Near, far. For here friendship does not go to war, far from the eyes, far from the heart, and so on. On the outer edge of the fringe: Death, life: for by these friendship endures. Therefore, since in uncertain matters a certain friend is recognised, remember that friendship is formed by both parties, as the saying goes, fortune makes a partnership with a companion. For a friend is recognised in the day of affliction, as is most brilliantly shown by the examples of David and Jonathan, Pylades and Orestes, and Damon and Phintias. Yet a friendship entered into should not bind a man to what is unjust or impious; rather, we ought to be friends even up to the altars. Those who agree in wrongdoing are not friends but conspirators, like the faction of Catiline, and those who conspired to kill Paul. Do not rashly break friendship because of the slanders of envious people. Rather, consider the law of friendship, which is: to admonish and to be admonished. Refrain from slander yourself, for nothing is more common than slander. Suspicion also has no place in friendship. Mend a quarrel as soon as possible: restore it. Do not offend a reconciled friend easily, and be wary for a while of one who has been reconciled.
O friends, behold, there is no friend [ὦ φίλοι, ἰδοὺ φίλων].
SPIRITUAL HONEY-MAKING: Great Things from the Smallest
