units.tr: [engraving: a sun with a face above an open book bearing the motto "The light shines in the darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend it"; beehives on a platform before a city and hills; described under notes]

units.la: Quam suauis liquor est verbum, bone Christe, tuum mi!
units.tr: How sweet is your word to me, good Christ, how sweet a liquid it is!
It tastes sweeter than Hybla's honey and its comb!

units.la: Hoc age perpetuo tantum mea corda rigentur,
units.tr: Let this be my constant care, that my heart may be watered by it,
and let no weariness seize my spirit.

units.la: De Apibus atq; mellificio multi scripserunt, nos moralem ex ipsorum ordine atq; opere sensum expresseruri sumus. Multarum autem & sane vtilium rerum per apiculas etiam lampade diuini verbi ductrice monemur. Principio monarchicum statum optumum esse, regimen ipsarum edocet, non totum examen vni paret, & eius nutui omnes audiunt: si duo in vno reperiantur alueario Reges, vnus damnas sit oportet: nimirum: vnus Deus. Vnus Sol, duos soles mundus non fert, ergo vnus & Rex sit, quemadmodum dicitur:
units.tr: Many have written about bees and honey-making, but we intend to draw out a moral sense from their order and their work. Moreover, through the little bees, under the guiding lamp of the divine Word, we are also taught many true and useful things. First, their governance teaches that the best state is a monarchy: the whole swarm obeys one, and all listen to his nod. If two kings are found in one hive, one of them must be condemned. Surely there is one God, one Sun, the world does not bear two suns, so there should be one king as well, as it is said: [ἐκ ἀρχῆς πολυκοιρανίη ἐς κοίρανος ἔστω] (Iliad 2: "Let the rule of many not be good; let there be one ruler").

units.la: ἐκ ἀρχῆς πολυκοιρανίη ἐς κοίρανος ἔστω
units.tr: ἐκ ἀρχῆς πολυκοιρανίη ἐς κοίρανος ἔστω

units.la: Dum enim multis paretur, nulli paretur recte, sed pro sua quisq; libidine rem gerit: itaq; ex πολυαρχία enascitur ἀναρχία, cui malo μοναρχίας beneficio optime occurritur, alioquin recte dicitur: Multitudo Imperatorum Cariam perdidit. Deinde ἀσπαζόμενος dedocet, id quod dolet Sapiens: Ne lau des quamquam de pulchritudine ipsius, nec abominerii vllum ex aspectu ipsius; parua est inter volucres apis, sed principatus est condimentorum dulcium fructus eius. Quod significanter admodum effert Cato noster. Corporis exigui vires contemnere noli Consilio pollet, cui vim natura negauit.
units.tr: For when many are obeyed, no one is obeyed rightly, but each man conducts affairs according to his own desire; thus from many rulers anarchy arises, and this evil is best met by the benefit of monarchy. Otherwise the saying is rightly given: The multitude of emperors ruined Caria. Then the bee teaches what the Wise Man laments, that one should not praise a man for his beauty, nor abhor anyone for his appearance: the bee is small among winged creatures, yet the fruit she yields is the chief of sweet things. Our Cato expresses this very aptly: Do not despise the strength of a small body; he excels in counsel to whom nature has denied strength.

units.la: Sub sordido sapepaltio latet sapientia: & in quo non credis gurgite piscis erit. Inimicitiarum etiam gerunt typum, quoniam Deus eos armauit aculeo side n sago agmine irruat, laedere graviter possunt: quare & David sub persona (Christi) de suis inimicis conqueritur: Circumdederunt me tanquam apes, &c. Inprimis boni ordinis exemplar praebent illustrissimum, cuius tam sunt tenaces, vt si intelligant esse quae non faciant officium, tolerare nequeunt, sed aculeorum suorum gladiis conficiunt, confodiunt, tollunt, quod a Poeta obseruatum est: Ignauum (inquit) fucos pecus a praesepibus arcet.
units.tr: Wisdom lies hidden under a humble cloak, and in whatever whirlpool you do not believe, there will be a fish. They also bear the figure of enmities, since God armed them with a sting; if they rush on in a swarm, they can wound grievously. Hence David, speaking in the person of Christ, complains of his enemies: They surrounded me like bees, etc. Above all, they provide a most notable example of good order. They are so tenacious of it that, if they perceive that some are not doing their duty, they cannot tolerate it, but despatch, pierce and remove them with the swords of their stings, as the poet observed: The idle herd keeps the drones away from the hives.

units.la: In nullis bene constitutis communitatibus vel Rebuspublicis tolerabitur pigri, ignaui, inertes, sed constitutum aut fustibus vt emendentur, aut exsuliis multentur: ne noceant exemplo, de quibus etiam Apostolus latissime, 2. Thess 3. v. d loc. Denique: iucundissimam allegoriam praebent, nam mellificia studiosissime exercent, & colligunt fauos pro quibus deinde ad necem dimicant. Fauus noster verbum Dei, quouis melle fauoq; Hyblaeo dulcius, quem fauum ex floridissimo scripturarum viridario, tanquam ex herbulis dinersissimi generis fugimus ac paramus, pro eo nostro suo decertemus vsq; ad necem, neq;, qui nos deprædetur, per inanem philosophiam & deceptionem ... hominum, admittamus, quemadmodum Syracides monet: pro veritate ad necem decerta, &c. sicut apes, &c. de diuinarum scientiarum flosculis suauia mella conficiamus, & quicquid ad medicinam animarum pertinet, arte componamus: quod fuse persequitur Ambros. ferm. de defect. Lun. 83.
units.tr: In no well-ordered communities or commonwealths will the lazy, the idle and the inert be tolerated; they are either corrected with cudgels or punished with exile, so that they do not harm by their example. On this the Apostle speaks at length, 2 Thess. 3. Finally, they offer a most pleasant allegory, for they practise honey-making with great diligence and gather combs, for which they then fight to the death. Our comb is the Word of God, sweeter than any honey or Hybla's comb. We flee to it and gather it from the flowery garden of Scripture, as from herbs of very diverse kinds, and for it we will contend to the death against anyone who would plunder us through empty philosophy and the deceit of men; we will not admit them. As Ecclesiasticus advises: fight to the death for the truth, etc. Like bees, we shall make sweet honey from the little flowers of the divine sciences, and skilfully compose whatever pertains to the medicine of souls, as Ambrose pursues at length: Ambros. ferm. de defect. Lun. 83.
Is Not Life a Warfare for Man?

units.la: Et Satanas, Mundusq;, Caro, Mors vltimus hostis, In te vnum ac solum spicula saeua vibrant: Sed IESVS CHRISTVS VICTOR te flamine sacroFirmabit, coelorum & trahet vsq; domos.
units.tr: Satan, the World, the Flesh, and Death, the last enemy, aim their cruel darts at you alone and at no one else. But Jesus Christ, the Victor, will strengthen you with His holy breath and will draw you up to the mansions of heaven.

units.la: Quemadmodum de Christo dicitur: Quod positus sit in signum cui contradicitur: Metaphora sumpta ab iis, qui tela sua mittunt ad scopum: ita & de fidelibus, imagini ipsius conformandis, in hac vita idem recte dicitur, significatur, figuratur: & huc collineat haec tabella Rochi imaginem gestans, undiq; telis petiti & confixi. Quemadmodum in Noctuam de die euolantem omnes undiq; volucres atq; auiculae irruunt atq; impetum faciunt, ita in pios ac probos omnes & omnis generis homines in hac vita irruunt, inq; eos tela venenatarum suarum linguarum & petulantium actionum vnos dirigunt: vt verissimum sit commune illud distichon:
units.tr: As is said of Christ: "that he is set for a sign which is spoken against" (Luke 2). The metaphor is taken from those who send their weapons at a target; and in the same way, of the faithful, who are to be conformed to His image, the same thing is rightly said, signified and figured in this life. To this point this little picture of Roch carrying an image, pierced and transfixed by weapons from every side, is aimed. As when a owl is pursued in daylight, all the birds and little birds from every side rush in and attack it, so upon the pious and upright, and upon men of every kind, they rush in during this life, and some of them direct the darts of their venomous tongues and wanton actions at them; so that that common couplet is most true:
"Wars and conflicts never fail the pious,

units.la: Et quo cum certet mens pia semper habet.
units.tr: And the pious mind always has something to contend with."

units.la: Vides Satanam quam cupide veneficas suas sagittas in hominem miserum eiaculetur, per tentationes a dextris & a sinistris, nimirum hoc illud est: Simon, Simon, Satanas expetiuit, quos cribraret sicut triticum: Aduersarius vester tanquam Leo rugiens circuit, quaerens quem deuoret: Qui ex superiori dimicant hostes loco, magno compendio vtuntur aduersum infra se positos, talem tanquam potentem Sagittarium habemus diabolum, ex aere in nos sua vibrat spicula: quo nomine etiam a D. Paulo nobis cauendus proponitur; Non est, inquit, nobis collustatio aduersus carnem & sanguinem, sed aduersus Principes ac potestates, aduersus mundi rectores tenebrarum harum, contra spiritualia nequitiae. Has Satanae technas alicubi deplorat Augustinus, inimicus, inquit, noster, vt occidat, semper vigilat sine somno. Ecce tetendit ante pedes nostros laqueos infinitos, & omnes vias nostras impleant decipulis ad capiendas animas nostras. Laqueos posuit in diuitiis, laqueos tetendit in paupertate, in cibo, in potu, in voluptate, in somno, in vigiliis, &c. non autem agit per seipsum semper, sed per fideles suos, mundum & carnem. Vides mundum etiam arcum intendere, vere enim Dn. Saluator: in mundo pressuram habetis: Vibrat mundus scandala, persecutiones. Mundus est mundus & mundus immundus manet, ait ille: quod Christus aliter effert: si de mundo esset, mundus quod suum esset diligeret, sed de mundo non estis, verum de mundo ego elegi vos. Mundus non potest vos non odisse, quoniam me odit. Et simil. Ex occultis, insidiis, & ab intus adoritur caro, diaboli & mundi fidelis intimus, contra huius spicula se munire difficillimum. Omnia enim vincես facilius, quam te: Heus vero tu! quo difficilior lucta, eo gloriosior erit victoria. Pro te ergo contra te tecum pugna, & peccato in te inhabitanti resiste. Deniq; vltimus hostis mors, cuius spicula iunt leuia, morbi: Gratia in fine vitae: sed bene confide: Spiritus Christi mitis, ma columba te solabitur, & deducent cum triumpho Angeli animam tuam, vt Lazari, in sinum Abrahae, ad sempiterna gaudia.
units.tr: See how eagerly Satan hurls his poisoned arrows at the wretched man, by temptations from the right and from the left. This is surely what is meant: "Simon, Simon, Satan has desired to sift you as wheat" (Luke 22); "Your adversary, like a roaring lion, walks about, seeking whom he may devour" (1 Pet. 5). Those who fight from a higher place enjoy great advantage against those placed below them; so we have the devil as a powerful archer, who from the air hurls his darts at us. By this name the devil is also set before us by St. Paul as one to be guarded against: "We do not wrestle," he says, "against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness" (Eph. 6). Augustine somewhere laments these snares of Satan: "Our enemy," he says, "watches always without sleep, that he may kill. Behold, he has stretched out countless snares before our feet, and fills all our ways with nets to catch our souls. He has laid snares in riches, he has stretched snares in poverty, in food, in drink, in pleasure, in sleep, in watching, etc." Yet he does not act always by himself, but through his faithful ones, the world and the flesh. You see that the world also bends its bow; for truly our Lord the Saviour says, "In the world you shall have tribulation" (John 16). The world hurls scandals and persecutions. "The world is the world, and the unclean world remains unclean," says one; and Christ expresses it otherwise: "If you were of the world, the world would love what is its own; but you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me" (John 15), and similar things. From hidden places, by ambush, and from within, the flesh, the inmost faithful friend of the devil and the world, attacks; it is most difficult to guard oneself against its darts. "For it conquers everything more easily than you." But look here, you! The harder the struggle, the more glorious the victory will be. Therefore fight for yourself, against yourself, with yourself, and resist the sin that dwells in you. Lastly, the last enemy is death, whose darts are light, the illnesses: a grace at the end of life. But trust well: the gentle Spirit of Christ, like a dove, will console you, and the angels will carry your soul with triumph, as Lazarus was carried into the bosom of Abraham, to eternal joys.
EMBLEM. REMEMBER THE END.

units.la: Nil Pullata iuuat quæ Carmina Præfica cantet, Funeribus cygnus concinit ipse suis: Nil post Fata iuuant aliorum munera, censusq; Alma fides, Pietas atq; præacta[?] iuuant.
units.tr: Neither does the mourner in her dark robe help, singing the funeral dirges; the swan itself sings at its own funeral. Nothing helps after death, the gifts of others and wealth; but kindly faith and piety and deeds done before death help.

units.la: Breuitatem arq; fragilitatem vitæ humanæ plurimi deplorarunt, sed plerique sine vera Dei suique ipsorum cognitione. Incertum admodum ᾿Ε῾ν ὀνπω Aristoteles appellat: flet Heraclitus lubricitatem vitæ huius, sed incertus causæ cum propinquæ tum remotæ, efficientis & finalis. Stulte admodum Imp. Seuerus, omnia, exclamat fui, & nihil mihi prodest. Deniq; Vandalorum Rex Gilimerus forte sine fundamento. Μακιότης μακροτητων ... μακροτης.
units.tr: Many have lamented the brevity and frailty of human life, but most of them without a true knowledge of God and of themselves. Aristotle calls it something uncertain; Heraclitus weeps over the slipperiness of this life, but is uncertain about its cause, both near and remote, efficient and final. Very foolishly the Emperor Severus cries out, "I have been everything, and nothing profits me." Lastly, the Vandal king Gelimer (said, perhaps without foundation) ... "Patience is the longest of long things."

units.la: Nos autem & breue esse vitam hanc scimus, & cur tam breuis ea sit, nos sugit minus: nos verbo diuino edocti succinimus Moysi Theandro & Prophetarum primo: DOMINE facis nos diffluere sicut nimbum, somnium fumus, sicut gran e, quod cito arescit: quod mane floret, & mutatur vespere, exciditur & arescit: quia defecimus in ira tua, in furore tuo turbati sumus: Posuisti iniquitates nostras in conspectu tuo, occulta nostra in lumen vultus tui: verbo dicā: causa breuitatis ac fragilitatis vitæ nostræ sunt peccata; Originis, seu primum, & actualis, seu à primo orta: nisi peccato inquinati essemus, neq; mors iuris quid in nos haberet, neq; tam inopina morte adobrui possemus. per peccatum fit, quod homo Bulla: quod dies hominis transeunt tanquam fumus: & quod vere dicitur:
units.tr: But we both know that this life is brief, and we know little why it is so brief; taught by the divine word, we sing with Moses, the man of God, and the first of the prophets: "LORD, you make us flow away like a cloud; our days are like a dream, like smoke, like grass which quickly withers; in the morning it flourishes and is changed in the evening, it is cut down and withers; because we have failed under your wrath, and in your fury we have been troubled. You have set our iniquities before your face, our secrets in the light of your countenance" (Ps. 90). In a word, the causes of the brevity and frailty of our life are sins: original, that is the first, and actual, that is arising from the first. Unless we had been stained by sin, death would have no right over us, nor could we be overwhelmed by so unexpected a death. Through sin it comes about that man is a bubble, and that the days of man pass away like smoke; and what is truly said:
"We are born and we die, and the end depends on the beginning."

units.la: Omnia sunt hominum tenui pendentia filo, &c. Et iterum:
units.tr: "All the things of men hang by a slender thread," etc. And again:
"And the days flee, with no rein to restrain them."

units.la: Quare quom sciamus, & elapsuram clepsydram, vitamque hanc esse breuem, necesse est nos ad felicem excessum in tempore, inq; vero timore Domini præparari: laudandus igitur & illaudatus ex parte mos Cygni, qui hic pro hieroglyphico adpingitur: Cygnus certe vt rota vita sua sonoram nō ædat vocem, morti tamen vicinus cantat: eorum forte typus, qui in fine vitæ conuerti volunt & resipiscere, quod periculosum admodum est, nam dum vocantem in tempore gratia non audiunt Deum, sed obdurant corda (vt aliì) ecs nec Deus vocanteis audiet, animam iam de lingua exhalaturos. Legi, inquid Augustinus & relegi scripturam, & non inueni exemplum in morte saluati præter Latronis in cruce.
units.tr: Therefore, since we know that the water-clock runs out and that this life is brief, it is necessary that we be prepared for a happy departure in due time and in true fear of the Lord. Praiseworthy, then, and in part not praiseworthy, is the custom of the swan, which is here depicted as a hieroglyph. The swan, indeed, as a wheel, does not give forth a sonorous voice during its life, yet singing near death; perhaps it is a type of those who wish to be converted and to repent at the end of life, which is very dangerous indeed, for "while they do not hear God calling in time by grace, but harden their hearts" (as others say), then God will not hear them calling when they are about to breathe out their soul from the tongue. "I have read," says Augustine, "and re-read Scripture, and I have not found an example of salvation in death except that of the thief on the cross."

units.la: Deinde & eorum hieroglyphicon esse potest, qui in fine vitæ, quod plerique faciunt boni, pia vota, ominosa verba, & voces ædunt optimas, vnde prouerbium manauit: Cygnæa cantio. Nam quod non coacta sed suauis illa vltima Cygnorum vox sit, vel ex illo Virgilii adparet:
units.tr: Then this also may be the hieroglyph of those who, at the end of life, as most good people do, utter pious prayers, auspicious words and the best voices, whence the proverb arose: "a swan-song." For that this final voice of the swans is not forced but sweet, appears even from that line of Virgil:

units.la: Nam neq; adhuc Varo videor nec dicere Cinna Digna, sed arguto interstrepere anser olores.
units.tr: "For neither to Varus do I seem, nor to Cinna, to say worthy things, but like a goose I chatter among the melodious swans."

units.la: Quales piorum Cygneæ cantiones in sacris sunt: Scio quod redemptor meus viuit, &c. In manus tuas Domine, commendo spiritum meum, &c. Domine Iesu suscipe spiritum meum. Vnde & Martialis:
units.tr: Such are the swan-songs of the pious in the sacred writings: "I know that my Redeemer lives," etc.; "Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit," etc.; "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Whence also Martial:

units.la: Dulcia defecta modulatur carmina lingua: Cantator Cygnus funeris ipse sui.
units.tr: "The sweet songs the failing tongue modulates; the singer swan is himself the singer of his own funeral."
THE END
THE END OF ALL THINGS DRAWS NEAR.

units.la: Fundamenta ruunt orbis, fastigia rerum Quassantur, summæ concutiuntur opes. Proq; ope suppressi tendunt ad sydera palmas, Quodq; optant sancti, non procul: (EVGE, veni!) est.
units.tr: The foundations of the world collapse, the pinnacles of affairs are shaken, the greatest powers are struck down. The oppressed, having no help, stretch their palms up to the stars, and what the saints long for is not far off: (Come, Lord Jesus!).

units.la: Si fundamenta domus labefactantur & concutiuntur, domus ipsa diu stare non potest: ita prorsus cum hoc mundo comparatum est, nam cum fundamenta non labefactentur tantum, nec tantum concutiantur, sed propemodum omnino emarcuerint & diruantur, verisimile certe est, stare diu non posse, sed nec finem longe abfuturum. Fundamenta sunt Hierarchiæ & Principaliores status, spirituales seu Ecclesiasticus; & Mundanus, secularisque vel Politicus: hæc fundamenta autem non tam concuti quam plane ferme dirui in propatulo est: Arietes autem demolitionum sunt φιλοδεξίαι τελεσηφίαι, vt præsens tabella ἰμαλησκα perstringere conatur: Pedo Episcopali, Ecclesiasticum; gladio, politicum ordinem figurante: Saeculo autem aureis conferto & pecunia, auaritiam insatiabilem indicante. Et certe pecunia obediunt omnia. Auri gratia omnia fiunt. Auro expugnantur omnia fundamenta & munimenta.Venalia vbiq; Templa,sacerdotes,altaria,sacra,corona: Ignes * thura,preces,cœlum est venale,Deusq.
units.tr: If the foundations of a house are weakened and shaken, the house itself cannot stand for long. So it is with this world: when its foundations are not merely weakened and shaken, but almost wholly decayed and overthrown, it is surely likely that it cannot stand long, and that its end is not far away. The foundations are the hierarchies and the chief estates, the spiritual or ecclesiastical, and the worldly or secular, or political. That these foundations are not so much shaken as all but razed is plain to see. The battering rams of this demolition are φιλοδεξίαι τελεσηφίαι [ambitions and fraudulent contrivances], which this present picture tries to lay bare with its ἰμαλησκα [emblem]: the bishop's crook stands for the ecclesiastical order, the sword for the political order, and the world, crammed with golden coins, for insatiable avarice. And indeed all things obey money. Everything is done for the sake of gold. By gold all foundations and fortifications are overrun. Churches, priests, altars, sacred things, and crowns are for sale everywhere: fires, incense, prayers, heaven is for sale, and God too.

units.la: Omnes hierarchiæ alas demittunt ad aurum, præcipue sacer ordo: vt nō immerito exclamare libeat: Dicite Pontifices in templo quid facit aurum; quod omnia in templo auro prostant, auro veneunt, auro deniq; extruduntur; Non Vrbis hæc iniquitas est, sed Orbis. In plerosq; Pontifices cuiuscunq; sectæ competit illud: Propheta tua concionatur propter aurum.&c: lignei olim erant calices & aurei sacerdotes, nunc aurei calices, & ligni, & aurei sacerdotes! Imo, inquam, bone Bonif.& aurei, nam auri gratia prostituunt, doctrinā, Deum, corpora & animas: docent placentia: fingūt se ad pruritum aurium magnatum. Optimus is est, qui propter sanctum aurum & offam politicis adulari & fratres onerare potest. Non est, sacerdotes! ô boni Politicis exprobretis, pedum vestrum in sacculo pecuniario dextram occupauit, primi estis vos in emungenda pecunia, in extricanda offa, in corradendo auro. Nullæ rationes potiores sunt, quam tinnula illa: Nec tamen aberrat etiam à vobis hoc telum, Domini Politici, etiam vos ferit hoc iaculum: & vos pars estis oneris, quod pauperes premit, vt hic cernitis, pauperes inquam qui sublatis ad sydera palmis, oculis, gemitibus, ac suspiriis, votis & precibus opem atq; vindicatam à Deo exposcunt, qui et annuit precibus ipsorū, & ait: Propter miseriam inopum & gemitus pauperum, nunc exsurgam, ponā salutem, &c. Μὴ ταλαιπωρίαν ... Qui autem plantavit audit, qui oculum fecit, videt; qui gentes corripit arguet. ... Termini ætatum in nos inciderunt. Finis omnium rerum appetit. Fundamentis conquassatis domus minatur ruinam.
units.tr: All the hierarchies droop their wings toward gold, and the sacred order above all; so that one may not unjustly cry out: Tell me, priests, what is gold doing in the temple? For in the temple everything is put on sale for gold, bought with gold, and finally pushed out with gold. This wickedness belongs not to the city alone, but to the whole world. That saying fits most prelates of every sect: Your prophet preaches for the sake of gold, etc. Once the chalices were wooden and the priests golden; now the chalices are golden, and some are wooden, and the priests are golden! Indeed, I say, good Boniface, they are golden too, for for the sake of gold they prostitute doctrine, God, bodies and souls. They teach what is pleasing and pretend to tickle the ears of the great. He is the best man who can flatter the politicians and burden his brothers for the sake of holy gold and a morsel. No, priests! Oh good men, do not reproach the statesmen that his hand has taken hold of his purse; you are the first in squeezing out money, in scraping together the morsel, in raking up gold. No arguments are more powerful than that jingling sound. Yet this dart does not miss you either, my lords the statesmen; this javelin strikes you too, and you are part of the burden that presses the poor, as you see here: the poor, I say, who with palms raised to the stars, with eyes, groans and sighs, with vows and prayers, seek help and vindication from God, who also nods to their prayers and says: Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, I will set in safety, etc. [Μὴ ταλαιπωρίαν] ... He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? He who formed the eye, shall he not see? He who chastises the nations, shall he not rebuke? ... The ends of the ages have come upon us. The end of all things draws near. With the foundations shattered, the house threatens ruin.

units.la: DEVORANT PAUPEREM, ET devorantur à Satana.
units.tr: THEY DEVOUR THE POOR, AND ARE DEVOURED BY SATAN.

units.la: Pauperis immani consumit viscera rituDives, & à stygio carpitur ipse Lare: Væ qui prædaris, nam tu quoq; præda futurus, Ingrati hæredes quando furantur opes.
units.tr: The rich man consumes the poor man's entrails with savage custom, and he himself is seized by the Stygian Lar: woe to you who plunder, for you too will be prey, when ungrateful heirs steal wealth.

units.la: Mira quidem sed vera(&vero iterum,cheu! vera)effigies. Vides quomodo alter alterum voret: diues pauperem : diuitem Leo ille de quo P. t. u: Iudæus calcaneo pauperis insidiatur,sed& hunc infernalis illa rapit interimperia,voratque. Nimirum: Pauper vbiq; acet in hoc æuo malo,de ipsius corio ludunt omnes. Nunquam iustior forte fuit querela dominica : Devorant ple- bem meam,devorant sicut panem. Prolixissime infamata est hactenus carnificina Iudaeorum, annulos fuluos in anteriori vestium parte gestantium, sed non minus nocet vafrities illorum in digitis fuluos eosq; aureos gestantu, ad clauum sedentium, Optimatum scilicet, inquam, populi, quorum frequens in ore est,quærimonia Prophetæ, dicentis: Quando transiuerit hoc nouilunium, vt vendamus commeatum? & Sabbathum, vt aperiamus frumenti horrea? minuendo Ephim,& maius faciendo pondus,ac peruertendo lancibus dolosis; i parando pecunia tenuis, & egentem pari calceorum, vt deniq; quisquilias frumenti vendamus : Sed audiant tales Gurguliones & Vini-Iudæi , quid Dominus de illis:Audite(inquit)hoc,qui anhelatis deicere egentem, & deleturi pauperes terra, (neq; adficiuntur egritudine propter contritionem Iosephi) turat Iehoua per excellentiam Iacobi, ne viuam si obliuiscar in aeternum vllum operum istorum: Aurum & argentum non liberabit eos in die irae: rapiant, congerant, auferant, relinquendum erit: Aurum & argentum ipsorum aruginauit, sed arugo in testimonium ipsis erit, & manducabit (quemadmodum & ipsi vorarunt carnes pauperum , sudorefq; & sanguines ipsorum biberunt,ita vorabit Furia infernalis)carnes ipsorum sicut ignis:clamor pauperum eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introiuit. Aegre id quidem ferunt dici ipsis,quemadmodum vsurarius ille;quid(aiebat)opus est Pastorem dicere de auaritia, ad me pertinet hæc prouincia expilandi & excoriandi? tamen dici & inculcari oportet, si qui sint adhuc conuertendi. Mirum autem, quomodo Iudæis tantum indulgeant Magistratus Christiani, vt de subditis suis,de carne q.& sanguine suo tantam lanienam exerceant, & sudores& sanguines piorum exsugant:Ain'!pender mihi magnum tributum; verum heus tu,unde id habet, an non ex carne tua exsuxit: Eoq; nutritur, vt Saluatorem suum ac meum odio habeat,blasphemet,eiq; in faciem exspuat, quæ saliua adhuc in ore & barba ei hæret, quando tibi loquitur, req; omnibus intus diris devouet! o indignitatem rei! LL. cum nostræ tum vestræ, & quid de Iudæis eorumq; vsuris statuant ignotæ vobis esse non possunt. quas huius loci & institu ti non est persequi : est in manibus Hotomannus fuse haec pertractans,ex eo petat qui volet. Habendi erant vt m. scipia, prout & in ii olim mancipia,in primis Gibeonitas,tractarunt.Theologi qui volent, i. vel Lu herum possunt vel Ballingerum: Musculum item & alios. Et extat omnibus textus Extr.de Iudæis & Saracenis, quem sequi possunt & debent,qui suos sibi inde honores ac titulos acquisiuerunt.
units.tr: A marvellous image, and a true one (true again, alas!). You see how one devours the other: the rich man devours the poor. That lion of whom P. t. u: The Jew lies in wait for the poor man's heel, but that infernal power seizes him too, in his wealth, and devours him. Surely: The poor man is everywhere in this evil age, and all play with his hide. Perhaps never was the Lord's complaint more just: They devour my people as they devour bread. The butchery of the Jews, who wear yellow rings on the front of their garments, has been slandered at great length; yet the cunning of those who wear yellow and golden rings on their fingers, sitting at the helm, does no less harm. I mean the nobles of the people, whose complaint on the prophet's lips is frequent, saying: When will this new moon pass, that we may sell grain? And the Sabbath, that we may open the granaries of wheat? Diminishing the ephah and enlarging the weight, and perverting the balances with deceitful scales; buying the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of shoes, that we may sell the refuse of the wheat. But let such gluttons and wine-Jews hear what the Lord says to them: Hear this, you who pant to cast down the needy and destroy the poor of the land (who are not moved by grief over the affliction of Joseph). The Lord Jehovah has sworn by the excellency of Jacob that I will never forget any of their works. Gold and silver will not deliver them in the day of wrath. Let them snatch, heap up and carry off; it must all be left behind. Their gold and silver has rusted, but the rust will be a testimony against them, and will eat their flesh as fire does. (Just as they devoured the flesh of the poor and drank their sweat and blood, so the infernal Fury will devour them.) Their flesh, as fire: the cry of their poor has entered the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth. They take it hard when these things are said to them, just as that usurer did, who said: Why must the minister speak about avarice? Is it my business to plunder and flay? Yet it must be said and repeated, if any are still to be converted. It is strange, though, how Christian magistrates so indulge the Jews that they carry out such butchery upon their own subjects, of their own flesh and blood, and suck out the sweat and blood of the pious. "Do you say, I pay a great tax? But look here: where does he get it, if not by sucking it out of your flesh?" He is nourished so that he may hate his Saviour and mine, blaspheme him, and spit in his face, and that spittle still clings to his mouth and beard when he speaks to you, and he curses you inwardly with every curse! O the indignity of the matter! The laws, both ours and yours, and what they decide about the Jews and their usury, cannot be unknown to you; it is not the task of this place to pursue them. Hotomannus is in hand, treating these matters at length; let whoever wishes seek it from him. They were to be held as slaves, as slaves were also treated in former times, especially the Gibeonites. Theologians who wish may consult Luther or Ballinger, and also Musculus and others. And the text of the Extra, De Iudaeis et Saracenis, exists for all, which those who have acquired their honours and titles from it can and ought to follow.
EMBLEM: FORTUNE IS TO BE USED WITH MODERATION

units.la: [Woodcut engraving: winged figure standing on a globe over a hourglass, with a landscape below; not text.] Ecce, instar globuli Fortuna volubilis errat; Et facili motu voluitur, atq; ruit: Sic Honor Orbis Abit, sic transit gloria mundi; Palmamq; Humilitas Obtinet Arce poli.
units.tr: [Woodcut engraving: a winged figure standing on a globe above an hourglass, with a landscape below; not text.] Behold, Fortune wanders like a rolling little globe; it turns with an easy motion and falls. So the honour of the world departs, so the glory of the world passes away; and Humility wins the palm from the citadel of heaven.

units.la: Lusus Fortuna variatur imagine Luna, Crescit, decrescit, constans consistere nescit:
units.tr: Fortune's sport is varied, like the moon's image: she waxes and wanes, and knows not how to remain constant:

units.la: Quod in omnium, cum priorum tum prophanorum literis abúde decantatum est. Refricat autem eiusce rei considerationem præsens Ἀμέλαγμα. Omnibus autem hoc vnice incumbit, vt lusum fortunæ considerent, omni loco ac tempore, quam inconstans sit, quamq; incerta, instabilis, volubilis, & caduca, vt verbo dicam; sive blandiatur, quod piis rarum, sive irascatur; sive sese fronte sive à tergo conspiciendam exhibeat: certe in omni fortunæ statu attendendum prudenter, ne in alterutram partem peccemus vel fastu, si blandis aspiret Euris, vel demissione animi, si Nothis & Aquilone infesta sit, iuxta illud:
units.tr: This has been sung abundantly in the writings of all, both sacred and profane. The present emblem, Amelagma [Ἀμέλαγμα], revives the consideration of this matter. Yet everyone ought to take this one thing to heart: to consider the play of Fortune, in every place and at every time, how inconstant, uncertain, unstable, changeable and fleeting it is, to put it in a word. Whether it flatters, which is rare for the pious, or grows angry, whether it shows its face or turns its back, in every state of fortune we must attend to it prudently, lest we sin in either direction: by pride, if it blows with smooth east winds, or by dejection of spirit, if it is hostile with south winds and the north wind, according to that saying:

units.la: Si Fortuna fauet cauto tolli, Si Fortuna negat cauto mergi.
units.tr: If Fortune favours, let the cautious man be raised up; if Fortune denies, let the cautious man be sunk.

units.la: Memorabile exemplum habemus in superioris ævi Imp. gloriosissimo atq; invictissimo D. Carolo V. augustissimæ memoriæ, de quo Historiographus memorabilem prædicat constantiam, quod in adversis animum minime deponderit, neq; in successibus, insolenter sese gesserit unquam, sed æquabili semper vultu atq; moribus utrumq; fortunæ lusum temperarit. Id quod & vere prudentis est; cum inconstans, vt sæpe diximus, sit, & cum blanditur, maxime nocere cupiat: Vitrea est, ait ille, cum splendet frangitur. Nam
units.tr: We have a memorable example in the most glorious and unconquered emperor of the former age, the Lord Charles V, of most august memory. Of him a historian proclaims a memorable constancy: in adversity he never lost heart, and in success he never behaved insolently, but always tempered either play of fortune with an even countenance and manners. This is truly the mark of a prudent man, since fortune, as we have often said, is inconstant, and when it flatters it most of all wishes to harm: Glass, as he says, when it shines, is broken. For

units.la: Si Fortuna volet fies de Rhetore Consul Si volet hæc eadem fies de Consule Rhetor.
units.tr: If Fortune wills, a rhetorician will become a consul; and if she wills, the same consul will become a rhetorician.

units.la: Uno momento tota fortunæ alea conversa est, quemadmodum Sesostris Ægyptii rota sapientissime monet. Quis ignorat exempla? Iosephi: Hamanis. C. Iulii Cæsaris. Bibuli Boni. Ruffini. Et se excentorum aliorum. Multos salutat Fortuna, & comatam frontem porrigit, sed resalutare & apprehendere non possunt imprudentes. Multis sese offert benigna, sed ambabus apprehendentes ni-mu inhumaniter eam tractant, h. e. insolentes fiunt, quos illa deinde vicissim tractat longe inhumanissime. Crocodilus est Fortuna, persequentes fugit, fugientes persequitur. Nescis, inquit, quid ferus vesper vehat, quare Fortuna moderate vtendum, maxime in aulis, vbi Dominorum gratia multo leuior est & inconstantior iactu sagittae, & ibi vel maxime verum est quod Poeta canit: Passibus ambiguis Fortuna volubilis errat, Et manet in nullo certa tenaxque loco.
units.tr: In a single moment the whole throw of fortune is turned, as the wheel of Sesostris of Egypt most wisely reminds us. Who does not know the examples: of Joseph, of Haman, of Gaius Julius Caesar, of Bibulus Bonus, of Rufinus, and of other outstanding men? Fortune greets many and offers her forelock, but the imprudent cannot greet her in return or seize her. To many she presents herself kindly, but those who seize her with both hands handle her too inhumanly, that is, they become insolent, and she in turn treats them far more inhumanly. Fortune is a crocodile: she flees from those who pursue, and pursues those who flee. You do not know, she says, what the cruel evening brings. Hence Fortune must be used with moderation, especially at court, where the favour of masters is much lighter and more inconstant than the flight of an arrow, and there above all it is true what the poet sings: Fickle Fortune wanders with uncertain steps, and remains certain and steady in no place.

units.la: Sit igitur semper in conspectu inconstantia & fortunae & vitae, vt moderate sortem feras, & si cum Augustino, Basilio, aliisque fortunae nomen & casus ferre non possis DEI vtere: & memineris: Nemo tam Diuos habuit faventes Crastinum vt possit sibi polliceri Res Deus nostras celeri citatas Turbine versat.
units.tr: Let the inconstancy of both fortune and life therefore always be before your eyes, so that you may bear your lot with moderation; and if you cannot bear the name and chance of fortune, as with Augustine, Basil and others, then use God. And remember: No one has had gods so favourable that he can promise himself tomorrow; God turns our affairs, hurried along by a swift whirlwind.
THE WORD OF THE LORD SHALL NOT PASS AWAY.

units.la: Diuinum ingeniùs est omnibus omnia verbum,Quamuis sit paucis semita trita viris:Lux est in tenebris: sanctæ lex prætia vitæ,Est animæ cibus; & clara lucerna poli.
units.tr: The divine Word is for all men in all things, / though the beaten path is trodden by few. / It is light in darkness, the law and price of holy life, / food of the soul, and the bright lamp of heaven.

units.la: Solem, quem in supremo eminere loco cernis, verbi diuini hieroglyphicum esse intellige, quod ipsum etiam & Lucerna, & adposita significat Candela, vt inscriptum noema manifestum facit: VERBVM DOMINI MANET IN AETERNVM. Extensus ille nasus: exporrecta, longeq; super caput eminentes, aures; acumin oculorum; perspicillum simul; &propinata dapes, probant, dedisse nobis Deū propitium media ad odorandum, audiendum, videndum, contrectandum, imo etiam comedendum verbum suum, dum modo ipsi odorari, videre, audire, contrectare, imo & manducare non detrectemus: estq; ita: Non finit se Deus Prostat verbum Dei in omnibus linguis: dantur sinceri concionatores: Orthodoxi Magistratus: & omnia media ad studium diuini verbi, tantum ad praxin transferamus illud, dominicum: & probemus omnia, ad legem & ad testimonium. Nemo tam infans est in sacris, quin se ad eius captum demittat, saltem tot in locis intelligēdis, quot ad salutem sufficiunt: Mare quidem est scriptura, sed in quo musPeditat & elephas natat: abscondit Deus mysteria sua a sapientibus & revelat parvulis, ex horum ore sibi laudem parat ac firmat regnum: nam si quid obscurius dicitur in uno loco, id in altero dicitur ac ponitur apertissime, atq; ita scriptura per scripturam est intelligenda atq; exponenda: non importandus, sed inde referendus est sensus scripturarum: ut recte dixerit Georg. Brandemburgicus: Das Wort Gottes wer nicht zu schwer/ Wann nur der eigen Nutz nicht wer. Divina sunt oracula Manifesta saltem propriis Legantur absq; adfectibus. Quid autem proderit, Solem in meridie lucere, si sciens volens ad lucem meridianam oculos, aures, & omnia claudas atq; obthures? Lucis certa fraudas vsura. Ipse Ipsum: ita qui scientes volentes ad diuini verbi praeconium lucemq; scientes, volentes caecutiunt, obstupescunt, obbrutescunt, quid inde referent: Lucis vsura se priuabunt & hic & isthic. Non possumus igitur quin cum D. Chrysostomo exhortemur: Audite, quaso omnes vos quibus cura sunt qua ad hanc vitam pertinent, & parate vobis Biblia, anima medicamenta. Qualiter esuriens in campo quaerit eodem, Semen auis, stramen bos, leporemq; canis. Ingeniis ita diuersis diuersa ministrat Pabula, sydereï pagina sacra Patris. Lac capit hic infans, panem robustior atas, Nec caret optato curua seneēta cibo: Et tamen huic pauci invigilant, quia plaraq; turba Aures non animum consuluisse solet.
units.tr: Understand that the sun, which you see set in the highest place, is a hieroglyph of the divine Word. It also signifies a lantern and the candle placed beside it, as the inscription makes plain: THE WORD OF THE LORD ENDURES FOREVER. That stretched-out nose, the long ears rising far above the head, the sharpness of the eyes, the spectacles too, and the dishes set out for drinking all show that God has given us means to smell, hear, see, handle, and even eat his Word, provided that we do not refuse to smell, see, hear, handle, and indeed to eat it. And so it is: God does not withhold himself; the Word of God is set forth in all languages; faithful preachers are given; magistrates are Orthodox; and all the means for the study of the divine Word are at hand. We have only to carry that over into practice: the Lord's word, and test all things by the law and by the testimony. No one in sacred matters is so much a child that he cannot stoop to its grasp, at least in as many passages as suffice for salvation. Scripture is indeed a sea, but one in which the little ass walks and the elephant swims: God hides his mysteries from the wise and reveals them to babes, from whose mouths he prepares and establishes his praise and his kingdom. For if something is said more obscurely in one place, it is said and set down most plainly in another, and so Scripture is to be understood and explained through Scripture: the meaning of the Scriptures is not to be imported, but drawn out from them. Thus Georg of Brandenburg rightly said: "The Word of God is not too hard, provided only that self-interest does not get in the way." The divine oracles are plain, and may be read without prejudice at least in what pertains to oneself. But what good would it do to see the sun shining at noon if you knowingly and willingly shut and blind your eyes, ears, and all your senses to the noonday light? You cheat yourself of the sure enjoyment of the light. So those who knowingly and willingly grow blind to the proclamation of the divine Word and to its light, who become dulled and brutish, will bring upon themselves the loss of the use of the light, both here and hereafter. We cannot therefore but join with Chrysostom in exhorting: Hear me, I beg you all, you who take care for the things that pertain to this life, and prepare for yourselves the Bible, the medicine of the soul. As the hungry creature in the field seeks its own food: the bird seed, the ox straw, the hare for the hound. The sacred page of the Father supplies different food to different minds. The infant takes milk, the stronger age takes bread, and the bent old age lacks no food it desires. And yet few give heed to it, for the crowd usually consults its ears and not its mind.

units.la: EIICE PRIMVM TRABEM ex oculo tuo.
units.tr: Cast out first the beam from your own eye.

units.la: [woodcut emblem: two figures on pedestals, an owl on a stump, and a beam through one figure's eye; no text inside the frame] Faex odiosa virum næuis intenta propinqui. Non curat proprii crimina tanta laris: Excute stulte trabem prius, ac festuca notetur: Sis turpi liber crimine censor, age.
units.tr: [woodcut emblem: two figures on pedestals, an owl on a stump, and a beam through one figure's eye; no text inside the frame] A hateful dregs of humanity, intent on a neighbour's blemishes, does not care for the great crimes of his own household. Cast out the beam first, you fool, and only then let the splinter be marked. Be a free censor, but with no shameful crime of your own. Go on.

units.la: Manifestum est omnibus, quod illa desumpta sint ex notissima pericopa Dn. Saluatoris αὐτὸς ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας κεφαλῆς, quae extant Matth. 7. & Luc. 6. Quid autem vides festucam in oculo fratris tui, & trabem in oculo tuo non vides? Aut quomodo dicis fratri tuo: Frater sine eiiciam festucam de oculo tuo, & ecce trabs est in oculo tuo. Hypocrita eiice primum trabem de oculo tuo, & tunc videbis eicere festucam de oculo fratris tui. Est odiosissimum genus hominum, imo sex virorum, & senti na malorum, qui non horrent quemuis, quiduis, quouis tempore, quouis loco, quaqua ratione carpere ac traducere, ipsi interim omnium nequissimi, conscelleratissimi, flagitiosissimi existentes. Hos carpit & perstringit p sensus nostrum ἐμαυτῷ: & certe aperte obarietat haec peruersitas atq; malitia edicto diuino: Nolite iudicare. Nolite condemnare. Obarietat etiam diuino-Christianae charitati, quae comis est & malis non gaudet. Militat piae prudentiae, quae docet telam cesurae a seipso orditi, iuxta illud sapientis; iustus est accusator sui ipsius. &c. Non tollitur officium amicorum, quod est monere & moneri, iuxta illud Domini: Si peccauerit frater tuus, &c. Sed animus corripientis fingitur iuxta pietatis atque charitatis cynosuram, ne quid dicas faciasue lacerato (ut Augustinus loquitur) animae: & ut temetipsum accuses prius, plerunq; enim non videmus id mantice quod in tergo est: Nota est Christiana: Rosa non pungit: est autem inter spinas & pungitur: ne fis igitur inter susurrones, monet Sapientum Rex. Malorum id est, cum peius facere non possunt, inquiebat Philosophus: Lusus, aiunt, fit oportet ad minimum, qui inter caecos regnare vult, ita saltem criminibus defunctus sit oportet, qui naevos aliorum carpere vult, atq; corrigere. Calumnia turpissimum ut crimen est, in sacris & profanis damnatum, nouacula acutior: & cultro Theatrica, quare ab eo vltro abstinent omnes boni & sani, si vero calumniis impetantur, cogitant & dicunt cum Alexandro Rege: Regium (laudabile) est male audire, bene cum fecerit. &: Aduersus os loquentium iniqua, bonorum opinio, cum testimonio conscientia sufficit, ut loquitur Bernard. Conscia mens recti fama me di sicut: Est quis murus aheneus nil conscire sibi, nulla pallescere culpa: Inueniunt tales iudices mendaces calumniatores, susurrones, &similes tandem suos etiam iudices, vel hic vel isthic, ut Zoilus, Ptolomaeum: Daphitas Grammaticus, Reges: alii, alios: Interim si quem ex fratribus videamus praeoccupari: lapsu, eum subleuamus spiritu manssuetudinis, & suscipiamus, vel ad minimum Domino suo eum stare & tandem permittamus, & vbiuis inscriptum gestemus:
units.tr: It is well known to everyone that these words are taken from the most familiar passage of our Lord, [αὐτὸς ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας κεφαλῆς], which is found in Matthew 7 and Luke 6: "Why do you see the splinter in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, 'Brother, let me take the splinter out of your eye,' when there is a beam in your own eye? You hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to cast out the splinter from your brother's eye." There is no more hateful kind of man, indeed no more pestilential brood of wrongdoers, than those who do not shrink from carping at and slandering anyone, anything, at any time, in any place, by any means, while being themselves the worst, most wicked and most shameless of all. Such a person is pricked and stung by our own sense of ἐμαυτῷ, and this perversity and malice clearly runs counter to the divine command: "Do not judge. Do not condemn." It also runs counter to divine Christian charity, which is kind and does not rejoice in evil. It fights against sound prudence, which teaches that we weave the web of censure from ourselves, according to that saying of the wise man: "The righteous man is his own accuser." And so on. The duty of friends, which is to admonish and to be admonished, according to the Lord's words: "If your brother sins, etc.," is not removed. But the mind of one who rebukes must be shaped by the guiding star of piety and charity, so that you say or do nothing that wounds (as Augustine puts it) the soul, and so that you first accuse yourself. For, as the saying goes, "we do not see what is in the wallet on our back." There is a Christian saying: "The rose does not prick," yet it stands among thorns and does prick. "Do not, therefore, be among the whisperers," warns the King of the wise. The Philosopher used to say that those who cannot do worse are wicked; "a little play, they say, is needed at least by the one who wishes to rule among the blind." So too, whoever wishes to carp at and correct the spots of others ought at least to be free of crimes himself. Calumny is, as a crime, most shameful, condemned in sacred and profane writers alike, sharper than a razor, and like a knife in the theatre, which is why all good and sound people keep far away from it of their own accord. But if they are assailed by calumnies, they think and say with King Alexander: "It is kingly (and praiseworthy) to be ill-spoken of when one has done well." And: "Against the mouths of those who speak wickedness, the good opinion of good men, together with the testimony of a clear conscience, is enough," as Bernard says. "A mind conscious of what is right is a sure defence against rumour. There is a wall of bronze, to be conscious of nothing and to grow pale at no fault." Such false judges, calumniators and whisperers find that their own judges, here or there, sooner or later find them out: as Zoilus did to Ptolemy, the grammarian Daphitas to kings, and others to others. Meanwhile, if we see any of our brothers caught off guard by a fall, let us lift him up in a spirit of gentleness, and receive him, or at least leave him to stand before his own Lord, and at last let us bear everywhere the inscription:
Whoever loves to gnaw at an absent man's reputation with his words,
let him know that this table is forbidden to him.

units.la: Galat. 6. v. 1. Rom. 14. v. 4. Sap. 6. v. 1, 2. Hor. in Ser. 2. Hor. Ep. 1. v. 1, 2.
units.tr: Gal. 6, v. 1. Rom. 14, v. 4. Wisd. 6, v. 1, 2. Hor. in Serm. 2. Hor. Ep. 1, v. 1, 2.
ENVY, A SICKNESS ARISING FROM ANOTHER'S GOODS.

units.la: Quem vides hominem, INVIDIÆ Pictuam gerit. Est autem invidia dolor iniustissimus, conceptus ex alterius felicitate seu prosperitate, oppositus misericordiae, quæ est iustus dolor ex proximi calamitate atq; misericordia. Non est idem cum ἐπιχαιρεκακία: nam hæc est exultatio propter proximi mala: Invidia, dolor & ægritudo propter proximi bona. Est autem & INVIDIA virium omnino turpissimum, Christianæ charitati, è diametro oppositum: Christiana enim charitas non gaudet de malo, sed de bono, de malo autem ægritudinem animo concipit. Vitium est immediate à diabolo manans, ut tabella emblematica ostendit: quemadmodum canis canem os rodentem odit, ita figulum figulus, proximus proximum cui res prospere succedunt. Proxime autem ad hoc scelus accedit ἐπιχαιρεκακία subiecti ratione, non enim invidus est, nisi qui ἐπιχαιρεκακεῖ & vicissim: quisq; de alterius felicitate contristatur, ille de ægritudine gaudet, & si quid dolet, hoc certe dolet, quod malum non duplicíter intenditur: cuius gratia vel ipse oculum poneret. Nota est fabula de deab. infernalibus, quibus per Mercurium Iuppiter optionem dat eligendi, ut quod una eligat & optet sibi, id alteri in duplo contingat, tum INVIDIA eruit oculum sibi optat, ut alteri utrique oculus cadat: tales sunt serpentes ac circa caput pendentes furiæ, quib. invidi & ἐπιχαιρεκακοι stimulantur dignissime. Hoc autem INVIDIA præ omnibus aliis flagitium habet, ut cum omnia alia scelera obiecto (cui vel quod) noceant, hoc subiecto (in quo) incommodet, & non noceat, nisi ei, qui invidet, non cui invidetur. Unde proprium exedere cor fingitur, ac pingitur macie faciem suffusa horrendam: Hinc lepide Horatius: Invidus alterius rebus macrescit opimis, Et: Invidia Siculi non invenere tyranni Maius tormentum, &c.
units.tr: The man you see bears the picture of ENVY. Envy is a most unjust grief, conceived from another's happiness or prosperity, opposed to pity, which is a just grief at a neighbour's calamity. It is not the same as malicious gloating [ἐπιχαιρεκακία], for that is exultation at a neighbour's misfortunes, whereas envy is grief and sickness at a neighbour's goods. Envy is also a vice wholly base and diametrically opposed to Christian love, for Christian love does not rejoice in evil but in good, while envy conceives sorrow in the mind at another's good. It is a vice flowing directly from the devil, as the emblem picture shows: just as a dog hates the dog that gnaws its bone, so a potter hates a potter, and a neighbour hates a neighbour to whom things go well. Closest to this crime, by reason of the subject, is malicious gloating [ἐπιχαιρεκακεῖ]. For only one who gloats over others' misfortunes [ἐπιχαιρεκακεῖ] is envious, and conversely: whoever is saddened by another's happiness rejoices in another's distress, and if he grieves over anything, he certainly grieves only that evil is not doubled. For this reason he would even pluck out his own eye. The fable about the infernal goddesses is well known: Jupiter, through Mercury, gives them the choice that whatever one of them chooses for herself, the other should receive twice over. Then Envy, tearing out her own eye, wishes that the eyes of both of them should fall out. Such are the serpents and furies hanging about the head, by which the envious and the gloaters [ἐπιχαιρεκακοι] are most rightly goaded. Envy, moreover, has this disgrace beyond all other vices: while all other crimes harm the object (the one against whom or what they are directed), envy troubles the subject (the one in whom it dwells), and harms no one except the one who envies, not the one who is envied. Hence it is fancifully said to eat away the heart, and it is painted with a face horribly suffused with leanness. Hence Horace wittily says: "The envious man wastes away at another's rich possessions," and: "The tyrants of Sicily never found a greater torment than envy," and so on.

units.la: Bernhard. alicubi ait: esse Basilisci similem, qui venenum in oculo gerit, pessimum & præcaterorum ex tali. Nosse (inquit) cupio oculum venenatum, oculum nequam, oculum fascinantem; INVIDIA Mcogitato. Quid v. invidere, nisi malum videre est? Exempla sunt in sacris & profanis: Cain invidet, Abel i: Ismael, Isaaco: Eliab, & Saul, Davidi: Pharisaei, Christo: Severinus, Chrysostomus, Marius, Syllæ: Pompeius, Cæsari: & sexcentis aliis. Cum autem misericordiæ obiectum sit calamitas: Invidiæ v. Fortuna: quemadmodum dicitur: INVIDIA FORTUNÆ COMES. Malis invidiam sustinere quam misericordiam; quam in rem commode Poetanoster: Liuore quisquis improbo Caret, vir est iniserrimus, Nam summa liuor murmure Oppugnat acri, maxima Vt perflat Aufert robora.
units.tr: Bernard says somewhere that envy is like the basilisk, which bears poison in its eye, the worst of all such creatures. "I wish to know," he says, "the poisonous eye, the wicked eye, the bewitching eye; consider envy. For what is it to envy, except to look upon evil?" There are examples in sacred and profane history: Cain envied Abel; Ishmael envied Isaac; Eliab and Saul envied David; the Pharisees envied Christ; Severinus and Chrysostom envied others; Marius envied Sulla; Pompey envied Caesar; and countless others. Since the object of pity is calamity, the object of envy is good fortune, as the saying goes: "Envy is the companion of fortune." It is better to bear envy than pity, as our poet says well in this matter: "Whoever is free of wicked envy is a most wretched man, for envy assails the highest with bitter murmuring, and as the strongest wind blows, it carries away the mightiest oaks."

units.la: Augustinus: Invidia vitium diabolicum, quo solo diabolus reus (intelligo quoniam homini invidit felicitatem) & inexpiabiliter reus. Ex hoc sunt invidi.
units.tr: Augustine: Envy is a diabolical vice, by which alone the devil is guilty (I mean, because he envies man's happiness), and he is guilty beyond atonement. From this come the envious.

units.la: SINE CERERE ET BACCHO friget venus.
units.tr: Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold.

units.la: In vino esse [Greek word], Paulus testatur ad Ephesios: veteres dixerunt: ebrium esse seruum omnium peccatorum: & vere quidem, non enim vitium est, quod à vino calescentibus perpetrari non possit. Ebrii longe vltra beluinam feritatem assurgunt: non quidem culpa vini, sed vini abusu. Audias ex vino calentib. horridissimas calumnias, atq; blasphemias, ad quas vel ipse Phoebus expalescere possit: qui vino sese ingurgitant, non attendunt ad opus Domini: neq; adficiuntur super contritione Ioseph. Per ebrietatem designantur furta, caedes, committuntur latrocinia & homicidia, quemadmodum ebriosus indeq; furiosus Alexander interficit alterum suum ocellum & amicum intimum, non ob quoddam commissum facinus, sed quoniam in gratiam Regis Paternarum Praeconem laudu sese gesserat. Insunt ebrietati stupra, furtiui amores, adulteria, incestus, vt in sacris de incestu Lothi apertum est: & memorat Augustinus historiam de quodam adolescente, qui per ebrietatem caecidit Patrem: vitiarit matrem: & duabus fororib. vim attulerit: Ceres & Bacchus gignunt venerem. Et quod cum turpissimum, tum nocentissimum est: Vitia vino concepta etiam sine vino durant, vt refert noster Seneca. Per ebrietatem multi fiunt diserti, tametsi vix balbutire possint, nam dum bibo vinum, ait Rythmicus, loquitur mea lingua Latinum: iuxta illud Martialis:
units.tr: "In wine there is excess" [ἀσωτία], as Paul testifies to the Ephesians. The ancients said that a drunkard is the slave of all sins, and truly so, for there is no vice that a man warmed with wine cannot commit. Drunkards rise far above beastly savagery, not indeed through the fault of wine but through its abuse. You may hear from men heated with wine the most horrible slanders and blasphemies, at which Phoebus himself might turn pale. Those who gorge themselves on wine do not regard the work of the Lord, nor are they grieved over the affliction of Joseph. Drunkenness brings thefts, murders, robberies and manslaughters, just as the drunken and then raving Alexander killed his other eye and most intimate friend, not for any crime committed but because, to please the king, he had acted as a praiser of his father's deeds. Drunkenness brings debauchery, furtive love affairs, adulteries and incest, as is plain in the sacred pages concerning the incest of Lot. And Augustine records the history of a certain young man who, in drunkenness, struck his father dead, violated his mother, and laid hands on two of his sisters. Ceres and Bacchus beget Venus. And what is as shameful as it is harmful: vices conceived in wine endure even without wine, as our Seneca reports. Through drunkenness many become eloquent, though they can scarcely stammer; for, as the rhymester says, while I drink wine, my tongue speaks Latin, in line with that saying of Martial:
I can compose nothing when sober, but when I drink
Fifteen poets come rushing to me.

units.la: Ebrii Apollines fiunt alii, & suauem mulcere se cantu sibi persuadent, tametsi ftentores sint: [German text] (quod caninum est, & porcos oblectat) [German text] (saluo honore decoris) [German text] ita non tam in bestias, vt diximus, euadunt homines, sed etiam bestialem immanitatem saepissime superant. Bacchho & Cerere propitiis saltat venus, multisq; saltatorib. aures asininae longissime supra caput eminent: posset hic vel ille pro viro reputari grauissimo, si loco considere suo, & gestus simiae omittere posset. Ebrietas studio quaesita insania est, & omnes vires corporis & animae exhaurit, quare vini vsus intraturis domum Domini sacerdotibus interdicitur, & rectissime dixerunt veteres: esse in laico crimen, in sacerdote sacrilegium. Magistratus etiam diuini Spiritus oraculo ab ebrietate arcentur. Ne regibus, inquit sapientissimus, des vinum, neq; siceram Principibus, ne cum bibant, obliuiscantur statuti, & mutent ius adflictorum. Si sexum distinguas, mulieribus turpissima est ebrietas, apud Romanos capitale fuit, vnde Ouidius:
units.tr: Some drunkards turn into Apollos and persuade themselves that they soothe others with sweet song, though they are only screechers (a noise that is dog-like and delights pigs) [German text] (with the honour of decency preserved) [German text]. So men do not, as we have said, pass over merely into beasts; they very often surpass even bestial savagery. With Bacchus and Ceres propitious, Venus dances, and among the many dancers the ears of asses stick up far above their heads. One of them might be taken for a most grave man if he could sit in his own place and refrain from the gestures of an ape. Drunkenness is a madness sought out by choice, and it drains all the strength of body and soul. For this reason the use of wine is forbidden to priests who are about to enter the house of the Lord, and the ancients rightly said: in a layman it is a crime, in a priest it is sacrilege. Magistrates too are kept from drunkenness by the oracle of the divine Spirit. Do not give wine to kings, says the wisest of men, nor strong drink to princes, lest when they drink they forget what is decreed and alter the right of the afflicted. If you distinguish by sex, drunkenness is most shameful in women; among the Romans it was a capital offence, whence Ovid:
A woman lying shamefully soaked in much Lyaeus
Is worthy to suffer any lover at all.

units.la: Si at ates: non adolescentioribus: prisci Gentiles studio inebriabant seruos, vt horum turpitudine morum ab hoc turpi vitio abhorrere discerent: & dicitur in versu Ebrietas commune malum crimenq; iuuenta.
units.tr: If you look to the ages, not only to the young: the ancient Gentiles deliberately got their slaves drunk, so that by seeing their disgraceful conduct they might learn to shrink from this shameful vice; and it is said in a verse that drunkenness is the common evil and crime of youth.

units.la: Sponsa ergo Christi (vt cum D. Hieron. pie loquar) vini abusum vinum sugiat pro veneno: haec prima arma sunt daemonum: non sic auaritia quatit; inflet superbia, delectet ambitio, facile alius caremus vitiis, si hic hostis nobis inclusus est.
units.tr: So let the bride of Christ (to speak piously with St. Jerome) shun wine as poison when it is abused. This is the first weapon of the demons. Avarice does not shake us so, pride does not puff us up, ambition does not delight us in this way; we can easily be free of the other vices if this enemy is shut in with us.
CERES AND BACCHUS DRIVE OUT VENUS.

units.la: [engraving: Ceres and Bacchus expel Venus; not transcribed as text]
units.tr: [engraving: Ceres and Bacchus expel Venus; not transcribed as text]

units.la: Conserit Oenotrius solida bonus arte racemos, Brutorumq; ipsos stercore pinguat humo: Hinc simul ac gignunt generosa animantia vina, Exsiliunt veneris mente procace capræ.
units.tr: The good Oenotrian plants his vines with skilled hand, and enriches the very soil with the dung of beasts. So as soon as the wines are born, the spirited animals spring up, and goats leap out with the lustful mind of Venus.

units.la: ABYSVM ABVSVM vini, nascentemq; inde degenerem τὰ λεγόμενα ο͂ν... vtrescentiam omnes boni semper detestati sunt. Hinc ortum duxisse arbitramur fabulam de animantibus, bestiis, ac feris circa Bacchum, de quibus Ouidius.
units.tr: Everyone good has always detested the abyss, that is, the abuse of wine, and the degenerate offspring born from it [τὰ λεγόμενα ὄν...], and the corruption. From this, we think, arose the fable about the animals, beasts and wild creatures around Bacchus, of which Ovid writes.

units.la: Quem circa Tigres, simulacraq; inania Lyncum,Pictarumq; iacent fera corpora Pantherarum.
units.tr: Around him lie tigers, the empty images of lynxes, and the spotted bodies of panthers.

units.la: Idem eundem significasse statuerunt fabula illa sua de sociis Vlyssis à Circe nobilissima Lamia in omnis generis bestias atq; animantia couersis, quum illi apud Circen intemperanter admodum vixerunt, eoq; ab hac in animantia conuersi finguntur quoniam illic immodicis escis potationibusq; quasi in hara saginati sunt. Et significanter admodum Poeta inquit in historia seu fabula Vlyssis:
units.tr: The same fable of the companions of Ulysses, transformed by Circe, that most famous enchantress, into beasts and animals of every kind, has been taken to signify the same thing. They lived intemperately with Circe, and so they are said to have been changed by her into animals, because there they were fattened on immoderate feasting and drinking, as if in a pigsty. And the poet, in his story or fable of Ulysses, says this with great aptness:

units.la: Osq; meum sensi pardo occallescere rostroColla tumtre torus, & qua modo pocu'a parteSumpta mihi fuerant, illa vestigia feci.
units.tr: "My mouth I felt harden into a leopard's snout, my neck swell with a thick bristling mass, and the parts through which I had lately taken the cup became footprints."

units.la: Ebriosi enim tales gestus ad viuum imitantur atq; exprimunt. Quare apologus noster ait: Oenotrium quoniam plantasse vineam, consensisse vites, quas omnis generis animalium sterc ore impinguant q. vina autem isthac bibentes, eorum animalium moribus praeditos euasisse, quorum stercore stercorata et aut vites, nimirum: ouium Leonum, simiarum, caprarum, porcorum, canum, similium.
units.tr: For such drunkards imitate and express to the life these gestures. Hence our fable says: since the Oenotrian planted the vineyard and set the vines, which he enriches with dung of every kind of animal, and those who drink these wines have turned out with the dispositions of those animals whose dung fattened the vines, namely sheep, lions, monkeys, goats, pigs, dogs, and the like.

units.la: Varie pro varietate ingeniorum adficiuntur ebrii: quod enim in corde sobrij hoc est in ore & opere ebrii. Oues multi fiunt: mites, mansueti. & in omnes partes versatiles. Multi simiae, gesticulantur & in Protheis, Polypiq; morem vertuntur. Porci alii: vt in superioribus. Non pauci Leones, omnia sursum deorsum vertentes: raptantes: quasi tantes: conterentes: confringentes: quod in sacris etiam perstrictum crimen est. Inprimis autem capra fiunt plaerique, quando Cerere & Baccho irritatur venus. Quem in sensum Virgilius Ouidianam herbulam obscene satis interpretatur, dicens:
units.tr: Drunkards are affected in various ways according to the variety of their dispositions. For what is in the heart of the sober man is in the mouth and deeds of the drunk. Many become sheep: meek, gentle, and changeable in every direction. Many become monkeys, gesticulating and turning themselves about like Proteus or Polyphemus. Some become pigs, as in the passages above. Not a few become lions, turning everything upside down: plundering, tearing, crushing, breaking, a crime which is even censured in sacred writings. Above all, most become goats, when lust is aroused by Ceres and Bacchus. In this sense Virgil interprets Ovid's little herb rather obscenely, saying:

units.la: Hinc legitur radix, de qua flos lacteus exit, Quamcunque Molyvocant? &c.
units.tr: "Hence is read the root from which the milky flower springs, which they call moly..."

units.la: Huc nostrum collineat ἐμεσῶ. & ex vino prouenientes libidines taxat: quo de expertis loquitur sapiens: Ne respicito vinum cum rubescit, quum exhibet in poculo colorem, &c. Oculi tui respicient alienas, & animus tuus eloquetur perversitates. Non quidem (vt hoc denuo meneamus) vsu sed abusu vini. Hinc Chrysost.Laqueus maximus (inquit) mulieris, forma est, sed lasciuus aspectus, &c.
units.tr: This passage aims at [ἐμεσῶ] and censures the lusts arising from wine, of which the wise man speaks from experience: "Do not look upon wine when it reddens, when it shows its colour in the cup... Your eyes will look upon strange women, and your heart will utter perversities." Not, indeed (to repeat this again), the use of wine but its abuse. Hence Chrysostom says: "The greatest snare of a woman is beauty, but a wanton glance..."

units.la: Deq; Lothi incestu Aegiptus Ebrietas decepit, quem Sodoma non cepit: Vritur ille flamma mulierum, quem sulphurea flamma non vrit. Et idem alibi: Valde turpe est, vt quem non vincit homo, vincat libido: & obruatur vino, qui non vincitur ferro. Sunt mortifera talia pocula: Mors iuuat infundere, & diabolus euacuare, quare in fine plerumq; grauissime plectitur hoc peccatum, certe isthic, nisi respiscatur, sed & hic, vt in exemplis Holofernis, Amnonis: & inprimis Legatorum, apud Amyntam Regem Macedonia, Persarum sinus matrum licentius contrectantium, eoq; iusta Nemesi a filio Amyntae occisorum.
units.tr: And concerning Lot's incest, Egypt, drunkenness, deceived him, whom Sodom did not catch: he burns with the flame of women, whom the sulphurous flame did not burn. And elsewhere the same writer: "It is very shameful that lust should conquer the man whom no man conquers, and that he should be overwhelmed by wine, who is not conquered by the sword." Such cups are deadly: "Death delights to pour out, and the devil to empty out." Therefore at the end this sin is usually punished most severely, certainly there, unless it is repented of, but also here, as in the examples of Holofernes and Amnon, and above all of the envoys of Amyntas, King of Macedonia, who, too freely handling the wives of the Persians, were then slain by the son of Amyntas in just retribution.
IN THE LAST DAYS there shall be scoffers.

units.la: Pastores stolidi nunc sunt ludibria vulgi, Nec tamen à sannis temperat aula sibi. Sit desiderium vestrum ergo Κοιμ[?]ων ἀνδρῶν, Pastores ! merces arce reposita poli est. Iure gentium cautum est, ne quis Legatos violet aut aspernetur: quod ex Tullii Hostilii oratione ad Legatos, &c. apparet: Vt erpopulus prius aspernatus fuerit Legatos: & historia Dauidis id luculenter confirmare videtur. At hocius Legatorum, † Dei Legatis, sacerdotibus Domini, ministris verbi obtingere & exhiberi nullo vnquam tempore potuit: verum quo maior fuit Legantis Maiestas, eo grauior est & fuit Legatorum adflictio & calamitas. Experientia omnium temporum istud confirmat. Primaeuatis vltimus Legatum & iustitiae praeconem Noam cum Mathusalemo, aliisq; omnino renuebat audire, & obseruare: Non ampli⁹ (inquit Dn.) disceptabit spiritus meus cum homine, quia caro est. Secundae status Lothum comprehendere & grauiter plecti volebant. Eadem fortuna cum talibus monstris luctati sunt Moses. Samuel. Elias. Elisaeus. Esaias, ferra a Manasse Rege Idololatricis mo(vt statuit Hieron.) dissectus, vsq; ad Paranymphum Dn. Ioannem, quos Dn. Saluator omnes ab iis, ad quos missi erant, persecutionem passos esse adserit plurimis in locis noui Instrumenti, praecipue vero in Parabola de Nuptiis filii regis: & seq. c. Matth. Sortem vero Legatorum suorum post tempora sua vsq; ad finem mundi describit in vltima concione ad discipulos. Si, inquit, verbum meum seruarunt & vestrum seruabunt: si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur: quod ipsum adeo euenisse exemplo suo & collegarū edocet Paulus: &c. Reliquorum inde quaestus scientes volentes omittimus: quibus haud mitior fuit fortuna, nam cum illud in viridi fieret, quid in Arido factum fuisse coniicies; &c: si Patrefamilias Beelzebub vocauerunt, quanto magis domesticos eius vocauerint. Non igitur mirum tam indigna atq; nefanda sacerdotes atq; ministros Dei pati a malis etiamnum. Carnificem hodie quam sacerdotem esse atq; vocari satius atmitius est, maxime si quis solicite & cum zelo officio praeesse suo velit, nam muti illi canes: vulpes: dolosi operarij: Dominorum assentatores: Fratrum oppressores, populi opplausum quarentes non digni sunt qui in Legatorum Domini ordinem allegantur, reperient illi mercedem suam dignam operibus suis cum infidelibus: quare concludimus cum Augusto. Nihil est in hac vita & maxime hoc tempore facilius & latius, & hominibus acceptabilius Episcopi aut presbyteri aut Diaconi officio, si perfunctorie & adulatorieres agatur, sed nihil apud Deum miserius & tristius & damnabilius. Vicissim, nihil est in hac vita & maxime hoc tempore difficilius, laboriosius, periculosius, Episcopi, Presbyteri, aut Diaconi officio: sed apud Deum nil beatius, si eo modo militetur, quo Imperator nosier iubet. Bonorum Legatorum, qui exsequuntur officium, merces & scutum Deus est, & copiosa ipsorum merces in caelo: In hoc autem saeculo nunquam impune quis ipsos persequutus est, persequitur, nec persequetur.
units.tr: Foolish ministers are now the mockery of the crowd, yet the court does not keep itself free from jeers. Let your desire then be for the shepherding of men [Κοιμ[?]ων ἀνδρῶν]. Ministers! Your reward is laid up in the citadel of heaven. By the law of nations it is provided that no one shall violate or spurn envoys, as appears from the speech of Tullus Hostilius to the envoys, etc., where the people had first spurned the envoys; and the history of David seems clearly to confirm this. But this right, owed to the envoys of God, the priests of the Lord, the ministers of the Word †, could never at any time be granted or shown to them. Rather, the greater the majesty of the one who sends, the heavier has been the affliction and calamity of the envoys. Experience of all ages confirms this. In the first age, the last of the line, Noah, herald of righteousness, together with Methuselah and others, altogether refused to hear and heed him. "My Spirit," says the Lord, "shall not strive with man any longer, because he is flesh." In the second age they wanted to seize Lot and punish him severely. Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, and the others wrestled with such monsters under the same fate; Isaiah was sawn in two by King Manasseh, the idolater (as Jerome holds), and so on down to John, the Lord's friend of the bridegroom. The Lord Saviour asserts that all of these suffered persecution from those to whom they were sent, in many places of the New Testament, especially in the parable of the wedding of the king's son, and in the following chapter of Matthew. He describes the lot of his envoys after their time, down to the end of the world, in his last discourse to the disciples: "If they have kept my word, they will keep yours; if they have persecuted me, they will persecute you". Paul teaches by his own example and that of his colleagues that this very thing came to pass, etc. We knowingly and willingly pass over the sufferings of the others; their fate was no milder. For if this was done when the wood is green, consider what was done when it is dry; etc.; if they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more will they call his household. It is therefore no wonder that priests and ministers of God still suffer such unworthy and wicked treatment from evil men. Today it is better to be called an executioner than a priest, especially if someone wishes to carry out his office diligently and with zeal. For those dumb dogs, foxes, deceitful workers, flatterers of masters, oppressors of brethren, seekers of popular applause, are not worthy to be enrolled in the order of the Lord's envoys; they will receive their wages, fitting for their works, with the unfaithful. Wherefore we conclude with Augustine: "Nothing in this life, and especially at this time, is easier, broader, and more acceptable to men than the office of bishop, presbyter or deacon, if it is done perfunctorily and flatteringly; but nothing is more wretched, sad and damnable before God. Conversely, nothing in this life, and especially at this time, is more difficult, laborious and perilous than the office of bishop, presbyter or deacon; but nothing is more blessed before God, if it is carried on in the way our Emperor commands." God is the reward and shield of good envoys who carry out their office, and their reward in heaven is abundant. But in this age no one has ever persecuted them with impunity, nor does anyone do so now, nor will anyone in future.

units.la: OPES ET GLORIA HVIVS mundi vanitas.
units.tr: The vanity of the wealth and glory of this world.
All things pass away, and man is more fleeting than a thin shadow,
Shaken from his crest, every man perishes:

units.la: Sis licet excelsi sublatus ad æthera cœli,
units.tr: Though you be raised up high to the heights of the lofty heaven,
Beneath the depths of the earth you will be cast down.

units.la: Iterum vinuehimur in vanitatem studiorum huius aeui, maxime vero in corradendis diuitiis, & aucupanda gloria occupati, quae omnia in fumum tandem abire atq; euanescere luce clarius ex hac tabella perspicitur: Alligat hic homo terrenus, & terrenorum studiosus manus & cor suum Regina P. Cunis, eius frena capessit, seq; ei regendum praebet quantus, quantus est, totum. sed omnis honos, omnis gloria, omnis affluentia concedit in fumum, fumus ut ante fuit: quare in stabilioribus figendum, fundandum, haerendum erat: Omnia hic vana sunt, & VANITAS VANITATVM, ut Ecclesiastes infit: & omnis gloria carnis, tanquam flos agri, tanquam foenum, deniq; tanquam fumus, a summo venerandissimo Imperii vertice ad infimas stabuli vsq; quisquilias, ut recte Cyprian. sanctus Christi praeco & martyr: quid & quos honores putas [?] quam affluentia in diuitiis? quam potentiam in castris? in Magistratu Purpurae sPLECTENTEM? in principatu lucentia potestatem? malorum blandientium virus occultum est, & arridentis nequitiae facies quidem lata, sed calamitatis abstrusae illecebrosa fallacia, instar quoddam veneni, vbi in lethales succos dulcedine adspersa calliditate fallendi sapore medicato poculum videtur esse quod sumitur, vbi epotaueris, pernicies haustā, grassatur. Hactenus Cyprian. Nec aliter aestimat Simonides: Greek text. Perinde ac si cum Mose voluisset dicere: Greek text. Et cum Dauide: vniuersa vanitas est omnis homo viuens, & frustra tumultuatur. Exemplis res fiet clarior: confidentes ad vrnam Alexandri Magni Regis Philosophi, & funebres planctus aedentes, cum diu potentiam regis momentaneam dilaudassent: nunc in vrna iacet, inquit, vermium esca futurus. Imperator Alexander Seuerus, dixit se perhibetur de se & omni sua potentia atque gloria, qua vsus erat in vita: Omnia fui & nihil mihi prodest. Gilimerus Rex Vandalorum pro triumpho ductus a Bellisario in Vrbem Greek text Constantinopolim, dixisse fertur ex Salomone: Greek text. Et de Magno Turcorum Imperatore ferunt, quod vrna suam funeream secum vehere semper solitus fuerit, & ante eum pannum, iusseritq; ferialem ante se proclamare: Ecce, Magnus Turcorum Imp. Saladinus de omnibus thesauris suis nihil inde reportat, quam hunc pannum. Deniq; qualis, quanta sit gloria, maiestas, opulentia omnium etiam summorum, apparet ex doctissimi Imp. Adriani vltimis verbis, quibus ludit ad animam: Ani mula vagula, blandula, hospes, comesque corporis, quae nunc abibit in loca; pallidula, rigida, nudula. Nec vt soles dabit iocos. O vanitatem vanitatum vanissimam! quam ergo missis factis terrenis, ad coelestia vnice adspiramus!
units.tr: Again we are carried away into the vanities of this age, and are busy above all with heaping up riches and hunting after glory.
