That all these things at last vanish into smoke and fade away is plainer than daylight from this picture: here the earthly man, a devotee of earthly things, binds his hands and heart to Regina P. Cunis, takes up its reins, and offers himself wholly to be governed by it, however great or small he is. But every honour, every glory, every abundance gives way to smoke, and becomes smoke as it was before. Therefore we ought to fix, found and cling to what is more stable. Here all things are vain, and VANITY OF VANITIES, as Ecclesiastes begins. And all the glory of the flesh, like the flower of the field, like hay, and finally like smoke, from the highest and most venerable summit of empire down to the lowest trifles of the stable, as rightly Cyprian, the holy herald and martyr of Christ, says: what honours, what do you think of them? What abundance in riches? What power in camps? What in the magistracy, glittering in purple? What in the principate, shining with authority? The poison of flattering evils is hidden, and the face of smiling wickedness is indeed cheerful, but the enticing deceit of hidden calamity is like a kind of poison: where the cup that is taken seems to have a medicinal flavour, sweetened with the honey of deceitful cunning and mixed into deadly juices; when you have drunk it off, the destruction once swallowed spreads through you. Thus far Cyprian. Simonides judges no differently: Greek text. As if he wished to say with Moses: Greek text. And with David: every man living is altogether vanity, and he stirs himself up in vain. The matter will become clearer by examples. Those who sat by the urn of Alexander the Great, the king's philosopher, and began funeral lamentations, after they had long praised the king's fleeting power, said: now he lies in an urn, destined to be food for worms. The emperor Alexander Severus is said to have declared of himself and of all his power and glory, which he had enjoyed in life: I have been everything, and it profits me nothing. Gelimer, king of the Vandals, led in triumph by Belisarius into the city of Constantinople, is said to have spoken the words of Solomon: Greek text. And of the great emperor of the Turks they report that he was always accustomed to carry his funeral urn with him, and had a servant's cloth carried before him, and ordered it to be proclaimed before him: Behold, the great emperor of the Turks, Saladin, carries away from all his treasures nothing but this cloth. Finally, what sort of glory, majesty and wealth even the greatest men have is shown by the last words of the most learned emperor Hadrian, with which he addresses his soul: Little wandering soul, pleasant one, guest and companion of the body, now you are going off to places pale, stiff and bare, and you will not make jokes as you used to. O vanity of vanities, most vain! How wholly, then, we should set aside earthly things and aspire only to heavenly ones!

units.la: Spartian. in Hadr. Imp. Colos. 3. v. 1. 2. 3
units.tr: Spartian. in Hadr. Imp. Colos. 3. v. 1. 2. 3
FAME, THE WORST OF EVILS! Than which there is none worse.

units.la: Sunt, qui eminere, & obtinere primas in hoc æuo gestiunt, & hoc vanum est. Est quidem fama bonum, & quidem bonum non mediocre, sed inter bona huius ævi cū primis, Fama enim, aiunt, & vita aquiparantur: paribusq; passibus ambulant, HONORES, FAMA, VITA. VIRTVTIS Comes est, bona fama qua semel amissa postea nullus eris, vt Cato noster in Moralibus. Famam dico, quæ recte facta, pietate, & studio virtutum non fucato, acquiritur. Quæ autem fama quæritur secus quam diximus, neq; legitimo fine, ea fama vanissima est. Quærunt alii studiosissime Famam ex congestis thesauris auri & argenti, vana hæc fama est, & mallent hi beati quam boni dici er in hoc seculo. Quaerenit ex opibus fama, prophana venit. Possunt vel pessimi quique esse diuites: & ingentes thesauros per phas & nephas hinc inde corradere, harpagare, concumulare & contumulare
units.tr: There are those who long to stand out and hold the first place in this age, and this is vain. Fame is indeed a good, and no small good, but among the goods of this life it is one of the foremost, for, as they say, fame and life are reckoned equal, and they walk with equal steps: HONOURS, FAME, LIFE. Good fame is the companion of virtue, which, once lost, is never regained, as our Cato says in the Moralia. I mean the fame that is won by right actions, by piety, and by an unfeigned zeal for virtue. But fame that is sought otherwise than I have said, and not for a lawful end, is most vain. Others seek fame most eagerly from heaped-up treasures of gold and silver; this fame is empty, and such men would rather be called rich than good in this age. Fame that comes from wealth is a profane thing. Even the very worst men can be rich, and by right or wrong can scrape together, snatch, heap up and bury huge treasures on every side.

units.la: Nil nostro in corpore gazæ Proficiunt, vt inquit Lucretius.
units.tr: Such treasures profit nothing for our body, as Lucretius says.

units.la: Non domus & fundus, non aris aceruus & auri.
units.tr: Neither house and land, nor a heap of bronze and gold.

units.la: Non iam dicam: quando tale studium cancrinos sæpe imitetur grecsus, & Satanam habeat ductorem & rectorem: Nam omnis dives aut iniquus est aut iniqui hæres. Non enim gazæ, nec consularis, &c.
units.tr: I will not even mention that such a pursuit often imitates the crab's backward gait, and has Satan for its leader and guide. For every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man. For neither treasures nor consular rank, etc.

units.la: Sunt qui famam quærunt ex fumosis maiorum clypeis, ex multorum seclorum prosapia, ex laudatorum maiorum præclare factis, sed & hoc vanissimum est: Nam virtus nobilitat, non aliena sed propria, quare præclarissime dictum ab Ouidio:
units.tr: There are those who seek fame from the smoky shields of their ancestors, from the lineage of many generations, from the noble deeds of praised forefathers. But this too is most vain, for virtue ennobles, not what belongs to others but what is one's own; hence Ovid says most aptly:

units.la: Et genus & proavos & quæ non fecimus ipsi Non ea nostra puto. Et Lucretius —Nil Proficiunt vel nobilitas vel gloria Patrum, &c.
units.tr: Both birth and ancestors, and whatever we have not done ourselves, I do not count as ours. And Lucretius: Neither nobility nor the glory of one's forefathers avails anything, etc.

units.la: Sunt qui malis factis inclarescere cupiunt, quemadmodum Herostrat. qui vt memoriam nominis sui post se relinqueret, celebratissimum Ephesiæ Dianæ templum incendit: Maledicta hæc est fama, qualis & Epicureorum atq; Empedoclarum illorum qui dicunt: vbiq; relinquamus memoriam latitia, nam hæc est portio nostra & fors huiusmodi.
units.tr: There are those who desire to become famous by evil deeds, as Herostratus did, who, so that he might leave the memory of his name after him, burned the most celebrated temple of Ephesian Diana. This is cursed fame, like that of the Epicureans and of Empedocles, who say: let us leave everywhere the memory of joy, for this is our portion and such is our lot.

units.la: Quicquid fit, quippe bonum dici possit fama, etiam gloriose parta caducum tamen est & fragile bonum, & est vbi gloriosum & ignobilu nihil differunt, quemadmodum dicitur:
units.tr: Whatever the case, fame may rightly be called a good, but even fame won by glorious deeds is a frail and fleeting good, and where there is glory, nothing differs from the ignoble, as the saying goes:

units.la: Est vbi nobilitas, honor atq; potentia mundi Hic forma vultus conspicuis esse pares Ecce quis his pauper, quu diues iure vocandus? Qualibet offa suis osibus æqua vides.
units.tr: Here there is nobility, honour and the power of the world; here beauty of face and bearing are equal among the conspicuous. Behold, who is poor here, and who rightly to be called rich? Every bone is equal to the others in its bones.

units.la: Quare consultissimum fuerit missa fama & gloria terrena quærere cæleftem illam & gloriam perennem, de qua dicitur: Gloria, honor, pax, omni opevanti bonum: Interim Stet quicunq; volet potens aula culmine lubrico: Me dulcis saturet quies: obscuro positus loco leni perfruar otio.
units.tr: Therefore it will be wisest to set aside the pursuit of earthly fame and glory and to seek that heavenly and everlasting glory, of which it is said: Glory, honour and peace to everyone who works good. Meanwhile, let whoever wishes stand powerful on the slippery summit of a court: may sweet quiet satisfy me, and may I, placed in an obscure spot, enjoy a gentle leisure.
MINE: THINE: HIS.

units.la: [woodcut illustration, no text] Iusta licent in præsenti commercia seclo, Sistere non alias ciuica vita potest: Verum absint fraudesq; doliq;, & crimina falsi, Sistere non alias ciuica vita potest.
units.tr: Just dealings are allowed in the present age; civic life cannot otherwise endure. But let fraud and trickery, and crimes of falsehood, be absent; civic life cannot otherwise endure.

units.la: Inter eas res, quarum virum ingenuum probumq; pudere non debeat, numeratur etiā à sapiente hæc: Attendere de varia mercatorum venditione. Quare & nobis licitum esse arbitramur de iis disputare, & sententiam nostram interponere: PRINCIPIO autem tenendum est, licita esse mercimonia, & concedi contractus civiles per se: quod tam certum est, quam est distinctio mei & tui: quæ certe quarta secundæ duarum tabularum lege diuino oraculo expressè cauta atq; confirmata: & ostendunt exempla utriusque Instrumenti, quod commercia semper exercita strenul atq; à Christiana plebe per se probata sint, nihil ergo moramur, quæ hæc vel illa Sus Cata-Baptistica oggrūniat. Adstringuntur autem mercimonia legibus, cum diuinis tum positiuis seu humanis: illis quidem, ut ne vt antur statera dolosis: ne Epham minuant: ne sortes adulterent: ne paleam pro tritico vendant, deniq; ne in mercimoniis agant dolose cum fratribus, sed omnia fieri curent in charitate. Et quod quis sibi fieri nolit, alteri id faciat minus, quod etiam ex L. Naturæ defumptū, & adeo probatum est laudatissimo Imperatori Seuero, ut omnibus tabulis insculpi & mandari id iusserit. His vero ut omnes contractus nitantur, ÆQVO ET BONO, exclusis omnibus fraudibus & dolis malis. Nam dolosus contra rectam rationem, æquitatem iuris & fas, & Deum ipsum agere instituit, sed non perficiet cæpta: imo ipse suo dolo (res hominum miro suo iudicio temperante Iehouah;) velut venator suis laqueis capietur atq; irretitus pessimè peribit malis verissimum q; experietur quod
units.tr: Among those matters which an honourable and upright man should not be ashamed to take up, this one is counted by the wise: to attend to the varied selling of merchants. Therefore we judge that it is also lawful for us to discuss these things and to set forth our opinion. First, however, it must be held that trade is lawful in itself and that civil contracts are permitted, which is as certain as the distinction of mine and thine. This is expressly guarded and confirmed by the divine oracle in the law of the second table, the eighth commandment. The examples of both Testaments show that commerce has always been practised vigorously and has been approved by the Christian people in itself. So we need not linger over whatever this or that Anabaptist sow grunts. Trade is bound by laws, both divine and positive or human. The divine laws say: not to use deceitful scales; not to diminish the ephah; not to adulterate the lots; not to sell chaff for wheat; and finally, not to wrong a brother in business, but to see that all things are done in love. And: what one does not wish done to himself, let him not do to another. This precept is taken from the law of nature, and it was so approved by the most praiseworthy emperor Severus that he ordered it to be engraved and posted on all tablets. Moreover, all contracts ought to rest on what is EQUITABLE AND GOOD, with every fraud and wicked trickery excluded. For the deceiver acts against right reason, the equity of law and justice, and against God himself. He does not bring his undertakings to completion; indeed, by his own trickery (God, by his wonderful judgment, tempers human affairs, Jehovah), he is caught like a hunter in his own snares, and, entangled, he perishes most wretchedly by his wickedness, and he will truly find what is said: Nobody has ever been happy for long through crimes.
Nobody has ever been happy for long through crimes.

units.la: Μυξιομμοκρατίαν est in Iustitia, studioq; æqui & boni, ac proinde id omnes boni vnice pensi habebunt, vt iustitiæ distributiuæ; commutatiuæq; in hoc ordine studeant, & scientes volentes neminem dolo malo circumscribant.
units.tr: Mixiommocratia [Μυξιομμοκρατίαν] lies in justice and in zeal for what is equitable and good. Accordingly, all good people will make it their sole concern to strive for distributive and commutative justice in this sphere, and knowingly and willingly to cheat no one by wicked trickery.

units.la: Χερίμετ... Pie & præclare D. Gregorius: credite mihi, quia sicut experimento multorum didicimus, in damno expenditur, quicquid cum peccato congregatur. Si vultis igitur nihil iniuste perdere, summopere fludete de iniustitia nihil habere. In terrenis etenim rebus semper causa damni est origo peccati. Hactenus Gregor. Frequens dici solet: male partum, male dilabitur.
units.tr: Cherimet... [Χερίμετ...] Piously and admirably St Gregory says: Believe me, for as we have learned by the experience of many, whatever is gathered together with sin is spent in loss. If you wish therefore to lose nothing unjustly, take great care to have nothing of injustice. For in earthly things the cause of loss is always the origin of sin. Thus far Gregory. It is commonly said: what is ill-gotten is ill-spent.

units.la: De male quæsitis non gaudet tertius hares, &c.
units.tr: The third heir does not rejoice in ill-gotten goods, etc.

units.la: Quare & hic pia cautione opus est: Es ist ein böser Pfenning der einem zween schadet/ mediocri igitur compendio vel lucello contentus esto, ut augeat Deus reliqua. Sed ô tempora! ô mores! quot mercimoniorum genera, tot decipiendi modi, in diuendenda annona: pannu! libris etiam limo & in oui, cæpis, holeribus, butyro, & quis omnia auri & argenti retia percensebit.
units.tr: Therefore here too there is need of pious caution: It is a bad penny that harms the one who holds it twice over; be content, then, with a modest gain or a little profit, so that God may increase the rest. But oh the times! Oh the morals! As many kinds of merchandise, so many ways of deceiving in the selling of grain, cloth, books, even mud, and in eggs, onions, vegetables, butter; and who could count up all the nets of gold and silver?

units.la: EMBLEM- A AURO UBIQUE RETIA ponuntur.
units.tr: EMBLEM: Nets are laid everywhere with gold.

units.la: Aurea divini quæruntur ubiq; metalli Munera, sub criptis aucupio, atq; mari. Improba ter stolidum quatit hæc vasania mundum, Cum quærenda prius cælica regna forent.
units.tr: Golden gifts of the divine metal are sought everywhere, by digging under the earth, by fowling, and by the sea. This wicked madness shakes the foolish world three times over, when the heavenly kingdoms ought rather to be sought.

units.la: Non omnino improbamus maximam illam folertiam & sagacitatem mortalium ægrorum in perscrutandis terrę viscceribus inueniendorum pretiosissimorum metallorum gratia.Nam cum aurum,argentum,as, & alia metalla bonum Dei donum sint,consequens est,etiam illa à nobis perquiri nō omnino illicitum esse. Verbum diuinum, virtutes, inprimisq; virtutes,auro defæcato & pretiosissimo comparantur. Iob venas seu meatus auri in terrę viscceribus laudat.Etiam piissimi multi auro,argento,æ,aliisq; metallis ditissimi fuerunt, neq; tamen propterea male audierunt, dānares: ex fluminibus gemma & aurum datum esse cum sacra tum prophana testantur.Quamuis nimium auri studium, & perfodiendorum montium libido auri gratia merito à piis adstringenda paulisper aut minuenda videatur:&ietfet * optandū homines to studio ferri in cœlum, quo scrutantur terra viscera, sola diuitiarum cupiditate pelleāi, qua beatum hominem adeo facere non possunt, vt multos admodum, idq; non raro insumpta opera ac factorum sumptuū pœniteat:Nota est historia Pythii Metallarii, & quomodo vxor ipsius auri ἀπλήσιον in ipso correxerit,confectis affabre aureis tragematis & esurienti propinatis, quibus tñ esuriem illę suam solari, nedum animam tranquillare & conscientiam non possit.Huc pertinet & Midæ auriritis, quem tamen cito stultissimæ optionis pœnituisse historiæ tradunt. Ponenda igitur erat hæc μοχθηρία in perquirendis thesauris spiritualibus, docente Christo, præ quibus tamen stolidissimi homines terrena tam frequenter expetunt: quod & Ouid. deridet,inquiens itum est in viscera terra Quaq; recondiderat,stygiisq; reconderat vmbris Iamq; nocens ferrum,ferroq; nocentius aurum, Prodierat cuius dira cupidine tandem Omne nephas fugere procul verumq; fidesq; In quorum subiere locum fraudesq; dolique, Insidiaq; & vis,& amor sceleratus habendi.
units.tr: We do not altogether disapprove of the great cleverness and shrewdness of mortals in searching the bowels of the earth for the sake of the most precious metals. For since gold, silver, copper and the other metals are a good gift of God, it follows that it is not wholly unlawful for us to seek them too. The divine Word and the virtues, above all, are compared to gold refined and most precious. Job praises the veins or seams of gold in the bowels of the earth. Many most pious men have also been very rich in gold, silver, copper and other metals, and yet they were not on that account badly spoken of. Both sacred and profane writers testify that gem and gold have been given from rivers. Although an excessive zeal for gold, and a lust for digging up mountains for the sake of gold, rightly seems to be something the pious should restrain or lessen a little, and it is to be wished that men were drawn by the iron of heaven rather than by the desire of riches alone, which cannot make a man so happy; so that many, and not rarely, regret the effort and expense they have spent. The story of Pythius the miner is well known, and how his wife corrected his insatiable [ἄπληστον] desire for gold: she made golden dainties skilfully and gave them to him when he was hungry, and yet they could not relieve his hunger, much less calm his soul and conscience. To this belongs also the greed of Midas for gold, whom the histories say soon repented of his most foolish choice. This wickedness, then, was bound to be set down in the search for spiritual treasures, as Christ teaches, compared with which yet the most foolish men so often seek earthly things. Ovid also mocks this, saying: They went into the bowels of the earth, and what she had hidden in the Stygian shades; and now iron, harmful, and gold, more harmful than iron, had come forth, by whose dire lust at last every wickedness fled far away, and truth and faith; in their place came frauds and tricks, ambushes and force, and wicked love of possessing.

units.la: Eadem opera etiam impostura Alchimistica, capite censenda, taxatur. Vt iam non dicam de nobili illa fatuitate, qua in tentandis montium fastigiis virgæ auellanæ, vel alii confidunt,& ex virgæ vel sonitu, vel tractu, vel susurro de pretiosi vel ignobilis metalli præsentia augurantur.De Aucupio & piscatione dicere quid attinet, quibus tamen multi adeoediti fuere, vt auieis retibus,hamisq;, aucuparentur, piscarentur. Et quidem modica harum rerum oblectatio cum quod culinæ etiam seruiunt, non inuidenda erat, verum id temporis in aucupio & piscatione insumitur, quod sæpe in studio verbi diuini, dicendo iure secundum leges & aliis exequendis officiis vocationis insumi conueniebat: quare non immerito Viyssis filium Telemachum ab hoc studio omnino abstinuisse proditum est.
units.tr: By the same token, the alchemical fraud is also condemned, and deserves to be condemned. Not to mention that noble folly by which some trust in hazel rods, or other things, for probing the tops of mountains, and from the rod's sound, or its pull, or its whispering, foretell the presence of a precious or base metal. What need is there to speak of fowling and fishing, by which many have been so addicted that they were caught with bird-nets and hooks, that is, they went fowling and fishing? Indeed, a moderate enjoyment of these things, since they also serve the kitchen, was not to be begrudged; but the time spent on fowling and fishing is the very time which ought often to be spent on the study of the divine Word, on speaking justly according to the laws, and on carrying out the other duties of one's calling. Therefore it is not without reason that Telemachus, son of Ulysses, is recorded to have wholly abstained from this pursuit.
Snatching, heaping up and carrying off must be given up.

units.la: Vt si quem videas fodiendis lege metallis, Damnatum, vano se macerare labore: Sic auro quisquis studet, argentoq; parandis, Deserit, & Stygias fors vehitur sub aquas!
units.tr: As when you see someone condemned to dig metals in the mines, wearing himself out with empty labour, so whoever strives to get gold and silver deserts everything, and perhaps is carried beneath the Stygian waters!
THEFT

units.la: FVRVNCVLVS vel mus ille agrinus,( quem marem fennicum, vel glirem fennicum alii dictum arbitrantur ) qui toros frugum acervos in terram deportat, æstatis tempore, vt ingrauescente hyeme, vnde viuat, habeat, typum nobis præbet eorum, qui nimio labore se macerant & torquent in hac vita. & magnos thesauros congerunt, quos tamen deserere coguntur tum cum minime putant: quibus sepe ne contrectandi datur facultas, poena diuinitus infl icta, eaq; iustissima pro tali malitia: quod non semel in sacris videas cum deploratum tum reprehensum: Quam nihil ( inquit Dauid ) nisi vanitas omnis homo: eheu! quam si ut umbra pertransit homo. Et quam vane sollicitti sunt! Colligit & ignorat quibus ea sit congregaturus: & iterum Propheta: vt perdix colligit oua sed non excludit: ita comparans diuitias sed iniuria medio diebus suis derelinquet eas, & tandem erit stultus: & Rex sapientissimus: est malum quod vidi sub sole, idq; maximum super homines: viro cui dederit Deus ipse diuitias, facultatesq; & honorem, & cuius animus non desiderat vlla re qua delectetur, cum huic non facit copiam Deus ipse fruendi re illa, sed vir alienus fruitur re illa; hoc vanitatem & ægritudinem pessimam esse. Non aliter sitiens vicinas Tantalus vndas Captat, & oppositis abstinet ora cibis. Magnum sane vi- tium esse, iners & ignauum otium omnes boni semper fassi, iuxta atq; detestati sunt, multa mala docet, & Satana puluinar est, homo desidia diffluens nec hominis nomine nec lucis vsura dignus deputetur, vt sapientissimis Gentium etiam visum est, sterquilinium ille hominis verius dicetur, & qui recta contrauenit fini creationis suæ qui est, ad laborem, sed labore nimio sibi ipse decurtare vitâ, quid etiâ est aliud quam sui ipsius homicida esse & fieri, quare laborandum quidem sed tamen & orandum, h.e. pietati studendum, & precibus aliisq; pietatis & honestatis, vocationisq; officia faciet... enda. Quarendum regnum Dei & iustitia eius, vt pro Domini Saluatoris promissione, reliqua adiiciantur. Laborantes vt vmbra sequitur mors: & nisi in timore Domini laboraueris, etiam infernus patulo rictu & flammas ructantibus faucibus, exhalantibusq; fauillas, fumumque natibus patet, in quem procurrere curriculo credatur is, qui laborat. Quare semper infoneret auribus auaris, & laboribus sese torquentibus, enecantibusq;: Hac nocte repetent animam & cuius erit qua congregasti. Haud vllas portabis opes Acherontis ad vndas Nudus ad infernas stulta vehere rates. Pendentem ergo ab arbore verbi Euangelici Christum respice & contuere fide, ille dat requiem in labore, solatium in tentatione, vitam in morte.
units.tr: The dormouse, or that field mouse (which some think is called the Finnish marten or the Finnish dormouse), which in summer drags heaps of grain into the ground so that it has something to live on when winter grows harsh, gives us a type of those who wear themselves out and torment themselves with excessive labour in this life. They pile up great treasures, which they are compelled to leave behind just when they least expect it. Often they are given no chance to handle them, a punishment inflicted by God, and a most just one for such wickedness. You may see this in Scripture more than once, where it is both lamented and rebuked. How nothing, says David, is every man but vanity; alas, how like a shadow man passes through! And how vainly they are troubled! He gathers and does not know for whom he will gather. And again the prophet: like the partridge that gathers eggs but does not hatch them, so he who gets riches but not justly will leave them in the middle of his days, and in the end will be a fool. And the wisest king: there is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and that the greatest among men: to a man to whom God himself has given riches, wealth and honour, and whose soul lacks nothing that he might enjoy, yet God does not grant him the power to enjoy those things, but a stranger enjoys them; this is vanity and a most grievous affliction. Not otherwise does thirsty Tantalus catch at the waters nearby, and his mouth refrains from the food set before him. Indeed all good men have always confessed, and equally detested, that idle and lazy leisure is a great vice, and teaches many evils; and man, dissolving in sloth, is a pillow for Satan. Such a man, neither worthy of the name of man nor of the use of light, is rightly called, as even the wisest of the Gentiles have thought, rather a dunghill; and he who acts against the purpose of his creation, which is labour, but by excessive toil shortens his own life, what else is he but his own murderer? Therefore one must labour, but also pray, that is, devote oneself to piety, and fulfil the duties of piety, honesty and one's calling, with prayers and other means. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and the rest will be added, according to the promise of the Lord and Saviour. Death follows the labourers like a shadow, and unless you labour in the fear of the Lord, hell too lies open with its gaping jaws and fiery throat, breathing out sparks and smoke from its backside, into which he who labours is likely to run headlong. Therefore let there always ring in the ears of the greedy, and of those who torment and wear themselves out with toil: This night they will require your soul, and whose will be the things you have gathered? You will carry no wealth at all to the waters of Acheron; naked, you will be ferried in a foolish boat to the infernal shores. Therefore look to Christ, hanging from the tree of the Gospel word, and gaze upon him in faith: he gives rest in labour, comfort in temptation, life in death.

units.la: VIRTVTES VITIIS INQVINAN- tur, vt virtutes esse desinant.
units.tr: Virtues are defiled by vices, so that they cease to be virtues.

units.la: Viuit in hoc æuo nemo, qui criminis exsors Exstet, & à vitiis libera corda gerat: Ne tamen enormes magno cum crimine lapsus Committas, prudens mente tremente caue.
units.tr: No one lives in this age who is free of wrongdoing, or who keeps a heart free from vices. Yet, lest you commit grave falls with great guilt, act with a wise and trembling mind.

units.la: EXCELLENTIA ingenia, excellentia vitia: quod proverbio fertur. Dolendum certe est, in multis inesse artes, disciplinas, sapientiam civilem, sortitudinem, aliarumq; virtutum nobilissimarum initia, sed iuxta has habitare in eodem etiam ignobilissimos neques, & turpissima vitia, ut virtutes vitiis certent, & vicissim, quemadmodum de Alexandro Magno Iustinus ex Trogo refert. Perinde est, ac si opiparum edulium & magno conquisitae lautitiae in sordido apponantur vasculo, quod non potest non esse fastidiosum, & inquinatum. In Scipione est magna fortitudo & continentia summopere laudanda, sed in eodem turpissima concurrit φιλαυτία & vanae gloriolae aucupandae detestanda cupiditas. Est in Xenocrate temperantia & continentia, sed laudis stimulis promicat nimius. Alexander fortitudinis ac prudentiae bellicae immortalem habet laudem, quam tamen ambitio, ingluvies & libidines obscurant simul & obturpant. Adeoq; etiam in Socrate insignis est Patientia, sed ob defectum fidei ac verae cognitionis (qua etiam sapientissimi & moratissimi Gentilium oës destituuntur) ita inquinatur, ut ne virtutis quidem nomen mereatur, sed larua virtutis verius dici possit. Ad eundem modum invenias hodie in vno aut altero eximiam cognitionem, eruditionemq;, vel sapientiam vel eloquentiam, cum quo eodem habitat vel intolerabilis superbia, qua bonis operibus insidiatur, ut pereant, dicente Augustino, vel temulentia, vel incontinentia, vel libido, vel praecipitantia, vel alia: ut qui in uno delinquit, reliquorum reus censeatur, ut Iacobus loquitur. Quare faciendum est omnibus modis iis, qui donaDei in sese mediocria deprehendunt, ne aliis iisq; enormibus vitiis ea obturpent & deperdant, sed ut ipsorum usus aliquis esset, monente Syracide, esse possit: Alias donorum abusus, talentum defodere esset, quod a Deo graviter puniendum esse docet parabola Domini de talentis: fideles igitur dispensatores esse debemus variae gratiae divinae, prout cuique datum est. Inprimis autem cavere a praesumptione, superbia, & fiducia propriarum virium: Melior enim est in malis factis humilis confessio, quam in bonis factis superba gloriatio, Omnibus quidem in vniuersum naevis in hac corruptione naturae defungi non possumus, manet in nobis peccatum inhabitans, & lucta Spiritus cum carne: sed id cavendum est ne naevi in vitia, vitia in crimina, crimina in scelera atque flagitia evadant; ne peccatum regnet in corpore nostro, neq; obediamus eius in concupiscentiis suis, sed Spiritu peccata carnis mortificemus.
units.tr: EXCELLENT minds, excellent vices, as the proverb goes. It is certainly regrettable that many people have the beginnings of arts, learning, civil wisdom, courage and other most noble virtues, yet beside these dwell the most worthless and wicked people and the most shameful vices, so that virtues and vices contend with one another, and vice versa. This is what Justin reports of Alexander the Great, drawing on Trogus. It is as if a rich dish and delicacies sought out at great cost were set out in a filthy bowl, which cannot help but be distasteful and defiled. In Scipio there is great courage and self-restraint, deserving the highest praise, but in the same man there meet most shameful self-love [φιλαυτία] and a desire to hunt after empty glory, which is to be detested. In Xenocrates there is temperance and self-control, but too much of him is driven by the spur of praise. Alexander has an immortal reputation for courage and military prudence, which nevertheless ambition, gluttony and lusts both obscure and disfigure. Indeed, even in Socrates there is remarkable patience, but because of his lack of faith and of true knowledge (which all the wisest and most upright of the Gentiles also lack), it is so defiled that he does not deserve even the name of virtue, and could more truly be called a mask of virtue. In the same way you will find today, in one or another person, outstanding knowledge and learning, wisdom or eloquence, and living alongside it there is either intolerable pride, which lies in wait against good works so that they perish, as Augustine says, or drunkenness, or incontinence, or lust, or rashness, or something else; so that whoever offends in one point is counted guilty of all, as James puts it. Therefore, by every means, those who find in themselves modest gifts of God must take care that they are not disfigured and destroyed by other and grave vices, but that they may be of some use to themselves, as the Son of Sirach advises. Otherwise the abuse of the gifts would be burying the talent, which the parable of the Lord about the talents teaches is to be severely punished by God. Faithful stewards we ought to be of the manifold grace of God, as each has received a gift. Above all we must beware of presumption, pride, and trust in our own strength, for a humble confession of evil deeds is better than a proud boasting of good deeds. Indeed, we cannot in general be wholly free of blemishes while in this corrupt state of nature: sin dwelling within us remains, and the struggle of the Spirit with the flesh. But we must take care that blemishes do not grow into vices, vices into crimes, and crimes into wickedness and shameful deeds; so that sin does not reign in our mortal body, nor do we obey its lusts, but by the Spirit we put to death the deeds of the flesh.

units.la: LVX ET TENEBRÆ NON coharent sibi mutuo.
units.tr: LVX ET TENEBRÆ NON coharent sibi mutuo.

units.la: [Engraving: a lit candle on a globe with a devil figure, flanked by smoke and flames; not transcribed as text.] Omnia cum prima sumunt exordia luce, Optima lux, louæ est cunEti creantis opus? Non opus est σκότος: est tantum priuatio lucis, Lux Christi, tenebræ sunt Satanæq; typus.
units.tr: [Engraving: a lit candle on a globe with a devil figure, flanked by smoke and flames; not transcribed as text.] When all things take their first beginning from light, is the best light not the work of God, the Creator of all? Darkness [σκότος] is no work at all: it is merely the privation of light. Light is Christ, and darkness is the type of Satan.

units.la: Duo contraria iuxta se posita magis elucescunt. Adparet id hic ex oppositione lucis ac tenebrarum. Lux est creaturarum τῶν ἀλόγων nobilissima ac praestantissima, & primo a Deo condita, concreata primo moli, nihil enim esse potest sine luce. Tenebrae autem a Deo creatae non sunt, imo ne sunt quidem: non enim sunt quiddam positivum, sed tantum priuatio nobilissimae creaturae lucis. Quo non quid magis est, eo est perfectius: quo quid minus est, eo est imperfectius, quare ut essentia & creatio lucis perfectionem, ita priuatio tenebrarum imperfectionem arguit. Unde & Deus sese lucem dicere, & in luce habitare inaccessa non abhorret: qui & ex tenebris lucem splendescere iussit, ut Apostolus loquitur: unde efficitur, quo quid est perfectius eo magis lucis habet, ut ante de essentia Dei dictum, & ex natura Angelorum: animarum hominum patet, adeoq; etiam aer & aqua, quoniam sunt corpora diaphana, praestantiora sunt terra, creatura minime pellucida; quam oppositionem lucis & tenebrarum sancti ac prophani homines agnouerunt: Tobias ait: Quae mihi potest esse laetitia, qui in tenebris sedeo, & lumen caeli non video? Ouidius initio suarum metamorphoseon:
units.tr: Two contraries set side by side shine out all the more. This appears here from the opposition of light and darkness. Light is the most noble and excellent of the irrational [τῶν ἀλόγων] creatures, created first by God, and made together with the first mass, for nothing can exist without light. Darkness, however, was not created by God; indeed it is not even a thing at all. For it is not something positive, but merely the privation of the most noble creature, light. Whatever is more of a thing is more perfect, and whatever is less of a thing is more imperfect. Therefore, just as the being and creation of light show its perfection, so the privation of darkness shows its imperfection. Hence it is not unfitting that God calls himself light, and dwells in light unapproachable, and that he commanded light to shine out of darkness, as the Apostle puts it. From this it follows that the more perfect a thing is, the more it has of light, as was said earlier of the essence of God, and as is evident from the nature of the angels and of human souls. Even air and water, since they are transparent bodies, are more excellent than earth, a creature not at all transparent. Holy and profane men alike have recognised this opposition of light and darkness. Tobias says: What joy can be mine, who sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven? Ovid at the beginning of his Metamorphoses:
As yet no Titan gave light to the world, &c.

units.la: Quare in sacris lux, rerum integrarum: tenebra, rerum adflictarum sunt hieroglyphicum: haec lux veritatis: tenebra falsitatis, & errorum: item, lux pietatis, fidei atq; virtutum, tenebra vero impietatis, infidelitatis & criminum hieroglyphicum gestant. Nam qui mala agit, in lucem non venit, scit enim opera sua a luce arguui, qui vero bona, in lucem venit, nec formidat χρίσιν lucu. Lucis igitur sectanda opera, & refugiendae tenebrae, nam qui hic lucis operibus studet, is theic in aeternam lucem suscipietur, inq; lumine lumen, & gaudium videbit perpetim, sed qui tenebrarum opera facit, in tenebris exterioribus aeternos sustinebit cruciatus: hinc deducit conclusionem Apostolus: Deponenda opera tenebrarum, & tanquam in luce ambulandum: compotationes & comessationes, cubilia, stupra, adulteria, furta, caedes, obtrectationes odia, & similia sunt tenebrarum opera, quae qui facit, regnum lucis & gaudii non possidebit unquam: Filii lucis sumus, opera tenebrarum non facere sed arguere potius debemus: quemadmodum autem lux & tenebra coniungi non possunt, sed se mutuo tollunt, ita non possumus pietatis simul esse studiosi, & magnis sudare criminibus, nec Christum cum Belial, coniungere: qui non est mecum (ait, Dn. Saluator) contra me est, & qui non colligit mecum dispergit.
units.tr: Therefore in the sacred writings light is the hieroglyph of things whole and prosperous, and darkness of things afflicted. Light is the symbol of truth, darkness of falsehood and errors; likewise light stands for piety, faith and virtues, while darkness stands for impiety, unbelief and crimes. For he who does evil does not come to the light, for he knows that his deeds are reproved by the light; but he who does good comes to the light and does not fear the judgment [κρίσιν] of the light. Therefore the works of light are to be pursued and darkness is to be shunned. For he who here devotes himself to the works of light will be received into eternal light, and will see light in light, and joy for evermore; but he who does the works of darkness will endure eternal torments in the outer darkness. From this the Apostle draws his conclusion: Let us cast off the works of darkness, and walk as in the light: revelling and drunkenness, chambering and wantonness, strife and envy, adulteries, thefts, murders, slanders, hatreds, and similar things, are the works of darkness; whoever does these will never possess the kingdom of light and joy. We are sons of the light; we ought not to do the works of darkness, but rather to reprove them. Just as light and darkness cannot be joined, but cancel each other out, so we cannot at the same time be devoted to piety and wallow in great crimes, nor can we join Christ with Belial. He who is not with me (says the Lord Saviour) is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters.
VIRTUE IS POSTPONED TO MONEY.

units.la: [Woodcut emblem: a figure above a globe holding a crown and sword, with a balance on the globe and a sea monster below. No printed text.] Est via decliuis nummorum immensa cupido, Excutit ad stygias sæua machera Rates. Nobilitas virtus, Pietasq; ad sydera ducit, Humilitatis Ouans Astra subibit opus.
units.tr: There is a downhill path of boundless lust for money, and cruel sword-blades drive ships down to the Stygian shores. Nobility, virtue and piety lead to the stars, and humility, triumphing, climbs to the heavenly stars as its work.

units.la: BILANCE eadem ventilatur Alma virtus & flauum æs, sed illa ab hoc longissime superatur. Nimirum, corrupti æui huius mores depinguntur, quod virtutis minimam, nummorum rationem ducit maximam, & illam hisce longissime posthabet: iteratq; illud Gentilis Poetæ O ciues, ciues, quærenda pecunia primum est Virtus post nummos, &c.
units.tr: The balance is tilted: kindly virtue is weighed against yellow bronze, and virtue is far outweighed by it. Clearly this portrays the morals of this corrupt age, which counts virtue as least and money as greatest, and places virtue far below money. It repeats the saying of the Gentile poet: O citizens, citizens, money must be sought first; virtue comes after money, etc.

units.la: Quantum quisq; nummorum possidet arca, tantum habet & fidei: vt nunc re- ctius quam vnquam. Ætas Aurea & Argentea dici posset: quoniam proscripta virtute sola fere regnat Philargyria. Creuerunt & opes & opum furiosa libido, Et cum possideant plurima plura petunt Crescit amor nummi quantum ipsa pecunia crescit Deficit virtus, exulat alma Fides.
units.tr: As much faith as each man's chest holds in money, so much he has: now more truly than ever. This could be called the Age of Gold and Silver, since virtue has been banned and the love of silver almost alone reigns. Wealth and the frenzied lust for wealth have grown; and though they possess very much, they seek more. The love of money grows as money itself grows; virtue fails, and kindly faith is exiled.

units.la: Egregie autem pingitur ac fingitur huius ævi labes, seu potius malitia hisce Phaleucis: Sine me vocari pessimum, dum diues vocer: Nemo an bonus, an diues; omnes quaerimus: Non quare & vnde, quid habeas tantum rogant: Vbi quantum quisq; habuit, tanti fuit: Quid habere nobis turpe fit, nihil: An diues omnes quaerimus, nemo an bonus? Aut diues opto viuere, aut pauper mori: Bene moritur quisquis moritur, dum lucrum facit Pecunia ingens generis humani bonum.
units.tr: This age's disgrace, or rather its malice, is portrayed and shaped well in these Phalaecian verses: Let me be called worst, provided I am called rich. Everyone asks whether a man is rich or good; we all seek riches. No one asks why or whence you have what you have; they ask only how much. Wherever a man has as much as he has, he is worth that much. To have nothing is the shameful thing. Do we all seek to be rich, and not to be good? I choose to live rich, or to die poor. He dies well who dies while making profit. Money is the great good of the human race.

units.la: Sed, heu cæcitatem ac turpitudinem! non aduertimus stupidi, quo magis vincit grauitate pecunia, eo magis demergit & demergitur ad Orcû: & quo magis vincitur eleuaturque virtus, eo magis sustollitur ad astra & aspirat ad coronam. Nam virtus, detrusò & prolapso ad inferos cacodæmone, sedes æthereas occupat & victrix triumphat. Olim apud Romanos bina ædes sacra conjuncta stabant, vt per vnam ad alteram fieret accessus & transitus, vnæ virtutis, alteræ Honoris ædes dicebantur, per illam ad hanc patebat ingressus. Videlicet, tantum per Virtutes ad Honorem recta via contenditur: præcipitia nummorum demergunt in laqueos, tentationem, & mortem. Via virtutis est, inquit Augustinus, qua nititur ad possessionis finem, id est, ad gloriam, Honorem, Imperium. Hoc insitum habuisse Romanos, etiam Deorum apud illos edes, Virtutis & Honoris, quas coniunctissimas constituerunt, indicant. Gloriam ergo & Honorem & Imperium non debet sequi virtus, sed ipsa VIRTVTEM.
units.tr: But alas, what blindness and baseness! We stupid people do not notice that the more money prevails by its weight, the more it sinks and is sunk down to Orcus; and the more virtue is overcome and cast down, the more it is raised up to the stars and aspires to the crown. For virtue, once the evil demon has been thrust down and cast into the depths, occupies the heavenly seats and triumphs as victor. Long ago among the Romans two sacred temples stood side by side, so that access and passage was made from one to the other. One was called the temple of Virtue, the other of Honour, and the way into the second lay through the first. Clearly, the straight road to Honour runs only through the Virtues; the precipices of money plunge men into snares, temptation and death. The way of virtue, says Augustine, is that by which one strives towards the end of possession, that is, towards glory, honour and power. That the Romans held this as innate is shown by their temples of Virtue and Honour, which they set up as most closely joined, even among their gods. Therefore virtue ought not to follow glory, honour and empire, but virtue itself.
DEATH LEVELS ALL THINGS.

units.la: Pallida per similli mors trutinat omnia lance:
units.tr: Pale death weighs all things on one and the same scale,

units.la: Quæq; subis hodie, cras ego forte luo.
units.tr: and what you rule over today, I may perhaps pay for tomorrow.
Therefore humility, and wise self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια], hope and
dear faith should always rule our hearts.

units.la: Mors æqua lance omnes ponderat, & lance sua demetit congrue omnia: Est commune mori, mors nulli parcit honori:
units.tr: Death weighs all men on an equal balance and measures out everything fittingly by its own standard: It is common to die; death spares no one's honour.
The weak and the strong come to the threshold of death.

units.la: Non exhorrescit triplicem coronam: non expauescit ad diadema Cæsareum: Regium sceptrum non formidat: aularum culmina conscendit imperterrita: nec humiles subire dedignatur casas, & ruguriola: huius spiculis cadit mas & fœmina: vir & puer: iuuenis & senex: doctus & indoctus: infulatus & paludatus pariter succumbunt: decutit galeas: excutit romphæam: præcipitat galeros: excutit furcam & calamum: fortitudo vincitur: pulcritudo deformatur: cursu nemo effugit: latebrarum indago non oculit: verbo dicam: à mortis spiculis nihil est immune: est nascendi & moriendi tempus: omnia in hac uno incerta sunt, sola certissima mors: incertissima hora, Nam
units.tr: Death does not shrink from the triple crown; it does not tremble at the imperial diadem; it does not fear the royal sceptre; it climbs the roofs of palaces undaunted, and it does not disdain to enter humble cottages and hovels. Men and women fall by its darts, man and boy, young and old, learned and unlearned; the mitred and the cloaked alike succumb. It strikes off helmets, knocks the sword from the hand, casts down crowns, and takes the rake and the pen from the hand. Strength is overcome; beauty is disfigured; no one escapes by running; no hiding place eludes its search. In a word, nothing is immune from the darts of death; there is a time to be born and a time to die; all things in this life are uncertain, only death is most certain, and the hour most uncertain. For

units.la: Nemo tam Diuos habuit fauentes Crastinum vt possit sibi polliceri:
units.tr: No one has had the gods so favourable that he can promise himself tomorrow:
God whirls our swiftly driven
affairs about in a rapid whirlwind.

units.la: Nemo natus vnquam est, qui non fuerit vel moriturus vel mortalis.
units.tr: No one has ever been born who will not either be about to die or be mortal.

units.la: Oriens hac lege intraui, vt exirem, inquit Seneca:
units.tr: I entered this life on the condition that I should leave it, says Seneca.

units.la: Pallida mors æquo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas
units.tr: Pale death with even foot knocks at the huts of the poor
and at the towers of kings, O blessed Sextius!

units.la: Vita summa breuis spem nos vetat incoare longam.
units.tr: Our short life forbids us to begin a long hope.
Soon night and the myth will press upon you, the shades.

units.la: Si de diuitiis & honoribus & morum nobilitate, te iactas, de patria & pulchritudine corporis & honoribus, quæ tibi ab hominibus exhibentur: respice teipsum quia mortalis terra es, & in terram ibis. Circumspice qui similibus fluxere splendoribus. Vbi sunt qui ambiebant currum potestatis? vbi i-superab. les Imperatores? vbi sunt qui conuentus disponebant, & festa: & equorum spendidi nutritores? vbi nunc vestes & ornamenta peregrina: vbi seruorum turba? vbi iocus & latitia? vbi exercituum duces? vbi satrapa & tyranni? nonne omnes puluis & fauilla; morte omnes simus similes, absque discrimine:
units.tr: If you boast of riches and honours and nobility of character, of your homeland, your bodily beauty and the honours men pay you, look at yourself: you are mortal earth, and you will go into the earth. Look around at those who flowed away in similar splendours. Where are those who sought after the chariot of power? Where are the conquering emperors? Where are those who arranged assemblies and festivals, and the splendid breeders of horses? Where now are the foreign robes and ornaments? Where is the crowd of slaves? Where are jest and merriment? Where are the leaders of armies? Where are the satraps and tyrants? Are they not all dust and ashes? We are all alike in death, without distinction:
King Croesus, your image, richest of kings,
Diogenes the Cynic saw among the shades.
He looked at it, and shaken with a louder laugh than usual,
he said: "What good now do riches do you,

units.la: Nunc prosunt rex ô Regum ditissime? cum fis
units.tr: O richest of kings? Since you are
just as poor as I, even poorer than me;

units.la: Nam quantunq; habui mecum fero, cum nihil ipse
units.tr: for whatever I had, I carry with me; you, having nothing,
from such great wealth, Croesus, will carry nothing with you."
Look to the end, and you will not sin.

units.la: [Woodcut emblem: a skeleton beneath a winged globe with a figure, a crowned chest above the clouds, trumpets, and a landscape below; not transcribed as text.] Pectore vt intrepidus læto vltima fata capessas, Diuina mentem religione liga, Exerceq; Fidem, mentem dilectio firmet, In Domino fidens spiçula Mortis aret.
units.tr: With a fearless heart you may meet your last fate cheerfully: bind your mind with divine religion, exercise your faith, let love strengthen your mind, and, trusting in the Lord, ward off the darts of death.
VINCV
LXXVIII.

units.la: VINCVLA, plagas, compedes, retia vbiq; ponit mors, pedé non figimus, vbi suas non tetenderit mors pedicas; vbi arcú mors suum non intenderit, tela missurus: Et quia resistit morte? Resistitur ignibus, vndiu, ferro, resistitur potestatibus, resistitur regib. venit vna mors, quis ei resistit? nihil est illa fortius. Vbiq; tedit plagas, siue comedas, seu bibas: siue vigiles, seu dormias: siue moreris, seu iter facias siue stes, seu sedeas: & dum haec scribimus, mors intendit, & dum haec legis, mors intendit. Quomodo pisces hamo capiuntur & retibus: & aues per aerem libera laqueo dum nesciunt alligantur: sic & homines pro merito suo deducuntur, cum repente mors venerit, & iudicium in omnes, &c.
units.tr: Death sets its chains, snares and nets everywhere. We cannot set our foot anywhere that death has not spread its traps, or where it has not bent its bow, ready to loose its arrows. "And who can resist death? Fire can be resisted, water, iron; powers can be resisted, kings can be resisted. Once death comes, who resists it? Nothing is stronger than it." Death spreads its snares everywhere, whether you eat or drink, whether you watch or sleep, whether you stay put or travel, whether you stand or sit. While we write these words, death is aiming, and while you read them, death is aiming. "As fish are caught with hooks and nets, and birds taken in the air are snared in a noose while they do not know it, so men are carried off according to their deserts, when death comes suddenly, and judgement falls upon all," etc.

units.la: Plagas has euitare omnino nullo modo possumus, sed quomodo in mortis casses incidamus, pia sollicitudine & sollicita pietate agendum est: Et primo quidem opus est humilitate vera, ac demissione animi cum coram Deo tum coram hominibus: Quid enim superbiret cinis & pulvis; cum lutum fit & figmentum fragilimum, longam infirmitatem resecat medicus, & qui Rex est hodie, cras etiam moriturus est: Et mortuus homo heres est serpentum, & bestiarum ac vermium futurus; recte Rythmicus. Cum sex cum limus cum terra leuissima fimus, Unde superbimus, nescimus, quando perimus.
units.tr: We can by no means altogether avoid these snares, but we must take care, with a devout anxiety and a careful piety, that we do not fall into the nets of death. And first of all we need true humility, and a lowering of the spirit, both before God and before men. "For why should dust and ashes be proud, since man is mire and most fragile clay? The physician cuts short a long illness, and the one who is king today will die tomorrow. And a dead man becomes the heir of serpents, beasts and worms." As the rhymester rightly says: "Since you are mud, and dung, and the lightest earth, we do not know why we are proud; we do not know when we shall perish."

units.la: Deinde [Greek] nostram consolidat, &c, vt praesentibus, quae diuina obtingunt bonitate, contenti viuamus, monet: quomodo enim de conquirendis multis bonis maxime sollicitus esset, cui per aures cordi insonat illud ferale: Hac nocte tollent animam tuam? facile omnia contemnit, qui moriturum se cogitat. Restringet etiam haec meditatio gulam & luxuriam, comessationes & compotationes, cauetq; ne corda nostra grauentur. Atheorum & Epicureorum haec vox est: edamus & bibamus, cras enim moriemur: pro quo dicendum erat: Pie ac moderate aeuum hoc transmittamus, cras enim, si Deo ita videbitur, spiritum exhalabimus, vt eum fortiter in sinum redemptoris deponere possimus. Integer vita scelerisq; purus Non pauet mortis iaculum, nec arcum
units.tr: Next, [Greek] strengthens our ... (etc.), and it urges us to live contentedly with the present blessings that come from divine goodness. For how could a man be anxious to gather up many goods, when that deadly saying sounds in his ears: "This night they will take away your soul"? He who thinks he is about to die easily despises everything. This meditation will also restrain the belly and luxury, feasting and drinking bouts, and it guards against our hearts being weighed down. "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" is the saying of the atheists and Epicureans; against it we ought to say: "Let us pass this life piously and temperately, for tomorrow, if it so pleases God, we shall breathe out our spirit, so that we may bravely lay it in the bosom of our Redeemer. He whose life is whole and whose conscience is pure does not fear the dart of death, nor the bow,"

units.la: Nec venenatus grauida sagittas, Fusce, pharetra.
units.tr: "Nor the poisoned arrows that your quiver, Fuscus, carries pregnant with venom."

units.la: Deniq; quicunq; se moriturum cogitat, & quidem necem sibi vbiuis imminere, ille in tempore prospicit de felici excessu, omnibus locis, iuxta illud Seneca: Cum quo loco te mors moretur haud scias Tu fac locis mortem moreris omnibus.
units.tr: Finally, whoever considers that he must die, and that death hangs over him everywhere, will in time look ahead to a happy departure, in every place, according to that saying of Seneca: "You do not know in what place death awaits you; so prepare to meet death in every place."

units.la: Acerbitatem autem mortis, mortis Christi consideratione, tanquam letiferas aquas iniecta arbore vita edulcat, nouit enim morte Christi nos victuros in aeternum beate.
units.tr: Moreover, the bitterness of death is sweetened by the consideration of Christ's death, as the tree of life thrown into bitter waters sweetens them; for by the death of Christ we know that we shall live blessedly for ever.
DEATH IS CERTAIN, THE HOUR UNCERTAIN.

units.la: Sola Dei pietas vitarum stamina ducit, Prorogat & rumpit fila Pronæa Dei. Quare cum veluti filum sit vita caducum, Ad momenta vide singula, teqs; para.
units.tr: God's sole piety draws out the threads of our lives; the providence of God lengthens and breaks the threads. Therefore, since life is like a fragile thread, look at each moment separately, and prepare yourself.

units.la: Alludit hæc hieroglyphica tabella ad Parcarum stamina Poetarum, de quibus fabulantur: quod tres sint Deæ apud inferos, quæ cuiuis homini suâ vitam & fata destinent atq; temperent: dictas volunt hoc ordine.[Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos,] de quibus Lactantius: Omnia tribus temporibus contineri necesse est, praeterito, praesenti & futuro. Praeteriti est origo: praesentis substantia: futuri dissolutio. Incipimus cum nascimur: summus, cum vivimus: definimus, cum interimus. Unde (pergit Lactantius) tres esse Parcas volunt Poetæ: unam quæ hominis vitam ordinat, alteram quæ contexat, tertiam quæ rumpat & finiat, iuxta versiculum: Clotho colum baiulat, Lachesis trahit, Atropos occat.
units.tr: This hieroglyphic picture alludes to the threads of the Fates, as the poets tell of them: that there are three goddesses in the underworld, who assign and regulate the life and destiny of each man. They are said to be named in this order [Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos], of whom Lactantius says: "Everything must be contained in three times: past, present and future. The past is the origin, the present the substance, the future the dissolution. We begin when we are born, we proceed while we live, we end when we die. Hence" (Lactantius goes on) "the poets want there to be three Fates: one which orders the life of a man, another which weaves it, a third which breaks and finishes it," according to the little verse: "Clotho carries the distaff, Lachesis draws the thread, Atropos cuts it."

units.la: Significari autem hisce omnibus liquido apparet: Primo certitudinem fati, & quod, si rem recte expendas, nihil fiat fortuito nec contingenter, sed omnia diuinitus in numero, pondere, & mensura disponantur: cum vitæ introitus, tum excitus per quem stat vita & nex nostra, & est tempus nascendi & moriendi, dicitq; Deus reuertimini filii hominum: qui limites posuit vitæ nostræ, quos transgredi nemo: adeoq; nos & omnia nostra à Dei nutu atq; arbitrio pendere. Deinde certum esse & immotum fatum mortis, & nulli parci, nam dicuntur Parcæ per ἀνυτίφεξαπ, quod minime parcant, quemadmodum & bellum ἀνυτι φεξηκας ita dicitur, quod minime bellum sit: nam omnes nascimur, aliquando moriturî: hæc lex firmata est diuino eoq; verissimo oraculo: Quocunq; die comederit ex eo, morte morietur: unde Martialis:
units.tr: It is clear that all these things signify, first, the certainty of fate; and that, if you weigh the matter rightly, nothing happens by chance or contingently, but all things are arranged by divine providence in number, weight and measure: both the entrance into life and the exit by which our life and death stand, and there is a time to be born and a time to die. And God says, "Turn back, sons of men, who has set the limits of our life, which no one may pass," so that we and all our affairs depend upon the nod and will of God. Second, the fate of death is certain and unchanging, and it spares no one. For the Fates are called [ἀνυτίφεξαπ], because they spare no one, just as war is called [ἀνυτι φεξηκας], because it is not war at all (that is, not a thing to be spared). For we are all born, and at some time shall die; this law is confirmed by the divine and most true oracle: "On whatever day you eat of it, you shall surely die." Hence Martial:
"Not to any woman has it been granted to entreat the three spinning girls,"
"they keep the day that they have appointed."

units.la: Inprimis autem notari hocipso apparet, fragilitatem vitæ nostræ, quæ a serico, quod aiunt, filo pendet: Homo Bulla, aiunt, quam facile occatur filum, rumpitur: ita vita nostra abrumpitur: affirmante Hiiobo: induit caro mea vermes, & ramentum puluerii, cutis mea disrupit se & liquefit: dies mei velociores fuerunt radio textoris, & consumpti sunt cum inopia spei. Pauci ac mali sunt dies vitæ nostræ, finis ab origine pendet, πνεῦμα ὀρθῶς: & instar rapidissimi torrentis abripimur: Eodem plane modo nobiscum comparatum est quo cum Damocle, cuius ceruici acinaces imminebat: quod nos prudenter ac pie considerare iubet, mellifluus Doctor, dicens: Septem sunt de essentia hominis, quæ si homo consideraret, in æternum non peccaret, scilicet, materia vilis, operatio turpis, exitus flebilis, status infabilis, mors tristabilis, dissolutio miserabilis, damnatio detestabilis, & consideratio gloriæ ineffabilis..
units.tr: Above all, this picture shows the fragility of our life, which hangs, as they say, by a silken thread. "Man is a bubble," they say; "how easily the thread is struck, and it breaks: so our life is cut off." Job affirms this: "My flesh is clothed with worms and a crust of dust; my skin breaks open and melts; my days have been swifter than the weaver's shuttle, and they are used up without hope. Few and evil are the days of our life; its end depends on its beginning, [πνεῦμα ὀρθῶς], and like a most rapid torrent we are swept away." In exactly the same way our situation is like that of Damocles, over whose neck a sword hung. The honeyed Doctor bids us consider this prudently and piously, saying: "There are seven things in the essence of man which, if a man considered them, he would never sin for ever: namely, vile matter, foul operation, tearful exit, unspeakable state, sad death, miserable dissolution, detestable damnation, and the ineffable consideration of glory."
Man is scattered like smoke.

units.la: [engraving: skeleton emblem, not transcribed as text] In ventos mordax fumus dispergitur; atq; Præterit, vt nunquam forte fuisse putes. Non secus hic transit cunctorum vita caduca, Vt ceu non fuerit præteriisse rere.
units.tr: The biting smoke is dispersed into the winds, and passes away so that you might think it had never been. In the same way the fleeting life of all men passes, so that you would suppose it had never existed at all.

units.la: Ἀὶς ᾧ τῆς τὸ κ̀αλὸν. Habuimus hactenus aliquot hieroglyphica vitæ huius fragilis atq; caducæ, recurrit tale etiam hęic, & aliquot eius rei statuisymbola. Primo, aristam. Secundo, sonitum tibiæ. Deniq; & fumum. Arif mile admodum quadrat: nam è terra nascitur: nimirum & homo terra terreus; unde eius etiam fragilitatem perspicere est: Quicquid soluitur in suum Principium: terra est homo, ergo & in terram revertetur. culum diuinum, quod iambi sequentes lepide declarant & exaggerant: Conceptus agro semine Mortalis infans editus Dolens gemensq; nascitur Diesq; quosuis conterit In maximis molestiis Nihilq; morte certius Incertiusq; tempore Vitam per omnem cogitat.
units.tr: A Greek motto, garbled in the scan [Ἀὶς ᾧ τῆς τὸ κ̀αλὸν]. Hitherto we have set out several hieroglyphs of this frail and transitory life, and the same theme recurs here, along with several emblematic symbols of the matter. First, an ear of grain. Second, the sound of a pipe. Finally, and smoke. The ear of grain fits very well, for it springs from the earth, and so does man, earth born of earth; hence his frailty may also be seen: Whatever is dissolved returns to its principle: man is earth, therefore he will return to earth. The divine oracle, which the following iambics neatly set out and amplify: Conceived from a seed sown in the field, the mortal child is born, grieving and groaning, and wears away his days amid the greatest troubles; nothing is more certain than death, nothing more uncertain than its time; he considers his life throughout.

units.la: Arista vel culmus principio pulcre viret: est & suus iuuentæ virorum: deniq; definit in pulcram atq; fructiferam aristam: & homo positus est, vt fructum ferat, & fructus eius manet, dicente Dn. Seruatore: fructus autem sunt: laudes Dei, invocatio, gratiarum actio, Fides, Dilectio, Spes, Patientia, Humilitas, Castitas, Moderatio, &c. quib. quo magis vita hominis turget, eo gloriosius assequitur finem suæ sationis & creationis. Interim tamen omni iniuria atq; intemperie aeris subditus est culmus, subdita arista: haud absimiliter homo subiectus est omnibus miseriis atq; calamitatibus, per quas Electos ingredi oportet in regnum cœlorum: vi- deatur inprimis Aug. de ciu. Dei, li. 22. c. 23. & in serm. ad Lippium, cū inquit, te Dominus magnis persecutionibus corripit, probat te in Electorum suorum numero ordinasse. Nam sine huiusmodi tribulationibus nequaquam ad Deum peruenire possumus. Omnes enim qui ad paradisum redire desiderant, oportet transire per ignem & aquam. & quæ sequuntur. ¶ Deniq; culmus cum arista breui demetitur, tritico collesto, deflagrant palea: Ita homo breuissime demetitur mortis falce, & qui bona egerunt: ibunt in cœlum ad cœlestia glaudia, qui mala in igni æterno flagrabunt in æternum. ¶ Sonus tibiæ leuitatem huius vitæ percommode audumbrat, dulce equidem canit fistula vel tibia, sed est tamen tantum transiens sonus: suauis est & illecebrosa vita hæc nostra, sed momento quasi transit, vt dulcedo eius nec videatur nec audiatur nec vere sentiatur: verbo dicam: sonitu leuius & breuius transit. ¶ Deniq; vita fumi instar in ventos dispergitur ac dissipatur. Quid n. fumus? Mordet & lacrymas elicit, nempe: in lacrymis orin.ur, in lacrymis morimur: expletur lacrymis egeriturq; dolor: Discutitur à ventis vt ne vestigium eius appareat: ita breui discutitur vita hominis præ flatu diuinæ iræ, vt perinde transeamus tanquam euolemus: & vestigium non videtur, vt est in Psalmo.
units.tr: The ear of grain, or stalk, flourishes finely at its beginning, and has its own youth like men; at last it ends in a fine and fruitful ear, and man is appointed to bear fruit, and his fruit remains, as our Lord the Saviour says. The fruits are: the praise of God, invocation, thanksgiving, faith, love, hope, patience, humility, chastity, moderation, etc., and the more the life of man flourishes in these, the more gloriously he attains the end of his sowing and creation. Meanwhile, however, the stalk is subject to every injury and inclemency of the air, and the ear to the same; in much the same way man is subject to all miseries and calamities, through which the elect must enter the kingdom of heaven. See especially Augustine, On the City of God, book 22, chapter 23, and in his sermon to Lippius, where he says: when the Lord chastises you with great persecutions, he proves that he has ordained you among the number of his elect. For without tribulations of this kind we can by no means come to God. For all who desire to return to paradise must pass through fire and water, and what follows. ¶ Finally, when the stalk with its ear is cut down in a short time, and the grain is gathered in, the chaff is burned up. So man is very quickly cut down by the sickle of death, and those who have done good will go into heaven to heavenly joys, while those who have done evil will burn in eternal fire for ever. ¶ The sound of the pipe very aptly shadows the lightness of this life. The flute or pipe indeed plays a sweet tune, but it is only a passing sound: this life of ours is pleasant and alluring, but it passes in a moment, so that its sweetness is neither seen nor heard nor truly felt; in a word, it passes more lightly and briefly than a sound. ¶ Finally, life is scattered and dissipated into the winds like smoke. For what is smoke? It bites and draws tears: indeed we are born in tears, we die in tears: grief is filled with tears and driven out. It is dispelled by the winds so that no trace of it appears; so in a short time the life of man is dispelled before the blast of divine wrath, so that we pass by as if we flew away, and no trace is seen, as it says in the Psalm.

units.la: PECCATA ET POENÆ PECCATORUM in æquilibrio.
units.tr: Sins and the Punishments of Sinners in Balance.

units.la: Vt truculenta metit sæua mors omnia falce!Vt magnas strages cedit, & interimit!Nimirum, cum PECCATI mensura repleta est,Accelerat flagrans vindicis ira Dei.
units.tr: How the cruel scythe of death mows down all things! How it cuts down great slaughters and destroys them! Surely, when the measure of sin is full, the flaming anger of the avenging God hastens on.

units.la: Quemadmodum maturù herbulù, agrìq; frugib falx imminet, ita hominib. lectaritate diffluentibus cõpleta peccatorum mensura imminent pœnæ & λεψία iusto Dei iudicio. Ad multa peccata Deus sapienter & per multam μαχροθυμίαν conniuet, tanquam ad pœnam nõ vigilaturus, vbi autem expleta est iniquitas, tum in furore corripit & punit, quemadmodum Apostolus: An nescis, longanimitatem te Dei ad poenitentiam prouocare, tu autem corde poenitere nescio, cumulas tibi ipsi iram in die ira & iusti iudicii diuini: Iustus enim Iudex Deus est, si non conuertatur impius, gladium suum acuet, arcum suum adduxit, & sagittam aptauit ei: Deniq; aptauit in eum arma lethifera, sagittas suas in feruidos occupaturus est: Depluit super improbos, prunas, ignem & sulphur: ventusq; procellosissimus portio calicis eorum futurus est, dum scopu perditionis verrat & euertat, vt Propheta loquitur. Longanimis equidem & multa misericordia Deus est, sed nec minus iustus super irreuipi-cibiles, quare sapiens: Misericordia(inquit) & ira apud eum citae sunt, & super peccatores incubabit eius indignatio, &c. Nemo igitur diuina lenitate & ad pœnam tarditate atque conniuentia abutatur ad peccandum, sed potius sibi certo persuadeat peccata sequi pœnas peccatis dignas, nisi fiat resipiscentia & remissio, non enim de nihilo est quod Gentilis ait, Deum ad vindictam quidem tardum esse, sed tarditatem morae grauitate pœnae plerunque compensare: idque fieri certo, diuino, iusto, atque sancto consilio, quod Deus ante pœnas & πανολεπῖαν peccata crescere & homines sinit efferari, &in suas clades furenter irruere, vt dicitur Iratus ad pœnam Deus si quos trahit, Auferre mentem talibus primum solet, Calignemq; offundit, vt ruant suas Furenter in clades sibi quas noxiis Accersierunt vltro consilio malis.
units.tr: Just as the sickle hangs over the ripening grass and the grain, so when the measure of sins is full among men who are dissolute in their wickedness, punishment and impunity [πανολεψίαν] hang over them by the just judgment of God. God, wisely and through much long-suffering [μακροθυμίαν], overlooks many sins, as though he would not keep watch for punishment; but when iniquity is complete, then he seizes and punishes in wrath, as the Apostle says: "Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But you, by your hard and impenitent heart, are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God" (Rom. 2:4-5). "For God is a just judge; if the wicked does not turn, he will whet his sword, he has bent his bow and made ready his arrow for him. He has also prepared for him deadly weapons, and he will make his arrows for those who pursue him. He rains on the wicked coals, fire and brimstone, and a horrible tempest shall be the portion of their cup" (Ps. 7:12-13, Vulgate). And the prophet speaks of God sweeping and overturning them with the broom of destruction. God is indeed long-suffering and of great mercy, but no less just toward the incorrigible. Therefore the wise man says: "Mercy and wrath are with him, swift are they, and his indignation rests upon sinners," etc. No one, then, should abuse divine gentleness, the delay of punishment and the overlooking of sin, to sin the more; rather let him firmly persuade himself that sins are followed by punishments worthy of them, unless repentance and forgiveness intervene. For it is not without reason that a Gentile writer said that God is indeed slow to avenge, but that the slowness of his delay is usually made up for by the severity of the punishment. This happens by a certain, divine, just and holy counsel: God allows sins to grow and men to become unrestrained before punishment and impunity [πανολεψίαν], so that they rush madly into their own ruin. As it is said: "When God, angry, drags some to punishment, he usually first takes away their mind and casts a darkness over them, so that they rush madly to the ruin which they have of their own accord brought upon themselves by their harmful counsels."

units.la: Nota sunt exempla; Diluuii: Sodomorum & Gomorrhaeorum Euersorum Hierosolymorum, vbi tanta peccandi licentia & securitas erat, vt etiam Iosephus ipse fateatur, nisi Titus iustitia diuina executor venisset, & puniuisset rebelles, Sodoma eos atq; Gomorrha incendia passuros fuisse. Ex quibus omnib. ita recensitis efficitur, cum ad summum fastigium ascederint omnis generis peccata, vel vnquam fando audita, &librae peccatorum lingua recta inflet, non procul abesse diuinâ Nemesin Adraftian, & euenturum quod tabella nostra Emblematica monet. Quos autem Deus flagello temporali non castigat, eos in iudicium aeternum puniendos relinquit, iuxta Caesarium Arelatensem.
units.tr: The examples are well known: the Flood; Sodom and Gomorrah overthrown; Jerusalem destroyed. In Jerusalem's case the licence to sin and the sense of security were so great that even Josephus himself confesses that, had Titus not come as the executor of divine justice and punished the rebels, they would have suffered burning like Sodom and Gomorrah. From all these examples thus reviewed it follows that when every kind of sin, or any ever heard of, has climbed to its highest peak, and the tongue of the scales of sinners has swelled upward, the divine Adrastian Nemesis is not far off, and what our emblematic tablet warns will come to pass. "But those whom God does not chastise with temporal scourge, he leaves to be punished in eternal judgment," according to Caesarius of Arles.
THE MOST FOUL MORALS OF THE LAST AGE.

units.la: [illegible, ~5 letters]ia, & Sordes, Calumnia, Fœda Voluptas, [illegible, ~4 letters]tus, & officii obliuio, tumq; Rigor: [illegible, ~8 letters]ra extremum teneant cum singula seclum, [illegible, ~1 letter]xtremum Satanæ tibia rauca canit.
units.tr: [...]ia, and Filth, Slander, Foul Pleasure, [...]tus, and forgetfulness of duty, and then Harshness: [...] when each age holds its last place, [...] Satan's hoarse pipe sings the last.

units.la: Summa huius est: ostendere conatur, in quibus maxime regimen suum exerceat Satanas in hac mundi sece: nempe in iis, qui harum circumstantium bestiarum mores atq; peruersitates sectantur, quales sunt: Bufo, Sus, Canis, Hircus vel Capra, Pauo, Asinus. Leo, &c.
units.tr: The summary of this is: he tries to show in which things Satan especially exercises his rule in this world, namely in those who follow the manners and perversities of these beasts around us, such as: the Toad, the Sow, the Dog, the He-goat or Goat, the Peacock, the Ass, the Lion, etc.

units.la: BVFO inuidiae auaritiae & auarae inuidiae hieroglyphicum: inuidus n. qui successus proximi videt, ringitur, & instar bufonis turget, adeoque sibi alterius felicitate aliquid decessisse opinatur. Vitium diabolicum! & qua noxa diabolus primos nostros parentes seduxit, inuidens paradisi delitias & fauorem diuinum, aeternaq; olim possidenda gaudia. Regnat igitur in inuidis Satan, imo, si Augustino credimus, omnia sua excrementa & foetores in inuidi exonerat Satan. Nec minoris turpitudinis est auaritia. Auarus enim omnia licet habeat, seipsum tamen non habet: pie, plane, ac pulcre August. Tolle inuidiam, & tuum est quod habeo, tolle inuidiam & meum est quod habes. o diuinam sententiam! o opus exoptatissimum!
units.tr: THE TOAD is the hieroglyph of envy and of greedy envy. For the envious man, who sees his neighbour's success, pines away and swells like a toad, and so he thinks that something has been taken from himself by another's happiness. It is a devilish vice! By this harm the devil seduced our first parents, envying the delights of paradise, the favour of God, and the joys to be possessed eternally. Satan therefore reigns in the envious; indeed, if we believe Augustine, Satan unloads all his excrement and stench into the envious man. Covetousness is no less shameful. For the covetous man, though he has everything, does not have himself. Piously, plainly, and beautifully Augustine says: Take away envy, and what I have is yours; take away envy, and what you have is mine. O divine saying! O most desirable work!

units.la: SVS figurat eos, qui caeno voluptatum in hoc aeuo se prouoluunt & ingurgitant, mūditiem nihil penis habentes: Animam pro sale habet Porcus: Ita omnes voluptuarii & inprimis Lurcones & Eluones, qui noctes diesq;, dies noctisq; compotant, eluantur, pergręcantur, obliti pietatis atq, honestatis. Inest autem vino Satanas est, vbi ergo regnat, ibi regnat Satanas ipse. Temulentia furor est Satani, us, & ebriosus gubernacula omnium adfectuum & actuum diabolo resignat, qua de re supra plura.
units.tr: THE SOW represents those who wallow and gorge themselves in the mire of pleasures in this age, having no cleanliness in them: the pig has its soul in place of salt. So all voluptuaries, and above all gluttons and wine-bibbers, who drink through the nights and days, day and night, who are washed out and soaked, forgetful of piety and honour. Satan is present in wine; where wine rules, there Satan himself rules. Drunkenness is the fury of Satan, and the drunkard hands over the helm of all passions and actions to the devil; on which matter, more above.

units.la: CANIS denotat osores, & qui rancori & obtrectationibus dediti sunt. Ignobilia sane, seruiliaq; ingenia. Nihil enim magnum est, quod non aeque sit placidum. Inprimis autem grande peccatum est, odisse corripientem, maxime si te non odio sed amore corripiat, & non studio detrahendi, sed tua emendationis, vt Hieronymus in Prophetam Amos. c. 5 loquitur, quod hodie frequens. Sunt autem & hi Osores ex Satanae aulicis, in quibus potens est. Eph. 2.
units.tr: THE DOG signifies haters and those given over to spite and backbiting. These are indeed ignoble and servile dispositions. For nothing is great that is not equally calm. Above all, it is a grave sin to hate one who rebukes you, especially if he rebukes you not out of hatred but out of love, and not with a desire to slander you but for your correction, as Jerome says in his commentary on the Prophet Amos, chapter 5, which is common today. Moreover, these haters are also among Satan's courtiers, over whom he has power: Eph. 2.

units.la: CAPRA procacitatis & salacitatis, figurat scortatores, moechos, fornicarios & libinarios: qui vel a diabolo abripiuntur ad bestiales libidines, & irritantur ad foedas atque illicitas concupiscentias & concubitus, quod crimen multis populis, nationibus, vrbibus, regionibus extremam pernitiem attulit.
units.tr: THE GOAT signifies lewdness and lust, and represents fornicators, adulterers, whoremongers and the lustful, who are either carried off by the devil into bestial lusts or are provoked to foul and unlawful desires and couplings. This crime has brought extreme ruin upon many peoples, nations, cities and regions.

units.la: PAVO, superbiae hieroglyphicum refricat nobis exprobratq; fastum atq; supercilium, qua plus de nobis, minus sentimus de aliis quam decet: Conueniebat autem vngues Pauonios (h.e. naevos, vitia, crimina & fragilitatem nostram) contemplari, nec dubium est quin cristas confestim simus dimissuri, in hoc scelere regnat Satanas: & in iis qui eo capti ac dementati sunt.
units.tr: THE PEACOCK, a hieroglyph of pride, reminds us and reproaches us for haughtiness and arrogance, by which we think more of ourselves and less of others than we should. It was fitting to contemplate the peacock's claws (that is, our blemishes, vices, crimes and frailty), and there is no doubt that we would at once lay down our crests. Satan reigns in this sin, and in those who are captured and driven mad by it.

units.la: ASINVS, tarditatis ad labores & facienda officia vocationis: diabolicum hoc vitium est, & plerumq; confine.
units.tr: THE ASS signifies slowness toward labours and the performance of the duties of one's calling. This is a devilish vice, and very often closely bound to others.

units.la: LEO, Tyrannorum hieroglyphicum, & in his dominatum gerit Satan: nihil hi rectum faciunt, quam cum, vt aiunt, moriuntur. Sed de his supra latius.
units.tr: THE LION is the hieroglyph of tyrants, and Satan holds dominion over them. They do nothing right, except when, as they say, they die. But more on these above.
THE CHARIOT OF PRIDE IS DRAWN TO HELL.

units.la: SVPERBIÆ quanta insint mala, hoc Emblematicum commentum aruguere atq; ob oculos ponere annitur.
