Estq; adeo turpissimum sane crimen & flagitium vere diabolicum, reproborum, vt Gregor. inquit, certissima nota, quemadmodum humilitatem filiorum Dei τεκμήριον esse, nemo dubitat. Vnde Augustt. Delictum magnum arbitror esse superbiam. Quaeritis, quam magnum sit hoc delictum; quod deiecit Angelum, quod ex Angelo fecit diabolum, eiq; in aeternum interclusit regnum coelorum. Magnum hoc delictum est, & caput a q; causa omnium delictorum, scriptum est enim: initium omnis peccati superbia, & ne quid aliud contemnas, initium, inquit, superbia homīnis Apostatare à Deo creatore. Et vt euidenter ostendamus, ipsa est peccatorum omnium initium, & finis & causa, quoniam non solum peccatum est superbia, sed et nullum peccatum potuit aut potest aut poterit esse sine superbia. Vere tu quidem, Augustine beatissime, nam non est peccatum tam grande quod non committat superbus, efferus, & insolens homo. Invidet proximi prosperitati, nam id quarit, vt ipse solus emineat: vt rectissime idem Augustin. Prior est vitiis superbia: Non enim invidia parit superbiam, sed superbia parit invidiam. Non enim invidet nisi amor excellentiae: Amor autem excellentiae superbia vocatur: Superbus divitias quaerit, corradit, coacervat, vt habeat unde supercilium suum alere possit. Pecunia nervus superbiae est, vt est in Psal. 49. Superbus impingit in charitatem Christianam, nam in quo est superbia, in eo non est charitas, charitas sese demittit, superbia effert inflat, turget: illa autem charitas de proximo semper plus sentit quam de se. Superbus colla proximi premit, eumq; opprimit: crudelis tyrannus est, cuius finis, infamia, ignominia, interitus: Superbia Charybdis est, à cuius vortice qui abripitur, demergitur ac suffocatur: Hydrops est cuius tumor non potest sanari. Superbia inducit securitatem, & facile omnia diuina simul ac humana iura ridet, quod enim libet, licere putat, habet voluptatem pro ratione. Quare hanc Pupam suam & charam genuinam, qq; sobolem Satanae in curru exaltauit, ditauit duplici crumena: duplex poculum capiti pro corolla imposuit, breuiter, egregie admodum pinxit & finxit, vt ad excellentiam nihil addi possit, quare omnis generis homines eius currum trahunt, nam superbus ab omnibus vitiis atq; flagitiis praeceps trahitur ad inferos: Deus a superbis resistit: Deponit potentes de sede. Vir superbus non decorabitur, (ait Hieron.) nec voluntatem suam perducet ad finem, tametsi hic propter aurum ab omnibus manibus gestetur, tollatur in altum; sed lapsu graviore ruet.
units.tr: This emblematic commentary strives to set before our eyes how many evils lie in pride. It is so shameful and truly devilish a crime and disgrace, a most certain mark of the reprobate, as Gregory says, just as humility is a token [τεκμήριον] of the sons of God, as no one doubts. Hence Augustine: I consider pride a great offence. You ask how great this offence is: it cast down the angel, it made the angel into the devil, and shut him out for ever from the kingdom of heaven. This offence is great, and it is the head and cause of all offences, for it is written: "The beginning of all sin is pride" (Ecclus. 10). And do not despise anything else: the beginning, he says, is "pride, the apostasy of man from God his creator." And that we may clearly show it, pride itself is the beginning, end and cause of all sins, since pride is not only a sin, but no sin could or can or will be without pride. Truly you are right, most blessed Augustine, for there is no sin so great that the proud, haughty and insolent man does not commit it. He envies his neighbour's prosperity, for he seeks this, that he alone may stand out: as the same Augustine most rightly says: Pride is prior to vices. For envy does not give birth to pride, but pride gives birth to envy. For no one envies unless he loves excellence; and the love of excellence is called pride. The proud man seeks riches, hoards them and heaps them up, so that he may have something to feed his arrogance. Money is the sinew of pride, as it is said in Psalm 49. The proud man runs against Christian love, for where there is pride there is no love; love humbles itself, pride puffs up, swells and bloats; and that love always thinks more of its neighbour than of itself. The proud man presses down the necks of his neighbour and oppresses him: he is a cruel tyrant, whose end is infamy, ignominy and destruction. Pride is Charybdis: whoever is snatched into its whirlpool is sunk and suffocated. It is dropsy, whose swelling cannot be cured. Pride induces carelessness, and easily mocks all divine and human laws together, for it thinks that whatever it pleases is lawful, and it makes pleasure its rule. Therefore Satan has raised this his doll and dear true offspring in the chariot, enriched her with a double purse, and placed a double cup upon her head for a crown; in short, he has painted and fashioned her so admirably that nothing can be added to her excellence. Hence men of every kind draw his chariot, for the proud man is dragged headlong from all vices and crimes to hell. God resists the proud; he casts the mighty down from their seat. A proud man will not be honoured (says Jerome), nor will he bring his will to its goal, though on account of his gold he is carried in all hands and lifted on high; but he will fall with a heavier fall.
Let him perish who prefers gold to virtues,
A noble mind surpasses all riches.
O MAN, BE TIMELY, AND COME TO YOUR SENSES.

units.la: [Woodcut engraving: devils leading a procession of the damned past burning buildings and gallows; not transcribed as text.] Quæcunq; possunt sensibus Et cogitatu percipi Tormenta, sunt ludibria, Si cum dolore conferas Quem sustinebunt reprobi In inferorum sedibus.
units.tr: [Woodcut engraving: devils leading a procession of the damned past burning buildings and gallows; not transcribed as text.] Whatever torments can be perceived by the senses or grasped by thought are mere mockeries, if you compare them with the pain that the reprobate will endure in the abodes of the underworld.

units.la: INFERNI cruciatus ostendere, quomodo, ac prælibando quasi propinare hęc Emblematica tabella molitur: hic Infernalis Rhadamantus, cuique pro vt meruit, & à Domino Iehoua iussus est, dispefat, pœnas atq; cruciatus horrendos: de quibus verbo q. Augustinus, grauiora, inquit, esse tormenta, quam quæ & qualia hoc in seculo possint formidari. Nihil aiunt Poetæ, fabulantes, de voluente saxum sisypho: fictile dolium implentibus Danaidum sororibus: Tantalo fugientes aquas & retrocedentia poma captante, alia, alia sunt illa tormenta, quibus nunquam morituros Satanas enecat reprobos: Iocularia sunt illa fictitia & commentitia, præhisce veris & omni opinione humana maioribus: lacus inferni (sic quidem Aug.) plenus est tenebrarum, discordiæ, odii, sultitiæ, miseriæ, turpitudinis, amaritudinis, offensionis, doloris, adustionis, sitis, famis, ignis inextinguibilis, tristitiæ, vindictæ perennis, & omnis ineffabilis mali, quod nec dici nec cogitari potest. Dubitandum quidem non est, ipsas pœnas, quibus cruciabuntur, quia regnum Dei non possidebunt pro diuersitate criminum esse diuersas, & alias aliis esse acriores, vt in ipso igne æterno pro disparibus ponderibus peccatorum sint disparia tormenta pœnarum, dicente Domino: Tolerabilius erit Sodomis quam vobis in die iudicii. Verum ipsa per se pœna inferorum nec cogitatione concipi nec verbis calamoue describi potest. Et vocabula tenebrarum: stridoris dentium: Et similiter saltem aliquantisper ostendere & eminus spectanda conantur propinare tormenta, quemadmodum Euangelica historia testatur. Nihil aut parum admodum ait Virgilius, dicēs: Ergo exercentur pœnis, veterumq; malorum Supplicia expendunt, alia panduntur inanes Suspensa ad ventos, alii sub gurgite vasto Infectum eluitur scelus, aut exuritur igne, Hinc metuunt, cupiuntq;, dolent, gaudentq;, nec auras Suspiciunt, clausa tenebris & carcere cæco, &c.
units.tr: This emblematic tablet sets out to show the torments of hell, and, by offering a foretaste, as it were, to pour them out for the viewer. Here is the infernal Rhadamanthus, who, as each has deserved, and as he is commanded by the Lord Jehovah, distributes punishments and horrible torments. Augustine says of them briefly: they are heavier, he says, than those which can be feared in this age, both in kind and in degree. The poets, in their fables, say nothing of Sisyphus rolling his stone, of the sisters of the Danaids filling a leaky jar, or of Tantalus grasping at waters that flee and fruit that recedes from him. Other, other are those torments by which Satan will destroy the reprobate, who will never die. Those fictitious and invented fancies are jests, set beside these true torments, which exceed every human opinion. The pit of hell (so Augustine says) is full of darkness, discord, hatred, folly, misery, filthiness, bitterness, offence, pain, burning, thirst, hunger, unquenchable fire, sadness, perpetual vengeance, and every ineffable evil, which can neither be said nor thought. There is certainly no doubt that the punishments themselves, by which they will be tormented, since they will not possess the kingdom of God, are diverse according to the diversity of their crimes, and some more severe than others, so that in that eternal fire itself, according to the unequal weight of sins, there are unequal torments of punishment. The Lord says: "It will be more tolerable for Sodom than for you in the day of judgment." But the punishment of hell in itself can be conceived neither in thought nor described in words or with the pen. The words darkness and gnashing of teeth are used, and in a similar way they try, at least for a little while, to show the torments and to offer them to be viewed from afar, as the history of the Gospel bears witness. Virgil says little or nothing of this, saying: "Therefore they are exercised with punishments, and pay the penalties of their ancient evils: some are stretched out, hanging to the empty winds; others under a vast whirlpool wash away their infected guilt, or are burned out by fire. From here they fear, desire, grieve and rejoice, nor do they look up to the breezes, shut in darkness and a blind prison," and so on.

units.la: Rectius Rythmicus nolter licet minus eleganter vel Latine: Sunt ibi tortores serpentibus horridiores: Deformes, nigri, sed non ad verbera pigri, Nunquam lassantur, sed semper ad hoc renouantur: Sem per trstati, semperq; ferire parati: Semper mordescunt, nec cessant nec requiescunt.
units.tr: Our own rhymer speaks more correctly, though less elegantly and not in Latin: "There are torturers there more horrid than serpents: deformed, black, yet not slow to strike; they never tire, but are always renewed for this purpose; always savage, always ready to strike; always they bite, and neither cease nor rest."

units.la: Origenes diabolos & reprobos aliquando saluandos esse putat, verum cum Christus dicat: Ite in ignem æternum: videtur illa opinio manifeste refelli: Quicquid sit, non magnopere de hisce inquirendum, sed potius cauendum ne ingrediare. Et: vtinam vbiq; de gehenna dissertaretur, nam gehenna meminisse, non sinet in gehennam incidere.
units.tr: Origen thinks that the devils and the reprobate will sometimes be saved. But since Christ says, Depart into eternal fire, that opinion seems plainly refuted. Whatever the truth, this is not something to inquire into much; rather, one must take care not to enter it. Would that everywhere one spoke of Gehenna, for remembering Gehenna will not let you fall into Gehenna.
The delirium of Origen himself.

units.la: VIA LATA QVÆ DVCIT ad inferos.
units.tr: The broad way that leads to hell.

units.la: Fige pedem, properare caue, non est via recta, Ad cælum haud præsens ingredieris iter! Horrida crudelis trahit hic ad tartara saltus, Ergo gratum reuoca, quæso, pedemq; refer.
units.tr: Plant your foot and take care not to hurry: this is not the straight road, and by this path you will not enter heaven. Here the cruel thickets drag you down horribly to hell. So, I beg you, call back your pleasure and turn your foot back.

units.la: De choraeis & saltationibus multi multa commentati, plerique autem illam leuitatem, & libidinū fomenta exsecrati sunt atq; detestati: sed choraea, quam hic vides, & quam omnium ordinum homines saltant, alia est & omnium perniciosissima & exitialissima, nam recta ducit ad inferos, oftendit enim quomodo cacodaemones omnis generis homines trahant & abripiant sub se & iugum suum, aeternamq; damnationem: Fistula, quam inflat, rauc umq; cornu quo perstrepit, aliud nihil est quam diabolica suggestio, saltare vero & movere pedem corpusve, est diabolicis suggestionibus locum dare & gerere morem, qua de saltatione sic infit Augustinus Implere dicitur Satanas mentem a iciuus, & principale cordis, non ingrediens quidem in eum, & in sensum eius, sed fraude & iniquitate atq; omni malitia illum alliciens atq; seducens, affectu malitiae trahit per cogitationes & in entiua vitiorum, quibus ipse plenus est, utpote fallax, nequam & fraudulentus deceptor animarum. Non enim, &c. Sed per deceptionem fraudulentam & malitiam, &c. Verum o miserrimos nos qui ad tibiam ipsius tam leuiter salimus, & tentationibus ipsius quibuscunq; tam leui motu cedimus; cedūt Ecclesiastici, perperos sensus in sacrosanctum verbum Dei ingerentes, animas veneno haeresem inficientes, errore circumscribētes quos sanguine Christus suo mercatus est: scandalosa nocentes actione: peruersitates & vitia non increpantes, nec reprehendentes canes muti: fratres & conseruos percutientes: politicis adsentantes: Coepiscopos calumniis grauantes, multa mala facientes hypocritae, dealbati saepe parietes: &c. Cedunt politici, verbum diuinum adspernantes, ministros verbi prementes & longe infra pedum subsellia suorum abicientes, pro asinis ipsis vtentes, exitiali ... praefinientes quid, cur, quomodo, quousq; ex suggestu dicere debeant: semper discentes & nunquam ad agnitionem veritatis peruenientes: iuris baculum rectum infringentes, sententiam pro lubitu temperantes, personam respicientes, munera sumentes. Cedunt plerique persuadenti impietates, odia, rancorem, caedes, stupra, incestus, adulteria, furta, obtrectationes, rapinas: & omnis generis vitia atque flagitia. Bene equidem haberet: persuadere potest, cogere non potest, ideoque restitendum illi erat fortiter & in fide, atq; fiducia D.N. Iesu Christi victoris, sed nimis ad hanc luctam molles nos praebemus, ideoq; tam frequens & copiosa est choraea & cursus ad lacum infernalem. Sed tu Domine, libera nos d[?]queo venantium, & a verbo aspero, ne nos inducas in tentationem, sed libera nos a malo, ut latum tibi aliquando in vix ... psallere: eat: Benedictus Dominus, qui non dedit nos in captionem dentibus eorum. Anima nostra sicut passer erepta est, de laqueo venantium: Laqueus contritus est & nos liberati sumus.
units.tr: Many have written much about dances and capering, and most have cursed and detested their levity and their fuel for lust. But the dance you see here, which people of every rank perform, is another kind, the most deadly and destructive of all, for it leads straight to hell. It shows how the cacodaemons drag and snatch away men of every sort beneath their sway and yoke, into eternal damnation. The pipe he blows and the hoarse horn with which he makes it ring is nothing other than a diabolical suggestion, and to leap and move foot or body is to give place to diabolical suggestions and to humour them. On this kind of dancing Augustine speaks thus: Satan is said to fill the mind with a fool's joy and the seat of the heart. He does not enter in, indeed, nor into its perception, but by fraud and iniquity and all malice he entices and seduces it, and by the emotion of malice he draws it through thoughts and the inventions of the vices with which he himself is full, as a deceitful, wicked and fraudulent deceiver of souls. For not, etc. But by fraudulent deception and malice, etc. Truly we are most wretched, who leap so lightly to his pipe and give way so easily to all his temptations, with such a slight movement. Churchmen yield, bringing perverse senses into the most holy Word of God, infecting souls with the poison of heresy, ensnaring the errant whom Christ bought with his own blood, harming by scandalous conduct, not rebuking or reproving perversities and vices, dumb dogs, striking their fellow brothers and servants, flattering the politicians, burdening their fellow bishops with slanders, hypocrites doing many evils, whitewashed walls often, etc. Politicians yield, spurning the divine Word, pressing the ministers of the Word and casting them far below the footstools of their own feet, using them as asses, prescribing to them what, why, how and how long they ought to say from the pulpit; always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth, bending the straight staff of law, tempering sentence at will, respecting persons, taking bribes. Most yield to one who persuades them to impieties, hatreds, rancour, murders, debaucheries, incest, adulteries, thefts, slanders, robberies, and every kind of vice and shameful deed. It would indeed be well: he can persuade, but he cannot compel; therefore we ought to have resisted him bravely and in the faith and confidence of our Lord Jesus Christ, the victor. But we show ourselves too soft for this struggle, and therefore the dance and the rush to the infernal pit is so frequent and abundant. But you, O Lord, deliver us from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word, and do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil, so that we may one day sing to you ... let him go: Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as a prey to their teeth. Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the fowlers. The snare is broken and we are set free.
To you be glory.
ALL THINGS HAVE THEIR TIME.

units.la: [Engraving: a wreath enclosing an hourglass with wings, under a sun in a cloudy sky, with a hill and a building at the right.] Cura creatoris sapienti singula lege Nexuit, vt fiant tempore quæq; suo: Temporibus seruire decet, decet omnia Καιρῷ[?] Confieri, Sapiens, tempore quæq; facit.
units.tr: [Engraving: a wreath enclosing a winged hourglass, under a sun in a cloudy sky, with a hill and a building on the right.] The Creator's care has bound each thing by wise law, so that each comes to pass in its own time. It becomes us to serve the times; it becomes everything to be done in its [Kairos]. The wise man does each thing in its time.

units.la: Sapientissimus Deus tam sapienter omnia disposuit in numero, pondere, & mensura, vt omnia quae sub sole fiunt, singula suo tempore fiunt, quemadmodū Sapiens ait: cuiusq; rei suae est tempestas, & tempus cuiusq; voluntati sub caelo. Soles eunt & redeunt, sicut modum ipsis statuit Deus.
units.tr: The most wise God has arranged all things so wisely in number, weight, and measure that everything which happens under the sun happens in its own time, as the wise man says: for every matter there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven. The suns go and return, as God has set their course for them.

units.la: Et noua crescendo reparat sua cornua Phoebe:
units.tr: And Phoebe, growing new, renews her horns.

units.la: Labuntur stellae, fydera oriuntur & occidunt, prout Deus sanxit, & ire iussit. Tempus (inquit Tertullian.) est omni rei. Adspice ipsam creaturam paulatim ad fructum promoueri: Granum est primo; & de grano frutex oritur: & de frutice arbuscula enititur, deinde rami & frondes inuae fcunt, & totum arboris nomen expanditur: inde germinis tumor, & flos de germine soluitur, & de flore fructus aperitur: Ipsa vices natura subit, variataq; cursus Ordinat, inuersis & frondibus explicat annum; Cessat hyems, madidos & siccat vere capillos, Ver fugit aestates, aestatum terga lacessit Pomifer autumnus, nimbis cessurus & vndis: &c.
units.tr: The stars slip away, the constellations rise and set, as God has ordained and commanded them to go. Time (says Tertullian) is for every thing. Look at the creature itself, gradually brought forward to fruit: it is first a grain; from the grain a shrub arises; from the shrub a little tree puts forth, then branches and leaves unfold, and the whole name of the tree is spread out; then the swelling of the bud, and a flower breaks out from the bud, and fruit opens from the flower. Nature itself undergoes its changes, and ordering its varied course, unfolds the year with its leaves reversed; winter ceases, and spring dries the damp locks; spring flees, and autumn, bringing fruit, lashes the backs of summers, about to yield to rains and waves, etc.

units.la: Quod ipsum q. in fasciculum colligit & compingit Graecus ille scriptor: Πρὸς τῶ κρύπτε μηδὲν, ὡς ἁπάντ' ὀρῶν Καὶ πάντ' ἀκούων, πᾶντ' αὐαπτίσαι χρόνῳ.
units.tr: That same Greek writer also gathers and binds this into a bundle: "Do not hide anything, since time, which sees all and hears all, will bring everything to light" [Πρὸς τῶ κρύπτε μηδὲν, ὡς ἁπάντ' ὀρῶν Καὶ πάντ' ἀκούων, πᾶντ' αὐαπτίσαι χρόνῳ].

units.la: Omnium autem optime verbum Dei de tempore loquitur, & qui illud regit, disponit, ordinat Deus: Deus omnia facit tempore suo. Tempore opportuno. Tempore gratia. Die salutis. Et simil.
units.tr: Most excellently, however, the word of God speaks of time, and God, who rules, arranges and orders it: God does all things in his own time. In an opportune time. In a time of grace. On the day of salvation. And the like.

units.la: Quare prudentem temporis rationem subducere semper debemus, seu, temporibus (quod aiunt) seruire, id enim hominis prudentis est: quod ipsum etiam mellifluus doctor monet, dicens: Omne tempus tibi impensum requiretur a te, qualiter fuerit expensum, &c. Parum non astimes tempus, quod in dictis vel factis expenditur otiosis. Volat verbum irreuocabile, transfit tempus irremeabile, &c.
units.tr: Therefore we must always make a prudent reckoning of time, or, as they say, serve the times, for this belongs to the prudent man. The honeyed teacher himself advises this, saying: Every time given to you will be required of you, in what manner it was spent, etc. Do not think lightly of the time that is spent in idle words or deeds. The word once uttered cannot be recalled, and time, once passed, cannot return, etc.

units.la: Imo diuinum hoc habet oraculum: Quarite Dominum, dum inueniri potest & inuocate eum dum prope est: & Apostolus: Aptate vos tempori quoniam mali sunt dies:
units.tr: Indeed, the divine oracle has this: Seek the Lord while he may be found, and call upon him while he is near; and the Apostle: Make the most of the time, because the days are evil;

units.la: Nullum est pretiosius compendium tempore, nec maius dispendium eodem, quare cum Deus omnia faciat tempore suo, & omnia creata obseruet tempus & positum diuinum, id ergo nos multo magis facere est aequum, qui cum ratione & ad imaginem Dei creati sumus.
units.tr: There is no more precious gain than time, and no greater loss than the same. Therefore, since God does all things in his own time, and all created things observe time and the divine appointment, it is only right that we do so much more, since we have been created rational and in the image of God.

units.la: Est tamen quod adhuc temporis respectu fiduciam nostram grauiter firmat ac suffulcit, nempe: cum Deus omnia tempore suo faciat, veniet etiam tempus, quo nos ex malis huius vita eripiet, & fiet gloriosos in regno suo. Certe tempus est satisfactionis, est & messis: hic ferimus in lacrymis, sed ibi in exultatione metemus; interim patienter expectemus tempus, quod reuelabitur in Christo Iesu,
units.tr: Yet there is something which, with regard to time, greatly strengthens and supports our confidence: since God does all things in his own time, a time will also come when he will rescue us from the evils of this life and make us glorious in his kingdom. Surely there is a time of satisfaction, and also of harvest: here we sow in tears, but there we shall reap in exultation; meanwhile let us patiently await the time that will be revealed in Christ Jesus,
he shall make all things whole [πανσώσεται].
The resurrection of the dead is certain.

units.la: [engraving: angels blowing trumpets above a church; the dead rising from graves and gathering below. Described under notes.]
units.tr: [Engraving: angels blowing trumpets above a church, and the dead rising from their graves and gathering below. Described under notes.]

units.la: Meta æui, clangorq; tubæ, reparatioq; huius Corporis, arbitrio stant, venientq; Dei: Ergo iustitia, Pietateq;(age) imbue mentem, Quisquis aues gelida surgere faustus humo.
units.tr: The end of the age, the clangour of the trumpet, and the restoration of this body stand at the judgment and coming of God. Therefore imbue your mind with justice and piety, you who rise fortunate from the cold earth like birds.

units.la: Paucis Pauцis credita plærisq; derisa est Resurrectio mortuorum, quod ex sacris simul & profanis peripicue apparet. Sic Epicuri de grege porci loquuntur libro Sapientiæ: Casu nati sumus, postea vero ita futuri sumus, quasi non fuissemus, quia sumus est respiratio narium nostrarum, & sermo prolatus motu cordis nostri scintilla est: Quia extinctum in cinerem abiturum est corpus nostrum, & spiritus noster vt aer mollis diffunditur. Vt umbra transitus est tempus nostrum, neque est remeatio a morte nostra, quia obsignata est & nemo reuertitur. Age ergo fruamur praesentibus bonis, &c. Perinde atque prophani Gentiles dixerunt: ede, bibe, lude, &c. praesentibus exple
units.tr: The resurrection of the dead has been believed by a few and mocked by most, as is plain from both sacred and profane writings. Thus the book of Wisdom speaks of "the herd of Epicurus' pigs": "We were born by chance, and afterwards we shall be as though we had never been, for the breath in our nostrils is smoke, and speech is a spark kindled by the beating of our heart. When it is extinguished, our body will turn to ash, and our spirit will be dispersed like soft air. Our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no return from our death, for it is sealed and no one comes back. Come, then, let us enjoy the good things that are at hand, etc." In the same way the profane Gentiles said: "Eat, drink, play, etc.; fill yourself with present pleasures."
"Fill your mind with delights; after death there is no pleasure."
And this is commonly held: "There is no hope for the tomb."

units.la: Empedocles, Soles ire ac redire posse vident, sed vicissim statuunt ipsi, robis quando breue lux occidat, & dies huius vita finitur, quod nox sit perpetuo vna dormienda.
units.tr: Empedocles says: "We see that the suns can set and rise again, but for ourselves, once the brief light of this life goes out and our day is finished, we must sleep through one night that never ends."

units.la: Astruitur tamen resurrectio mortuorum firmis atque immotis argumentis, rationibusq; cum ex sacris, tum ex natura. Cuiusmodi sunt: Mortui tui viuent & interfecti tui resurgent: & apud Ezechielem, cum restitutionem populi Israelitici promittit Deus, vtitur simili resuscitationis mortuorum: Ecce, inquit ego aperiam tumulos vestros, & educam vos de sepulcris vestris, quem in loc. Hieron. Nunquam poneretur similitudo resurrectionis ad reditum populi Israelitici significandam, nisi esset ipsa resurrectio & futura crederetur, quae nemo de rebus non existentibus incerta confirmat, &c. Multi qui dormiunt, inquit Daniel, in pulvere terrae, resurgent, isti in vitam aeternam, illi in opprobrium sempiternum. Veniet, ait Dominus salvator, tempus quo mortui in sepulcris audient vocem filii hominis & prodibunt, alii &c.
units.tr: Nevertheless, the resurrection of the dead is established by firm and unshaken arguments and reasons, both from the sacred writings and from nature. Of the first kind are these: "Your dead shall live, and your slain shall rise" (Isa. 26.). In Ezekiel, when God promises the restoration of the people of Israel, he uses the likeness of the resurrection of the dead: "Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up out of your sepulchres" (Ezek. 37.). On this passage Jerome says: "A likeness of resurrection would never be used to signify the return of the people of Israel unless the resurrection itself were real and believed to be future. No one confirms uncertain things about what does not exist, etc." Daniel says: "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall rise; these to everlasting life, those to everlasting shame" (Dan. 12.). The Lord Saviour says: "The time will come when the dead in their tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of Man and come forth, some etc." (John 5.).

units.la: Viuificabit (Apostoli est) mortalia corpora nostra, & conformia faciet corpori suo glorioso. Quod & capitis nostri, Dn. Saluatoris resurrectione liquido euincere ipse Dominus & Apostoli confirmarunt. Confirmat idem in nobis inhabitans Spiritus sanctus. Resurrectio Christi, resurrectionu nostra est fideiussor. Quid? an non & natura id docet? Quod feminae non reuiref it nisi resurgas! quis ex mortuo cinere vitrum pulcerrimum conficit ignorat? quis reiuuenefcentiam aquilae infitebitur? quis Phoenicis reparationem? quem rugitu Leonem mortuos suos pullos resuscitare latebit? vt infinita alia obmittam. Quare ad resurrectionem iustorum fide atque respipiscentia adspiremus. Firmamentum Christianorum resurrectio mortuorum, miserrimi omnium creaturarum essemus, si non esset resurrectio. At scimus, Goelem noštrum viuere nos resuscitaturum. Semper igitur, insonet auribus nostris vox tubae & iudicii: surgite mortui, & venite ad iudicium.
units.tr: "He will also quicken our mortal bodies and make them like his glorious body" (Rom. 8.; Phil. 3.). The Lord himself and the Apostles clearly confirmed this by the resurrection of our Head, the Lord Saviour. The indwelling Holy Spirit confirms the same in us. The resurrection of Christ is the guarantee of ours. Moreover, does not nature itself teach this? Does not the seed come to life unless it rises again? Who does not know that a most beautiful glass is made from dead ashes? Who will confess the rejuvenation of the eagle? Who the restoration of the phoenix? Who does not know that the lion revives its dead cubs with its roar? I pass over countless other examples. Therefore let us aspire, by faith and repentance, to the resurrection of the just. "The resurrection of the dead is the firmament of Christians; we would be the most wretched of all creatures if there were no resurrection." But we know that "our Redeemer lives and will raise us up" (Job 19.). Therefore let the voice of the trumpet and of judgment always sound in our ears: "Arise, you dead, and come to judgment."
All Stand Before the Tribunal of Christ.

units.la: Iudicis aduentu micat æthra, & cuncta tremiscit Κτήσις, & ad sancti Iudicis ora stupet. Qui vigilat fidens est parte beatus ab omni, Ad dextram stabit, & cœlica regna petet.
units.tr: At the Judge's coming the sky blazes, and all creation [Κτήσις] trembles and is struck dumb before the face of the holy Judge. Whoever keeps watch, trusting, is blessed above all others: he will stand at the right hand and seek the heavenly kingdoms.

units.la: SOLIDA atq; immota rupe diuini decreti fundatum est extremum iudicium in fine seculorum celebrandum Dei nomine à filio Dei Dn.nostro Iesu Christo, iisdemq; fere, quibus resurrectio, astruitur argumentorum rationumq; fundamentis. De hoc septimo ab Ada Enoch prophetauit dicens: Ecce venit Dominus in sanctis millibus suis, facere iudicium contra omnes, & arguere omnes impios de omnibus operibus impietatis eorum quibus impie egerunt, & de omnibus duris, quæ locuti sunt contra eum peccatores impii. Omnia aget Deus, inquit Ecclesiastes, in iudicium, etiam ea quæ occulta sunt, siue bona ea sint, siue mala: Repletur adhuc verbum Dei, mihi flectetur omne genu: Omnes sistemur ad tribunal Christi, vt vnusquisq; accipiat prout meruit in vita, siue bona, siue mala. Totus iudicii diuini processus in sacris ordine descriptus est. Veniet Iudex conspicuus in humana nostra natura, quam de nobis sumpsit. Veniet non in humilitate, tanquam olim iudicandus, sed in maiestate tanquam omnem carnem iudicaturus. Venientem stipant Angeli, & Archangeli, omnesq; electi tum beati: Vorax ignis circa eum, & flamma lambens iuxta eum. Veniens insonabit de solio gloriæ: Surgite mortui & venite ad iudicium, hæc est tuba Archangeli & vox filii hominis, quam audient qui in sepulcris sunt, audient & reuiuiscent, reuiuiscent ac prodibunt: Superstites autem quos inuenerit dies Domini censoria, immutabuntur momento q.à corruptione ad incorruptibilitatem, à mortalitate ad immortalitatem, omnes autem rapientur in occursum gloriosissimi Iudicis, & sistentur tribunali eius, in nubibus: fiet autem sequestratio, piorum fideliumq; cœtus à dextris, lerna impiorum atq; infidelium sistetur à sinistris iudicis, quemadmodum segregat Pastor à pecore, hædos: in illos definitiuam feret sententiam: Venite patris mei benedicti, in regnū quod paratum est vobis ab initio. His dicetur: Ite maledicti in ignem æternum, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius. Iustissimum erit Iudicium istud, feretur sententia ex legis Euangel. conscientiarum. Feretur & mandabitur executioni è vestigio, venient illi in vitam æternam: ibunt hi in ignem æternum, eritq; durum, his contra stimulum calcitrasse, videbunt enim in quem pupugerint, ridentque quidem hæc Empeftæ, dicuntq;: vbi est promissio aduentus eius, sed eo ipso probat filios esse se Satanæ. Beatos autem, qui cum virginibus sapientibus, oleum in lampadib. habentes, vigilantes atque orantes per multas tribulationes & angustias expectant sponsum Iesum Christum, vt cum eo in Nympheion perrennis gaudii ingrediantur. O iterum! & terq; quaterq; beatos! ex horum numero nos esse velit faciatque Dominus Iesus Christus, salus nostra. Ea veni! Fiat. Fiat.
units.tr: The final judgment, to be held at the end of the ages in the name of God by the Son of God our Lord Jesus Christ, is founded on a solid and immovable rock of divine decree, and it is established by the same kinds of arguments and grounds of reasoning as the resurrection. Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of it, saying: Behold, the Lord comes with his holy thousands, to execute judgment upon all, and to convict all the ungodly of all their works of ungodliness, which they have ungodly committed, and of all the hard things which ungodly sinners have spoken against him. God will bring every work into judgment, says Ecclesiastes, including everything hidden, whether it be good or evil. The word of God still stands: every knee shall bow to me. We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive what he has deserved in this life, whether good or evil. The whole course of the divine judgment is set out in order in the sacred writings. The Judge will come visibly in our human nature, which he took from us. He will come not in humility, as once to be judged, but in majesty, as one who is about to judge all flesh. Angels and archangels will attend him as he comes, and all the elect, who are then blessed. A devouring fire goes before him, and a flame burns round about him. Coming down from the throne of glory, he will sound out: Arise, you dead, and come to judgment. This is the trumpet of the archangel and the voice of the Son of Man, which those who are in their graves will hear; they will hear it and come back to life, they will come back to life and come forth. But those who are still alive, whom the day of the Lord will find, will be changed in a moment, from corruption to incorruptibility, from mortality to immortality; and all will be caught up to meet the most glorious Judge and will be brought before his tribunal in the clouds. There will then be a separation: the company of the pious and faithful will be placed at his right hand, while the lerna of the impious and unbelieving will be set at the judge's left, just as the Shepherd separates the kids from the sheep. To those on the right he will pronounce the final sentence: Come, you blessed of my Father, into the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning. To the others it will be said: Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. This judgment will be most just; the sentence will be pronounced according to the law of the Gospel, the conscience. It will also be carried out at once: those will go into eternal life, these will go into eternal fire; and it will be harsh for them, that they kicked against the goad, for they will see him whom they pierced. These scoffers may laugh and say, where is the promise of his coming? but by that very fact they prove that they are children of Satan. Blessed, however, are those who, with the wise virgins, having oil in their lamps, keep watch and pray through many tribulations and distresses, awaiting the bridegroom Jesus Christ, so that they may enter with him into the bridal chamber of everlasting joy. O again and again, and three and four times blessed! May the Lord Jesus Christ, our salvation, will and grant that we be of their number. So be it! Amen. Amen.
